INTRODUCTION 

It is a well known fact that a substantial portion of the cases being tried in our courts arise out of automobile accidents. A great number of claims for injuries resulting from automobile collisions are settled without being litigated. In the last two decades the mass of litigation in Michigan, growing out of such accidents, is reflected in the large number of decisions handed down by the Michigan Supreme Court. So much law has been made by the 

Michigan Court on almost every phase of automobile accidents that it is seldom that the law of other states need be consulted at a trial involving an accident which occurred in Michigan. It was therefore felt that a book on Michigan automobile law would be of much practical aid to the attorney handling an automobile case.

The attorney for the plaintiff or defendant in such a case ordinarily is not particularly interested in the general rules of law. If a point of law arises, he wants a precedent case containing a set of facts very similar to his own case. He must know the facts of the precedent case in order to determine whether or not it is in point. 

There are so many types of automobile cases, with such a great latitude for fact situations, that it is extremely difficult to run down precedents from general statements and mere citations. Consequently, with this in mind, this book has been compiled without footnotes. The material facts of all cases contributing to the law have been set forth, and the cases under each subject for the most part have been put in chronological order.

An attempt has been made to treat the chapters, covering the various types of cases, exhaustively. The facts and statements of the Court in each case have been given iii

INTRODUCTION 

so that a minimum of comment is necessary. The conclusions are put in a summary at the end of each subject considered in these chapters. 

Michigan procedure and pleading practice and the law of evidence and damages have been covered in other works. Therefore, the chapters in this book dealing with these topics are confined to subject matter peculiarly applicable to the automobile case, and to those questions not considered in other works.

No attempt has been made to discuss the Michigan motor vehicle statutes in a separate chapter. The important statutes are given in the Appendix. Practically all of these statutes are discussed in the chapters dealing with the types of cases. By consulting the index, the discussion pertaining to any statute can be located. 

The index in this book has been made as complete as possible for the purpose of enabling the reader to find the precedent case which he is after, if it is in the book. Naturally, in a work of this kind, it is not practical to insert the facts of a case under every conceivable heading. But reference can be made to the case under such headings through the index. Thus, by using the index, cases may be found, which would not be turned up by consulting the headings in the book itself.

The civil case arising out of an automobile accident is the chief concern of this book. Therefore, little space is given to criminal cases and to insurance law. 

The cases considered in this book include those reported in Volume 271 of the Michigan reports.

Sec. 14. Miscellaneous Cases. 

Decisions involving pedestrian cases are so numerous in Michigan, and the statutes affecting the cases have been changed so much, that, in considering the law on pedestrians, decisions of the court prior to 1910 are not discussed in this chapter. It is important to remember, if an attempt is made to apply the rules of law in an old case to a pending one, that the old case was probably governed by statutes and ordinances now repealed or greatly changed. For instance, many of the pedestrian 1

§ 1] 

decisions before 1925 were based, to some extent, upon a statute found in Compiled Laws 1915, section 4818. 

This statute required a car driver, in approaching a person walking on a highway, to slow down to a speed not in excess of 10 miles per hour, and to give a warning of the approach of the car. In 1925 this section was re pealed. See 1925 Public Acts. No. 287. 

Many important pedestrian cases, involving a situation where the pedestrian is dead at the time of trial, are not considered in this chapter as they are discussed in the chapter on the presumption of due care. There are also a few cases which are treated more in detail in the chapter on subsequent or discovered negligence.

The rules of law developed by the Michigan Supreme Court in country highway cases are different from those in city street cases. Quite obviously a higher degree of care is required of an adult than a seven-year-old child. 

Consequently, the decisions have been put into groups, according to the nature of the case. Only opinions which have tended to develop the law are treated in detail. At the end of each group of cases a list of other decisions is given, the facts of which are not discussed. The divisions are: 

I. Crossing city street.

II. Children cases. 

III. Country highway cases. 

IV. Backing car. 

V. Car on wrong side of street. 

VI. Traffic signal cases.

Sec. 1. Crossing City Street. 

Bouma v. Dubois, 169 Mich. 422.

In this case the plaintiff was crossing a city street at night. When in the center of the street she stopped and 2

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[$ 1 looked in both directions but saw no car approaching. 

After taking a few steps she was struck by defendant's automobile and carried about 50 feet according to some of the testimony. There was evidence that the head lights were not on and that two oil lamps were not visible for any distance because of the rain. 

The question of the plaintiff's negligence was for the jury. 

Tolmie v. Woodward Taxicab Co., 178 Mich. 426.

The plaintiff with two companions was walking across 

Jefferson avenue in Detroit, going north on a crosswalk.

When they reached the north rail of the street car tracks the defendant's car approached from the east. The plaintiff continued north, but his companion stepped back. The car was stopped at about the point where it struck the plaintiff. The accident happened in the daytime, but the plaintiff testified that he did not see the car until it was nearly up to him. 

In reversing the judgment for the plaintiff, the court said that the testimony of the plaintiff showed that he failed to use a reasonable degree of care. 

Fulton v. Mohr, 200 Mich. 538.

In the daytime, while a heavy snow was falling, the deceased stepped from the west curb of a 30-foot city street just in front of a parked car and walked in a southeast direction with his head down and coat collar up. Just as he cleared the parked car he was seen by the defendant whose truck was then three feet north of the rear of the parked car. The left front of the truck struck the deceased. There was some testimony that the deceased had reached a point east of the center of the street when struck.

The Supreme Court said that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. 3

§ 1] 

Benjamin v. McGraw, 208 Mich. 75.

The plaintiff started to cross Kercheval avenue in Detroit from the south curb at a crosswalk. After leaving the curb about five feet he looked west and saw the defendant's car 60 to 70 feet west, traveling east at a speed of 30 to 35 miles per hour. He turned and went back to the curb and was struck after he had reached the curb. The court said: "There is no imperative rule of law requiring a pedestrian when approaching a street crossing to look both ways before stepping off the curb. He is only required to exercise such reasonable care as the surrounding circumstances require. In crowded centers where there is much traffic, the danger is greater, and greater precaution must be taken to avoid collisions. The plaintiff at the time he was struck by the car was on the curb, a place which should have been to him one of safety. The defendant had no right to have his machine there. Whether he was justified in so running it, in his effort to avoid injury to the plaintiff, as claimed by him, was a question for the jury."

It was held that the negligence of the plaintiff and defendant was for the jury. 

Darish v. Scott, 212 Mich. 139.

The defendant was driving his car west on Grand 

River avenue in Detroit and was crossing Woodward avenue with a "go" semaphore operated by an officer. 

When he reached the west curb line of Woodward he slowed almost to a stop on account of a large number of pedestrians. There was an opening and he increased his speed to 8 to 10 miles per hour. The plaintiff's decedent, a girl of 14 years of age, stepped from the north curb, at the building line, into the path of the car and was struck. 4

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 1 It was held that her negligence was for the jury. The 

Court said that under the direct testimony of the witness she was not guilty of negligence as a matter of law. The cross-examination clearly showed that she was. The 

Court felt that because of the circumstances and the nature of the testimony the case should have been submitted to the jury. 

Perkins v. Holser, 213 Mich. 579.

The plaintiff was crossing South Saginaw street in Pontiac in the daytime. After leaving the east curb he looked to the north and saw two south bound cars. He let these cars pass and then walked west 20 to 25 feet without looking again to the north and was struck by the defendant's south bound car.

The Supreme Court said that the failure of the plaintiff to see the defendant's car did not make him negligent as a matter of law and distinguished the case from 

Tolmie v. Taxicab Co., 178 Mich. 426. 

Metcalf v. Peerless Laundry & Dye Co., 215 Mich. 601.

This was another case in which the plaintiff failed to see the defendant's car and it was held that there was a question for the jury as to contributory negligence. 

There was a parked car which interfered with the view of the plaintiff. In addition, the plaintiff was walking out into the street for the purpose of boarding an approaching street car. 

Frary v. Grand Rapids Taxicab Co., 227 Mich. 445.

The plaintiff alighted from the east side of a street car which was headed north on Monroe avenue in Grand Rapids. He passed to the rear of this street car and looked north. There was a street car on the west track which partially blocked his view. He walked west to the

§ 1] 

west rail and looked to the north again and saw no south bound car.

He was then 17 feet from the west curb. 

Before he had gone half of this distance he was struck by the defendant's south bound cab which was going at least 25 miles per hour.

The Court held that he was not negligent as a matter of law in not seeing the car. A curve in the street and the street car cut off his view to the north for any great distance. It was pointed out that the cab could have been out of sight when he last made an observation. 

The accident occurred in a business district, and the Court said that the plaintiff had a right to assume that any car approaching would proceed at a legal rate of speed. 

Jones v. Armstrong, 231 Mich. 637.

The plaintiff started from the west curb of the street, which was 55 feet wide, after looking to the south for traffic. He walked east on or near the crosswalk for two-thirds of the width of the street, then turned northeast and walked toward a bus. When near the bus he was struck by defendant's car, which was moving north at 10 miles per hour. The Court said that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. There was nothing to interfere with the view of defendant's car. The plaintiff admitted that he did not look after he started across the street. 

Halzle v. Hargreaves, 233 Mich. 234.

The plaintiff started from the east curb of Second avenue in Highland Park. She looked to the south before leaving the curb and saw no car although she could see for a block. She traveled about 13 feet without again

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 1 looking and was struck. In holding the plaintiff negligent the Court said: "Vigilance is an essential and available safeguard to life and limb in this automobile age, and reasonable care requires constant exercise of the faculty of sight while crossing a city street." 

Arnell v. Gordon, 234 Mich. 140.

The plaintiff alighted from the rear end of a street car on Detroit street in Flint and, after looking north for a block, she started to walk toward the west curb 14 feet away. When two feet from the curb she saw the defendant's car, which struck her as it turned to the right. There was some evidence indicating that the defendant's car was traveling faster than 14 miles per hour.

It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law for not seeing defendant's car. The Court said that it could not be said, as a matter of law, that the car was within the plaintiff's vision at the time she started to cross the street. 

Molda v. Clark, 236 Mich. 277.

The defendant was driving north on Washington avenue in Lansing and intended to make a right turn onto Michigan avenue. The signal light at the corner was red against the defendant, but right turns were permitted. The plaintiff was walking east on the south crosswalk. She passed a standing street car and an automobile headed north waiting for the light to change. 

When the plaintiff passed this car the defendant's automobile was within a few feet of her. She testified that wwwww

§ 1] 

she looked but did not see the approaching car which was traveling 5 to 8 miles per hour.

"Assuming negligence of defendants, plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law. 

That she testified of looking and seeing nothing is of no avail when the physical facts demonstrate that, had she looked, using ordinary care, she could and must have seen defendant's approaching car, and had she so used ordinary care, she could have avoided injury." 

Stobbelaar v. Berg, 247 Mich. 121.

The plaintiff was walking across a city street at night in an easterly direction on a crosswalk. She testified that she looked each way several times and saw lights of cars but thought she could get across safely and was nearly across when struck by defendant's north bound car.

It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury. 

Nickels v. Hallen, 247 Mich. 291.

The plaintiff, at night, was crossing Main street in Ann Arbor at the intersection of Huron. He testified that he looked before and while crossing the street. He saw a car 100 feet away but did not see the defendant's car until it struck him.

It was held that the question of plaintiff's negligence was for the jury. However, the Court held that the instruction, requiring a driver to have such control over his car that he could stop soon enough to avoid an accident, was improper.

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 1 

Bosma v. Daniels, 250 Mich. 261.

The plaintiff, in the daytime, was attempting to cross a 292-foot street in Grand Rapids in a westerly direction. When he left the east curb he noticed two south bound cars, one following the other. He saw defendant's car coming north and 400 feet away. He walked to the center of the street and stopped, allowing the first south bound car to pass. He then saw defendant's car 150 feet away and traveling 40 miles per hour. He turned and ran in a northeasterly direction for 25 feet and was struck when he was about to step on the curb. At the time the plaintiff turned back the other south bound car was only 10 feet from him and was on its right side and was traveling 30 miles per hour. The lower Court directed a verdict for the defendant, which was affirmed by an equally divided court. 

Szekeres v. Detroit Motorbus Co., 252 Mich. 46.

The plaintiff's decedent attempted to cross the street at a point 10 feet from the crosswalk, running between parked cars in front of the bus which had proper lights and brakes and was being operated at a reasonable rate of speed.

It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. 

Gray v. Elliot, 254 Mich. 275.

The plaintiff alighted from a street car on Grand 

River in Detroit, at night, and started to walk to the south curb 40 feet away. The nearest car at that time was 450 feet west. When two-thirds across, the nearest car was 60 feet away. It slowed and the plaintiff passed in front of it. According to the plaintiff, she looked and saw no car running along the curb. However, the defendant suddenly swerved his car from behind this car and,

§ 1] 

passing to the right of it, struck the plaintiff when she was about to step on the curb. 

In holding that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, the Court pointed out the fact that the defendant swung out to pass a car on the wrong side after the plaintiff had observed that the space was clear. 

Tio v. Molter, 262 Mich. 655.

The defendant testified that he was driving east on Main street in the Village of Millburg, at night, at a speed of 10 miles per hour; that his lights were on and in good condition; that he was watching ahead but did not see the plaintiff. He heard a bump and stopped.

He saw the plaintiff lying on the pavement three to five feet in from the south edge. The plaintiff claimed that he was struck on the shoulder of the road. The lower court held that as a matter of law the plaintiff was not, and the defendant was negligent. 

The decision of the lower court was reversed and a new trial ordered. The lower court should have submitted the theory of the defendant that the plaintiff stepped onto the pavement directly into the path of the defendant's car. The Court said that, if the jury believed the defendant's testimony, it would almost of necessity have found that the driver did not see any one ahead of the car because the plaintiff stepped upon the pavement at the point of the accident immediately in front of the automobile. 

Orme v. Farmer, 268 Mich. 425. 

At about 1:30 a. m. the plaintiff with two companions was walking across Saginaw street in Flint near the intersection of Alma street. There was sufficient visibility from the street lights so that a car or person could be seen almost a block away. The plaintiff claimed that 10

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 1 he and his companions looked in each direction before leaving the curb and again in the center of the street but did not see defendant's car. There was testimony that the street was almost deserted; that the defendant did not see the plaintiff until he struck him; that the car was swerved just before the impact and, had it not swerved, the plaintiff would not have been hit. There was also testimony that the defendant had his head turned just before the impact.

In holding that the case was properly sent to the jury, the Court said that the testimony did not show that plaintiff's alleged failure to see defendant's car was the proximate cause of the accident. 

Lapachin v. Standard Oil Co., 268 Mich. 477.

The plaintiff was walking east on McLeod avenue in 

Ironwood. There were no sidewalks and the street was used by pedestrians. The street was covered by snow and there were banks of snow on each side. The plaintiff claimed that he was walking on the right side of the street when hit by defendant's car. 

In holding that the case was properly submitted to the jury the Court, by citation, stated that one walking along the highway may assume that an approaching driver will give a signal of warning.

Other Cases. 

Patterson v. Wagner, 204 Mich. 593; Degens v. Langridge, 214 Mich. 573; Quigley v. Taxicab Co., 225 Mich. 

275; Bacon v. McKay, 227 Mich. 667; Kuitula v. Abbott, 229 Mich. 84; Petersen v. Lundin, 236 Mich. 590; Szabo v. 

Feiler, 239 Mich. 380; Hinchey v. J. P. Burroughs & Son, 240 Mich. 273; Barriger v. Ziegler, 241 Mich. 83; Fenn v. 

Mills, 243 Mich. 634; Walker v. Rebeuhr, 255 Mich. 204; 

Watrous v. Conor, 266 Mich. 397; Fraser v. McArthur, 271 Mich. 622. 11

Sec. 2. Summary of Cases Under Group I. 

It is difficult to reconcile some of these cases. For instance, if the same rule of a pedestrian's duty to look, as was given in Halzle v. Hargreaves, had been applied in 

Perkins v. Holser, it seems that the plaintiff in the latter case would have been guilty of negligence as a matter of law. In many of the cases, where the pedestrian failed to see the car, there was an excuse such as atmospheric conditions, absence of lights on the defendant's car, or excessive speed which carried the car into the field of vision after a proper observation had been made. 

In this group of cases it is usually much easier to make a jury question as to the defendant's negligence than it is to prove that the plaintiff is free from negligence as a matter of law.

If the pedestrian runs into the street between parked cars directly in front of the car, he is negligent as a matter of law. (Szekeres v. Detroit Motorbus Co.) He should look to the left before starting to cross. He is not required to look to the right. (Benjamin v. McGraw.)

If he has a clear view to his left for a long distance, and is struck by a car coming from his left before he reaches the center of the street, and he does not see this car, he is probably negligent. (Halzle v. Hargreaves.) If he sees the car and has any reason to believe that he can get across safely, he is not negligent as a matter of law. (Darish v. Scott.) If he reaches the center of the street he should look to the right for traffic. If he can see a considerable distance and is struck by a car coming from his right without seeing it although it was within his vision, he is negligent. (Tolmie v. Taxicab Co.) However, if the car, because of excessive speed, was beyond the vision of the pedestrian, he is not negligent as a matter of law. (Frary v. Taxicab Co.) If he sees a car and 12

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 3 has any reason to believe that he can get across safely, his case goes to the jury. (Stobbelaar v. Berg.)

Sec. 3. Children Cases. 

Zoltovski v. Gzella, 159 Mich. 620. 

The plaintiff, a boy 13 years old, was playing tag in a public street. He started to run across the street pursued by an older boy and was struck by defendant's automobile. The accident occurred 30 feet from an intersection, the place being well lighted. There was evidence tending to show that there were no lights on the car. The boy ran immediately in front of the car. It was held that the boy was negligent as a matter of law to have become so engrossed in play as to run across a city street in front of a car without looking. 

Winckowski v. Dodge, 183 Mich. 303.

This accident occurred in Detroit on Joseph Campau avenue. The plaintiff had been riding on a north bound lumber wagon and, when the wagon started to turn left into an intersecting street, the plaintiff jumped from the wagon and ran toward the east curb. The defendant's south bound auto had been swerved to the left onto the east side of the street because of the wagon making its turn. The auto struck the boy, who was 8 or 9 years of age.

It was held that there were excusing circumstances in this case, as the defendant's auto was on the wrong side of the street, and consequently, the boy's negligence was for the jury to decide. 

Barger v. Bissell, 188 Mich. 366.

The plaintiff, six years and ten months old, started hurriedly to cross Gratiot avenue in Detroit from the north 13

§ 

curb in the middle of a block. The accident occurred in the daytime. The defendant's car was being driven within the speed limit, 7 to 9 miles per hour. It was claimed that the driver should have stopped quicker than he did.

As the automobile, proceeding west, was passing a hightopped wagon standing at the north curb, the plaintiff passing in front of the horse and wagon started quickly across the street in front of the auto. It was held that there was no proper proof of negligence on the part of the defendant. The testimony showed that the driver did all that he could, under the circumstances, to avoid the plaintiff. 

Gardiner v. Studebaker Corporation, 204 Mich. 313. 

In this case a four-year-old girl was killed when struck by defendant's trailer. The driver of the truck was the only witness. He testified that he was driving west on 

McGraw avenue in Detroit, a street about 28 feet in width. He proceeded across Linwood avenue at a speed of 10 to 12 miles per hour. The girl came out from behind a dump wagon at the south side of the street. He sounded his horn, applied his brakes and turned to the right but the trailer ran over her. It was held that there was no evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. 

Apps v. Walters, 216 Mich. 17.

While the defendant was driving south on Garland avenue, a 26-foot street in Detroit, near the center of the street, the plaintiff, a boy 9 years old, ran from the west curb diagonally across the street. There was testimony that the car was from 20 to 100 feet from the boy when he left the curb. The boy was three to four feet from the east curb when hit by the car. 

The Supreme Court said that the boy was negligent as a matter of law; that the accident happened very quickly, 14

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 3 and that the boy had a clear view of the car if he had looked before leaving the curb. There were a number of boys playing near the west curb as the defendant's car approached. 

Bade v. Nies, 239 Mich. 37. 

The plaintiff, a boy 6 years and 4 months of age, was crossing Eighth street in Holland, which was 56 feet wide. 

The boy attempted to cross from the south to the north near the center of the block, going into the street between parked cars. There was proof that defendant was driving west at a speed in excess of the statutory limit of 15 miles per hour. The case was submitted to the jury as to defendant's negligence and plaintiff's contributory negligence.

It was held that there was sufficient evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant to take the case to the jury.  

"He must always have regard for the situation and must drive his car in a reasonably safe manner so as not to endanger the persons and property of others, and, if to accomplish this it is necessary to drive at a lesser speed than the maximum provided by statute, he must do so." 

Oakes v. Van Zomeren, 255 Mich. 372.

The defendant was driving his car west on Main street in Fremont in the daytime. The pavement was 30 feet wide and was slippery, and the car was going down a rather sharp grade. There was testimony that the plaintiff's decedent, a boy 7 years old, was well toward the center of the street from the north curb before defendant's car came into view. The defendant had admitted that his car was 40 to 50 feet from the boy when he started to run into the street. 15

§ 3] 

It was held that the boy was not negligent as a matter of law, and that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. 

Braxton v. Gazdecki, 255 Mich. 518.

In the daytime, a five-year-old boy ran from the south curb of a 38-foot street in Detroit. The defendant drove his car west and did not see the boy until the car struck him at the left front fender. The car went about 10 or 15 feet and stopped.

It was held that there was no proof of negligence on the part of the defendant. The Court said that there was no duty on the part of the defendant to see the boy leave the curb or to anticipate that he would leave the curb. 

Franks v. Woodward, 258 Mich. 447.

The plaintiff, 10 years old, was walking with other boys in a southerly direction along the easterly edge of U. S. 28 in Munising. He testified that he looked north before he started to cross the road but did not see defendant's car. His companion saw the car and avoided it. The road was straight and the accident occurred at night.

It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law; that had he looked he could and must have seen the approaching car, and in that event, with reasonable care, he could have avoided the accident. 

Severson v. Family Creamery Co., 268 Mich. 348.

The defendant's truck was being driven south on John R. street in Hazel Park in the daytime. There was a 

20-foot pavement with shoulders of crushed stone and cinders with a foot path of cinders on the west side. The driver testified that his speed was 20 to 22 miles per hour. 

He saw the decedent, a boy four years old, on the cinder 16

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 4 path 18 feet from the pavement when the truck was a block north. He sounded his horn and slowed down when one-half block away. When he was nearly up to the boy he glanced to the left at a car approaching from the south. 

He looked back and saw the boy running in front of his truck. He could not avoid striking him. There was testimony that the driver did not sound his horn and that the boy was a foot or two from the pavement as the truck approached. 

The Supreme Court held that the case was properly submitted to the jury and affirmed the judgment for the defendant.

Other Cases. 

Beno v. Kloka, 211 Mich. 116; Church v. Stoldt, 215 

Mich. 469; Werney v. Reid, 219 Mich. 257; Zylstra v. Graham, 244 Mich. 319; Edgerton v. Lynch, 255 Mich. 456;

Sec. 4. Contributory Negligence Age. 

A most important question in this group of cases is how old must a child be to be chargeable with contributory negligence. In the case of Winckowski v. Dodge, 183 Mich. 303, the court discusses the degree of care required of children, saying that it must be proportioned according to their age and capacity. In Barger v. Bissell, the plaintiff was six years ten months old. The court said that had she been an adult she would clearly have been negligent as a matter of law, but that because of her age it was a question for the jury. In Beno v. Kloka, 211 

Mich. 116, it was held that the child five years and eleven months old could not be guilty of contributory negligence. 

In Zylstra v. Graham, 244 Mich. 319, the court said that 17

§ 5] 

the lower court was justified in refusing to direct a verdict for the defendant but did not say that the child six years old was too young to be guilty of contributory negligence. In Zebell v. Buck, 263 Mich. 93, a child seven years and two months old was held to be negligent. 

From these decisions it seems to be clear that a child of seven years or over can be barred from recovering because of contributory negligence. There is a good discussion of the question in Easton v. Medema, 246 Mich. 

130, where the court was evenly divided on the question as to whether a child under six could be negligent. Probably the court would now hold that under six a child could not be negligent. Between six and seven it would be a question as to the child's knowledge, capacity, and experience.

Sec. 5. Summary of Cases Under Group II. 

The decisions in this group of cases indicate that the court recognizes the emergency situation often presented to a driver of a car where a child runs into the street. 

Even though the child may be too young to be guilty of negligence, the child's act may be such as to take the driver by surprise and make the accident unavoidable. (Braxton v. Gazdecki.) On the other hand a driver may be required by circumstances to drive at a speed under the legal rate. (Bade v. Nies.)

Sec. 6. Country Highway Cases. 

Hill v. Lappley, 199 Mich. 369.

The plaintiff, a woman 76 years old, alighted from a truck on the south side of a 24-foot gravel road in the country running east and west. She looked to the east and west before alighting from the truck. After taking 18

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 6 three or four steps onto the highway she was struck by defendant's east bound car. The testimony showed that the plaintiff had defective sight, but, although she could see a car four rods away, she did not see defendant's car although the accident occurred in the daytime. In holding that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law, the 

Supreme Court said: 

"It is obvious, I think, from all the testimony, that the plaintiff most unfortunately stepped into the highway directly in front of the defendant's car. The most ordinary care on her part should have prevented her from doing so.' 

Deal v. Snyder, 203 Mich. 273.

The plaintiff was in a car which was driven north and stopped a little west of the center line of a highway in the country. The plaintiff alighted from the car on the right side and, without looking to the south, took a step or two toward the east and was struck by defendant's north bound car. It was shown that if the plaintiff had looked, he could have seen defendant's car. 

The plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law for not looking before attempting to cross the highway, even though the defendant was violating a statute in passing to the right of the other car. 

Hanser v. Youngs, 212 Mich. 508.

The plaintiff was standing on the concrete road just to the rear of a disabled truck which was partly on the concrete and had no tail light burning. There was some testimony that the defendant tried to pass a car on the right going the same way. dark on Woodward avenue near the Eight Mile road.

The accident happened after which was about 18 feet wide

The truck was on the west 3 19

§ 6]  

edge of the concrete and the defendant's car was traveling south.

It was held that the plaintiff's contributory negligence was for the jury. The court said that it could be inferred that the plaintiff was standing to the rear of the truck to warn south bound traffic of the truck. 

Reynolds v. Knowles, 223 Mich. 70.

At night the plaintiff was helping to remove some wreckage from the highway. He was struck by defendant's car while he was leaving the road at a point near the edge of the pavement. The defendant's car was traveling 

12 miles per hour. It was misting. The defendant did not see the plaintiff before the car struck him. The plaintiff testified that he was watching for traffic but that a minute had elapsed since he had last looked. 

The negligence of the plaintiff and defendant was for the jury. 

Richardson v. Williams, 249 Mich. 350.

The plaintiff's decedent, at the south edge of an 18-foot pavement, had an unobstructed view each way for onehalf mile. He was struck by defendant's car when four feet south of the north edge of the pavement. The car traveling west had come onto the highway three blocks east.

In granting a new trial because of an erroneous instruction, the court said that the car must have been a great deal less than three blocks away when the deceased started across; that if the deceased looked he must be held to have seen the car, and the jury should have been instructed that his act in crossing should be viewed as though he saw defendant's car approaching. 1 20

Volay v. Williams, 258 Mich. 184. 

The plaintiff was walking north, at night, on U. S. 31, a macadam road 16 feet in width, with shoulders three to five feet wide. He was on the shoulder on the east side when he noticed the reflection of approaching cars from the south. One car passed him without swerving but the defendant's car following struck the plaintiff. No testimony was offered by the defendant. 

It was held that the case was for the jury as to any contributory negligence. 

Korstange v. Kroeze, 261 Mich. 298.

This accident occurred at night on a 40-foot paved highway. The plaintiff was walking down a hill, having just come over its crest. He was walking east about three feet in from the south edge of the road and testified that just before he was struck he had looked back but saw no car coming. The driver of defendant's car testified that just as he came over the crest he dimmed his lights for an approaching car, and he did not see the plaintiff until within 15 or 20 feet of him.

In holding the negligence of the plaintiff a question for the jury, the Court said: "No statute required plaintiff to walk upon any particular part of the pavement, and he had a legal right to walk on any part thereof, exercising, however, the care of a reasonably prudent man for his own protection and preservation.' 

Zebell v. Buck, 263 Mich. 93. 

The plaintiff's decedent, a girl seven years and two months old, had alighted from a car which had been stopped headed west on the north side of a 20-foot macadam highway. The defendant's car, west bound, struck the girl, her body being 90 feet from the point of impact 21

§ 7]  

after the accident. There was testimony that the defendant's car was going 30 to 35 miles per hour. The girl ran from the rear of the parked car directly into the path of defendant's automobile.

It was held that no negligence on the part of the defendant was shown and that the deceased was negligent as a matter of law. 

Janse v. Haywood, 270 Mich. 632.

The defendant, driving his car north on a highway in the country, attempted to pass a north bound car and when abreast of it killed two of three girls, who were walking side by side on the west side of the highway facing approaching traffic. It was held that the decedent had a right to walk in the highway, facing approaching traffic, and the question of contributory negligence was an issue of fact for the jury.

Other Cases. 

Budnick v. Peterson, 215 Mich. 678; White v. Edwards, 222 Mich. 321; Gibbard v. Cursan, 225 Mich. 311; Sudinski v. Krohn, 242 Mich. 497; Wilkins v. Bradford, 247 Mich.

Sec. 7. Summary of Cases Under Group III. 

Naturally, in this type of case, on an open road in the country there is little or no excuse for the pedestrian not seeing the car where he is crossing the highway. (Hill v. 

Lappley.) If one is standing on the highway at night, with a reason for so doing, he is probably not negligent as a matter of law. (Hanser v. Youngs.) If he is walk- 22

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[88 ing along the highway at night and is struck by a car from the rear, he is probably not negligent as a matter of law, assuming that he has made some previous observation. (Korstange v. Kroeze.) If the pedestrian steps into the path of a car or runs across the highway and is struck he is probably negligent. (Zebell v. Buck.) 

Sec. 8. Backing Car. 

Ottaway v. Gutman, 207 Mich. 393.

While walking on a sidewalk across a private driveway the plaintiff was struck by defendant's backing automobile. The plaintiff testified that before crossing the driveway he looked up the driveway and saw no car although he could see to the garage 92 feet from the sidewalk. It was held by the Supreme Court that the plaintiff's contributory negligence was for the jury, although two judges dissented. 

Kinsler v. Simpson, 257 Mich. 7.

The defendant was backing his car from his garage to the street on a private driveway. There was a hedge along the edge of the driveway, and the defendant, while backing, was looking out of the window to his left to see that he cleared the hedge. A 17-month-old girl walked back of the car on the sidewalk and was struck. 

In holding that there was evidence of negligence, the court pointed out that the defendant knew that a large number of small children lived in the neighborhood. 

While another young man was in the car no attempt was made to have him keep a lookout, and no warning was given of the approach of the car to the sidewalk. 

Ogland v. Detroit Edison Co., 261 Mich. 583.

The plaintiff stepped between two cars parked at the curb about two and one-half feet apart. When she had 23

§ 9] 

taken two steps the car ahead started to back and struck her. The plaintiff had a verdict; the court did not submit a question of contributory negligence, and no request was made for such an instruction. 

It was held that there was no error in the instructions, the defendant having made no claim that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of fact and having made no request for an instruction on the question. 

Other Cases. 

Roach v. Petrequin, 234 Mich. 551.

Sec. 9. Summary of Cases Under Group IV. 

Where a driver backs his car from a driveway across a sidewalk there is a high degree of care required of him. (Kinsler v. Simpson.) When backing a car from a parked position at the curb the driver has a duty to look to the rear. (Ogland v. Detroit Edison Co.) 

Sec. 10. Car on Wrong Side of Street. 

Wilson v. Johnson, 195 Mich. 94.

The plaintiff's decedent was crossing a city street walking east on the south crosswalk. He was struck by the defendant's car which was traveling north and made a short left turn, striking the decedent before he had reached the center of the street. It was held that the case was properly left to the jury. 

Rowland v. Brown, 237 Mich. 570.

The plaintiff testified that she was walking east across Cass avenue in Detroit at night; that she had reached the east side of the street when struck by defendant's south 24

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 10 bound car which she did not see and that the impact occurred near the east curb.  "We know of no authority holding it is contributory negligence as a matter of law if a pedestrian does not continue to look after passing the center of the street for automobiles running on the wrong side of the street." 

Leary v. Fisher, 248 Mich. 574.

This accident occurred on Coolidge highway in Wayne County. There was proof that the plaintiff ran in a northwesterly direction across the road and was struck by defendant's north bound car off the pavement on the west side. The accident took place in a repair zone, and there was evidence that the defendant was driving at an unreasonable speed and that the plaintiff saw the car when it was 150 feet away.

In holding that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, the court said, that if the defendant had stayed on his own side of the highway, the accident would not have occurred. 

Dreyfuss v. Daronco, 253 Mich. 235.

The plaintiff was crossing an east and west street in Ironwood. It was the plaintiff's claim that the defendant's car was driven east on the north half of the street and struck him just after he had left the north curb. The defendant contended that the plaintiff was negligent in not looking to the west or to his right as he left the curb. 

The Court said: 

"He was not guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law if he failed to look in the direction where automobiles may not travel without violating the law of the road." 1 25

$11] 

Lawrence v. Bartling & Dull Co., 255 Mich. 580.

The plaintiff was walking east across a street in Pontiac at an intersection when the defendant's truck, going west, made a short left turn and struck the plaintiff when she was about two feet from the east curb. The trial court directed a verdict for the defendant because the plaintiff had not looked for traffic.

It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law as the truck was on the wrong side of the street, and the plaintiff was not required to continue to look, after she had passed the center of the street, for automobiles running on the wrong side. 

Sanderson v. Barkman, 264 Mich. 152.

The plaintiff testified that he alighted from the left side of a south bound tractor at a point two and one-third feet west of the center of the highway, having previously looked both ways and feeling assured there was no danger. He was struck by defendant's north bound car which was on the wrong side of the road traveling at a high rate of speed.

The plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law under the Supreme Court's decision.

Other Cases. 

Winckowski v. Dodge, 183 Mich. 303; Siegel v. Detroit 

Cab Co., 246 Mich. 620; Wood v. Priborsky, 259 Mich. 556; 

Bither v. Jacks, 265 Mich. 481.

Sec. 11. Summary of Cases Under Group V. 

There is no duty to look for cars proceeding on the wrong side of the street. It is significant that in this group of cases there is not one where the plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law. If the plaintiff's story 26

PEDESTRIAN CASES 

[§ 12 puts the defendant's car, of necessity, on the wrong side of the street, even though the plaintiff does not see the car, practically no other proof of negligence on the part of the defendant is needed.

Sec. 12. Traffic Signal Cases. 

Steele v. Hamilton, 218 Mich. 522.

The plaintiff was attempting to cross Lafayette street in Detroit at the intersection of Griswold. She looked for approaching cars before leaving the south curb but saw none. She also observed that the semaphore was turned against east and west traffic on Lafayette. She started north and when 20 feet out into the street she was struck by the side of defendant's car at the point where the fender joins the running board. She was held negligent as a matter of law. It was said: "It is obvious that the car occupied that part of the street immediately in front of her before she did, and, had she been making the use of her eyes that most people do when traveling in a busy section of the city, she would have seen the car in season to have stopped before it struck her."

The Court said that the semaphore did not wholly relieve the plaintiff of exercising ordinary care. 

Russo v. City of Grand Rapids, 255 Mich. 474.

A city truck had stopped near the center of Franklin street at the intersection of Ionia street in Grand Rapids. 

Another sanding truck coming from the rear of this truck struck the plaintiff's decedent who had walked in front of the standing truck and who was crossing the street against a red light. 27

§ 12] 

It was held that the plaintiff made no case. The Court pointed out that the pedestrian had just as good an opportunity to see the truck as the truck driver had to see him. 

The Court also said that to walk against a red light was not negligence as a matter of law. 

Willis v. Tucker, 261 Mich. 83.

The plaintiff was walking north across Macomb street on the west crosswalk at the intersection of Beaubien street in Detroit. The traffic signal was green for the plaintiff or red against Macomb traffic. When the plaintiff was north of the center of Macomb street he was struck by defendant's car which was driven across the intersection in a westerly direction against the red signal and at an excessive rate of speed.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the lower court that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law in failing to observe the defendant's car. 

Smarinsky v. Markowitz, 265 Mich. 412.

The plaintiff's decedent started to cross a street in Detroit at an intersection with the traffic light in his favor. The light changed while he was crossing, and he was struck by defendant's car and knocked to the center of the intersection.

It was held that the case presented a question of sub sequent negligence.  

"Such invitation to cross and protection while doing so did not cease upon change of light while the pedestrian was in the act of crossing. The change of light did not authorize defendant to continue his course at high speed, regardless of circumstances open to view."

Other Cases. 

Darish v. Scott, 212 Mich. 139; Molda v. Clark, 236 

Mich. 277. 28

Sec. 13. Summary of Cases Under Group VI. 

The plaintiff may be negligent as a matter of law even if walking with the signal, if he walks into the side of the car. (Steele v. Hamilton.) However, it is safe to say that the duty for observation is not the same. He has a right to rely. He is not negligent as a matter of law for not seeing a car running against a red light. (Willis v. 

Tucker.) If he starts on a green light and it changes before he is across the street, the driver of a car does not have a right to proceed. (Smarinsky v. Markowitz.)

Sec. 24. Summary-Where Traffic Signal Light Is Involved. 

This chapter does not purport to cover all intersection cases in Michigan of whatsoever nature. It covers only cases arising from collisions between vehicles traveling on right angle streets; consequently, cases where a left hand turn was made by one car have been excluded and, also, with one exception, cases involving street cars. 

The cases considered are divided into five groups. It is obvious that the Michigan Supreme Court has applied different rules of law to intersection cases according to the nature of the intersection involved. Although the 

Court has not mentioned any such divisions, its decisions 30

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 15 can be reconciled more easily by grouping the cases in the following five divisions.

It is natural that a street intersection case, where the view is obscured, should be treated differently from a country intersection case, where the vision is unlimited. 

It is also natural that an intersection involving a stop highway should make a case more different as to treatment from a case where no stop highway is involved. 

The five groups are as follows: 

I. Where each car was moving in approaching intersection and visibility was limited. (Usual City Intersection.)

II. Where each car was moving in approaching the intersection and visibility was unlimited. 

(Usual Country Intersection.) 

III.

Cases involving duties of a driver crossing a stop highway. 

IV. Cases involving duties of a driver on a stop highway. 

V. Where a traffic signal light is involved.

Sec. 15. Cases Under Group I. 

Brown v. Mitts, 187 Mich. 469.

In this case a judgment was rendered in favor of the plaintiff and the defendant appealed. The Supreme 

Court affirmed the decision of the lower Court. 

The plaintiff's car was traveling west at 1 p. m. on a street in Saginaw. The plaintiff testified that his car was moving at a speed of about seven miles per hour, and that he intended to stop on the northwest corner where there was a post office. The defendant's car was moving north. When ten feet from the intersection the plaintiff saw defendant's car traveling north in the center of the street. The defendant was traveling at about twenty to 31

§ 15] 

twenty-five miles per hour. The plaintiff honked his horn three times but the defendant continued to look toward the southwest corner of the intersection. The plaintiff then shouted at the defendant, but the defendant drove straight ahead into the left rear wheel of the plaintiff's car. An ordinance of Saginaw set the maximum speed as eight miles per hour. There was a large billboard on the southeast corner which obscured the view of the drivers until they arrived at or near the intersection.

The Court held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law.  "It cannot be said that under the law it is the duty of a party to stop his car when he sees another approaching him at a rapid rate of speed and there is ample room for the other party to pass him in the rear or elsewhere." The Court emphasized the fact that the defendant was driving down the center of the street and could have passed to the rear of plaintiff's car. It is not brought out as to how far the defendant's car was away from the intersection when the plaintiff saw said car. 

Kovacevic v. Reid, 196 Mich. 288.

In this case a judgment was rendered for the plaintiff against one defendant, and that defendant appealed.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision in the lower Court. The defendant was driving west on Grand Boulevard in the City of Detroit. He testified that he slowed to a speed of nine miles per hour at Chene Street. The view to the north was obstructed by a building, which was flush with the street line. The defendant testified that he looked to his left or south when he entered the intersection, but he did not look to the north until he reached the first car track. He then saw another car coming south on Chene Street at a fast rate of speed. 32

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 15 He turned to the left sharply and ran into the pedestrian who was the plaintiff and who was crossing the Boulevard on foot. It was brought out that the defendant could have stopped his car within 12 feet. 

The Court held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant although the defendant claimed that he was subjected to an emergency and was not negligent. The Court held him negligent in not looking to the north when he reached the intersection. The 

Court said that if he had looked to the north at the time he reached the intersection he could have put on his brakes and stopped before he reached the car track and thus no injury would have been done to the plaintiff. 

The Court also mentioned the fact that the defendant was traveling over the ordinance limit. 

Harris v. Bernstein, 204 Mich. 685.

In this case the Court heard only the testimony of plaintiff's witness, and directed verdict for the defendant. The plaintiff appealed, and the Supreme Court reversed the decision. The plaintiff was an occupant in a car traveling south on Antoine Street in the City of Detroit. The defendant's car was traveling west on Columbia. The only testimony was that when the plaintiff's car was at the north curb line of Columbia, the defendant's car was some distance east of the intersection. The witness would not state exactly how far the car was away but said that it might have been 50 feet away from their car. The testimony also showed that the plaintiff's car was south of the center line of Columbia when struck. 

There was no testimony as to the exact speed or distance. 

The plaintiff's car was struck on the left rear wheel. 

The Court said there was no negligence as a matter of law on the part of the plaintiff. The Court emphasized 33

§ 15] 

the statute requiring cars in passing at an intersection to keep to the right of the center of the intersection in passing. The Court emphasized the fact that the defendant's car had not kept to the right of the center of the street in passing. 

Tregonning v. Castantini, 243 Mich. 233.

In this case there was a judgment for plaintiff, and defendant appealed. The Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The plaintiff's truck was moving west, and the defendant's sedan was moving north. The plaintiff testified that he slowed to 10 to 15 miles per hour in approaching the intersection.. When about 10 feet from the intersection he saw the defendant's sedan moving north and 25 feet from the intersection. The plaintiff testified that he thought the defendant would yield the right of way to him, and it was not until plaintiff's truck was 6 to 8 feet into the intersection and about 20 feet from the point of impact that the plaintiff realized the defendant was not yielding the right of way. The defendant admitted that he was traveling about 25 miles per hour and that he did not see the plaintiff's truck until the impact occurred. The roadways were wet and muddy, and the plaintiff's truck slid about 8 feet after he applied his brakes. When the plaintiff's truck was about 8 feet into the intersection, and he knew the defendant was not yielding to him the right of way, he applied his brakes and his car struck the right rear side of the defendant's sedan. 

It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the plaintiff had the right of way and had a right to assume that the defendant would operate his car in accordance with the provisions of the law. The impact occurred somewhat east of the center line of the north and south street, and south of the center line of the east and west street. 34

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 15 

Kerr v. Hayes, 250 Mich. 19.

In this case the lower court gave a judgment for the plaintiff, and the defendant appealed. The Supreme 

Court reversed the decision without a new trial, holding that the plaintiff was guilty of negligence as a matter of law. The plaintiff was traveling south, and the defendant was traveling west. The plaintiff's car was traveling at a speed of about 15 miles per hour, and the defendant's car was going 35 miles per hour. The collision occurred in the center of the intersection. The plaintiff, at any point within 85 feet of the center of the crossing, had a clear view of an equal or greater distance along the other street. The plaintiff drove into the intersection, looking straight ahead, until he arrived at the edge of the intersection and looked to his right. He did not look to the left nor see defendant's car at any time until an instant before the collision and too late to avoid it. He relied upon the right of way statute entirely. 

The Supreme Court held the plaintiff negligent in not looking to his left upon entering the intersection. The 

Court said: "As the plaintiff did not look to the left he could not have formed any belief from the conditions. He is chargeable with having seen what he should have seen, that defendant's car was about twice the distance from the crossing as his own, approaching at about twice his own speed, without at any time giving any indication of according plaintiff the right of way and that the collision was inevitable unless he took measures to avoid it." 

Sellon v. Tanner, 252 Mich. 231.

The plaintiff was driving north on Cedar Street in the residential section in Lansing at night. The driver was watching the center line of the road to avoid approaching 35

§ 15] 

cars and did not see a truck which backed out from a side street into the intersection. Witnesses for the plaintiff testified that the truck could have been seen in time for the driver to stop. The judgment for the plaintiff in the lower court was reversed and the Court held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law as he should have looked ahead of him and should have seen objects ahead. 

Fabbro v. Soderstrom, 252 Mich. 455.

The plaintiff was driving south on Willard Street in Grand Rapids. When he reached the intersection he slowed his speed to allow an eastbound car to pass. When it passed he proceeded across and had gone far enough for the defendant, westbound, to pass behind him. The defendant, instead of passing behind the plaintiff's car, turned to the left and ran into the plaintiff's car. The plaintiff testified that he was closer to the corner than the defendant as he approached the intersection. It was held in this case that the question of right-of-way was for the jury. 

Swainston v. Kennedy, 253 Mich. 518.

In this case the accident occurred in Muskegon in the afternoon on a clear, dry day. Each street involved was paved and 30 feet wide. The plaintiff was riding in a car driven by her husband, which was being driven south on 

Fourth Street at the rate of 12 to 14 miles an hour. At the first opportunity and when 40 to 45 feet north of the crossing, he looked to the west and saw defendant's car 

250 feet from the intersection. He then looked to the left.

He thought there was no danger and proceeded without varying his speed and without again looking to the right. 

His car was struck by defendant's at the rear wheel when the front end was about at the south curb line of the 36

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 15 crossing, and was turned completely around and thrown across the street to the east curb. Defendant's car passed on, made a right hand turn at the east corner, jumped a five inch curb, and ran over the sidewalk on a lawn. The defendant did not see the plaintiff's car until he was 6 to 10 feet from it.

The Court said that under plaintiff's testimony the defendant drove about four times as fast as the plaintiff, causing him to travel four times as far in the same time. 

The Court said the case was not one for the discussion of authorities but for the application of familiar rules that each driver was bound to make the observations at the intersection, which, and to do what, an ordinarily prudent person would have made, seen, and done, and each could assume that the other would conduct himself as a reasonably prudent driver, unless, until, and insofar as a reasonably prudent person would have apprehended to the contrary. The Court said that the fact, that the driver of plaintiff's car saw the defendant approaching at a much greater distance from the intersection than the plaintiff's car was, did not as a matter of law justify the plaintiff's driver in proceeding. The Court said that the testimony showed the issue as to his care in so doing rested with the jury. His failure to look to the right the second time did not establish his negligence as a matter of law, and he was not guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law. The Court said also that the jury could fairly find the defendant guilty of negligence in driving at an excessive rate of speed, and neglecting to make proper observations in failing to accord the plaintiff the right of way as the first to enter the intersection. 

Smith v. Wassink, 262 Mich. 639.

The plaintiff's car was going north on Pine Street in Lansing. The defendant was driving east on Genesee 37

§ 15] 

Street. Each car was traveling at about 20 miles per hour and neither slackened its pace. Neither driver saw the other automobile until practically at the point of impact. When the plaintiff's car was 37 feet south of the intersection the driver had an unobstructed view sufficient to have seen defendant's car. The defendant's car turned to the left, and the impact occurred north of the center of Genesee Street. The Court held that the plaintiff's driver was negligent as a matter of law. 

Fraley v. J. Calvert's Sons, 266 Mich. 460.

When the plaintiff's car was 25 feet from the intersection the defendant's truck, being towed, was entering the intersection from the right. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent in colliding with the truck. 

Security Storage Co. v. Quimby, 268 Mich. 259.

In this case the view was obscured. The plaintiff, traveling 7 to 8 miles per hour, looked before entering but did not see the defendant's car. He did not look upon entering. If he had he could have stopped and avoided the collision. The defendant first saw plaintiff when he was a car length from the intersection. He applied his brakes but too late to avoid the collision. It was held that each driver was negligent. 

Izzo v. Weiss, 270 Mich. 372.

The plaintiff's car was being driven east on Otis avenue in Detroit at night. The defendant was driving north on Lockwood avenue. Upon arriving at the intersection, plaintiff's driver saw defendant's car 250 feet away. The defendant testified that he thought he would be given the right of way. It was held that the plaintiff had presented a question for the jury. The Court pointed 38

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 16 out that the plaintiff's car was in the intersection first, and entered when the defendant was more than 100 feet away, intimating that the plaintiff's car had the right of way. 

Rak v. Lake, 271 Mich. 274.

The plaintiff's driver was going west and the defendant north. When the plaintiff's car was 15 feet from the intersection the driver saw the defendant's car nearly 50 feet south of the intersection. When entering the intersection he saw the other car slowing down and not yet up to the south curb line. He believed the defendant was going to stop and consequently accelerated his speed. 

The plaintiff's car was beyond the center of the intersection when struck. It was held that the plaintiff's driver was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Sec. 16. Summary of Cases Under Group I. 

It is difficult to lay down any hard and fast rules from the decisions in this group of cases. In approaching an intersection, where the view of the other street is obstructed until the intersection is almost reached, a driver must slow down so as to be able to stop and avoid a collision from the point where he can make an observation. 

He must look to the left in approaching the intersection. (Kerr v. Hayes.) If the intersection is absolutely a "blind" one (Kovacevic v. Reid), he must also look to the right at the edge. If he sees a car to his left, he may rely upon the right of way, if he has reason to believe the other car will not violate it (Tregonning v. Castantini), but the right of way is not absolute (Smith v. Wassink; Kerr v. Hayes). There may be situations where a driver, having seen another car a long distance from 39

§ 17] 

the intersection, is excused from making further observation in entering and crossing the intersection. (Swainston v. Kennedy.) If a driver does not see the other car until too late to avoid a collision, he is probably negligent as a matter of law. (Smith v. Wassink; Security Storage Co. v. Quimby.)

Probably, it is true that in the usual city intersection case, where the vision is obstructed for the drivers up to a point near the intersection, it is quite common for the plaintiff to be held negligent as a matter of law. The plaintiff, as driver of a car, ordinarily has difficulty in establishing facts showing that he made the observation required, and at the time had his car under control and proceeded across the intersection after having formed a judgment that he could do so safely. 

Sec. 17. Cases Under Group II. 

Geeck v. Luckenbill, 215 Mich. 288.

In this case there was a judgment for plaintiff in the lower court, and the Supreme Court reversed the decision. The collision took place at an intersection in the country. The approach of either car was visible for about 700 feet. The plaintiff testified that when 15 rods or 250 feet from the intersection, he saw defendant's car about 500 feet from the intersection. When defendant's car was 120 feet from the intersection, plaintiff testified that his car was about 60 feet away. At this point plaintiff admitted that he could see defendant was coming rapidly. The plaintiff testified that he kept right on going and did not blow his horn. The plaintiff was traveling about 18 to 20 miles per hour and testified that he could have stopped his car within twice the length of his car. There was no other traffic. 40

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 17 It was held that the 'plaintiff was guilty of negligence as a matter of law.  

"It seems incredible that a collision could have occurred without negligence on the part of both drivers." 

The Court emphasized the fact that proper observation by the plaintiff could have shown him that the defendant was going twice as fast, and in addition to this the plaintiff's car was not under control at the intersection. 

Smith v. Ormiston, 242 Mich. 600.

In this case the lower Court entered a judgment for the defendant notwithstanding the verdict for plaintiff. The 

Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The intersection was in the country. The defendant's car was seen 1000 feet from corner, traveling very fast. An occupant of the plaintiff's car testified that plaintiff's car was then 

400 feet from the intersection, traveling 20 miles per hour. The speed was reduced as plaintiff's car approached the intersection. When one block away, defendant's car was three blocks from the intersection. 

The occupant testified that so far as he knew the plaintiff looked straight ahead and did not look to the right or left until they had passed into the intersection. Held, that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The 

Court said that had the plaintiff looked to the left with any degree of care he could have seen the defendant's car and would have had ample time to stop. The Court said that it was impossible to distinguish the case from 

Geeck v. Luckenbill. 

Grodi v. Mierow, 244 Mich. 511.

This was an open country intersection case. Each driver could see 1000 feet. The defendant was moving 41

§ 17]  

east and did not see plaintiff until the collision occurred. 

The plaintiff testified that he was traveling north and saw defendant 500 feet from the intersection when he was 150 feet away. He paid no attention to defendant until he arrived at the edge of the east and west road, which was 24 feet wide. Defendant was then 50 feet from the intersection. Plaintiff had slowed to 10 miles per hour. He did not undertake to estimate defendant's speed but testified that he thought that he could get safely across. Plaintiff's car was struck at the rear door when it had passed the center of the intersection. Held, that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

The Court distinguished the case from Geeck v. Luckenbill and Smith v. Ormiston, on the ground that here the plaintiff had his car under control when he arrived at the intersection, and then formed a judgment that he could get across safely. The Court emphasized the place of collision and stated that the defendant's car did not have a right on the left side of the road. "It was defendant's duty to pass plaintiff on the right." 

Kerns v. Lewis, 246 Mich. 423.

This was an open country intersection case. Plaintiff's car was traveling on a trunk line highway, and the defendant's car was on a crossroad. The facts of the case are not given.  "While the law accords the right of way it requires as well the exercise of at least horse sense." 

Zuidema v. Bekkering, 256 Mich. 327.

The plaintiff's car was being driven west on a country highway in the daytime. The defendant was going north on a paved road. There was a dispute as to whether the plaintiff's car was stopped before crossing the paved 42

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 17 highway. When near this road the plaintiff had practically a clear view for 1100 feet. The case was submitted to the jury, which returned a verdict in favor of the defendant. The Supreme Court said: "If plaintiff's husband looked down the highway to the left and saw defendant's automobile approaching and drove onto the pavement in front of defendant's automobile with knowledge of its approach, he was guilty of contributory negligence."

The Court also said that he was negligent, if he did not see the defendant's car approaching, if he stopped and looked down the road. 

Boerema v. Cook, 256 Mich. 266.

In this case the plaintiff was driving north on a country road. The defendant was driving west. The plaintiff, when 60 feet from the intersection, saw the defendant 160 feet away traveling 50 to 60 miles per hour.

He thought he could get across and proceeded 20 to 25 miles an hour without again looking. There was a collision near the center of the intersection. The Supreme 

Court said that the negligence of the plaintiff consisted in his failure to make further observation, considering the circumstances. The situation was such as to call for further observation. If he had looked he could have stopped or accelerated his speed and escaped the collision. He was negligent as a matter of law. 

Kok v. Lattin, 261 Mich. 362.

Each car in this case was on a gravel country road, and each driver had a clear view of the other when one-half mile from the intersection and up to the time of collision. 

The plaintiff slowed from a speed of 40 to 20 miles per hour on entering the intersection. The defendant main- 43

§ 18] 

tained a speed of 40 miles per hour. The plaintiff testi-
