The cars reached the fied that he looked but saw no car. until the cars were six feet apart. intersection at about the same time. It was held that the lower court was correct in directing a verdict for the defendant. The Court said that as the view was unobstructed the plaintiff must not have looked and was therefore negligent. 

Scurlock v. Peglow, 263 Mich. 658.

The plaintiff, approaching the intersection traveling west, saw a car from the north enter the intersection, turn west and stop. When the plaintiff entered the intersection he looked to the north but could see only 100 feet and saw no car. He looked to the left, and when he had crossed the center of the 16 foot highway saw the defendant's south bound car 10 to 15 feet away. The defendant's car skidded 35 feet and demolished the plaintiff's automobile. The plaintiff testified that his own speed was 7 to 8 miles per hour. It was held that he was not negligent as a matter of law. Intervening obstructions interfered with the plaintiff's view. The Court said that it was inferable that when the plaintiff entered the intersection the defendant was more than 100 feet north, and therefore the right of way did not apply. There were also a number of other factors which excused the plaintiff for not seeing the defendant's car.

Sec. 18. Summary of Cases Under Group II. 

It can be seen from a study of these cases that a driver, who makes several observations of an approaching car, has trouble in recovering. His repeated observations apprise him of the speed of the other car in its approach to the intersection. If one observation is made some dis- 44

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 19 tance from the intersection and no other is made, the driver is probably negligent as a matter of law. (Boerema v. Cook.) Where no judgment is formed as to the speed of the other car, and the car is under control at the edge of the intersection, when observation is made, the driver's negligence may be a question for the jury. (Grodi v. Mierow.) If a driver does not see the other car until just before the collision, the cars entering the intersection at about the same time, he is negligent as a matter of law. (Kok v. Lattin.) Sec. 19. Cases Under Group III. 

Ude v. Fuller, 187 Mich. 483.

There was a judgment for the plaintiff in the lower court, and the defendant appealed. The Supreme Court reversed the decision. This collision occurred in Grand 

Rapids. The plaintiff was a boy riding a bicycle at about noon on a street in Grand Rapids, and traveling about two feet from the curb. When at the west curb line he saw defendant's car one hundred feet away, going south, on the east side of the street and at a speed of about 20 miles per hour. There was a building on the northwest corner under construction, and the defendant testified that this construction work forced him to travel on the east side of the street. The street was 67 feet wide. 

Plaintiff admitted that he realized the car was coming 20 miles per hour and did not look again until the car was 10 feet away. He admitted that he knew the danger and could have started later or stopped and let the car go by. 

The Court held the plaintiff negligent as a matter of law. 

Weber v. Beeson, 197 Mich. 607.

There was a judgment for the defendant rendered, notwithstanding the verdict. The Supreme Court reversed 45

§ 19] 

the decision. The plaintiff was riding with his brother on a motorcycle north on St. Aubin street in Detroit.

When at the south line of Gratiot they stopped for a moment and then started up after looking each way. 

When on the north car tracks, the driver of the motorcycle saw a car coming west on the north side of Gratiot and about 150 feet away. They were moving 6 to 10 miles per hour. The motorcycle driver sounded his horn and proceeded. Just as the motorcycle cleared Gratiot, defendant turned in on St. Aubin and struck the rear wheel. This was the plaintiff's testimony. 

The Court said that as a matter of law it could not be held that the plaintiff was negligent, and that, although plaintiff was violating the speed ordinance, it was only evidence of negligence. 

Pline v. Parsons, 231 Mich. 466.

In this case there was a judgment for the plaintiff, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The plaintiff was moving west on a highway and came up to a trunk line highway and stopped at the stop sign about 55 feet from the east side of the road. Then he started up and traveled at a speed of 7 or 8 miles per hour towards the stop highway. Bushes along the road and intersection obscured the plaintiff's view of the traffic on the highway until he was 60 feet from said highway. Plaintiff's witnesses testified that the defendant was going about 50 miles per hour. When 34 feet from the center of the stop highway, the plaintiff could see the defendant's car about 238 feet away. The plaintiff's car was at the edge of the 

18 foot road or stop highway when defendant's car was 

132 feet away.

The Court held the plaintiff was not guilty of negligence as a matter of law. It discussed the statute giv- 46

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 19 ing defendant the right of way on a trunk line highway and said that the statute did not apply if the car on the trunk line highway was not near enough to demand the right of way. The Court said that the plaintiff was not bound to discover the high rate of speed of the defendant's truck. 

Anderson v. Detroit Motorbus Co., 239 Mich. 390.

In this case there was a judgment for the plaintiff, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The plaintiff, moving south on a street in Detroit and approaching Jefferson Avenue, a stop street, stopped at a stop sign 

40 feet from Jefferson. The plaintiff at that point saw the motorbus about one-half block away, coming west.

Desiring to make a left turn, the plaintiff pulled out onto Jefferson and got as far as the center of the street, when the bus swerved to the left and struck plaintiff's car in the middle of the left side.

It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court stressed the point that the plaintiff reached the intersection first and had the right of way. As the bus was one block away, the plaintiff felt that he could get across safely. The Court said that the plaintiff had the right to assume that the bus would observe the ordinance speed of 15 miles per hour and would travel on the north side of the street. The Court cited Pline v. Parsons in support, and said that the plaintiff had substantially complied with the stop ordinance by stopping opposite the stop sign. 

Hale v. Rogers, 244 Mich. 69.

In this case there was a judgment for the plaintiff, and the defendant appealed. The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the lower court. The plaintiff was traveling south on a graveled street in a city. He slowed his 47

§ 19] 

car to about five miles per hour at the intersection of West Saginaw Street, an asphalt street. He noticed the defendant's car coming east, and about 400 feet away.

The plaintiff continued across the asphalt street and was struck when he had almost crossed the intersection. 

The Court held that he was not negligent as a matter of law; that the plaintiff had a right to assume that defendant would slow down and have his car under control in entering the intersection. The defendant admitted that he was traveling at a speed of 40 miles per hour. 

Scott v. Wallace, 251 Mich. 28.

In this case the plaintiff was driving west in Saginaw on a street 26 feet wide. The plaintiff stopped at the stop sign for Fayette Street, a stop street. His view was unobstructed so far as buildings were concerned. He proceeded across Fayette Street at eight miles per hour and was struck by the defendant's car. The accident happened on December 1, 1928, at 5:30 p. m. It was dark and raining and the witnesses testified it was quite misty. The defendant was driving south on Fayette 

Street and claims he was going 20 miles per hour and looking ahead. The plaintiff's car was struck near the right rear end. The plaintiff claimed that he stopped and looked but did not see defendant until he was on top of him. The plaintiff's car was hurled against a telegraph pole at the southwest corner, 32 feet from the point of impact. The case was sent to the jury and a verdict was given for the plaintiff. The defendant had his dim lights on. The Supreme Court said that the failure of the plaintiff to see the defendant was not negligence as a matter of law, and the case was for the jury. 

Lefevre v. Roberts, 250 Mich. 675.

In this case the plaintiff stopped his truck ten feet from the cement approach leading to Gratiot Road which 48

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 19 was concrete. 

Gratiot Road was a trunk line road and plaintiff was bound to stop. He saw the defendant about 

400 feet or more away from the intersection and started to cross, and while going three miles per hour the defendant's car struck the truck near the rear. The truck driver made no further observation after he started to cross. The defendant testified that when 70 feet from the intersection he was first able to see the truck and saw it. He was going 35 miles per hour, the pavement was slippery, and he could not stop short of 100 feet. 

He accelerated his speed to get by the truck but was struck by the truck. The lower Court directed a verdict for the defendant. The Supreme Court said that if the auto was 400 feet away when plaintiff started to cross, he was not negligent as a matter of law even if he did not look again. The defendant, being on a trunk line highway, had the right of way but was bound to use care. A new trial was ordered. 

Howell v. Hakes, 251 Mich. 372.

The plaintiff was on a trunk line highway between Lansing and Charlotte. He intended to turn left onto a county road and when the intersection was reached his car was stopped. He saw the other car approaching on the trunk line highway about 300 to 500 feet away. He turned and as the car was nearly over the pavement the crash came. The defendant testified that he saw the car stop and thought that he would stay in that position until he passed. He skidded 70 to 80 feet. There was a verdict for the defendant. The Supreme Court said that the negligence of the plaintiff consisted, not so much in crossing, but in failing to look while crossing. The Court said that there was concurrent negligence. The Court also commented on the fact that if the plaintiff had looked he could have accelerated his speed and got out of the way. 49

§ 19] 

The Court said that, assuming the cars collided on the pavement, there was concurrent negligence. 

Szost v. Dykman, 252 Mich. 151.

The plaintiff was driving north on Lane Street in Grand Rapids and stopped at Bridge Street which was a stop street with a car track. The plaintiff looked to the left and saw the defendant 265 to 300 feet away. He did not notice the defendant's speed. He proceeded across at a speed of five miles per hour. He did not look to the left again until he reached the car track. He then saw the defendant 10 to 20 feet away. The defendant testified that he did not see the plaintiff until the collision occurred. He was traveling 15 to 25 miles per hour and looked down Lane Street and saw nothing. The collision occurred south of the center of the street. The verdict of the jury was "no cause of action" each way. The 

Supreme Court held that the defendant might be negligent in not seeing the plaintiff and in driving at an excessive rate of speed. The plaintiff might be negligent in driving too slow. 

Bunker v. Reid, 255 Mich. 536.

In this case the plaintiff was traveling south on M-114 and testified that he stopped opposite a building on the northwest corner of the intersection. He was bound to stop for the road he was crossing. The stop highway was forty feet wide, there being four lanes of traffic, two each way. He looked west and saw no car just before he stopped. He looked east and saw a car approaching and drove ahead enough for clearance and looking west saw the defendant 100 feet away traveling 70 miles per hour in an easterly direction. He claimed he stopped his car on the center line of the road, leaving 20 feet in front for the defendant to pass. The Supreme Court held that the 50

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 19 plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law for so doing. Although he might have looked sooner, he stopped at the center of the road, leaving plenty of room for the defendant to pass. 

Sak v. Waldecker, 256 Mich. 219.

The plaintiff, driving a horse and buggy, stopped 17 feet from the property line and 40 feet from the concrete road which was a stop highway. The concrete road was 

20 feet wide. When the plaintiff stopped he saw defendant 960 feet west, going in an easterly direction. The plaintiff was driving north. The plaintiff started to drive his buggy across the road at a walk. The buggy was past the middle of the road and the horse and front part of the buggy were off the concrete when struck by defendant's car. The Supreme Court held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law and said: "The plaintiff had a right to assume that when he reached the side of the road where he had a right to be that defendant would observe the traffic laws." The Court commented on the fact that the plaintiff thought he could get across and did get across the south half of the road. 

The Court held that it was a question for the jury. 

Adams v. Canfield, 263 Mich. 666.

The plaintiff's car was driven west on a gravel road. 

It was stopped 5 feet from a 20 foot through highway. 

The driver could see 180 feet to the north. The car was driven across the highway and was struck at the rear wheel when nearly across by the defendant's auto, which was traveling 40 to 45 miles per hour. The driver of plaintiff's car made no observation to the north after starting to cross. The lower court directed a verdict for the defendant. The Supreme Court reversed the lower 51

§ 19] 

court and ordered a new trial, holding that the negligence of the plaintiff's driver was for the jury. 

Parker v. England, 266 Mich. 467.

The plaintiff was crossing a through highway after having stopped. He could see 365 feet to the south and saw no vehicle approaching. When near the center of the highway he saw the defendant's car 125 feet away.

He stopped, but the defendant drove into his car. It was held that this presented a question of fact for the jury as to contributory negligence. 

McKelvey v. Hill, 259 Mich. 16.

The plaintiff was driving west on a highway in the country and was crossing a trunk line highway when his car was struck by the defendant's automobile. The plaintiff was required to stop. He testified that he saw the defendant approaching but did not observe the speed carefully. He said that he stopped momentarily and started ahead at low speed, trying to get across the trunk line highway fast enough to avoid a collision. The Supreme Court held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. It said that the plaintiff, knowing of the danger, took a chance on getting across without being hit. 

Cox v. Bell, 259 Mich. 555.

In this case the plaintiff's decedent was driving west on Sixth Street in Monroe. The testimony showed that the decedent drove 35 miles per hour across the Dixie highway without stopping for the stop street. The Court held that he was negligent as a matter of law. 

Henry v. Sanderson, 260 Mich. 563.

The plaintiff was on a gravel road, driving east. In approaching a trunk line highway he shifted into low 52

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 20 gear when opposite the stop sign which was 28 feet west of the trunk line highway. He proceeded at a speed of seven to eight miles per hour. The defendant was driving north 50 miles per hour. When at the west edge of the highway the plaintiff looked to the south. He could see 10 to 12 rods down the easterly side of the highway.

An embankment limited his vision so that he could not see so far down the west half. No vehicle was seen in this space. There was testimony that the defendant was driving on the west half or in the middle of the road. 

The plaintiff did not see the defendant's car before the collision which occurred at the center of the intersection. 

The trunk line highway was 24 feet wide.

The Supreme Court held that the failure of the plaintiff to stop was not negligence as a matter of law because he was not bound to anticipate that the defendant would approach the intersection on the wrong side of the high way. The Court cited Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4713, subdivision (e), but did not comment on subdivision (c) of this section, which, coupled with section 4715, gives the state highway commissioner the right to erect stop signs at certain through highways.

Sec. 20. Summary of Cases Under Group III. 

It is noteworthy that in this group there are but few decisions holding the plaintiff guilty of negligence as a matter of law. It is usually a question of fact as to whether a driver, who has stopped for a stop highway, was negligent in crossing with a car approaching. However, where the car is seen, there may be a duty to continue observation. (Howell v. Hakes.) If the driver tries to cross the path of an approaching car, having stopped only momentarily and knowing the danger, he is probably negligent as a matter of law. (McKelvey v. Hill.) 53

§ 21] 

If no stop is made for a stop street or highway and the car is driven across the intersection at a fair rate of speed, the driver is negligent. (Cox v. Bell.) However, if the car is slowed almost to a stop and proper observation is made, the failure to stop may not be a proximate cause of the collision, especially if the view of the drivers is limited. (Henry v. Sanderson.) In this case the Court based its opinion on a statute and not proximate cause. The decision would be more consistent if the opinion had said that the failure to stop for the stop sign, although negligence per se, was not a proximate cause of the collision.

Sec. 21. Cases Under Group IV. 

Michaels v. Smith, 240 Mich. 671.

In this case there was a judgment for plaintiff, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The plaintiff was driving north on Military Street in the City of Port Huron. This was a trunk line street, with car tracks, and a stop street. The collision occurred in the business district. Plaintiff testified that he was moving ten to fifteen miles per hour and that when 40 feet from the intersection he looked to the left where he could see 40 feet west on Pine Street. There was a building near the corner which prevented further vision. He saw no car. 

He then looked to the right and ahead for pedestrians and continued into the intersection and did not see the defendant's car until it was upon him. 

It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court emphasized the fact that plaintiff was on a main street and in the business district. The 

Court said that the plaintiff had the right of way and was not bound to know that the defendant would disobey the law. 54

[§ 21 

Kerns v. Lewis, 246 Mich. 423.

This was an open country intersection case. Plain 

The facts of the tiff's car was traveling on a trunk line highway, and the defendant's car was on a cross road. case are not given.  "While the law accords the right of way it requires as well the exercise of at least horse sense. 

Wehling v. Linder, 248 Mich. 241. 22 In this case the plaintiff was an occupant in her husband's car. The car was traveling east on Cort Street in Flint at 20 miles per hour. Cort Street was a stop street. As they approached Liberty Street they saw a 

Ford truck about 100 feet distant and traveling south at about 30 miles per hour. Plaintiff continued across 

Liberty Street at the same speed and, when near the center of the street, the Ford struck the left side of plaintiff's car. There was an ordinance making the speed limit 12 miles per hour.

The Court held the plaintiff guilty of negligence as a matter of law and said that the violation of the ordinance, coupled with the failure of the plaintiff's driver to make reasonable observation, constituted contributory negligence. 

Kellstrom v. City of Detroit, 249 Mich. 431.

In this case plaintiff was riding in an automobile with two other men. The car was traveling east on West 

Grand Boulevard in the City of Detroit. The collision occurred just before daylight. The street car was moving north on Hamilton. No other vehicles or cars were near the intersection at the time. The auto slowed for the intersection to between seven and nine miles per hour, and when at or near the building line on the west 55

§ 21] 

side of Hamilton, the driver saw the street car about 25 or 30 feet from the sidewalk line. It appeared to be coming to a stop. The driver, who had run street cars, knew the street car was required to stop on the near side of the Boulevard before crossing and that he had such requirement in mind at the time. He proceeded to cross after looking north on Hamilton, and the accident resulted. Plaintiff's witnesses testified the street car did not stop before crossing the Boulevard. An ordinance required such stop. The Court said the driver of the auto was not bound to anticipate that the street car was going to cross the Boulevard without stopping. The

Court said it was a question of fact for the jury as to the contributory negligence of the plaintiff. 

Townshend v. Reader, 252 Mich. 465.

In this case plaintiff was riding a bicycle north on 

Turner Avenue, Grand Rapids. By ordinance Turner

Avenue was a stop street. The defendant was driving a truck west on Sixth Street. The plaintiff's testimony was that he was going north on the through street. He saw the defendant approaching on the side street from the east. He knew the ordinance gave him the right of way and required the defendant to stop his truck before entering the intersection and wait until traffic on the through street had passed. He testified that the movement on the part of the truck indicated that it was going to stop; that it slowed down, then suddenly shot ahead and ran into him just as he was about to pass. 

The Supreme Court said that under this testimony he had a right to assume that the truck would stop. It said that if, as he testified, there was no circumstance indicating that the defendant was not going to stop the plaintiff was not negligent in proceeding to cross. The Su- 56

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 21 preme Court said that the lower court did not err in refusing to hold that the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law.

The lower court instructed the jury that the ordinance required all vehicles approaching a through street from the side street to stop and wait until the traffic on the through street had passed. The defendant contended that under such an instruction the driver on a protected street could never be guilty of contributory negligence. 

The Supreme Court said that the defendant's counsel did not observe that the Court further instructed the jury that, while the plaintiff had a right to assume that defendant would obey the law and stop, it was nevertheless his duty to be watchful and, if the circumstances indicated he was not going to stop, then plaintiff would be guilty of negligence if he attempted to cross. The Court said that this charge correctly stated the law and clearly explained to the jury how to apply it to the facts as they found them. 

Haynes v. Clark, 252 Mich. 295.

In this case the plaintiff was driving west on Allen Street, a stop street in Grand Rapids. The defendant was traveling south on a paved street. Plaintiff testified that when he came to the intersection he slowed his car to a speed of 4 to 5 miles per hour and looked both ways and saw car lights 150 feet to the north. When he reached the center of the street he looked again and saw the other car was 50 feet away and presumed the other car would stop.

The Supreme Court held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law and said that he had a right to assume that the other car would come to a stop. The 

Court also commented on the fact that the defendant did 57

§ 21] 

not stop at the stop sign although she almost came to a stop. The Court said that the ordinance bound her to make a complete stop.

National Liberty Insurance Co. v. Foth, 254 Mich. 152. 

In this case the plaintiff was driving his car north on a stop highway and the defendant was driving south. The defendant, to avoid a car coming onto the stop highway from a side road, swung his car onto the plaintiff's side of the road, causing a collision. The defendant claimed that a car on the cross road did not stop for the stop highway and forced him over. The lower court directed a verdict for the defendant on the ground that there was no negligence shown.

The Supreme Court reversed this decision and said there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant, and it should have been submitted to the jury. 

The Court said that it must be assumed that the defendant saw the car on the side road as it approached the intersection in determining whether the verdict was properly directed. The Court said that if the car was running at a rate of speed and in a way which indicated that the driver did not intend to stop, then the defendant's failure to reduce the speed of his car was negligence on his part and the proximate cause of the collision. 

Shoniker v. English, 254 Mich. 76.

In this case the plaintiff was traveling north on U. S. 

131, a stop trunk line highway. The defendant was traveling east on M-114, a state trunk line highway. Both highways were paved and 40 feet wide at the intersection. 

There was a stop sign 80 feet west of the intersection on M-114 requiring cars to stop for U. S. 131. There was no 58

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 21 stop sign on U. S. 131 for cars to stop for M-114. The defendant testified that he stopped at the stop sign west of the intersection. A gas station obstructed his view from the point where he stopped. The plaintiff testified that he did not stop.

The Supreme Court held that the plaintiff was bound as a matter of law to stop for the state trunk line highway even though there was no stop sign and even though he was traveling on a road at which the defendant was bound to stop. The Court also said that the defendant did not perform his whole duty in stopping at the stop sign. The Court said that where his view was obstructed it was not sufficient for him to merely stop at the stop sign and make observation. The Court said that there was a duty upon the part of the defendant to make observation at a place where the view was clear and to keep the car under such control as would enable the driver to stop at once if observation disclosed approaching vehicles. The Court said that neither was his car under control, nor was he able to stop when he saw the other and this was in spite of being warned. 

Bunker v. Reid, 255 Mich. 536.

In this case the defendant was driving his car in an easterly direction on a stop highway. There was a building on the northwest corner and the other car was being driven south. The lower court instructed the jury that the defendant, although he was on a stop highway, should have looked to the north behind the building and was negligent for not seeing the plaintiff.

The Supreme Court said that this instruction was in error because the defendant, had he looked and seen plaintiff, would have had a right to rely upon the plaintiff stopping. The instruction was also in error as the defendant testified that he did look. 59

§ 21] 

Weil v. Longyear, 263 Mich. 22.

This collision occurred at the intersection of Clairmount and Fourteenth streets in Detroit. Longyear was driving south on Fourteenth, a stop street. He slowed for the intersection but not quite enough to comply with the city ordinance. A truck was driven into Fourteenth on Clairmount without stopping and at high speed into the side of the Longyear car. The Court held that the speed of the Longyear car was not a proximate cause of the accident. The Court said that if Longyear had observed the truck he would have had the right to assume that it would come to a full stop. 

Lindzy v. Swaab, 263 Mich. 264.

The plaintiff was east bound on Packard Road in Washtenaw County. She testified that she stopped near the edge of U. S. 23 and looked to the north. She could see 372 feet and saw no car. She claimed that she was just past the center of the 40 foot highway when she was struck by the defendant's south bound car. It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury. The 

Court said that if the defendant came over the hill while the plaintiff was crossing the intersection and drove 35 to 40 miles per hour into the plaintiff's car he was negligent. 

Hilliker v. Nelson, 269 Mich. 359.

The plaintiff was driving on a trunk line highway at a speed of 20 to 25 miles per hour. He saw the defendant approaching on an intersecting road. The defendant was required to stop, there being a stop sign about 60 feet from the intersection, and was traveling 25 miles per hour. He believed the defendant would stop and did not see his car again until just before the collision took place. 60

INTERSECTION CASES 

[§ 23 It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 22. Summary of Cases Under Group IV. 

As in the third group of cases, the driver on a stop highway is not often held to be negligent as a matter of law. Where he sees a car approaching the stop highway and slowing down as if to stop, he is not negligent as a matter of law in proceeding. (Townshend v. Reader.) On the other hand, he may be negligent in taking too much for granted. (National Liberty Insurance Co. v. Foth.) 

It is difficult to reconcile Wehling v. Linder with the other cases in this group, especially with Weil v. Longyear, a later decision. A seemingly unfair statute requires a driver on a trunk line highway to stop for an intersecting trunk line road even though there is no stop sign, and even though the other car is bound to stop by reason of a stop sign. (Shoniker v. English.)

Sec. 23. Cases Under Group V. 

Travis v. Eisenlord, 256 Mich. 264.

The plaintiff's car was going east on Plymouth Road. 

The defendant's auto was being driven north on Middlebelt in Wayne County. There was a traffic signal light at the intersection which was green for the plaintiff as he approached and entered the intersection. When the plaintiff was 400 or 500 feet from the intersection he saw the defendant 1000 feet away. The lower court directed a verdict for the defendant on the ground that the plaintiff was negligent in not observing the approach of the defendant's car. The judgment was reversed and a new trial ordered. "It was the duty of plaintiff's driver to look for the green light and to see that the intersection was 61

§ 24] 

clear before attempting to cross, but he was not required to look to the right for the defendant, because he had good reason to believe that he was protected from danger in that direction by the red light." 

Oppenheimer v. Simpson, 263 Mich. 156.

This was an intersection case involving a traffic light. 

The case was reversed and a new trial given to the plaintiff, the Court citing Travis v. Eisenlord as controlling.

Sec. 24. Summary of Cases Under Group V. 

There are only a few cases in the United States involving the duties of drivers at intersections controlled by a signal light. The green light excuses a driver from the absolute duty of making observation of traffic on the intersecting highway. (Travis v. Eisenlord.) However, he may be negligent in fact for not seeing and avoiding the other car which is proceeding against a red light. 62

Sec. 40. Summary-Cases Under the Statute. 

Before 1929, when the so-called Guest Statute was passed in Michigan, the action of a guest against the driver of his car was based upon the common law. The common law cases, which arose before the Guest Statute was passed, will be discussed in this chapter along with the cases which arose after the statute was passed. 

Sec. 25. Cases Before the Statute. 

Roy v. Kirn, 208 Mich. 571.

The accident in this case occurred on March 3, 1916, and the plaintiff was a guest in the defendant's automobile. The accident occurred at an intersection, the 63

§ 25] 

defendant's car striking another automobile. The defendant argued that in order to hold him liable it was necessary to show that he was guilty of gross negligence. 

The Court held, however, that one who invites another to ride with him as his guest is not absolved from responsibility for negligence merely because he is performing a gratuitous service or favor to his guest. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Wood v. Brennan Truck Company, 227 Mich. 545.

In this case the defendant was a carrier for hire. 

However, a question arose as to whether the plaintiff, who was riding on the defendant's truck, was contributorily negligent in not warning the driver of the approach of the interurban car. The lower court directed a verdict for the defendant on the ground that the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law. The judgment was reversed and a new trial was ordered by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court pointed out the fact that the defendant was a carrier for hire, and there is an implication in the case that, if the defendant had not been a carrier for hire and the plaintiff had been a guest, plaintiff might have been negligent as a matter of law. 

Hemington v. Hemington, 221 Mich. 206.

In this case the plaintiff was the defendant's mother. 

She was riding as a guest in the daughter's new automobile and was injured when the car went into a ditch to avoid a horse and buggy at an intersecting highway in the country. The defendant contended that the plaintiff voluntarily put herself in a place of danger and assumed the risk by remaining in the automobile after she knew of the apparent danger. The facts showed that the plaintiff was aware of the defendant's fast 64

GUEST CASES 

[§ 25 driving, and was frightened and repeatedly asked defendant to reduce the speed of the car. It was claimed that the plaintiff voluntarily put herself in a place of danger by re-entering the car after having warned her daughter against the fast driving. It was held this presented a question of fact for the jury, and that the plaintiff as a matter of law did not assume the risk. The 

Court said that if the defendant had been intoxicated, the plaintiff would have been negligent in riding with her, as no one with sense would submit to the peril of riding with such a person. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. The Court said that there was a duty on the part of the driver to exercise reasonable care in the operation of the car, and failing in this duty, the driver would be liable to the guest. 

Ford v. Maney's Estate, 251 Mich. 461.

In this case the defendant contended that the guest passenger was guilty of negligence. The accident occurred at the intersection of two trunk line highways when the defendant's car struck another automobile. 

The Supreme Court made this statement: 

"An invited passenger may have and usually has, no control of the car or the driver. Danger ordinarily appears suddenly. Whether and when the passenger should warn the driver, grasp the wheel or take other action in the particular emergency may be a matter of judgment upon which men may fairly disagree. Even an inopportune warning cry may startle the driver and cause him to swerve from a safe course upon which he has determined or may induce a mental hesitation or uncertainty or involuntary action which will tend to produce rather than to avoid an accident. The duty of the invited passenger, in a case where it is not obvious to him that 65

§ 25] 

the driver is unaware of the danger, depends so completely upon the special circumstances and upon such varied and conflicting notions of the propriety of interference in the management of the car that the courts are loath to hold such a passenger guilty of negligence as a matter of law.”

The Supreme Court said that the testimony did not show when the danger became apparent or what the plaintiff could have done to avoid it. 

Kalso v. Wilson, 252 Mich. 520.

The plaintiff in this case was riding with the defendant as his guest. The only allegation of negligence, on the part of the defendant, was operating the car at an excessive rate of speed. At the conclusion of the testimony the trial court directed a verdict for the defendant, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The undisputed testimony showed that the plaintiff was on a pleasure ride with the defendant and was coming home at night, the street being slippery. A car coming from behind the defendant went by and cut in ahead of him sharply in order to avoid a collision with an oncoming car. The defendant was compelled to cut down the speed of his car and applied his brakes, and the car slid off the highway striking a telephone pole. There was no testimony that the defendant was driving at an excessive rate of speed. The Court said that the proofs showed the defendant was confronted with a sudden emergency by the car cutting in ahead of him, and under the circumstances there was no proof of negligence. 

Devlin v. Morse, 254 Mich. 113.

The plaintiff and defendant on the night of the accident visited a number of places where they danced and partook of refreshments. The plaintiff admitted drink- 66

GUEST CASES 

[§ 26 ing a glass of beer and the defendant admitted that he had several drinks. The defendant while driving the plaintiff home, and while driving at a speed of 30 miles an hour, fell asleep at the wheel and the car ran into a post, injuring the plaintiff. The testimony showed the defendant had been up all night and had taxed his powers of endurance with drink and by loss of sleep. The 

Court said it was actionable negligence under the circumstances for him to continue driving till overcome by sleep. 

Cusick v. Feldpausch, 259 Mich. 349.

The defendant's automobile skidded on ice and turned over injuring the plaintiff, who was a guest in the car. 

The testimony showed that the defendant drove from Grand Rapids to the place of the accident, a distance of 47 miles, in approximately an hour and that he knew that because of ice the road was in a dangerous condition for fast driving. There was a verdict for the plaintiff, and the decision was affirmed by the Supreme Court. The 

Court said that to the usual perils of riding in an automobile, which must have been in the contemplation of the guest when she accepted the invitation, the defendant added unnecessarily another peril, driving at a high rate of speed on a road which he recognized as unsafe for such driving. The opinion did not comment upon assumed risk.

Sec. 26. Summary of Cases Before the Statute. 

It can be seen from the above cases that in Michigan, before the Guest Statute was passed, there was a duty on the part of the driver of a car toward his guest to exercise reasonable care. It was not necessary for the plaintiff to prove gross negligence on the part of the 67

§ 27] 

defendant in order to recover. The decisions indicate a tendency on the part of the Court to put the burden on the defendant in proving contributory negligence. 

The Court intimated in some of the decisions that the plaintiff might be barred from recovering because of assumed risk in certain situations such as where the defendant was intoxicated. It also admitted that in certain situations the plaintiff might be guilty of contributory negligence, but it is noteworthy that in none of the above decisions was the plaintiff defeated because of contributory negligence.

Sec. 27. Cases Under the Statute. 

The Michigan so-called Guest Statute was passed in 1929. It provides that no person, transported by the owner or operator of a motor vehicle as his guest, without payment for such transportation, shall have a cause of action for damages against such owner or operator for injury, death or loss in case of accident unless such accident shall have been caused by the gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct of the owner or operator of such motor vehicle, and unless such gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct contributed to the injury, death or loss for which the action was brought. See 1929 Compiled Laws, Section 4648. 

The statute was held constitutional in the case of Naudzius v. Lahr, 253 Mich. 216. In this case the Court held that the statute would apply to minors as well as adults. In the case of Devlin v. Morse, 254 Mich. 113, it was held that the statute was not retroactive, and would not apply to an accident occurring before the statute became effective. Also see Cusick v. Feldpausch, 259 Mich. 349. 68

GUEST CASES 

[§ 28 As soon as this statute was passed a question arose as to what the legislature meant by gross negligence and wanton and wilful misconduct. A number of decisions have been given by the Michigan Supreme Court involving various types of cases, the overwhelming majority of which have been for the defendant. The decisions for the defendant will be considered first and will be grouped into divisions according to the type of case involved. 

Sec. 28. Intersection Cases. 

Werner v. Wegusen, 252 Mich. 41.

This accident occurred at an intersection in Grand Rapids, the defendant's automobile colliding with another car at the intersection. The driver of the other car was also sued as a defendant in this case. The driver of the car in which the plaintiff was riding made a motion for a directed verdict which was granted. A judgment was rendered against the driver of the other car and both the plaintiff and that defendant appealed. 

The decision of the lower court was affirmed. 

Finkler v. Zimmer, 258 Mich. 336.

This was a guest action, plaintiff's decedent having died of injuries suffered in the collision of automobiles at the intersection of highways. At the conclusion of the plaintiff's case a verdict was directed for the defendant on the ground that the evidence showed no gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct. The accident occurred in the day time and there was no important obstruction to the view of either driver. The defendant was driving his car north on a paved trunk line highway, and the other car was being driven in an easterly direction on an intersecting gravel road. The other driver admitted 69

§ 28] 

that he did not stop for the trunk line highway on which the defendant was traveling but slowed almost to a stop. 

The defendant testified that he slowed to a speed of 45 miles per hour and believed the other car would come to a stop before crossing the trunk line highway. The decision of the lower court was affirmed. In its opinion the Court said that gross negligence, subsequent negligence, antecedent negligence, discovered negligence, last clear chance, and intervening negligence were the same thing. The 

Court said that when it passed to the field of wilful or wanton misconduct it left the field of negligence, as wilful and wanton misconduct was something above ordinary negligence. In this case the Court also said that to a charge of wilfulness or wantonness contributory negligence was no defense. The Court pointed out that the defendant, as he approached the intersecting road, thought the other car would stop and that at the very most he was guilty of ordinary negligence only, and not wilfulness or wantonness. It should be noted in this case that three 

Justices concurred in the result but dissented from the majority opinion that gross negligence had no place in the law of negligence other than meaning discovered or subsequent negligence. 

Mogill v. Resnick, 263 Mich. 103.

Plaintiff in this case was a guest passenger of the defendant, who was driving her car in a westerly direction on Chicago Boulevard in Detroit, and at the intersection of Fourteenth Street made a left turn. Chicago Boulevard was divided by a parkway in the center. Plaintiff testified that she remonstrated with the defendant not to travel so fast but that the defendant speeded up her car to 35 miles per hour approaching the intersection of Fourteenth Street. There was a traffic signal light at the 70

GUEST CASES 

[§ 29 intersection which was green for traffic on Chicago Boulevard when the defendant made her turn. It was claimed by the plaintiff that she was still traveling 35 miles per hour when she made her turn and that she lost control of her car, did not stop in the center of the intersection to wait for the traffic light to change, but continued to make the turn and collided with an eastbound car. The plaintiff contended that the defendant drove her car recklessly in a wanton and wilful manner, disregarding warnings and threats to jump out of the car. The case was sent to the jury, and a verdict of $1,500 was rendered for the plaintiff. The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the lower court without a new trial. The Court said that there was no question but that the defendant should have stopped in the center of the intersection and waited until the light changed, permitting the traffic on Fourteenth Street to proceed. The Court, however, held that she was not guilty of gross negligence or wanton and wilful misconduct in making a left turn on the red light. The Court pointed out the fact that there was no showing of heavy traffic on Chicago Boulevard, or that the defendant was aware of the oncoming car in time to avoid a collision. 

Sec. 29. Running Off Highway. 

Bobich v. Rogers, 258 Mich. 343.

The defendant in this case was driving east approaching a small village. Plaintiff claimed that the defendant drove his automobile at a high rate of speed, and that he was unable to make a sharp turn to the right and lost control of his car, overturning it off the road. Plaintiff testified that before reaching the turn he told the defendant he was driving too fast, and that he wanted to get out. 

The defendant testified that as he was making the turn something happened to his car and he lost control of it. 71

§ 29] 

After the accident it was found that one tire was flat. 

The judgment for the plaintiff was reversed and a new trial was granted, although it was said in the Court's opinion that the plaintiff had only made out a case of ordinary negligence. The Court made this statement: "Whether a turn of the road can be made with reasonable safety at any particular speed depends, of course, upon the character and condition of the road and the skill of the driver. We cannot draw a line beyond which mere speed in making a turn departs from negligence and becomes wilful and wanton misconduct. Conceding that defendant was negligent in making the turn at high speed, it would not constitute wilful and wanton misconduct."

In its opinion the Court said that the term gross negligence as employed in the statute did not mean something of less degree than wilful and wanton misconduct. The 

Court also pointed out that the violation of the speed statute in residence or business districts was not gross negligence or wanton and wilful misconduct. 

Boyle v. Moseley, 258 Mich. 347.

The defendant was driving in a southerly direction on 

U. S. No. 2 at about nine o'clock in the evening. Defendant met a car that had very blinding lights. He testified he could not see where he was driving after he got close to this car. He said he was driving 45 miles an hour and was in a hurry to get to a party. As the approaching car neared him it swerved somewhat in his direction, and the defendant turned his car to the right so that the right hand wheels left the pavement. He testified that he was afraid to apply his brakes for fear he would go into the ditch. While traveling off the road he hit a post and turned over. There was testimony that his car ran one 72

GUEST CASES 

[§ 29 hundred feet after passing the other car before hitting the post. A judgment was directed for the defendant in the lower court and the plaintiff appealed. The decision of the lower court was affirmed by an equally divided Court. Four Justices held that there was evidence of gross negligence and four held there was not evidence of gross negligence. 

Willett v. Smith, 260 Mich. 101.

The plaintiff, seven years of age and a guest in the automobile of the defendant, sued for injuries sustained when the car went into a ditch. Mrs. Smith was driving the car when the accident occurred. She had been used to driving her husband's model T Ford but had driven the car involved in the accident, a Model A Ford, but a few times. The accident occurred a short time after she started to drive. She was using the hand throttle, and was traveling at a speed of 25 to 30 miles an hour, and had gone but a short distance when she apparently lost her head and lost control of the car. An experienced driver in the car grabbed the wheel but the car swayed and went into a ditch. It was held that there was no gross negligence or wanton and wilful misconduct. The Court in this case defined wanton and wilful misconduct as follows: "(1) Knowledge of a situation requiring the exercise of ordinary care and diligence to avert injury to another; (2) ability to avoid the resulting harm by ordinary care and diligence in the use of the means at hand; (3) the omission to use such care and diligence to avert the threatened danger, when to the ordinary mind it must be apparent that the result is likely to prove disastrous to another."

The Court said it was not apparent to Mrs. Smith that her driving would prove disastrous. The Court said that ww 73

§ 29] 

she would not invite danger to herself, a neighbor or child, and to her own children. 

Mater v. Becraft, 261 Mich. 477.

In this case the accident occurred at night, the car leaving the road at a curve. Neither the plaintiff nor the defendant saw the curve until just prior to the accident. 

The judgment in the lower court for the plaintiff was reversed, the Supreme Court holding that there was no evidence of gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct. The Court said it was a fair inference from all the testimony that the defendant was confused and misled by the lights of an oil station near the curve. It was not claimed that the defendant intentionally drove off the highway. The Court said that the defendant may have been negligent in driving too fast and in not applying the brakes in time; however, this lack of care was at the most but ordinary negligence. 

Elowitz v. Miller, 265 Mich. 551. way Plaintiff was riding as a guest of the defendant in the city of Ann Arbor at night. The automobile left the highat a street intersection and struck a tree. There was testimony that the defendant drove at an immoderate rate of speed particularly when rounding corners, and that he was asked to slow down and watch his driving. 

The defendant testified that as he came down the street and was approaching the curve he knew there was a curve ahead but reached it sooner than he expected. As soon as he saw it he applied his brakes, and that had there been no ice or gravel at the corner, he guessed he could make the turn in safety. It was held there was no evidence of wanton or wilful misconduct on the part of the defendant. 74

GUEST CASES 

[§ 30 

Turney v. Meyer, 266 Mich. 87.

The plaintiff testified that he had driven with the defendant and knew he was a driver who drove quite fast, There was testimony that the defendant had informed the plaintiff that the front brakes were not working properly but were grabbing. There was also testimony that the defendant informed the plaintiff that he did not have any rear brakes. It was also claimed that the car was being driven.at a speed of 60 miles an hour down grade and that it left the road at the curve. The Court said that the facts in this case were similar to those in the case of Elowitz v. 

Miller, and held that a verdict should have been directed for the defendant. The Court said there was evidence, seemingly conclusive, that there was nothing wrong with the brakes on the car at the time of the accident. It should be noted that in this case the Court commented on the fact that the plaintiff had knowledge of the condition of the brakes, that they were defective, and the fact that the defendant was a fast driver and intimated that, if there was any gross negligence in the case, he assumed the risk.

Sec. 30. Car on Wrong Side of Road. 

Wyma v. Van Anrooy, 260 Mich. 295.

The plaintiff's decedent was a guest riding in an automobile driven by the defendant. The defendant endeavored to pass an automobile going in the same direction and collided with an approaching automobile. After the first collision the defendant increased the speed of his car, according to the plaintiff's claim, turned it to the wrong side of the road, and collided with another automobile. After the first collision the defendant's car started for the ditch on the right hand side of the road and he righted it. Then the car went to the left side of the road and into the second car. It was claimed that the 75

§ 30] 

defendant's car went a distance of four hundred feet from the first collision until it struck the second car. It was held that the defendant was not guilty of gross negligence or wanton and wilful misconduct. The Court said that it could assume that the speed of the car was 65 miles per hour but still there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

The Court also said that the testimony most favorable to the plaintiff's case showed that the defendant, in attempting to pass the automobile ahead of him, did not give due heed to the oncoming automobile and the situation in which it would place him. This was misjudgment or possibly judgment so carelessly exercised as to constitute negligence but was wanting in wilfulness or wantonness. 

Findlay v. Davis, 263 Mich. 179.

In this case the proof showed that the defendant was intoxicated and that the plaintiff had been drinking. 

Plaintiff denied that she had been drinking. The defendant denied that he was intoxicated. The road where the accident occurred was a one track sand road through a woods, and at the time of the accident there was a heavy fog. The accident occurred in the night time in a narrow hollow between two hills. The defendant's car struck an oncoming car and apparently was partly on the wrong side of the road when the collision occurred. It was held that the defendant was not guilty of wanton or wilful misconduct. The Court said in this case that gross negligence did not mean something of a lesser degree than wanton or wilful misconduct. The Court pointed out that when the defendant saw the other car approaching he attempted to get out of the track and avoid a collision. 

LeGroh v. Bennett, 271 Mich. 526.

The plaintiff was a guest passenger and was injured when the car in which she was riding collided with a truck. 76

GUEST CASES 

[§ 31 The accident occurred at night on a 40-foot pavement when the plaintiff's car in attempting to pass another north bound auto swerved and struck a south bound truck. 

The car then went a distance of nearly 400 feet and struck another south bound truck, killing the driver and two occupants of the car. There was testimony that the car was being driven at a speed of 50 to 60 miles an hour on a slippery road in a heavy fog. There was a space of about 

20 feet between the car which was overtaken and the south bound truck. It was held that there was no evidence of wanton or wilful misconduct.

Sec. 31. Not Stopping for Stop Highway. 

Oxenger v. Ward, 256 Mich. 499.

At the time of the accident in this case the defendant was driving a Ford car and there were ten persons in it. 

The defendant was driving along Territorial Road and was crossing Hillsdale Road, a through traffic highway, when the accident occurred. A stop sign had been placed on Territorial Road about seventy feet from the center of Hillsdale Road. Both roads were county roads 24 feet in width. There was not much traffic on either road at any time. The road commissioner estimated the average traffic on Hillsdale Road was about three hundred vehicles a day or less than one vehicle every two minutes. The main witness testified that the defendant slowed up somewhat in approaching the stop sign but did not stop, and when he got ready to cross Hillsdale Road he increased the speed of the car. The speed of the car was about twenty miles per hour. It was held that there was not evidence of gross negligence in this case. The Court made this statement: "Had he driven into a busy arterial highway or a city street without stopping when commanded to do 77

§ 32] 

so by an appropriate sign, his liability would have been a question for the jury to determine. Under the facts presented in the instant case, we are constrained to reverse the judgment, with costs to defendant, and remand the case to the trial court with instructions to enter a judgment in favor of defendant." 

Sec. 32. Railway Crossing Cases. 

Morgan v. Tourangeau, 259 Mich. 598.

The defendant in approaching a railroad track was driving 30 to 35 miles per hour and did not reduce her speed as she approached the track. When 50 to 60 feet from the crossing, the plaintiff saw a train approaching about 150 feet away and shouted a warning at the defendant, but the defendant made no effort to stop the car, apparently trying to cross ahead of the train, and a collision resulted. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence in this case. The Court said that the defendant was placed in a position of danger, and, while it might have been a safer course to try to stop the car, failure to do so was not gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct. 

Balcer v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 266 Mich. 538.

In this case the defendant, in driving his car across a railway crossing in Bay City, struck a train at the crossing. There were gates at the crossing, and they were up. 

The plaintiff testified that he noticed the gates were up and thought the way was clear and did not look for a train. When a block and a half from the track, however, he called the driver's attention to the train and suggested that he have his car under control. The street was icy near the crossing, and the car evidently skidded just be- 78

GUEST CASES 

[§ 33 fore reaching the crossing and struck the locomotive. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence or wanton and wilful misconduct in this case. 

Greenfield v. Duluth, South Shore & Atlantic Ry. Co., 268 

Mich. 277.

The accident in this case occurred at the crossing of a trunk line highway by railway tracks. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence or wilful or wanton misconduct on the part of the defendant. 

Sec. 33. Failure to Stop Within Assured Clear Distance. 

Van Blaircum v. Campbell, 256 Mich. 527.

The defendant, while driving on a highway at night, did not see a trailer which was parked on the highway and ran into it from the rear. The testimony showed that he was driving at about 45 miles per hour. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct on the part of the defendant. The 

Court said that the proximate cause of the accident was the defendant's failure to see the trailer, and this failure at the most was only ordinary negligence. 

Moore v. United States Truck Co., 260 Mich. 56.

In this case the plaintiff was injured in a rear end collision with a stalled truck with trailer standing upon a highway. At the close of the plaintiff's case, the court directed a verdict as to the driver of the plaintiff's car. 

The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment as to the defendant Moran, who was driving the car in which the plaintiff was riding, and reversed the judgment rendered against the owner of the truck. 

Grabowski v. Seyler, 261 Mich. 473.

In this case as the defendant was driving along a highway in a storm, it being dark, he noticed a truck ahead, 79

§ 34] 

which was poorly lighted, and turned out to pass it. The rear wheels of his car skidded on the ice, and the automobile hit the corner of the trailer. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct.

Sec. 34. Defendant Driving While Intoxicated. 

Findlay v. Davis, 263 Mich. 179.

In this case it was claimed that the defendant was intoxicated and that driving while intoxicated amounted to gross negligence and wilful and wanton misconduct. It was held that there was not sufficient evidence to send the case to the jury on the question of gross negligence. The 

Supreme Court said: 

"Driving a motor vehicle upon the public highways of the State while intoxicated is doing something prohibited by statute, and may constitute negligence, but the terms, 'gross and wanton and wilful,' when used in relation to misconduct which constitutes the violation of a statute or municipal ordinance enacted to promote the public safety and which is often called negligence per se, have no legal significance which imports other than simple negligence or want of due care, and are not equivalent to wilful or wanton, and it is error in advance to use them in that sense." 

The Court said that intoxication itself is not negligence as a matter of law.

Sec. 35. Defendant Asleep When Accident Occurred. 

Boos v. Sauer, 266 Mich. 230.

It was shown in this case that the defendant for about a year had been leaving Grand Rapids at about 3 a. m., driving to Otsego, and then returning to Grand Rapids in 80

GUEST CASES 

[§ 36 time to meet a 6 o'clock train in the morning. He did other work in the afternoon. The day before the accident he was awake at 3 a. m. to bedtime, or about 11 p. m. On the day in question he followed his usual routine. A witness testified that when he saw the defendant's car approaching it was weaving on the pavement and then ran off the pavement, striking a telephone pole. The defendant testified that he did not know how the accident occurred. It was the plaintiff's theory that the defendant fell asleep. The defendant testified that on the trip, as on other trips, he had felt a little sleepy but that he had full control of his mental processes up to the time of the accident. It was held that there was no evidence to take the case to the jury as to gross negligence. The Court said that the weight of authority was that the mere falling asleep was not gross negligence. The Court said, that to constitute gross negligence in falling asleep while driving, there must have been such prior warning of the likelihood of sleeping that to continue to drive constituted a reckless disregard of consequences. Also, see case of

Manser v. Eder, 263 Mich. 107, where the plaintiff was permitted to recover on a guest case.

Sec. 36. Operating Defective Car. 

Gifford v. Dice, 269 Mich. 293.

The plaintiff was riding with the defendant in his automobile when the left front tire blew out, causing the defendant to lose control of his car, resulting in a collision. 

The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was guilty of wilful and wanton misconduct in driving his car with knowledge of the worn and weakened condition of the tire. The lower court directed a verdict for the defendant, and the decision was affirmed. The Supreme Court said that, assuming the tire was worn through the tread 81

§ 37] 

and that the defendant was aware of the fact, there still was not evidence of wilful and wanton misconduct. The 

Court made this statement: "A guest in an automobile accepts the means of conveyance in the condition it is maintained by the owner, and cannot predicate an action for gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct upon failure of the owner to inspect the car and keep it in such repair as to avoid the possibility of an accident. So, in this case, defendant owed no duty to plaintiff as his guest to keep the car tire in such a condition of repair as to prevent a blowout or to replace the worn tire by another. The owner of a car, under circumstances such as in the case at bar, is only required to provide his guest with the conveyance he provides for himself."

Sec. 37. Cases in Which Plaintiff Recovered. 

Manser v. Eder, 263 Mich. 107.

The defendant was a dentist and had worked steadily from 9 a. m. to 9 p. m. the night of the accident. At about 

1 a. m. the plaintiff was returning from Pontiac to Detroit with the defendant. As he drove through Highland 

Park he fell asleep at the wheel and narrowly escaped running into a safety zone. The plaintiff testified that he aroused the defendant and informed him that he was driving in a dangerous manner. The plaintiff insisted that she be allowed to get out of the car, but the defendant stated that he would not permit her to do so and declared that he could drive her to her home safely. Shortly thereafter he went to sleep again and drove his car into a safety zone post. It was held that there was evidence of gross negligence in this case. 82

GUEST CASES 

[§ 37 

McLone v. Bean, 263 Mich. 113.

The accident occurred in the night time, the parties being on their way from a dance. The plaintiff and her escort were riding on the front seat with the defendant. 

They were traveling over a dusty gravel road used as a detour, and the defendant twice passed another automobile going in the same direction. The other automobile passed the defendant three times, both cars being driven at a high rate of speed in a cloud of dust. In an attempt to pass the other car a third time, the defendant's automobile left the road and turned over and injured the plaintiff. At the time of the accident the defendant was driving 68 to 70 miles an hour in a dense cloud of dust, so dense that he could not see the front of his own car. The testimony showed that the defendant was racing with the other car. It was held that there was evidence of wanton and wilful misconduct, the court saying that he acted in disregard of the probable consequences. The court pointed out that what happened was just what a man of ordinary intelligence ought to know would happen. 

Goss v. Overton, 266 Mich. 62.

The testimony in this case showed that late in the afternoon the defendant left a country club with three friends to return home. It was a hot, dry and dusty afternoon with practically no wind blowing. The road had been freshly graveled in the morning, and just before entering the city limits of Allegan there was a short curve. The defendant was driving at a speed of 60 miles per hour up to the time of the accident. Just before reaching the curve, Overton drove into a thick cloud of dust without decreasing his speed. Suddenly a road scraper loomed up ahead of him. He swerved out of its path and was unsuccessful in his effort to make the curve and hit a tele- 83

§ 38] 

phone pole at the side of the road. It was held that there was evidence of gross negligence and wilful and wanton misconduct in this case. It was shown that the driver had lived in Allegan all of his life and was well acquainted with the road and the turn. The court pointed out that when the driver saw the cloud of dust on the curve it meant that some moving vehicle had produced it. The court said that the defendant knew before he saw the scraper on the curve that he was in a dangerous situation, and yet, disregarding the consequences, he continued to drive at a high rate of speed and went recklessly ahead.

Sec. 38. Doctrine of Assumed Risk. 

It should be remembered that, even though the plaintiff produces proof which would take the case to a jury so far as the proof of gross negligence is concerned, the plaintiff might be barred from recovery. He still might not be able to recover because of assumed risk. The doctrine of assumed risk should be distinguished from the doctrine of contributory negligence. It could be argued that in a guest case where it is necessary to prove wilful and wanton misconduct the plaintiff could not be defeated because of contributory negligence. This would be on the theory that where the defendant is guilty of wilful misconduct, contributory negligence is not a bar to recovery. However, the plaintiff can be guilty of assumed risk without being guilty of contributory negligence. A guest in an automobile would be guilty of contributory negligence if there was a duty on the guest's part to make some observation at an intersection or a railway crossing and he failed to do so. He also might be guilty of negligence where he interfered with the defendant's operation of the car negligently. However, this would be entirely different from the doctrine of assumed risk. 84

GUEST CASES 

[§ 38 

In the case of Hemington v. Hemington, 221 Mich. 206, the court said that intoxication temporarily destroys the faculties essential to safe driving and that such was common knowledge; that no one with sense would submit to the peril of riding with such a person. Therefore, in this case, the court implied very strongly that a person riding with an intoxicated driver and knowing his condition could not recover. This would be because of assumed risk. It has already been pointed out in this chapter that the guest assumes the risk in riding in a car which is in need of repair or in need of better tires. For a case in which the court seems to have gone quite far in permitting the plaintiff to recover in spite of the doctrine of assumed risk, see Cusick v. Feldpausch, 259 Mich. 349, where the defendant was operating his car at a high rate of speed on a slippery road and had been operating it at a constant rate of speed for some time before the accident occurred. In the case of Turney v. Meyer, 266 Mich. 87, the Court made this statement: "But assuming that the defendant made the remark attributed to him as to their condition, these remarks were made when on the way from the home of the plaintiff's father to Ontonagon, and, with full knowledge thereof, plaintiff did not hesitate to go with the defendant on the trip in which he was injured. He knew that the defendant was a fast driver.

He was willing to and did ride with the defendant after the accident."

Therefore, the Court in this case definitely fell back on the doctrine of assumed risk to defeat the plaintiff. 

There seems to be no question that the doctrine of assumed risk will apply in a Michigan guest case in certain situations. 85

39] 

 Sec. 39. Whether Plaintiff Is a Guest. 

The Guest Statute, of course, applies only to guests. 

If the occupant is a passenger for hire, he is not a guest. 

Very often a question arises as to whether the occupant has become a passenger for hire by paying for gasoline or part of the expense of the trip. In the case of Morgan v. Tourangeau, 259 Mich. 598, the plaintiff was permitted to pay for the gasoline before the trip was started. The 

Court held that she was a gratuitous passenger and was a guest. The defendant had invited the plaintiff to accompany her on a trip which she intended taking to Green Bay, and the invitation was accepted. In the case of 

Wojewoda v. City of Detroit, 264 Mich. 277, it was held that the occupant was not a guest. The plaintiff with other workmen had made an arrangement with the defendant to be taken in the defendant's car to and from work from their homes. The plaintiff was to pay $1.00 per week for this transportation. The Court said that the arrangement was made in advance of the transportation. The Court said that, if the payment was not by way of voluntary or spontaneous courtesy of the guest or cooperative contribution to the expense of the trip, the fact that the driver made the expense the basis of his computation of the charge would not prevent the carrying being for hire. The Court said that, under the testimony, whether the plaintiff was a passenger for hire was a question for the jury. It should be remembered that where the plaintiff seeks to avoid the Guest Statute by showing that he was a passenger for hire in the defendant's automobile at the time of the accident he may not be able to recover from the defendant's insurance company because of the usual clause in automobile insurance policies, providing that the policyholder will not be protected where the car is used to carry passengers for hire. See Michaelson v. Simula, 264 Mich. 457. 86

GUEST CASES 

[§ 40 There are a number of situations in which the occupant of a car would not be a guest. For a discussion of the situation, see case of Monison v. McCoy, 266 Mich. 693.

In the opinion in this case it is suggested that a prospective buyer of an automobile, to whom it is being shown, would not be a guest, nor would one invited by a real estate salesman to look at real estate. Also see McQuire v. Armstrong, 268 Mich. 152. 

Hunter v. Baldwin, 268 Mich. 106.

The plaintiff was driven from his home to a town, a few miles away, by the defendant. They attended to some business for two or three hours. When coming back to the car, the motor would not start, and the plaintiff was asked to crank the car. The car was in gear and when the motor started the plaintiff was injured. It was held that he was not a guest after he left the car for a period of two or three hours, and he had not resumed the position of a guest passenger while cranking the car. 

Sec. 40. Summary of Cases Under the Statute. 

The Supreme Court has definitely defined gross negligence in the so-called Guest Statute in practically the same manner as wilful and wanton misconduct. In other words, the Court would not follow the definition of gross negligence found in the Last Clear Chance Doctrine. The following general rules can be gathered from the decisions involving guest cases: 

1. Before the Guest Statute will apply the plaintiff must have been a guest in the defendant's automobile. 

There must have been a relationship of host and guest. 

2. If the plaintiff pays part of the expenses of the trip spontaneously as a voluntary courtesy, he still may be a guest in the car. However, if the payment for gas or for 87

§ 40] 

expenses is not incidental to the trip but is given as a consideration for the carrying of the plaintiff, then the plaintiff probably would not be a guest. 

3. Plaintiff cannot recover by merely showing that the defendant was intoxicated at the time of the accident. 

The plaintiff must put proof in of certain actions on the part of the defendant that amount to wilful and wanton misconduct. 

4. In order to get his case to a jury, the plaintiff must show that the defendant was confronted with a known dangerous situation and acted in disregard of the consequences. 

5. The defendant would not be liable to a guest plaintiff because of an accident caused by defects in the car, such as a blowout of a well-worn tire. 

6. The plaintiff, although he could not be barred from recovery because of contributory negligence, may fail to recover because of the doctrine of assumed risk. If the plaintiff voluntarily rode with an intoxicated defendant, knowing his condition, he would be guilty of assuming the risk and could not recover.

From the cases considered in this chapter, it can be seen quite clearly that a guest cannot recover in the ordinary situation. Obviously, in order to recover, there must be rather peculiar circumstances or an unusual situation, as in the majority of accidents the driver at the most is guilty of only ordinary negligence. 888

CHAPTER IV  Sec. 41. Ordinary Crossing Cases. 

Sec. 42. Summary-Ordinary Crossing Cases. 

Sec. 43. Protected Crossings. 

Sec. 44. Summary-Protected Crossings. 

Automobiles Stalled on Track. 

Sec. 46. Street Railway Crossing Cases. 

Sec. 47. Summary-Street Railway Crossing Cases. 

The Michigan Supreme Court has placed a heavy duty on the driver of an automobile at a railway crossing. It has become increasingly more difficult for the driver or occupants of an automobile to recover from a railroad company for damages sustained in a railway crossing case. Therefore, in order to get a true picture of the law in Michigan on this type of case, the early decisions will not be considered. The duties of an automobile driver in respect to street railways will be considered under a separate heading near the end of this chapter. The operator of an automobile naturally would have a better chance to recover from the railroad, where his car was struck at a so-called protected crossing, than he would have at an ordinary crossing. Therefore, the cases are grouped in two divisions, dependent upon whether the crossing was or was not protected.

Sec. 41. Ordinary Crossing Cases. 

Davis v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 241 Mich. 166.

In this case, when the driver reached a point about 40 feet from the crossing, he stopped his car and looked and 89

§ 41] 

listened. At that point he could not see down the tracks because of an elevator, a box car, and a flag shanty. Hearing no train, he started across and was near the track when he was aware of an approaching train and applied his brakes, but due to the icy road his car skidded into the path of the train. It was held that the driver was guilty of negligence as a matter of law. The Michigan 

Supreme Court cited the United States Supreme Court case of Baltimore & Ohio Ry. Co. v. Goodman, 48 Supreme

Court 24. In that case it was said that, if a driver could not be sure otherwise whether a train was dangerously near, he must stop and get out of his vehicle, although obviously he would not often be required to do more than to stop and look. The Michigan Supreme Court pointed out that the plaintiff first stopped where he had no view of the track, and this placed upon him the duty of exercising precaution commensurate with the situation. 

Rosencranz v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 244 Mich. 137.

In this case the driver of the automobile was attempting to cross four tracks. He stopped his automobile near the first track and listened and made observation. He had crossed three tracks and was near the last track when he discovered the locomotive about 35 or 40 feet away. He could not stop in time to avoid the collision. His view was obscured by two cars loaded with coal, standing on the third track and about six feet from the roadway. It was held that the driver was negligent as a matter of law. 

The Court said that he should have stopped, looked and listened before crossing the last track and, if necessary, should have gotten out of his automobile and made observation. As he did not stop and not being able to see whether the way was clear, he was negligent in driving into the path of the locomotive. 90

[§ 

Brady v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 248 Mich. 406.

In this case the driver of the automobile testified that he stopped near the crossing and had a view of 700 feet down the track and looked and saw no train but was struck by a train in crossing. It was held that the driver was guilty of negligence as a matter of law in spite of the fact that he testified there was a wigwag signal at the crossing which was not working. The Court said that the driver had open to him a view of 700 feet down the track, over which the train came. When such a view was open, a collision between a train and an automobile moving across a railroad track was only possible by reason of want of care on the part of the automobile driver, according to the Court. 

Laurain v. Detroit, Toledo & Ironton Rd. Co., 249 Mich. 630. 

The plaintiff's decedent approached the crossing, traveling in a westerly direction, and brought his car to a stop. A large building near the road and a freight car blocked his view to some extent.
