The facts showed that, if the driver had gone to a point just 20 feet east of the main line, he had a view along defendant's main line track as far south as his eyesight would be able to carry. 

It was held that the driver was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the driver stopped before he reached the point where he could have had an unobstructed view in a place of safety. The accident occurred in daylight hours, and the testimony showed that the driver was familiar with the crossing.

Richman v. Detroit, Grand Haven & Milwaukee Ry. Co., 

254 Mich. 607.

This accident occurred at about 9:30 p. m. The driver had two street car tracks and three railway tracks to 91

§ 41] 

cross. As he approached the street car tracks, he stopped his car and, seeing no street cars were approaching, crossed the car tracks and again stopped at the first or more westerly railroad track. He saw a long freight train standing on this track. The rear of the caboose on the south end of the train was approximately five feet from the road. The plaintiff stopped his car and, as he looked and listened, a man came out of the rear door of the caboose and motioned and called to the plaintiff to come on. This man was not identified in any way as an employee of the defendant. After looking to the left and right, the plaintiff speeded up his car and drove onto the middle railroad track, where his car was struck by the locomotive of a southbound train. The plaintiff claimed that the locomotive had no lights and sounded no whistle. 

It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the invitation by the man who came from the caboose, and who was a stranger as far as the records showed, did not completely relax the plaintiff's duty to exercise due care and precaution in crossing the other tracks. The Court also pointed out the fact that the automobile was headed in a northeasterly direction in crossing the tracks and the headlights would shine upon the approaching locomotive. The Court said that if the plaintiff had looked he would necessarily have seen the approaching train. His mere statement that he looked did not overcome the physical facts of the case. 

Graham v. Ann Arbor Rd. Co., 259 Mich. 139.

In this case the testimony showed that the plaintiff was approaching a crossing; and, when 100 to 125 feet from the crossing, the approaching train was only two or three car lengths away. The plaintiff was driving her car at approximately 20 miles per hour while the train was moving at only eight miles per hour. The train was being 92

[§ backed across the crossing, and the head brakeman was stationed on top of the leading car. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that it conclusively appeared that the plaintiff was familiar, at least in a general way, with the railroad crossing and was guilty of negligence in driving in daylight upon the defendant's tracks at an unprotected crossing in front of approaching freight cars and without having looked at all in the direction from which they were coming. 

Heintzelman v. Pennsylvania Rd. Co., 260 Mich. 688.

Shortly after midnight the plaintiff was driving in an easterly direction on Goodrich street in Grand Rapids.

He was driving across twenty-seven tracks belonging to various railroads and had proceeded half-way across the tracks when he reached the three tracks belonging to the defendant company. Just east of one of these tracks, and also two hundred to three hundred feet to their west, were two street lamps lighted and suspended in the center of the street. There were two rows of box cars standing north of the street on each of the side tracks, the end of the cars being only five feet north of the sidewalk. 

The plaintiff testified that he stopped his car before attempting to cross the three tracks. He looked and saw no train and heard no signal. He testified that he proceeded at a speed of eight miles an hour, but just as he reached the center track a large black object suddenly loomed up before him. It was the end of a rear coach of a string of passenger cars that were being backed across Goodrich street from the north at a rate of speed about one-third in excess of that at which the plaintiff was driving. The testimony showed that as the car reached the most easterly rail of the first track the driver's view down the cen- 93

§ 42] 

ter track was unobstructed for a very great distance. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that when he reached the point where he could see a great distance down the main track he was in a zone of safety where, with the aid of his headlights and street lights, he could have seen the approaching train on the main track had he looked. The Court said that the moving train approached very slowly, and he had plenty of time to see it. 

Gardinear v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 265 Mich. 286.

In this case the driver of the car drove his automobile against the side of a moving freight train at night. It was held that the driver was guilty of negligence as a matter of law. The Court said that the driver was not operating his car at such a speed that he could stop within the range of his lights.

Sec. 42. Summary. 

Where an automobile is struck by a train at an ordinary railway crossing, not protected, the driver of the car or adult occupants would have little or no chance to recover against the railroad, especially if the accident occurred in the daytime. Where the view is unobstructed, there, of course, would be no excuse for the driver crossing the path of the train. Where the view is obstructed, the driver is bound to use a great deal of care, and it is difficult to conceive of a case where the driver could recover in the daytime. If the accident occurred at night and the train was not lighted, the driver, by exercising a great deal of care, might not be negligent as a matter of law. However, if the crossing is lighted to any extent or his lights would shine upon the train, he would probably be held negligent. It is not sufficient that the driver bring 94

[§ his car to a stop near the tracks. If his view is obscured, he must bring the car to a stop at a point where he can see down the tracks if that is possible. If the view is obstructed so that he cannot see a sufficient distance down the tracks by stopping close to the tracks, then it may be necessary for him to get out of his car as suggested in one or two Michigan cases.

Sec. 43. Protected Crossings. 

Miller v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 167 Mich. 21.

This accident occurred at a railroad crossing on Division street in the city of Dowagiac. The plaintiff was crossing five tracks. The crossing was protected by gates. 

The plaintiff was driving a load of hay. As he approached the crossing, the gates were down, and he had to wait about ten minutes before they were raised. When they were raised he proceeded across. As he was crossing he saw an engine standing ninety feet away. As he was about to cross the last track, this engine started up and struck his wagon. The case was submitted to the jury, and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Coston v. Ann Arbor Rd. Co., 201 Mich. 232.

The plaintiff in this case contended that the electric bell at the crossing was out of order due to negligence of the defendant. This bell was supposed to ring when the train was about eight hundred feet from the crossing. 

The defendant contended that the bell was frequently out of order and the deceased was familiar with that fact. 

The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court made this statement: "Such warning bells are not required or customary at ordinary highway crossings and, when installed, are inevitably a notice to the general public that the 95

§ 

ordinary means of warning at a highway crossing are inadequate for that particular place, which would naturally tend to divert the vigilance of those regularly using the highway from the ordinary methods of warning. This bell had been maintained by defendant at the crossing where the accident occurred for several years."

The accident occurred in the evening, and as the driver was killed there was no testimony as to whether he looked or not. 

Mohrloch v. Detroit, Jackson & Chicago Rd. Co., 223 

Mich. 586.

The crossing in this case was a protected one, there being a bell and a wigwag. The plaintiff contended that he observed the bell and wigwag and that neither was in operation and that he listened and no gong was sounded or whistle blown. The plaintiff also testified that there was an obstruction to the view to the west, from which direction the train came. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law.  "While this Court has repeatedly held that the fact that a crossing is a protected crossing does not absolve a traveler from contributory negligence and that he may not rely entirely or absolutely upon the railroad to perform its duty, its giving warning by sounding its bell or lowering its gate where they are maintained, it has also been held that the traveler may rely to some extent upon the railroad to properly operate the protecting device, and that the jury may take that fact into consideration, together with the other facts in the case, in determining the question of contributory negligence." 

Hudson v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 227 Mich. 1.

In this case the plaintiff contended that the electric crossing bell did not ring as the train approached and the 96

[§ train gave no sound of warning. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, and the question of his negligence was for the jury. The plaintiff's view was obstructed by buildings and foliage until he was very close to the defendant's tracks. 

Patton v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 236 Mich. 173.

The plaintiff's decedent was a drayman in Charlotte, Michigan. He was driving a Ford truck north when he reached the defendant's crossing, which was blocked by a freight train which was moving slowly in an easterly direction on the south track. A short distance west of the intersection the caboose was cut off from the train and stopped on the highway crossing, partly blocking travel. There was just enough room to drive around the west end of the caboose. After the caboose stopped, the brakeman walked along the south side of the caboose. 

After looking to the west and north, the brakeman motioned the plaintiff across. Two other cars went ahead of the plaintiff but, as he was crossing the track, he was struck by a fast passenger train, going west on the north track. The case was submitted to the jury, and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed by the Supreme Court. 

The Court said that the plaintiff had a right to assume that when he got the invitation to go around the end of the caboose he could do so with safety. 

Stone v. Duluth, South Shore & Atlantic Ry. Co., 248 

Mich. 538.

This accident occurred in the city of Ishpeming, Michigan, at 9 p. m. The crossing was protected by gates, but they were not operating at night and were up when the plaintiff approached the crossing. When the plaintiff approached the crossing he observed that the gates were 97

§ 43] 

not down, but he did not rely on that entirely. He looked in both directions before entering the crossing and saw no train. On the third track there was a box car close to the sidewalk and to the right of the plaintiff. They crossed the third track before they discovered a train approaching from the right. It was too late to avoid the collision at that time. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. Between the third track and the track upon which the car was struck was a safety zone of 38 feet. In this zone the view of the driver was unobstructed. The Supreme Court said that the driver must not have looked in this zone or he would have seen the train. He did not look until it was too late. 

Day v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 252 Mich. 589.

The plaintiff was driving east on Superior street in Alma, Michigan. When within five or ten feet of the track he stopped his car and waited until a northbound freight train had passed. There was a flagman at the crossing; and, as soon as the freight train had cleared, two automobiles, which had been waiting on the other side of the track, and pedestrians on the sidewalk proceeded to cross the tracks. While the freight train was passing, the flagman went over and stood on or near the northerly street curb. He saw the approaching passenger train and warned at least one of the pedestrians but told her she had time to cross. The flagman stopped the westbound automobile traffic and caused one vehicle to back off the track. In the meantime, the plaintiff started to cross the track. The flagman called to him and made motions to stop, but he proceeded until the wheels of his automobile were on the track, where he was struck by the southbound train. It was held that on the record the case was for the jury. The Court said that the flagman's 98

[§ conduct, in leaving the part of the street used by passing vehicles at a time when the defendant's passenger train was approaching, might indicate to a reasonably careful driver that the crossing was clear for his safe passing. 

The Court said that it did not hold that an accident at a so-called protected crossing always presented a question of fact on the issue of contributory negligence. It said that each case must depend upon its own circumstances. 

Motyka v. Detroit, Grand Haven & Milwaukee Ry. Co., 

253 Mich. 647.

In this case the plaintiff was a pedestrian and was struck while crossing the defendant's tracks in the daytime. By order of the Michigan Railroad Commission the defendant was required to have a watchman stationed at the crossing for twenty-four hours each day to warn the public of approaching trains. There was testimony that there was no watchman in sight at the crossing when the accident occurred. There was a small but sufficient safety zone from which the plaintiff, had he looked to the north, could have seen the locomotive approaching and avoided the injury. It was held that this was a case for the jury, and the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that if this had been an ordinary crossing case, the plaintiff would have probably been negligent. The Court made the following statement: "We think it was for the jury to say whether the absence of the watchman and the lack of any signal from him might indicate to a reasonably prudent person that the crossing was clear for safe passage, whether the conduct of the watchman was an invitation to proceed." 

See also 256 Mich. 417. 99

§ 44] 

 Sec. 44. Summary. 

The degree of care required of an automobile driver in approaching a so-called protected railway crossing is less than that required in approaching an ordinary crossing. He has a right to rely to some extent upon the gates, light, watchman or whatever protection is usually given at the particular crossing. His chance to recover, where the warning is not given, is probably improved, if his view of the track is obstructed. Whereas, in an ordinary crossing case the driver of the car is almost always negligent as a matter of law, in a protected crossing case the plaintiff has a fair chance to have his case submitted to the jury.

Sec. 45. Automobiles Stalled on Track. 

Deadman v. Detroit, Jackson & Chicago Ry., 223 Mich. 228. 

In this case the plaintiff's truck stalled on the defendant's track on a highway crossing, and before attempting to fix the gears the plaintiff looked both ways and no train was in sight for three-quarters of a mile. About a minute later he was struck by the defendant's interurban car, running at a great speed. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The 

Court said that the trial judge might correctly have said that the record presented a case of wanton and wilful negligence on the part of the defendant. The motorman in charge of the car had a plain view of the truck for a distance of three-quarters of a mile. 

Larsen v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 248 Mich. 506.

The plaintiff on his way to work just before daylight stalled his motor on the defendant's track. The train 100

[§ 

The trainmen probably was approaching on a curve. could have seen the car for 400 feet. The plaintiff contended that the defendant was guilty of gross negligence, but it was held that there was no gross negligence on the part of the defendant. When the plaintiff approached the crossing the bell was ringing and the wigwag was operating, showing a red light. It was held that the plaintiff's contributory negligence barred his recovery. 

Kraft v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 262 Mich. 494.

This accident occurred in the afternoon. The plaintiff's automobile was stalled upon defendant's track at a street crossing in the city of Bay City. As she was trying to start the motor, a train came along and struck the automobile, injuring her. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law in not seeing the approaching train.

Sec. 46. Street Railway Crossing Cases. 

Westover v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 180 Mich. 373.

The plaintiff's car was being driven west on Briggs avenue in the city of Grand Rapids. It was his intention on reaching the intersection of Grandville to cross over the street car tracks and drive south on Grandville avenue. As he approached Grandville, he looked to the south and saw the headlight of a street car about 200 feet away.

He proceeded across the car track, but, before he could clear the east track, the street car struck his automobile, turning it over. The lower court instructed the jury that merely looking at the car once at a distance was not enough and that the driver should have continued to observe the scene until he got to the track, and if he failed to do this the plaintiff could not recover. The judgment for the defendant in the lower 101

§ 46] 

77777 court was affirmed. The Supreme Court made this statement: "We think it can be said, as a matter of law, that when an ordinarily prudent person is about to cross a highway, whether on foot, on a bicycle, or in a carriage or automobile, and he observes an approaching street car or any other vehicle which may obstruct his passage, he is watchful of it or them until he has passed the danger point in reaching the place of safety." 

Prince v. D. U. R., 192 Mich. 194.

In this case the plaintiff was driving south on Woodward avenue in Detroit and, in making a left turn across the street car tracks, his car was struck by a northbound street car. A southbound car had just passed him, and his view to the south was limited to one hundred feet as he started his turn. While proceeding across the west track, he observed the northbound car about seventy-five feet away. He thought he could clear it and kept going. 

When starting across the east track, the street car was fifty feet away. He increased the speed of his automobile but could not clear the track before being struck. It was held that he was not guilty of negligence as a matter of law. The Court said that he had a right to expect the motorman would use reasonable care and slow down, if it became necessary, to enable him to cross in safety. 

Travelers' Indemnity Co. v. D. U. R., 193 Mich. 375.

This case involved a collision between an automobile and a street car. The Supreme Court made the following statement: "Mutual care to avoid collisions was demanded and was to be expected. Both parties were driving on a business street in a large city, which both had a right to use for their particular method of travel, but each in driving his conveyance was required to 102

[§ exercise all reasonable care and take precaution to avoid injuring others. Their duties were mutual. 

The questions of negligence and contributory negligence were questions of fact, properly left to the jury within the rule of the following cases, etc." 

Fox v. D. U. R., 218 Mich. 5.

The plaintiff was driving a horse and wagon to the north on Fifteenth street in the city of Detroit. As he approached the intersection of Warren avenue he stopped and waited for three eastbound street cars to pass. The last of the cars stopped with its rear end slightly protruding into the traveled portion of Fifteenth street. The plaintiff's view to the east was entirely obstructed by this car. After waiting for some time and listening for sounds of a westbound car, he attempted to cross and was struck by a westbound street car. It was held that he was not negligent as a matter of law. In discussing the question of contributory negligence, the Court said that the defendant had no greater right to the use of the street at this crossing than had the plaintiff. 

Hutton v. Michigan Railway Co., 220 Mich. 1.

The plaintiff, when 37½ feet from the car track, saw a heavy interurban car approaching and 100 feet away. 

Without again looking to ascertain its speed, he proceeded across the track and was struck. It was held that the plaintiff was guilty of negligence as a matter of law. 

Mills v. Michigan Electric Ry. Co., 237 Mich. 393.

This accident occurred in Jackson, Michigan, at a time when automobiles were thickly parked along Michigan avenue at the curb at an angle of approximately fortyfive degrees. Between the rear of the cars and the car track there was room for one automobile to drive and clear street cars. The plaintiff had driven north on Jack- 103

§ 47] 

son street and turned east on Michigan and was swinging his car to the left to get in a parking space when he was struck by an eastbound street car. It was held that he was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court commented on the fact that the plaintiff was driving on a main business street where cars were thickly parked and might back out at any time, where traffic was congested, and where cars might temporarily be forced upon the street car tracks at any time. The Court said that under such circumstances the right of the automobile drivers and the street car motormen were reciprocal. 

For a discussion of the rights and duties of a driver of an automobile whose car has become stalled on a street railway track, see Nagi v. D. U. R., 231 Mich. 452. 

Sec. 47.

Summary. 

The driver of an automobile unquestionably has a much greater duty to exercise care in crossing a railroad crossing than in crossing street car tracks at an intersection. If the driver of a car sees a street car approaching, he should observe it closely enough to determine to a reasonable extent whether he can get safely across the tracks. In a number of instances the Michigan 

Supreme Court has said that the duties of a car driver and of motormen on a street car are reciprocal and that each has the same right as the other upon the street. 

However, the duty of an automobile driver in crossing a street railway crossing is probably greater than that in crossing an ordinary intersection without street car tracks. The fact, that the motorman cannot swerve his street car and probably has more difficulty in stopping it than a car driver would have with his automobile, requires a higher degree of care on the part of an automobile driver where street cars approach him. 104

CHAPTER V WRONG SIDE OF ROAD CASES Sec. 48. Wrong Side of Road Cases. 

Sec. 49. Summary-Wrong Side of Road Cases. 

Sec. 48. Wrong Side of Road Cases. 

Section 4703, Compiled Laws 1929, requires a driver of a vehicle to drive upon the right half of the highway. 

Section 4705 requires drivers of vehicles proceeding in opposite directions to pass each other on the right, giving to the other at least one-half of the main traveled portion of the highway as nearly as possible. In this chapter, the cases which have added anything to the law on the interpretation of these statutes have been set forth. 

Corey v. Hartel, 216 Mich. 675.

The plaintiff was riding on some hay in the back part of a sleigh with her feet hanging over the left side. It was claimed that the defendant's truck approached the sleigh, with its left wheels on the wrong side of the road, and that the driver suddenly turned the front wheels, and it skidded and struck the plaintiff's legs. The Supreme Court said that the burden was on the defendant to satisfy the jury that he was justified in driving partly on the wrong side of the street. If the defendant did not do this, the happening of the unexpected would not relieve the defendant from liability. See Winckowski v. 

Dodge, 183 Mich. 303, for presumption raised when car is operated on the wrong side of the highway. 105

§ 48] 

Wiggins v. Ford Motor Co., 220 Mich. 269.

This accident occurred on Miller Road, which was 16 to 20 feet wide. The decedent was near the west edge of the road, sitting on a small wagon. Fifty to sixty feet. south of the boy on the east side of the road was a car parked which occupied about three feet of the width of the pavement. The Ford motor bus with a trailer was going north and turned to the left to pass the parked car. 

This put the wheels of the bus slightly over the center of the road. The bus was being driven slowly. The position of the bus did not require the southbound car to leave the pavement. The southbound car was still a considerable distance from the express wagon when the Ford bus started to pass the parked car. It was held that there was no showing of negligence on the part of the bus driver even though the bus was slightly over the center of the road. The Court said that there was no duty on his part to stop, and that it was clear that the reckless driving of the other defendant or the decedent's negligence was the cause of the accident. The driver of the southbound car claimed that the boy moved the express wagon onto the pavement into the path of his car when his car was close to it. 

Russell v. Twiss, 224 Mich. 532.

The plaintiff was driving south. The defendant, driving his car north, turned to the left to pass a parked motorcycle. In turning back to the right the defendant got so far over that he was afraid he would go into the ditch. In trying to avoid this he lost control of his car, and it ran diagonally across the road into the plaintiff's automobile. The plaintiff's car was at the extreme right hand side of the pavement, and its speed had been reduced to ten miles per hour. The lower court directed a 106

WRONG SIDE OF ROAD CASES 

[§ 48 verdict in favor of the plaintiff, leaving to the jury to fix the damages. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment, saying that the testimony of the defendant established very clearly that the provisions of the statute, requiring a driver to keep to the right in passing, were not obeyed. 

Nelson v. Glover, 231 Mich. 229.

The defendant was driving east on a tarvia strip which was eight feet wide and was in the center of the road with gravel at the sides. The plaintiff's decedent was driving west on the tarvia strip with a part of his car to the south of the center. When a short distance apart the cars both turned to the north and collided. The defendant claimed that when he saw the other car approaching south of the center of the tarvia strip, he thought the driver intended to turn into a driveway or go south on an intersecting street. The Court said that this was a miscalculation on defendant's part as the decedent turned to the north, evidently to let the defendant go by on the right side of the road, as he should have done. It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury. 

Milliman v. Spratt, 235 Mich. 521.

In this case each driver testified that his car was on the right side of the road when the collision occurred. 

The court instructed the jury that, if the defendant was driving on the wrong side of the road at the time of the accident, the burden shifted to him to show that his negligence in this respect was not the proximate cause of the plaintiff's injury. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment by an equally divided Court, although all of the judges thought the instruction was erroneous. The Court 107

§ 48] 

said there was no shifting of the burden. Four of the justices held that, although the burden did not shift, the defendant had the duty to justify his being on the wrong side of the road. They felt that, as the defendant did not admit being on the wrong side, the instruction was not applicable to the facts. The four dissenting justices thought that the instruction was erroneous and constituted reversible error. 

McConnell v. Elliott, 242 Mich. 145.

The plaintiff was driving his car east and the defendant was going west. The undisputed testimony was that the plaintiff at all times was on his own side of the road. 

The plaintiff testified that defendant's car came over in front of him when only 25 feet away, too short a distance within which to stop. The lower court instructed the jury that even though the plaintiff was exceeding the speed limit, unless it contributed to the accident, such fact would not prevent a recovery. The Court held that there was sufficient proof of negligence, and that the instruction was not erroneous. 

Essenberg v. Achterhof, 255 Mich. 55.

The plaintiff and four other boys were riding bicycles on a dirt street in the outskirts of Holland, Michigan. It was admitted that the plaintiff did not look for approaching vehicles and did not see the defendant's automobile until it was 10 feet from him. It was claimed that the defendant was on the wrong side of the street. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that to some extent he had a right to rely on the known fact that cars usually did not travel on the wrong side, and even if he had looked he would have had the right to rely on the assumption that the 108

WRONG SIDE OF ROAD CASES 

[§ 48 defendant would turn his car to the right. The Court also held that the lower court was justified in submitting the question of subsequent negligence to the jury. 

Harrison v. Eastern Michigan Motor Bus Co., 257 Mich. 329. 

In this accident the driver of the plaintiff's car tried to pass a line of traffic. He tried to get back into the line but, while his car was partly on the wrong side of the road, it was struck by the defendant's bus. It was held that the driver was negligent as a matter of law, and his negligence continued up to the time of the injury. The 

Court said: "One who drives on the wrong side of the highway assumes the risk of the experiment and is required to use greater care than as if he kept on the right side of the highway." 

Luck v. Gregory, 257 Mich. 562.

Just prior to the collision, the defendant swung his car to the right to avoid another automobile, and the right rear wheel went into a ditch on his right hand side of the highway. The driver of the plaintiff's car saw this situation in time to have stopped. In order to get back on the road the defendant cramped his wheels to the left so that when the hind wheels gained traction the car went across the center of the road and into the path of the plaintiff's car. It was held that the defendant's negligence, if any, in getting off the road had nothing to do with the accident as proximate cause, and the failure of the plaintiff to stop was contributory negligence. 

Loucks v. Fox, 261 Mich. 338.

The testimony in this case was that the deceased drove toward the defendant on the wrong side of the road, and 109

§ 48] 

the defendant when 30 to 40 feet from the approaching car turned to the left to avoid a collision. At the same time the decedent swerved his car to the right, the right side of the defendant's car striking the left side of the automobile driven by the deceased. The case was tried without a jury. The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the lower court and ordered a judgment entered for the defendant. The Court said that the defendant was confronted with an emergency and was forced to go to the south or turn right into a ditch five feet deep. If a reasonably prudent man would turn onto the wrong side of the road under such circumstances, the defendant was free from liability. The Court said that the course he adopted was a natural one in the emergency presented. 

Derby v. Culver, 270 Mich. 197.

The defendant was driving west on U. S. 16 when his right rear tire blew out. He turned onto the shoulder of the road where he ran for a short distance. Before this he had noticed the plaintiff's car approaching. He testified that he was afraid that his car would go into the ditch, and he turned it to the left and applied his brakes slightly. The car went out of control and crossed the center of the road, striking the plaintiff's automobile. 

The Court said that the defendant was negligent in attempting to turn to the left at his rate of speed when he knew or should have known the other car was near, there being no emergency confronting him. The Court also said that the plaintiff was not forewarned of any danger. 

Flynn v. Kramer, 271 Mich. 500.

In this case Flynn sued the owners of the two other cars involved in the accident which occurred on U. S. 31, a 40 foot pavement, in the daytime. Flynn, driving north, 110

WRONG SIDE OF ROAD CASES 

[§ 48 claimed that Bernstein's car, south bound, was over the center line and that Kramer's car was trying to pass Bernstein. Flynn testified that he took his foot off the accelerator and moved farther to the right. He considered the shoulder unsafe. After Flynn's car came in contact with that of Bernstein's it was thrown across the road to the west where it was struck by Kramer's car. It was held that the failure of Flynn to apply his brakes and to drive onto the shoulder was not negligence as a matter of law. 

Meisenheimer v. Pullen, 271 Mich. 509.

The defendant was driving east on a street in Grand Rapids. A truck was against the south curb, blocking nearly the south half of the street. The defendant drove 

The plaintiff, coming to the north and passed the truck. west, turned his car to the left to avoid a head-on collision. At that instant the defendant turned his car back to the right, and the collision occurred near the center of the street. It was held that the defendant was negligent but that there could be no recovery for the plaintiff's property damage as the plaintiff had ample opportunity to see the defendant approaching. In addition, it was obvious that the defendant would be forced to turn out around the truck. The plaintiff did not apply his brakes but merely released his accelerator. 

Saums v. Parfet, 270 Mich. 165.

The plaintiff claimed that she was riding a bicycle in a northerly direction on her side of the road when the defendant drove his car towards her around a curve and on her side of the highway. She turned to the west side of the road to avoid a collision, and the defendant turned to the west side, striking her. The defendant testified 111

§ 49] 

that he was on his own side of the road, and when the collision occurred his car was partly off the traveled portion of the road. It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury, and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed.

Other Cases. 

Marsh v. Burnham, 211 Mich. 675; Prove v. Interstate 

Stages, 250 Mich. 479; Miner v. Scholton, 250 Mich. 645; 

Bachand v. Rosemurgy, 261 Mich. 519; Soule v. Grimshaw, 266 Mich. 117; Leonard v. Hey, 269 Mich. 491; 

Hanna v. McClave, 271 Mich. 133.

Sec. 49. Summary. 

If one drives on the wrong side, the burden is on him to justify his act. (Corey v. Hartel.) A driver may be justified in driving to the wrong side to pass a parked car, if the approaching car is far enough away or has room to pass. (Wiggins v. Ford Co.) The negligence in getting off the road may not be the proximate cause of the accident when the car is turned back on the road and across the center line. (Luck v. Gregory.) However, a driver, if not confronted with an emergency, may be negligent in turning back on the road as an approaching car is ready to pass. (Derby v. Culver.) A driver may be justified in turning onto the wrong side of the road to avoid a car approaching him. (Loucks v. Fox.) But if the cars are approaching in the middle of the road, the drivers should turn to the right. (Nelson v. Glover.) A driver who tries to pass a line of traffic and cannot get back in line before colliding with an approaching car is probably negligent as a matter of law.
