CHAPTER VI  Sec. 50. Left Turn Cases. 

Sec. 51. Left Turn Against Approaching Vehicle. 

Sec. 52. Left Turn Into Vehicle from the Rear. 

Sec. 53. Summary-Left Turn Cases. 

Sec. 50. Left Turn Cases. 

Section 4710, Compiled Laws 1929, requires a driver intending to turn left at an intersection to pass beyond the center of the intersection and to pass as closely as practicable to the right of the center before turning to the left. Local authorities, by markers, may indicate another course to follow in making the turn. Section 4711 requires the driver, before he makes his turn, to first see that such movement can be made in safety. A signal must be given by extending the arm horizontally beyond the left side of the car, or by a mechanical or electric signal to another driver approaching from the rear. It should be noted that this statute seems to be applicable only to drivers from the rear and not for the benefit of approaching drivers. For statutes on passing vehicle, see Sections 4706 and 4708.

The left turn cases fall into two divisions. There are those decisions involving accidents between cars making left turns and vehicles approaching. Then there are a number of cases in which the party making the left turn collides with a vehicle coming up from the rear. 113

§ 51] 

 Sec. 51. Left Turn Against Approaching Vehicle. 

Everhard v. Dodge Bros., 202 Mich. 48.

The plaintiff claimed that she was driving her car west on Jefferson avenue in Detroit, and that a truck approaching from the west at a speed of 12 to 15 miles an hour, instead of keeping to the right of the center of the intersection, turned diagonally to the northeast ahead of her car, colliding with it. It was held that the plaintiff's contributory negligence was for the jury to determine. 

Black v. Parke, Davis & Co., 211 Mich. 274.

The plaintiff was riding a bicycle south on the west side of Clifford street in Detroit. The defendant's truck was being driven north on the east side of the street. 

The plaintiff, when 50 feet north of Adams avenue, saw the truck about 50 feet south of the intersection. The plaintiff testified that he did not see the truck again until he was hit. He said that had the truck gone to the center of the intersection before making the turn, he would have been past the place where he was hit. The negligence claimed was that the truck cut the corner in making the turn to the left. In holding that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, the Court said: "It was not the duty of the plaintiff to anticipate that the driver of the truck would cut across the corner and drive on the wrong side of the street.' 

Torbert v. Smith's Estate, 250 Mich. 62.

The plaintiff was driving north on Woodward avenue in Detroit. The defendant's truck and trailer, 60 feet in length, was moving south. There was testimony that the defendant's driver, without warning by hand or horn, made a sudden left hand turn, increased his speed, and 114

[§ ran across a double car track and into Savannah avenue close to the south curb, at which point the truck was struck near the rear wheel by the plaintiff's car. The plaintiff testified that he was driving 15 to 20 miles per hour and could stop in 18 feet. He first saw the truck when he was 30 feet from the corner, and he increased his speed with the intention of beating it to the intersection. The plaintiff also testified that the truck ran 

10 feet south after he first saw it and that it was going 10 miles per hour. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court argued that the plaintiff must have been 12 to 15 feet from the point of collision, on his own testimony, when the truck started to turn. This was too short a distance within which to stop. 

"A driver, about to make a left-hand turn, must give notice of his intention. He has not the right to dash across the street, closely in front of other vehicles, even though he is driving a heavy truck which will only be slightly injured in a collision with light cars. The ordinarily prudent driver may turn to the left when oncoming vehicles are near, but, if there is danger of collision, he will stop before he reaches the stream of traffic and await an opportunity to proceed."

Three justices dissented, holding that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. 

Pavela v. Tryloff, 251 Mich. 110.

The plaintiff's car was being driven east on U. S. 112. 

The defendant was in a car going west. Both drivers had a clear view. Intending to make a left turn from the highway to enter a driveway, the plaintiff's driver slowed down and gave a signal with his hand and turned to the 115

§ 51] 

left. He was nearly over the pavement when his car was struck. He claimed that the other car was 300 to 400 feet away when he started his turn and was traveling 60 to 65 miles per hour. The defendant's car was being driven by his son, 14 years of age. The boy turned the car to the right and the defendant grabbed the wheel and turned it to the left, causing it to zigzag. The Court held that this made the defendant the driver of the car. The plaintiff was a minor occupant. The Court held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant himself. 

Benson v. Tucker, 252 Mich. 385.

In this case the defendant made a left turn from a trunk line highway at a curve and collided with the plaintiff's car which was approaching. The defendant testified that he did not see the car approaching and did not look. The Supreme Court said that the instructions favored the defendant as the record would sustain an instruction that the defendant was negligent. 

Garton v. Powers, 252 Mich. 442.

The plaintiff was riding in an automobile driven by the defendant in Cleveland, Ohio. At an intersection the defendant stopped, then turned left and drove north across two lines of traffic directly in front of a westbound car, causing a collision. The defendant testified that he did not see the other car until just before he was hit. It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. The Court said that, if the defendant had kept a proper lookout, he could have seen the other car and avoided it. The plaintiff saw the car and warned the defendant. 116

[§ 

Barnum v. Berk, 256 Mich. 363.

The plaintiff's car, being driven east, collided with the defendant's automobile which was approaching the plaintiff and making a left turn. The defendant testified that the plaintiff's car was between 125 feet and 150 feet away when he started to turn. There was testimony by the other driver that the distance was only 10 or 15 feet. A verdict was rendered for the defendant and the judgment was affirmed. 

Bernstein v. Brody, 256 Mich. 512.

In this case the plaintiff's car was traveling north on Twelfth street in Detroit, and it collided with the defendant's car, which was making a left turn into Euclid avenue to go east. The plaintiff's car struck the defendant's automobile at the right rear wheel just as it was leaving Twelfth street. The accident occurred in a business district. The plaintiff's driver testified that he was driving at a speed of 15 to 18 miles per hour. One witness said 22 to 25 miles and another 30 to 35 miles. The case was tried without a jury, and a judgment was rendered for the plaintiff. The Supreme Court reversed the decision, holding that the plaintiff's driver was exceeding the speed limit and this negligence was a proximate cause of the accident. The Court assumed the defendant was negligent in cutting the corner. 

Van Dixhorn v. Central Motor Freight Co., 265 Mich. 81.

The defendant's truck was driven north on a 42 foot street in Kalamazoo, and, according to the plaintiff, when it was 50 feet from the intersection, the driver swung it to the left. The truck and trailer were 38 feet long. The plaintiff, southbound, slackened his speed and turned to the left as only six feet was left between the front of the 117

§ 52] 

truck and the west curb. The plaintiff found he could not get by on the other side and applied his brakes but skidded into the truck, striking it 10 feet from the front. 

It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Ulvund v. Sogge, 266 Mich. 548.

The plaintiff's car was going east, and the defendant was driving west. When the plaintiff's car was 80 to 90 feet west of a store, the driver dimmed and rebrightened his lights as a signal and made a left turn. At the time the car began to turn the defendant was over 190 feet away. He drove wholly or partly off the pavement and struck the plaintiff's car. It was held that the lower court was justified in finding the defendant negligent in not remaining on the pavement. The plaintiff's driver was not contributorily negligent. 

Sebastian v. Sherwood, 270 Mich. 339.

The plaintiff was driving west on U. S. 12. The defendant was driving east. He stopped and, after looking to the east and to the rear, he made a left turn without giving a signal, causing a collision. The trial court instructed the jury that the defendant was negligent as a matter of law in turning without giving a signal. It was held that the trial court was in error as the statute did not require a signal to be given to an approaching car. 

The question of the defendant's negligence on this point was for the jury.

Sec. 52. Left Turn Into Vehicle from the Rear. 

Greenleaf v. Lambert, 192 Mich. 411.

The plaintiff testified that he was driving his motorcycle south on a street in Bay City, and to the right of 118

[§ the center. The defendant's truck was ahead and nearer the west curb and was also southbound. At a point in the middle of the block, it was claimed that the defendant's truck was turned suddenly to the left, without a signal being given, so that it crossed the path of the plaintiff's car. The plaintiff's motorcycle collided with the truck. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Gates v. Landon, 216 Mich. 417.

The driver of the plaintiff's car testified that he was driving north on a city street, and when in the middle of a block he held his hand out while the car traveled 50 feet at 8 miles per hour. He looked back, being able to see 

150 feet, and there was no car in sight. He then swung his car to the left and was within 4 or 5 feet of the west curb when he was struck by the defendant's northbound car. The plaintiff's car was at the curb on the east side of the street when the turn was started. It was held that the plaintiff's driver was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court pointed out that, if the plaintiff's car traveled only 4 miles per hour in making the turn, the defendant's car could have gone more than 150 feet after the plaintiff's driver looked to the rear. The Court also said that the skid marks of 65 feet left by the defendant's car, and the damage done, indicated excessive speed. 

Greenwold v. Faber, 234 Mich. 217.

In this case one car going north was turned to the left to go west and came in contact with another northbound car which was passing the first car. A judgment was rendered against the driver of the first car only in favor of the plaintiff, who was a pedestrian. The plaintiff was struck by the second car. It was held that there was no error in the instructions, and the judgment was affirmed. 119

§ 52] 

McLaughlin v. Curry, 242 Mich. 228.

Both cars were going south on M-13. The plaintiff testified that he gave a horn signal to pass the defendant's car and sounded his horn again. He turned to the left side of the road, was about to pass when the defendant, without a signal, turned his car to the left to go into a driveway, and a collision resulted. The defendant admitted that he did not comply with the statute by extending his arm outside the car but testified that he held up his right hand within the car. It was held that the defendant was guilty of negligence in not giving a proper signal for his left turn. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. The Court said that the controversy was over the contributory negligence of the plaintiff, indicating that the failure of the defendant to give a proper signal was a proximate cause of the accident. 

Lauth v. Woodruff, 265 Mich. 34.

This accident occurred on U. S. 131, which was 20 feet wide at the point of the accident. The defendant was driving his car north, traveling 30 to 35 miles per hour. 

The decedent was riding a motorcycle north and some distance to the rear of the automobile. The defendant slowed down as he approached a driveway and made a left turn. Just at this instance the motorcycle struck the rear end of the car. It was claimed that the decedent had given a signal and was in the act of passing the car. 

There was testimony that the decedent was only 20 feet from the car when it turned and that the stop light did not show until then. There was contradictory testimony as to whether a hand signal was given. The Court held that the case was properly submitted to the jury and said that, even though the electric signal was given, there was a question as to whether it was sufficiently timely. Also, 120

[§ the fact that the motorcycle struck the rear end of the automobile would not preclude recovery. 

Felsenfeld v. Chattaway, 266 Mich. 234.

This accident occurred on U. S. 10, a 40 foot highway. 

The plaintiff, a minor, was in a car being driven north. 

The defendant was driving north and made a left turn, the two cars coming together. The plaintiff's testimony presented the theory that her car was about to pass the defendant when the turn was made. The defendant claimed that he applied his brakes, causing the stop light to show, and raised his right hand in the car to signal a turn. The Court held that the case was properly submitted to the jury. The judgment for the defendant was affirmed. The Court held that it was not necesary to determine whether the signal as given by the defendant was a sufficient compliance with the statute as under the plaintiff's theory the signal was unimportant as the car was alongside that of the defendant. It was said that, under the defendant's account, the effect of the signal on the plaintiff's driver was purely speculative as he did not testify. 

Jacoby v. Schafsnitz, 270 Mich. 515.

Both plaintiff and defendant were driving east on M-24, a 20 foot paved highway. The defendant was driving a truck, the body of which extended 14 inches beyond the cab. As the defendant was making a left turn the plaintiff was attempting to pass. There was testimony that a horn signal was given by the plaintiff before he started to pass defendant's car. In affirming the judgment for the plaintiff, the Court said that the greatest damage to the plaintiff's car was on the right side at the center which tended strongly to support the plaintiff's claim 121

§ 53] 

that he was well under way in passing defendant's truck before the latter turned to the left.

Sec. 53. Summary. 

A driver, in approaching an intersection, has a right to assume that a car approaching will not cut the corner. 

(Black v. Parke, Davis & Co.) There is no statutory duty to give a signal to the approaching car. (Sebastian v. 

Sherwood.) However, there may be negligence for failure to do so. It is a jury question. On this point see 

Torbert v. Smith's Estate. Even though a signal is given to the driver of the vehicle in the rear, it must be given in time to warn the driver of the turn. The failure to give a timely signal may amount to negligence. (Lauth v. Woodruff.) In this type of case, if the negligence of the turning driver is being relied upon, it is advisable to have the driver in the rear testify. (Felsenfeld v. Chattaway.) It is significant that in almost all of the left turn cases the defendant is the party making the turn. The question of contributory negligence is generally left to the jury. 122

CHAPTER VII REAR END COLLISIONS Sec. 54. Rear End Collisions. 

Sec. 55. Summary-Rear End Collisions. 

Sec. 54. Rear End Collisions. 

Section 4788, Compiled Laws, 1929, provides that when it is shown that a vehicle overtook and struck the rear end of another vehicle proceeding in the same direction or lawfully standing upon any highway, the driver of the vehicle in the rear shall be deemed prima facie guilty of negligence. Section 4709 provides that a driver of a motor vehicle shall not follow another vehicle more closely than is reasonable. A driver of a motor truck outside of a business or residence district shall not follow another motor truck within 100 feet. 

The cases given under this heading are those interpreting the so-called rear end collision statute. A number of the decisions listed under the heading "Assured Clear Distance" are also rear end collision cases, but the opinions do not discuss the rear end collision statute. A question might be raised as to the applicability of this statute to a situation in which the overtaking car struck the rear end of a car starting to make or making a left or right turn. It would depend upon whether the front car was proceeding in the same direction. 

Wilkowski v. Grant Iron & Metal Co., 219 Mich. 535.

In this case it was the plaintiff's claim that he left his car at the side of the street, and a trailer belonging to 123

§ 54] 

the defendant became detached from the truck and ran into the rear of the plaintiff's car. The jury found that a proper inspection had not been made and that the defendant was liable. The Court said that in view of the rear end collision statute there was an abundance of testimony to justify the verdict. 

Depue v. Schwarz, 222 Mich. 308.

The plaintiff was driving his wagon south. The defendant testified that he was driving south and started to pass the wagon when he discovered a car coming north, causing him to turn back of the plaintiff's wagon. He claimed that he had practically stopped when he was struck from behind, driving his car into the wagon. It was held that the question of the defendant's negligence was properly submitted to the jury. The plaintiff made out a prima facie case under the rear end collision statute, and the testimony offered by the defendant left a question of fact as to the sufficiency of his observation before he started to pass the wagon and as to his precautions regarding the car following. 

Cothran v. Cleenewerck & Son, 235 Mich. 351.

The defendant in this case testified that he saw the plaintiff's truck ahead of him when he was six rods from it. The road was icy. He planned to turn out and pass the truck on the left. As he turned he saw a car approaching, and he elected to strike the truck. It was held that the defendant was negligent as a matter of law, and that the absence of a tail light on the plaintiff's truck had nothing to do with the accident as the defendant saw the truck in ample time to avoid it. The Court said that, where there is evidence rebutting the presumption under the rear end collision statute, the presumption should not be considered. 124

REAR END COLLISIONS 

[§ 54 

Noonan v. Volek, 246 Mich. 377.

The plaintiff was driving his wagon on the right hand side of the street near the curb when the defendant drove his car into the rear end of the wagon. At the close of the plaintiff's case the defendant moved for a directed verdict on the ground that negligence on the defendant's part had not been shown. The motion was denied. The defendant then offered proof that the plaintiff negligently turned his wagon into the path of his car after he had signaled his intention to pass. The Court held that the plaintiff had made out a prima facie case under the rear end collision statute. The presumption, however, existed only in the absence of evidence and did not serve at all when the issue of negligence was tried out upon evidence.

Weaver v. Motor Transit Management Co., 252 Mich. 64. 

The plaintiff's car was being driven on a paved highway and was followed at a distance of 35 or 40 feet by a passenger bus owned by the defendant. An approaching car turned from the line of traffic, and the plaintiff's driver, in order to avoid a head-on collision, turned his car slightly to the right and stopped suddenly. The bus struck the plaintiff's car from the rear, and it was claimed that this caused the car to collide with the approaching automobile. The trial court instructed the jury that the bus driver was prima facie guilty of negligence and the burden was upon the defendant to show by a preponderance of evidence that he was not negligent. 

This instruction was held to constitute error.  "The presumption mentioned tentatively supplies enough to prevent a directed verdict against plaintiff and to require a defendant to go ahead with his 125

§ 55] 

proofs on the subject of negligence, and, if credible evidence is submitted, the plaintiff still has the burden of establishing defendant's negligence by a preponderance of the evidence."

The Court also said that, if the driver ahead, in an emergency, brings his car to a sudden stop without signal to a vehicle following at a reasonable distance, then the presumption of negligence is not to be indulged, unless opportunity to stop was afforded after need to do so was apparent. It was also held that the defendant was not entitled to a directed verdict, and a new trial was ordered. 

Botbyl v. Mackus, 261 Mich. 150.

This accident happened on U. S. 31 in the daytime. A wrecker had stopped traffic. The first car south heeded the signal and stopped. The defendant, following about 

50 feet behind, struck this car and drove it forward against the man who had given the signal to stop. The defendant testified that the car ahead traveled about 30 feet before stopping. He knew it was stopping, and consequently had 80 feet in which to stop his car. He admitted that he could stop at his speed in 30 feet. He gave no excuse for not doing so. The Court reversed the judgment of the lower court and ordered a judgment entered for the plaintiff, the case having been tried without a jury, the defendant having been found negligent. 

Sec. 55. Summary. 

Where there is evidence to rebut the presumption under the statute, the presumption should not be considered. (Cothran v. Cleenewerck & Son.) In this case it was held that the driver in the rear could be guilty of negligence as a matter of law. If evidence is submitted 126

REAR END COLLISIONS 

[§ 55 to rebut the presumption, the plaintiff still has the burden of establishing the defendant's negligence by a pre ponderance of the evidence. (Weaver v. Transit Co.) 

In this case the Court said that the presumption would not apply where a car was brought to a sudden stop without signal, if the car in the rear was a reasonable distance behind. 127

CHAPTER VIII PARKING ON HIGHWAY Sec. 56. Parking on Highway. 

Sec. 57. Summary-Parking on Highway. 

Sec. 56. Parking on Highway. 

"Parking" under the Motor Vehicle Act, Section 4693 

(S), Compiled Laws 1929, is defined as standing a vehicle upon a highway, when not loading or unloading except when making necessary repairs. Section 4718 makes it unlawful to park a vehicle on the beaten track or paved surface of any highway outside the limits of any village or city. For the requirements as to lights on a parked or stopped vehicle, see section 4740. The parking statute prior to 1927 has been changed, and no good service would be performed in considering cases which arose before 1927 and which were decided upon a difference in the wording of the statute. A large number of cases involving illegally parked or lighted vehicles may be found in the chapter entitled "Assured Clear Distance." Also see cases under the heading "Rear End Collisions." 

The chief question under the parking statute is the interpretation of the word "parking" in the face of the statutory definition. Therefore, the cases selected for consideration were those including a discussion of what constitutes parking. 

Hanser v. Youngs, 212 Mich. 508.

In this case a question arose as to whether the plaintiff's failure to have the tail light on his truck burning 128

PARKING ON HIGHWAY 

[§ 56 would bar his recovery. The truck was standing on the highway under an arc light. It was held that this presented a question for the jury respecting the contributory nature of the negligence. 

Sahms v. Marcus, 239 Mich. 682.

John Sahms was driving north on M-13 with his wife. 

Her hat blew off, and he backed the car on the east side of the road to a point near the hat. He then alighted, went around the north end of the car and crossed to the west side of the road. He was reaching down for the hat when the defendant's southbound car struck him. The defendant claimed that Sahms was negligent in parking his car in violation of the statute. It was held that he did not park his car within the meaning of the statute. 

The Court drew a distinction between stopping and parking. A temporary stop for a necessary reason was not prohibited. 

McAvon v. Brightmoor Transit Co., 245 Mich. 44.

In this case the defendant's bus was stopped on the 20 foot pavement with the rear end three feet from the edge and the front one foot from the edge. The bus was stopped for passengers. It was held that the bus, in stopping for this purpose, was not parked. 

Bowmaster v. De Pree Co., 252 Mich. 505.

The truck belonging to defendant De Pree Company was stopped at night on the south side of the pavement and headed west with headlights on for the purpose of aiding a car in the ditch. Bowmaster, driving from the west, stopped just west of the truck. Van Ark, the other defendant, driving east, struck Bowmaster's car, killing

Bowmaster. The Court said that Bowmaster was within 129

§ 56] 

www. his rights in stopping to make inquiries. He was not parking on the highway. A new trial was ordered. See following case: 

Bowmaster v. De Pree Co., 258 Mich. 538.

In the new trial of the above case a verdict was rendered against Van Ark only, and the plaintiff appealed. 

It was held that there was no negligence shown on the part of the De Pree Company which was a proximate cause of the accident. The Court said that the De Pree 

Company driver was not negligent in placing the truck on the wrong side of the road, and the only question was whether a proper warning was given. Evidently proper warning had been given. It was not the fault of the 

De Pree Company that Bowmaster placed his car in such a position that it obscured the lights. It should be noted that in the opinion the Court said that Bowmaster should have parked his car in a safe place off the pavement on the shoulder of the road. If Van Ark ran into his car because he failed to see the lights on the De Pree Company truck it was because Bowmaster's car obscured the lights. Van Ark did not appeal, and consequently the judgment against him stood, and the directed verdict and judgment for the De Pree Company was affirmed. 

Reed v. Ogden & Moffett, 252 Mich. 362.

This accident occurred on a dark, foggy night. The defendant's truck and trailer, headed north, had stopped because the rear lights on the trailer had gone out. The truck occupied the east side of the pavement and had been stopped several minutes when a northbound car skidded onto the wrong side of the highway, when the driver tried to stop for the truck, and struck plaintiff's southbound car. The truck driver testified that when he saw the northbound car he went behind the trailer and 130

PARKING ON HIGHWAY 

[§ 56 used a flashlight as a warning. This was contradicted.

It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. It was his duty to give warning by lantern or flashlight. Consequently, his negligence was a question for the jury. 

Camp v. Wilson, 258 Mich. 38.

A truck owned by defendant Hunt had broken down and was standing on the pavement. It had two green rear lights but no tail light. Wilson's car, coming up from the rear, swerved to the right and missed the truck but struck the plaintiff, who was 15 feet from the pavement. The Court held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of Hunt as he could have used a flashlight to warn drivers. Wilson testified that he discovered the truck when it was some distance away but did not realize it was standing. 

Edison v. Keene, 262 Mich. 611.

This accident occurred in Indiana, but the statute in that state was similar to the Michigan statute. The defendant's truck became disabled and its lights went out. 

Another of defendant's trucks was stopped back of the first truck with rear lights working. The drivers were repairing the first truck when the plaintiff drove into the rear end of the second truck. A verdict was directed for the defendant. The Court held that there was no negligence on the part of the defendant. Owing to the banks of snow, the trucks could not be removed from the pavement.  "While our statute makes no provision for an emergency, it has been construed as though it so provided." 10 131

§ 57]  

Ozga v. Clock, 266 Mich. 58.

The defendant Clock was called to the scene of an accident with his ambulance. The plaintiff, a pedestrian, had been struck by a car and was lying on the north part of the road. The ambulance was placed so that it was headed east on the north half of the road and with the rear end near the plaintiff. Part of the ambulance was on the pavement, and the headlights were on in addition to two spotlights. About a minute or so after stopping, while the cot was being unloaded, defendant Greiner, driving west, saw the lights of the ambulance and swerved to the left. Seeing the lights of another car parked south of the pavement, he swung back to the right, colliding with the ambulance and forcing it back over the plaintiff. The Court held that defendant Clock was justified in stopping where he did to give the quickest aid possible to the plaintiff. He had a right to rely upon the deputy sheriff, who was there directing traffic. 

Greiner arrived before the deputy could take his place to direct traffic. The judgment against Clock was reversed. 

See also Russell v. Szczawinski, 268 Mich. 112; Johnson v. Fremont Canning Co., 270 Mich. 524.

Sec. 57. Summary. 

The decisions in this group are virtually exceptions to the statutory definition. A temporary stop for a necessary purpose is not parking. (Sahms v. Marcus.) It is not necessarily negligence to stop a car on the wrong side of the road, if the need is urgent enough, and if warning lights are shown at night. (Bowmaster v. De Pree.) (Ozga v. Clock.) If the vehicle is stopped necessarily, a warning should be given, if possible, to vehicles approaching. (Reed v. Ogden & Moffett.) There may be 132

PARKING ON HIGHWAY 

[§ 57 a duty to drive the car off the pavement and on the shoulder, if possible. (Bowmaster v. De Pree, 258 Mich. 

538.) Even if a truck has some lights on the rear, there may be liability if the tail light is not on and no further warning is given. (Camp v. Wilson.) It should be remembered that, although there has been no violation of the parking statute, there may be negligence in leaving the vehicle on the traveled portion of the highway. 133

CHAPTER IX  Sec. 58. Assured Clear Distance Cases. 

Sec. 59. 

Summary-Assured Clear Distance Cases. 

Sec. 58. Assured Clear Distance Cases. 

Section 4697, Compiled Laws 1929, as amended by Act No. 119, Public Acts 1933, prohibits a person from driving at a speed greater than will permit him to bring the vehicle to a stop within the assured clear distance ahead. 

Section 4738 requires the vehicle to have head lamps which will produce a light sufficient to render a person discernible 200 feet ahead under normal atmospheric conditions, and on a level road, except when approaching an oncoming vehicle. In such a case the lights should render discernible a person 75 feet ahead. A great number of cases have reached the Michigan Supreme Court involving the question of the duty of a driver to drive at such a speed that he can stop within the range of his vision. As a result of these cases a rule has been adopted by the Michigan Court which has been followed in several other states. The Court has applied this rule relentlessly. For certain cases where the rule is not applied see cases under heading, "Miscellaneous Cases." How ever, when a plaintiff has driven his car into an illegally parked car at night, the Court has made it at least as difficult for him to recover as if he had been struck by a train at a railway crossing. 134

[§ 

Harnau v. Haight, 189 Mich. 600.

The plaintiff was riding a bicycle near the center of a city street going east. It was 6 o'clock in the evening and so dark that the street lamps had been lighted. The defendant's car, eastbound, struck the plaintiff from the rear. The defendant contended that the plaintiff was negligent in not keeping as close as possible to the curb on the right, as required by an ordinance of the city of 

Muskegon. The Court said in this regard: "Whether the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence or not in being near the center of the street, and in front of the car, such negligence could not have been a proximate cause of the accident. He was where the defendant, exercising any reasonable degree of care, should have seen him. 

He is required by law to have such lights as will show objects immediately in front of him, and he must have his machine under such control as not to overtake and run down people within the scope of his lights." 

Ott v. Wilson, 216 Mich. 499.

The plaintiff was riding in a wagon, going south, in the evening. The defendant had a lantern hanging on the front part of his car, his lights having gone out. The 

Court held that the driver was bound to drive his car at such a speed that he could stop within the vision of his lights and this rule applied where the regular lights were not working. 

Gleason v. Lowe, 232 Mich. 300.

While driving his wagon at night on a trunk line highway, the plaintiff was struck from the rear by the defendant's automobile. The defendant claimed that there was no light on the wagon. The defendant also claimed that when about 300 feet from the wagon he was partly 135

§ 58] 

blinded by the bright lights of an approaching automobile. He slowed down and dimmed his lights but did not see the wagon until it was 8 or 10 feet away. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed.  "Defendant's claim that he was blinded by the bright lights of an approaching automobile, taken in its most favorable aspect, presented a question for the jury of whether, under such circumstances, he was ordinarily prudent or was careless in going ahead while unable to view the way." However see 

Budnick v. Paterson, 215 Mich. 678. 

Diederichs v. Duke, 234 Mich. 136.

The plaintiff in the early morning drove her car into the rear end of the defendant's trailer, which she claimed was parked on the road without lights. The plaintiff testified that she had her dimmers on and could see 20 to 25 feet ahead. She was driving 12 miles per hour and could stop within 12 feet on a dry pavement. She claimed that she had been driving on a dry pavement. When she saw the trailer ahead she applied her brakes, but there was a strip of icy pavement just behind the trailer which was the same color as the pavement. Due to this ice she was unable to stop. It was held that this condition created a question of fact for the jury as to whether there was any negligence on the part of the plaintiff. 

Lett v. Summerfield & Hecht, 239 Mich. 699.

The defendant's furniture van was left partly on the 20 foot road. It had no tail light. It was a dark and foggy night, and some rain was falling. The plaintiff's driver drove his car into the rear end of the van. The plaintiff claimed that there was gross negligence on the part of the defendant. The decision of the lower court in directing a verdict for the defendant, on the ground 136

[§ that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law, was affirmed. The Court quoting from Spencer v. Taylor, 219 

Mich. 110, said: "It is well settled that it is negligence as a matter of law to drive an automobile along a public highway in the dark at such speed that it cannot be stopped within the distance that objects can be seen ahead of it."

The Court also said that it did not believe the rule should be weakened by engrafting exceptions on it or modifying it. 

Skaug v. Knappins, 241 Mich. 57.

The driver of the plaintiff's car testified that his lights showed up the road ahead for 200 feet but only that part of the road directly ahead of his car or 6 feet in width. 

He gave this as his reason for not seeing the truck which was traveling partly on the left side of the road and in the same direction as the plaintiff's car. The plaintiff's driver was held to be negligent as a matter of law. The 

Court held that the statute required lights which would show up the entire traveled portion of the road for a distance of 200 feet. 

Haney v. Troost, 242 Mich. 693.

The defendant's car skidded off the pavement and turned over so that the front end extended out into the road for two or three feet. The plaintiff's car struck the part extending over the pavement. The plaintiff testified that because of the snowstorm and darkness he could see only 30 feet ahead and could stop in less than that distance. He accounted for his failure to see the defendant's car because of the snow on it. The Court approved the decision of the lower court in directing a verdict for the defendant. 137

§ 58] 

Ruth v. Vroom, 245 Mich. 88.

The plaintiff's driver drove his car into the rear end of a trailer which was standing on the pavement with no rear lights. The plaintiff's car approached the trailer at a speed of 30 miles per hour. When 400 to 500 feet away from the trailer the car came to the crest of a grade sloping slightly down. The driver then saw the lights of an approaching car and dimmed his lights, reducing his speed to 15 to 20 miles per hour. The approaching lights bothered him some but he still could stop within the range of his vision which was then 50 feet. 

He drove to a point from 15 to 66 feet from the trailer, when he was blinded by the lights of the other car, which were defective. He ran 10 feet in the black spot before applying his emergency brake. He saw the trailer 12 feet ahead and turned to the left but skidded into the left rear corner. It was held that the plaintiff's driver was negligent as a matter of law. The Court admitted that emergencies, not to be fairly anticipated, might vary the application of the rule, but it found no emergency in this case. The following statement was made.

"Accidents due to their glare are frequent. prudent person would reasonably anticipate that the lights might interfere with his view ahead. When cars meet at night each driver must anticipate the possibility of interference with his vision by the headlights of an approaching car, and, if he cannot see the road beyond such car, must have his own automobile under control which will enable him to stop immediately, or within such distance as he can at all times see ahead." 

Bielecki v. United Trucking Service, 247 Mich. 661.

The defendant was carrying two iron beams on its trailer which projected several feet over the rear end. 138

[§ The night was dark and stormy. The truck in which the decedent was riding collided with one of the beams, forcing it through the windshield. The force of the collision was so great that it drove the beam against the cab of the defendant's truck, so that the driver was forced to break the windshield to get out. The driver of the truck in the rear was held to have been negligent as a matter of law. 

There was evidence that the lanterns hung upon the ends of the beams were not lighted and the other lights were defective. The plaintiff's driver did not discover the trailer until he was within 10 feet of the ends of the beams. He was driving 15 miles an hour with lights disclosing a view of not more than 10 feet. The Court said that the beams were of such size as to be clearly visible, if the plaintiff's truck had been equipped with proper lights. The Court held section 5a, title 3, Act No. 318, Pub. Acts 1927 unconstitutional. This Act provided that where each driver violated a statute the question of who should be held for damages should be a question of fact. 

Martin v. J. A. Mercier Co., 255 Mich. 587.

The plaintiff, at night, was driving north on a street which was within a repair zone. His testimony was that he came to a barrier extending only part way across the 20 foot pavement. He thought the road was open and proceeded. Before he could stop, his car went into an excavation which was not guarded. The plaintiff had encountered a number of similar barriers on the south bound road which was open. As to his duty to have seen the excavation the Court said: "The rule that a driver must see objects and be able to stop within the range of his lights, applied to things on the road, does not apply to holes in the road.' 

139

§ 58]  

His negligence was a question of fact. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. The Court also held that the requirement that a car must have lights capable of showing up the road for 200 feet applied only under ordinary conditions. 

Hollingshead v. Gunderman, 256 Mich. 299.

The plaintiff and defendant were driving their cars in opposite directions on a county highway which had recently been covered with loose gravel. There was a rut on each side of the middle of the road. The plaintiff was driving with his left wheels in one of the ruts close to his side of the road. The defendant was driving in the middle of the road, using both ruts. There was a fog which, to a considerable extent, interfered with visibility. The plaintiff testified that he had his lights on full and was driving 15 miles per hour when he saw the defendant's car suddenly emerge out of the fog about 40 or 50 feet away and without lights. He applied his brakes but was unable to avoid the collision. He claimed that the defendant was driving 30 miles per hour; that he could see 50 feet ahead and could stop within 10 feet. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed, the Court deciding that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Humphrey v. County of Wayne, 257 Mich. 398.

This accident occurred while it was dark. There was a heavy fog which made visibility bad. The driver testified that he was going less than 10 miles per hour and was well acquainted with the road and the turn. He failed to make the turn onto the bridge and went over an embankment. There was a barrier on each side of the road. The driver saw a barrier and thought it was the south barrier but learned too late that it was the one on the north side 140

[§ of the road. The case was tried without a jury and a judgment was given to the plaintiff. This was reversed by the Supreme Court on the ground that the driver was familiar with the conditions and knew the approach to the bridge was dangerous. The Court said he was negligent, but it was not necessary to find him negligent as a matter of law. It found the lower court's finding against the preponderance of the evidence. 

Boylon v. Reliable Cartage Co., 258 Mich. 5.

The plaintiff's decedent was killed when his car crashed into a truck, standing across the road on a curve. It was dark. The lights of the car showed up the road for 200 feet ahead. The car was rounding the curve at 35 miles per hour when the driver saw the truck 100 to 125 feet away. There was testimony that he applied his brakes and would have been able to stop had it not been for a strip of ice close to the truck; that the road up to this point had been dry. In rounding the curve the vision of the driver was reduced to about 100 feet. He could stop within 60 or 65 feet on a dry pavement. The Court affirmed the decision of the lower court in directing a verdict for the defendant, distinguishing this case from that of Diederichs v. Duke, 234 Mich. 136. The Court said that, regardless of the icy strip, he had opportunity to stop his car before the collision or at least to reduce the speed so as to render the impact comparatively harmless.

The damage done by the collision and the distance which the car went after striking the truck were facts indicating an unreasonable rate of speed or failure of the driver to apply his brakes. 

Angstman v. Wilson, 258 Mich. 195.

This accident occurred at 3 a. m. on Woodward avenue near Twelve Mile Road in Royal Oak, Michigan. The 141

§ 58] 

plaintiff testified that he was driving north at a speed of 20 miles per hour, and when within 35 or 40 feet of the point of impact, he saw the standing truck on the easterly side of the pavement, which was 18 feet in width. There was no light on the truck. It was plaintiff's theory that he was unable to stop the car in time because of grease or oil on the pavement. In driving from Detroit the plaintiff used his dim lights, being able to see only 40 to 50 feet ahead. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. No exceptional or unforeseen conditions were present to make this an exception to the rule. 

Marek v. City of Alpena, 258 Mich. 637.

The plaintiff claimed that the defendant was negligent in not making a bridge safe for travel. At night, his car struck a bump in the approach to the bridge, causing him to lose control of the car. It was foggy and he could see only 25 feet ahead. He was driving 25 miles per hour and could stop in 50 feet. The Court held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. It said that the rule that a driver must be able to stop within the assured clear distance ahead did not apply to a hole or bump on the road. The speed of the car in relation to the range of vision was not the proximate cause of the accident. 

Garrison v. City of Detroit, 270 Mich. 237.

While the plaintiff was driving north on First street in Detroit on a rainy, misty night her car struck a signal post in the center of an intersection. The post had a cement base and was painted black and yellow but was covered with mud and dirt. The post had been discontinued for signal purpose and had no warning lights. 

During the same week there had been two other collisions with the post and in a month seven collisions. The plain- 142

[§ tiff could see 50 feet, and could stop in 5 to 10 feet. The judgment for the defendant was affirmed.  "It would convert a rule of safety into a rule of danger to hold that drivers in a city, subject to distraction caused by pedestrians and vehicles, must anticipate at their peril, so unusual a thing as an unlighted traffic signal in the center of a street intersection."

However, the Court held that the testimony presented a close question as the plaintiff was going slowly and was not distracted by anything. The Court said that the case was so close that it could not say the trial court erred in holding the plaintiff contributorily negligent. The case was tried without a jury.

Other cases. 

Elrich v. Schwaderer, 251 Mich. 33; Bowmaster v. 

De Pree Co., 252 Mich. 505; Moore v. United States 

Truck Co., 260 Mich. 56; Russell v. Szczawinski, 268 

Mich. 112; Buwalda v. County of Ottawa, 270 Mich. 477; 

Johnson v. Fremont Canning Co., 270 Mich. 524.

Sec. 59. Summary. 

If the lights on a car go out, the driver is still bound to the rule that he must be able to stop within his range of vision. (Ott v. Wilson.) The lights should show up all of the road ahead. (Skaug v. Knappins.) Blinding lights of an approaching car will not excuse a driver. (Ruth v. Vroom.) The rule does not apply to a hole in the road. (Martin v. Mercier Co.) Nor does it apply to bumps. (Marek v. City of Alpena.) An emergency or unexpected condition of the road may make the case an 143

§ 59]  

exception to the rule. (Diederichs v. Duke.) However, see Boylon v. Cartage Co. If driving conditions are very bad the familiarity of the driver with the road may be a controlling factor. (Humphrey v. County of Wayne.)

Although in Haney v. Troost, the Court held that the driver must stop before striking a camouflaged object, the opinion in Garrison v. City of Detroit indicates a tendency to make the rule less exacting in such a situation. 144

CHAPTER X SKIDDING CASES Sec. 60. Skidding Cases. 

Sec. 61. Summary-Skidding Cases. 

Sec. 60. Skidding Cases. 

Corey v. Hartel, 216 Mich. 675.

The plaintiff claims that the defendant drove his truck toward the sleigh, in which she was riding, with the left wheels on the wrong side of the street and, in turning the truck, it skidded into the sleigh. The lower court instructed the jury that, if the unpreventable skidding of the truck or the sleigh or both caused the accident, the plaintiff could not recover. The Supreme Court said that this instruction negatived the force and effect of the statute requiring drivers to keep to the right of the center of the road in passing. The Court said that, if the operation of the car on the wrong side of the highway was not justified, the skidding of the car when the driver turned the wheels to the right, even though unexpected, would not relieve the defendant of liability. 

Kalso v. Wilson, 252 Mich. 520.

The plaintiff, riding with the defendant, claimed that the defendant was driving at an excessive rate of speed which caused the car to skid off the road. A car passed the defendant and cut in ahead sharply to avoid an approaching automobile. The defendant reduced his speed and applied the brakes, but the car skidded into a pole. 145

§ 60] 

It was held that there was no evidence of excessive speed or negligence, the defendant having applied his brakes upon being confronted with an emergency. 

Cosgrove v. Thomas, 257 Mich. 376.

The defendant, in approaching a bridge, saw the plaintiff's car on the bridge and applied his brakes to stop but skidded over the center of the road, his car coming in contact with the plaintiff's automobile. The defendant claimed that the road was icy at the point where the brakes were applied. The plaintiff's driver testified that the road was slippery all along. The defendant's car was stopped or just moving when the collision occurred. There was also testimony that the defendant had admitted that the accident was entirely his fault. The Court held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant in view of his admissions and the testimony that the road was generally slippery. 

Deyo v. Detroit Creamery Co., 257 Mich. 77.

A long truck with two trailers of the defendant company was moving north on Third avenue in Detroit. 

Third avenue was 46 feet wide and was "crowned," the center of the street being two inches higher than the edges. The plaintiff's testimony was that the truck was traveling 15 to 18 miles per hour and the driver turned it to the left suddenly, causing the trailer to skid. The jury found that the speed of the truck did not exceed 15 miles per hour. The defendant contended that the mere skidding of the trailer did not constitute negligence.

However, the Court held that there was sufficient evidence to take the case to the jury.  "It did not require expert testimony to show what is in everyone's knowledge; that one is apt to slide or skid on a slippery pavement and particularly so 146

SKIDDING CASES 

[§ 61 11 when making a sharp turn with a vehicle. The testimony does not show that the skidding was unpreventable. It is within the general or common knowledge of jurors, as well as almost everyone else, that, unless one moves very cautiously on an icy pavement, he is apt to skid, slide, or fall." 

Leonard v. Hey, 269 Mich. 491.

This case was tried without a jury. The plaintiff's car, driven south on Woodward avenue in Birmingham, was struck by the defendant's northbound car, which skidded on the rails of the car tracks. The collision occurred on the west half of the street. It was necessary for the defendant to cross the tracks, and it was claimed that the rear wheels caught in the car tracks, causing the car to skid to the left. It was raining at the time and the street was slippery. The lower court found for the defendant, and the decision was affirmed. The Court said that the failure to keep to the right when, through no fault of the driver, an automobile skids on a slippery pavement and is thrown across the road, is not negligence. 

Sec. 61. Summary. 

If a driver is operating his car on the wrong side of the road without justification and skids in trying to get back on the right side, he is not relieved from liability by reason of the skidding being unexpected. (Corey v. Hartel.)

Whether or not the road is generally icy or slippery is important in determining whether the skidding was due to negligence. (Cosgrove v. Thomas.) Ordinarily, a case of skidding will be left to the jury to decide whether there was negligence. (Deyo v. Detroit Creamery Co.) How ever, there may be a finding of no negligence even though the car has skidded to the wrong side of the highway. (Leonard v. Hey.) 147
