Sec. 62. Closing Door on Occupant's Hand. 

Camp v. Spring, 241 Mich. 700.

The defendant, a funeral director, closed the door of a car, catching the fingers of the plaintiff in the door jamb. 

The plaintiff was still standing in the car when he closed the door. Because the closing of the door after the plaintiff had entered the car was a usual and proper act, the Court said that the defendant was not bound to anticipate that the plaintiff would place her fingers in the door jamb. There was no claim that the defendant saw the position of the plaintiff's fingers. It was held that there was no evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. 

McIntyre v. Kunsky Theatres Corp., 256 Mich. 634.

The plaintiff, with two friends, came out of the defendants' theater and got into the automobile at the curb. 148

MISCELLANEOUS CASES 

[§ 64 The plaintiff, after getting into the back seat, stood up to permit one of the other women to pass her and take the left hand seat. She did not know that she had her right hand in the door jamb while bracing herself. The defendant's doorman closed the door, injuring the plaintiff's hand. In affirming the decision of the trial court in directing a verdict for the defendant, the Supreme Court could find no difference between this case and Camp v. Spring. 

Sec. 63. Collision Between Horse and Auto. 

Myler v. Bentley, 226 Mich. 384.

The plaintiff's automobile collided with the defendant's horse on a paved country highway at night. The defendant owned seven horses. He returned to his home at about 9 o'clock the night of the accident and found two of the horses out of the inclosure. He drove them back and retired without ascertaining whether there were other horses out. The collision followed soon after this. The plaintiff testified that the horse came across the road in front of the car. It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury, and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. It should be noted that in this case the plaintiff partly relied upon the statute prohibiting the running at large of animals in the highway. See section 

9037, Compiled Laws 1929.

For cases involving the liability of a car driver where horses are frightened, see: Prindle v. Allen, 164 Mich. 

553; Kasprzak v. Chapman, 197 Mich. 552.

Sec. 64. Part of Body Protruding from Car. 

Helber v. Harkins, 210 Mich. 580.

The plaintiff was delivering milk in Ann Arbor. He had just delivered milk at a residence just west of the 149

§ 65] 

defendant's home and was on the right running board to be in readiness to make the next delivery. As the car passed the defendant's premises, the plaintiff's legs were struck by some old stairs which protruded over the pavement about 18 inches. The defendant had placed them there while rebuilding his house. The driver and the plaintiff testified that they did not see the stairs although it was daylight. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the obstruction was small, near the ground and did not extend far into the traveled way. Consequently, the negligence of the driver or plaintiff was a question for the jury. 

Corey v. Hartel, 216 Mich. 675.

The plaintiff was riding on the back part of a sleigh with her feet hanging over the side and was injured when an automobile struck her legs. The lower court instructed the jury that the question of whether the plaintiff was negligent was for them to decide. It was held that this was error as the plaintiff was not called upon to anticipate that either driver would violate the statute. Her duty to avoid the danger of injury did not arise until it became apparent or the circumstances were such that an ordinarily prudent person would have apprehended its existence.

Sec. 65. Driving Through Smoke Screen. 

Marsh v. Burnham, 211 Mich. 675.

The plaintiff was driving his car north and the defendant south. The plaintiff testified that a fire alongside the road raised a smoke screen across the road, making it impossible to see. He slowed his car to five miles per hour and drove well over to the right side of the road. 150

MISCELLANEOUS CASES 

[§ 67 He had gone about a car length into the smoke when the collision occurred. The lower court instructed the jury that each driver had a right to enter the screen of smoke, using such caution as the circumstances rendered necessary and proper, and this instruction was approved. 

Sec. 66. Striking Object on Road. 

Creitz v. Wolverine Engineering Co., 213 Mich. 402.

In driving over a temporary bridge the plaintiff's car struck a gasoline engine which had been placed at the corner of the bridge. The bridge was 12 feet wide, and there was room to pass the engine which was on the floor of the bridge. It was daylight and the car was moving very slowly. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the slightest glance by the plaintiff to the roadbed ahead of him would have revealed the engine and avoided the accident. 

Sec. 67. Bicycles. 

Niedzinski v. Coryell, 215 Mich. 498.

The defendant's car was being driven south on a city street and struck the plaintiff, who was riding a bicycle south. At the time of the accident it was raining and daylight was fading. The street was 40 feet wide. The plaintiff testified that he was riding a few feet to the right of the center of the street and heard the car approaching but did not look back or change his course, and his bicycle was struck in the rear end. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that while the bicycle was a vehicle it was not the kind of a vehicle mentioned in the motor vehicle statute. The Court held that the plaintiff was not negligent in not turning to the right as there was room for the defendant to pass on either side. 151

§ 68] 

Stinson v. Payne, 231 Mich. 158.

A question arose in this case as to whether the plaintiff was negligent in riding a bicycle after dark without a light in violation of an ordinance. It was held that evidence, that after the installation of a boulevard lighting system the ordinance was not enforced, was admissible and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Sec. 68. Speed on Curve. 

Knope v. Springett, 229 Mich. 223.

In this case the plaintiff, while driving on a curve at night on his own side of the road, came into collision with a car which was attempting to pass a truck. The defendant's car was approaching the plaintiff and was admittedly on the wrong side. The defendant claimed that he did not see the lights of the plaintiff's car due to the curve, and he did not know of the curve. The plaintiff testified that he was driving at a speed of 20 to 25 miles per hour. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed by an equally divided court. Four justices felt that the plaintiff's speed on the curve was too high as the inside of the curve was obstructed and in rounding the curve the road was not illuminated, except immediately in front of the car. 

Quigley v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 234 Mich. 178.

The plaintiff's car failed to make a short left turn in approaching a bridge and struck a barrier. Signs along the road warned the driver of the turn. It was held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. 

Sec. 69. Striking Man Thrown from Vehicle. 

Morris v. Montgomery, 229 Mich. 509.

The plaintiff was driving his motorcycle along a gravel road in the country and claimed that, while turning 152

MISCELLANEOUS CASES 

[§ 70 slightly to avoid some loose gravel, the front wheel struck a rut and threw him onto the road where he was run over by defendant's car. The plaintiff's testimony was that the defendant was far enough behind to turn to either side and avoid striking him. It was held that the case was for the jury, and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Sec. 70. Avoiding Vehicle Coming Into Highway. 

Steinberg v. Builders Lumber & Wrecking Co., 238 Mich. 181.

The plaintiff's car was being driven west on a dry, asphalt street in the daytime. The driver saw a horse and wagon coming out of a driveway on the north side of the street when his car was 16 feet from the path of the horse and two or three feet from the curb. He testified that at a speed of 13 miles per hour he could stop in 12 feet, but he made no effort to do so, although he swerved slightly to the left. The driver made other statements which were contradictory to his specific testimony as to distances. It was held that he was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the specific facts were in explanation of the general statements and controlled. 

Door v. Valley Lumber Co., 254 Mich. 694.

The decedent, four years of age, was coasting in a little cart on the sidewalk along the north side of a city street.

She was going west, slightly downgrade, and suddenly turned down a driveway leading to the street, and the cart ran into the side of a westbound truck. The truck was traveling at a speed of 15 miles per hour, 10 feet from the north curb, and, when it was 10 feet from the driveway, the cart was turned from the sidewalk down the driveway. The truck driver swerved to the left and applied his brakes. It was held that there was no negligence 153

§ 71] 

upon the part of the driver. The Court said that the driver had no reason to anticipate that the girl would turn the cart down the drive. 

Hazzard v. Heneveld, 263 Mich. 253.

This case was tried without a jury. The plaintiff's car was being driven west on an 18-foot pavement near the limits of a village. The driver noticed the defendant's car starting or about to start from a gasoline station on the north side of the road. He blew his horn and crossed to the south side of the road. As he reached the easterly approach to the station, the defendant's car struck his car on the right side, shoving the car off the road. The road was covered with packed snow. The trial judge found no negligence on the part of the plaintiff's driver and gave a judgment to the plaintiff, reasoning that the defendant had not complied with the statute requiring a stop before entering the highway from a private drive, and saying that the plaintiff had a right to assume the stop would be made. The decision was affirmed.

Sec. 71. Speed on Rough Road. 

Collins v. Hull, 256 Mich. 507.

The defendant was driving east on M-44, a very rough gravel road with loose gravel in the center. He claimed that when 200 feet from the plaintiff's car, and while driving downgrade, his wheels struck a rut in spite of his effort to avoid it, and his car went out of control, going to the left and striking the plaintiff's automobile. The defendant did not apply his brakes, but the defendant claimed that his knee was cut when he started to apply his brakes, and that accounted for his failure to apply 154

MISCELLANEOUS CASES 

[§ 72 them. It was held that there was evidence of negligence.

"When, however, one drives at a rate of 40 to 45 miles per hour over a rough and pitted road cut up with ruts, and with loose gravel in the center, and strikes some uneven rut that causes his car to swerve, he is not without fault, nor is he driving in the manner that a careful and prudent driver would under like conditions."

Sec. 72. Vision Restricted by Car Cutting in. 

Moore v. United States Truck Co., 260 Mich. 56.

This accident occurred on a 40-foot paved highway at night. The defendant's truck and trailers, southbound, were stalled in the second lane from the west side and partly over the third lane. The plaintiff's car was traveling south at about 35 miles per hour and, while approaching the rear of the trailers, another car passed the plaintiff, swung in front of her car, and almost instantly cut out to avoid the truck. This car was only four feet in front of the plaintiff's car and cut off the driver's view of the road ahead. When it swerved to the left, the plaintiff's driver discovered the trailer 15 feet ahead, and he skidded into it. There was no light on the trailer. The 

Court held the plaintiff's driver negligent in driving without a view of the highway ahead of him. It was negligence for him to drive at a speed of 35 miles per hour, back of another automobile and within four feet of it, with all view ahead cut off. 

Bishop v. Gaudio, 263 Mich. 65.

This accident occurred in the daytime on U. S. 16 in a shallow gully. The plaintiff, with other children, was 155

§ 73]  

walking east. It had been raining and the pavement was slippery. Defendant Gaudio was driving a truck-train 

56 feet long. When going over 20 miles per hour he did not have control of the train. Defendant Allen overtook 

Gaudio about one-half mile east of the gully and followed him. As they came to the top of the grade he passed the truck-train at a speed of 35 to 45 miles per hour. 

Allen saw the children and a car approaching from the west. He got back on the right hand side when half way down the hill. He gradually reduced his speed until he was running at 5 to 10 miles per hour when he passed the children. The truck struck the rear end of his car. The truck then struck the plaintiff. A verdict was rendered against Allen only. The Supreme Court ordered a judgment entered against Gaudio and for Allen. The majority of the Court held that there was no negligence on Allen's part, saying that he observed more than ordinary care in slowing down for the children. The whole Court agreed that Gaudio was negligent in driving at an illegal rate of speed and in not having the truck under control. 

Sec. 73. Coasting on Highway. 

Van Dyke v. Knoll, 262 Mich. 644.

The plaintiff, while coasting on a bobsled on a city street in Grand Rapids, came in contact with the defendant's car. Municipal authorities permitted coasting on this street, having placed barriers eight feet long at intervals with a sign reading "Caution, Coasting Allowed."

An icy strip, three feet wide, was used for coasting. It was 13 feet from the north curb. The defendant backed his car across the street against the north curb. There was conflicting testimony as to whether the car was standing or moving when the impact occurred. The lower court instructed the jury that, if the slide was clear when the 156

MISCELLANEOUS CASES 

[§ 74 sled started down, it was the duty of anyone down the hill not to get in the way of the bobsled. It was held that this instruction was erroneous. The duty not to get in the way was not an absolute duty. A new trial was ordered. 

Sec. 74. Fainting at Wheel. 

Soule v. Grimshaw, 266 Mich. 117.

The defendant's car went over on the wrong side of the road, striking plaintiff's approaching car. The defendant testified that he became unconscious while driving. 

He claimed that he had never had a fainting spell before and had not used intoxicating liquors. The plaintiff's testimony was that the defendant slumped over in his car, and the car then went across the center line. The defendant admitted that he felt dizzy for some time before the accident. It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury on the question of whether the defendant was negligent in continuing to drive after feeling dizzy. The jury was instructed that, if he fainted immediately prior to the accident, he was not liable. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. Also see Armstrong v. Cook, 250 Mich. 180. 157

CHAPTER XII DISTINCTION BETWEEN  Sec. 75. The Distinction Between Death and Survival Actions. 

Sec. 76. Instantaneous Death Theory Adopted. 

Sec. 77. Interpretation of Word "Instantaneous."

Sec. 78. Summary-Distinction Between Death and Survival Actions. 

Sec. 75. The Distinction Between Death and Survival Actions. 

To understand the actions for death in Michigan, it is necessary to trace the history of the Death Act and the 

Survival Statute. The first Survival Statute in Michigan is found in Revised Statutes of Michigan, 1837-8, Chap ter 3, Section 7, Page 428: 

“In addition to the actions which survive by the common law, the following shall also survive, that is to say: actions of replevin and trover, actions of trespass for assault, battery or imprisonment, or for goods taken and carried away, and actions of trespass, and trespass on the case for damages done to real and personal estate.”

It should be noted that in this early statute there was no survival of an action for personal injuries, excluding the action for assault and battery. In 1885 this statute was amended to include actions for personal injuries and was as follows: Public Acts 1885, No. 113. 

"In addition to the actions which survive by the common law, the following shall also survive, that is to say: actions of replevin and trover; actions of 158

[§ assault and battery, false imprisonment, for goods taken and carried away, for negligent injuries to the person, and actions for damage done to real or personal estate."

The present form of the statute is found in 1929 Compiled Laws of Michigan, Sec. 14040: "In addition to the actions which survive by the common law, the following shall also survive, that is to say, actions of replevin, actions for the conversion of property, for deceit, for assault and battery, for false imprisonment, for negligent injuries to persons, for damages done to real and personal estate, and actions to recover real estate, or any interest therein, where persons have been induced to part with the same through fraudulent representations and deceit.' 99 The Death Act was passed in 1848 and was as follows:

Laws of Michigan, 1848, Act No. 38: 

(1) Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages, in respect thereof, then and in every case, the person who, or the corporation which would have been liable, if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured, and although the death shall have been caused under such circumstances as amount in law to felony." "(2) Every such action shall be brought by, and in the names of the personal representatives of such deceased persons, and the amount recovered in every such action shall be for the exclusive benefit of the widow and next of kin of such deceased person, and shall be distributed to such widow and next of kin in 159

§ 75] 

the proportions provided by law in relation to the distribution of personal property, left by persons dying intestate and in every such action, the jury may give such damages as they shall deem fair and just, with reference to the pecuniary injury resulting from such death, to the wife and next of kin of such deceased person. 

The second section of the Death Act was amended in 1873, and no change has been made since then. The first section of the Death Act has remained the same since it was passed in 1848. The second section, Compiled Laws 

1929, Sec. 14062 is as follows: 

"Every such action shall be brought by, and in the names of, the personal representatives of such deceased persons, and the amount recovered in every such action, shall be distributed to the persons and in the proportions provided by law in relation to the distribution of personal property left by persons dying intestate: and in every such action the jury may give such damages as they shall deem fair and just with reference to the pecuniary injury resulting from such death, to those persons who may be entitled to such damages when recovered."

Thus from 1848 to 1885 Michigan had a statute providing an action for wrongful death, but there was no action surviving death for personal injuries. Therefore, if a person was injured and died from a cause not due to the wrongful act, there was no remedy. It died with the person.

After the Survival Statute was changed in 1885, to include personal injury actions, a question arose as to the application of the Death Act. But it was not until 1898 that the Michigan Supreme Court took under consideration the meaning of the two statutes in an action for 160

[§ death. Quite naturally, the few death actions which reached the Supreme Court before 1898 generally found a railway company on the defense. There was a special death statute applying only to death actions against railroad companies. This act has been interpreted in the same manner as the general Death Act, and can be disregarded in this discussion.

Although the Michigan Court gave opinions on a number of actions for death between 1885 and 1898, it was not until the Court was presented with the case of Sweetland v. Chicago & Grand Trunk Railway Company, 117 Michigan 329, that the Survival Statute and the Death Act were interpreted together. To see the situation clearly, this case must be treated in detail. 

Sweetland v. Chicago & Grand Trunk Railway Company, f17 Mich. 329.

The declaration in this case contained three counts. 

Count I was for pain and suffering prior to death, the plaintiff contending that the action survived under the 

Survival Statute. Count II was for loss of personal property. Count III was for recovery of damages for wrongful death under the Death Act. The jury found for the plaintiff under Counts I and II and for the defendant under the third count. The deceased had been burned to death in a railway wreck, no definite testimony being offered as to any survival. The majority of the Court held that there could be no recovery under the Survival 

Statute for pain and suffering. Chief Justice Grant, in his opinion, based his decision on the lack of testimony on the survival of the deceased. Justice Long, concurring in the result, wrote a lengthy opinion, going into the history of the Death Act and the Survival Statute. He arrived at the conclusion that where an action was brought for 161

§ 75] 

death due to wrongful act the suit should be based upon the Death Act to the exclusion of any action under the 

Survival Statute. Chief Justice Grant concurred in this. 

Justice Montgomery dissented in a long opinion, arguing that an action should be permitted under the Death Act, and also under the Survival Statute for damages suffered by the deceased up to the time of death. Justice 

Hooker dissented, arguing that the Death Act should apply only where death was instantaneous and where the Survival Statute could not be relied upon because of the failure of the deceased to survive long enough to create an action capable of surviving. From this case which divided the court there came three theories. 

1. The Survival Statute applied only where death was not due to the wrongful act. If a person died as a result of injuries, an action would lie under the Death Act, and no action could be brought under the Survival Statute in conjunction with the Death Act. The reasoning was that the Survival Statute as to personal injuries was passed in 1885, not as affecting the Death Act, but merely to keep personal injury actions from abating with the natural death of the party injured. 

2. The recovery for damages up to the time of death could be had under the Survival Act, and for damages due to death and wrongful act under the Death Act. There could be two actions brought at the same time under the two statutes. The reasoning was that the Survival Statute, before the Death Act was passed, permitted a recovery for damages up to the time of death. There was no reason for interpreting the Death Act as repealing any part of the Survival Act. 

3. The Death Act should apply only where death was instantaneous; otherwise the Survival Statute was to be used. There could not be two actions under the two statutes. 162

[§ Which theory was supported by the law at the time the 

Sweetland case was decided? For law supporting each of the three theories in the Sweetland case, the opinions should be consulted as they are lengthy and for the most part well considered. So far as precedent was concerned in Michigan there were a number of decisions to support the first theory over the third. 

In the case of Van Brunt v. Cincinnati, Jackson & 

Mackinaw Railroad Company, 78 Mich. 530 (1889), an action was brought under the Death Act, although the deceased survived the accident five hours. The injury occurred in 1888, three years after the Survival Statute was passed. Yet the Court in its opinion does not even intimate that the action might not be properly brought. 

The decision was against the plaintiff for lack of proof as to damages. The Court did show its attitude by these words. "The point is suggested by plaintiff's counsel for the first time in this Court that the cause of action which the plaintiff's intestate had for his personal injuries survived to his personal representatives under Section 7397, Howell Statutes, as amended by Act No. 113, Laws of 

1885." This was the Survival Statute. The Court held that as the plaintiff had relied on the Death Act he must stand upon his pleadings in the Court below. Here was a clear case of survival permitted to be brought under the 

Death Act. For other cases similar to the Van Brunt decision, allowing action for death under the Death Act, although there was a survival, see: Hurst v. Detroit City 

Railway, 84 Mich. 539; Sweet v. Michigan Central Railway Company, 87 Mich. 559; Racho v. City of Detroit, 90 Mich. 92. In the Racho case the survival was for one year. All of these cases involved injuries which occurred after the Survival Statute was passed applying to personal injury actions. 12 163

§ 76] 

The second theory, mentioned above, which would permit an action under each statute, was supported by dicta in Hurst v. Detroit City Railway, 84 Mich. 539 at page 544, where the Court said that an action for injuries, suffered up to the time of death under the Survival Statute, would be a separate action from the death action under the Death Act. Additional support to this theory was given in the case of Racho v. City of Detroit, 90 Mich. 92 at page 95, where, after citing the Survival Statute, the

Court said: "We have no doubt that the right of action of Racho survived to his administrator, but this does not aid the plaintiff in this action." As the action in this case was brought under the Death Act, the Court in this decision recognized a right of action under the Survival Statute to recover for injuries sustained by the deceased in addition to an action as was brought. 

Sec. 76. Instantaneous Death Theory Adopted. 

In the case of Dolson v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Ry. Co., 128 Mich. 444, decided in 1901, the Michigan

Supreme Court definitely decided to follow the third theory as given by Justice Hooker. Justices Long and

Grant deserted theory number one and swung over to 

Hooker's argument that there should be but one right of action, and it should be based on the Death Act only where death was instantaneous. Otherwise the action should be brought under the Survival Statute. In this case the deceased survived the action several hours. In the declaration there were two counts, one under the Death Act and one under the Survival Statute. The majority of the 

Court held that an action would lie only under the Survival Statute, while two of the Judges maintained that an action should lie under each statute. 164

[§ Thus the Dolson decision laid down the law which has been followed consistently by the Michigan Supreme Court since 1901. The reasoning of Justice Hooker was that where death was instantaneous it prevented an action from accruing to the decedent's estate under the Survival Statute as there was nothing to survive. Hence the 

Death Act was passed by the legislature to furnish a remedy, otherwise not available where death was instantaneous. The difficulty in this reasoning is found in the chronology of the statutes. At the time the Death Act was passed in 1848, there was no survival of personal injury actions. Thus Justice Hooker would have had to contend that between 1848 and 1885 an action for death due to personal injuries could have been brought only where there was instantaneous death. But this was not true as has already been pointed out. In addition, it would have been repugnant to the language of the Death Act to refuse to permit an action where death resulted from injuries some time after the accident. However illogical the reasoning of Justice Hooker was, the decision settled the law, and was advantageous to that extent. 

Sec. 77. Interpretation of Word "Instantaneous.”

After the decision in the Dolson case, the Court was called upon to define "instantaneous death." The following cases developed the Court's interpretation and are given here in outline form. 

Olivier v. Houghton County Railroad Company, 134 Mich. 367. 

The Court in this case talked about a continuous injury resulting in death. It pointed out that death was not instantaneous because the period of survival was accompanied by a state of unconsciousness. In other words, the 165

§ 77] 

Court felt that merely because the period of survival found the deceased unconscious was no reason for making a death instantaneous. 

West v. Detroit United Railway, 159 Mich. 269.

This is one of the leading cases on the definition of instantaneous death. Deceased was carried under the street car for some distance and died within fifteen minutes while still under the car. The Court held that the death was instantaneous and said: "Where there is a continuing injury, resulting in death within a few moments, it is instantaneous within the meaning of the statute." 

Ely v. Detroit United Railway, 162 Mich. 287.

In this case the deceased lived ten to thirty minutes after the original blow. The Court pointed out that there was no continuous operation of the direct cause of death up to the time of death and held that it was a survival action.

Lobenstein v. Whitehead & Kales Iron Company, 179 

Mich. 279.

The deceased in this case fell a distance of 85 feet. 

There was testimony that he was alive ten to fifteen minutes afterward. The action was brought under the Death 

Act, and the Court held that the action was properly brought and quoted a Massachusetts decision as follows: "We are to ascertain what the intent of the legislature was when they passed the law. It is not to be supposed that they intended to make a distinction between a case where the death was so instantaneous that there was no manifestation of life whatsoever and a case where there might be some slight spasmodic action of the body of the sufferer to indicate that life was not quite extinct.” 166

[§ 

Wood v. Standard Drug Company, 190 Mich. 654.

The deceased in this case died twelve hours after taking a drug. It was held that the action was properly brought under the Survival Statute. The Court pointed out that, if there was a continuing injury up to the time of death, the death did not result in a few moments as required in the rule laid down in the case of West v. Detroit 

United Railway, cited above. 

Beach v. City of St. Joseph, 192 Mich. 296.

The Court in this case pointed out the fact that there was a conflict in the decisions in other states on the definition of instantaneous death. The Michigan Court stated that it followed the Federal Court decisions that death by drowning was instantaneous. For another case on drowning, see Clark v. Detroit & Mackinac Railway Company, 197 Mich. 489. 

Brabon v. Gladwin Light & Power Company, 201 Mich. 697. 

The decedent was killed by an electric shock. The action was brought under the Death Act. The Court held that the death was instantaneous, and said that whether one or two minutes elapsed before life was extinct was not material. 

Paperno v. Michigan Railway Engineering Company, 202 

Mich. 257.

The decedent came in contact with a third rail and was killed by an electric shock. There was conflicting testimony as to a survival. Some evidence was offered that the deceased lived eighteen minutes after being removed from the rail. There was also testimony that the decedent had expired when he was removed. The Court held that a question of fact for the jury was presented by the 167

§ 77] 

evidence as to whether death was instantaneous. For another case involving survival after electric shock, see 

Swaczyk v. Detroit Edison Company, 207 Mich. 494. 

Budnick v. Peterson, 215 Mich. 678.

The deceased was struck by an automobile and died. 

There was testimony that his death occurred fifteen minutes after the accident. The Court made this statement: "If there was competent evidence tending to show that deceased survived the injury, the judgment entered must be affirmed."

It was held in this case that the action was properly brought under the Survival Statute. 

Nelson v. Glover, 231 Mich. 229.

The decedent was injured in an automobile accident and lived for twenty minutes, being unconscious. It was held that the death was not instantaneous. For a similar case, see Kinsler v. Simpson, 257 Mich. 7. 

Olchefsky v. Mercier Brick Company, 240 Mich. 536.

The decedent in this case inhaled poisonous gas. The testimony tended to show that the decedent was alive when removed. The Court stated that there was enough evidence to put the case under the Survival Statute. 

Micks v. Norton, 256 Mich. 308.

This case was brought under the Survival Act. The facts were that after the accident the child was taken into a store. There was testimony that the child was living after being brought into the store. A doctor, who arrived later, answered a hypothetical question at the trial by saying that the death was instantaneous. The Court held that the evidence presented a question of fact for the jury as to survival. 168

[§ 

Janse v. Haywood, 270 Mich. 632.

This case was started under the Survival Statute. 

There was testimony that the decedent received a skull fracture at the back of her head, compound fractures of both legs and that blood spurted from her mouth and her pulse was beating for several minutes. It was held that while close to the line of instantaneous death there was sufficient evidence to bring the case within the survival statute.

For a discussion by the Court distinguishing between instantaneous death in applying the Death Act and instantaneous death in determining whether an action survived against the estate of a tort feasor, see Ford v. 

Maney's Estate, 251 Mich. 461.

Sec. 78. Summary. 

Where death results from a wrongful act, the following general rules are applicable: 

1. There cannot be a recovery under each Act, although the declaration may contain two counts to assure recovery under one of the two statutes. 

2. If the death was instantaneous as to time, or if there was an injury which continued as a cause of death up to the time of death, death occurring within a few moments after the injury, the action must be started under the 

Death Act. A space of fifteen minutes has been held to constitute a few moments. A continuing injury does not mean the actual injury sustained by the deceased, but rather the object which caused the injury. 

3. If the action is started under the Survival Statute, and the plaintiff can prove a survival for an appreciable length of time, that is, for a number of minutes, action is properly brought. This, of course, assumes that the cause of death does not continue up to the point of death. 169

CHAPTER XIII  Sec. 79. Death Actions for Minors. 

Sec. 80. 

Summary-Death Actions for Minors. 

Sec. 81. Death Actions for Adults. 

Sec. 82. Summary-Death Actions for Adults. 

The measure of damages in an action under the Death Act is entirely different from the measure of damages based upon the Survival Statute. As an action for wrongful death is purely statutory, the method of determining damages is set forth in the Death Act. The statute requires a jury to give damages with reference to the pecuniary injury resulting from death to those persons to whom the personal property of the deceased would go under the so-called statute of distributions. See Michi gan Compiled Laws 1929, section 14062. 

The cases which have developed the law of damages under the Death Act will be discussed in this chapter under two divisions. First, cases involving the death of a minor. Secondly, cases involving the death of an adult.

Sec. 79. Death Actions for Minors. 

The following decisions are given in their chronological order. They are all subsequent to the change in the damage clause of the Death Act, which change was made in 1873. 

Chicago & Northwestern Railway Co. v. Bayfield, 37 

Mich. 204.

In this case the deceased was seventeen years old and was living with his mother and sister. He was of feeble 170

[§ intellect and at the time of death was earning $1.40 per day. It was held that a verdict of $3,400 was excessive. 

Evidence was introduced at the trial to show the poverty of the mother and sister. The Supreme Court said that in this case the financial condition of the mother and sister was not material. The Court admitted that in the case of the death of a young child the circumstances of the family would be material in determining whether assistance would later be demanded. 

Cooper v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Railway Co., 66 Mich. 261.

This was an action brought for the death of an eleven year old girl. At one point in the instructions to the jury, the lower court informed the jury that it could take into consideration the pecuniary benefits, not including loss of services, which the parents might have expected to realize during the balance of the deceased's life and not longer than theirs. The Supreme Court expressed itself in this manner: "The jury, of course, must determine whether she would remain single or married. If she married, she might marry a husband in the same humble walk of life as herself. He might be without means, or he might have a competency of this world's goods; and the daughter might or might not be in a position, and have the means and desire, to make presents to her parents to a greater or less extent. Or she might marry a millionaire and be able and willing to supply her parents with all the luxuries of life, or she might remain single and be compelled to toil from morning until night to earn her livelihood. Who can place a pecuniary estimate upon chances such as these? It is evident at a glance that any estimate or value placed upon events so uncertain must be without any satisfactory basis to rest upon." 171

§ 79] 

A verdict of $1,550.00 was given in the lower court. The 

Supreme Court said that it could not see that this verdict was larger than the jury were authorized under the statute to render and that the value of the earnings or services of the child until she reached the age of twenty-one might have amounted to the amount of the verdict. The 

Court said that the instruction which was given regarding pecuniary benefits for the balance of the deceased's life above the age of twenty-one was not proper but they did not believe that it influenced the jury. 

Rajnowski v. Detroit, Bay City & Alpena Ry. Co., 74 

Mich. 20.

Suit was brought for the death of a five year old child. 

The Court said that the parents were deprived of the services and assistance of the child until he was twentyone. The Court also said that testimony, throwing any light upon what the pecuniary injury would be, was admissible. 

Hurst v. Detroit City Ry., 84 Mich. 539.

The deceased was an infant one year and eleven months old. No proof was made of any pecuniary loss and there was no such allegation in the declaration.  "The measure of such damages, if any are recoverable in such cases, is limited to the prospective earnings of the child until his arrival at the age of twenty-one years, taken in connection with his prospect of life, less the expenses of his care and support."

As no damages were proved the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment for the defendant. 172

[$ 

Snyder v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern Ry. Co., 131 

Mich. 418.

Here there was a suit for the death of an eleven year old boy. A verdict of $250.00 was given in the lower court, and it was appealed by the plaintiff. There was testimony that the boy had an unusual aptitude for drawing and wood carving and that at the age of fifteen he could have earned $15.00 per week. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment and said that the verdict was not inadequate. It was pointed out that the testimony did not definitely show what the future of the boy was, and that his future was problematical. The Court said that the conclusions to be drawn from the testimony were for the jury. 

McDonald v. Champion Iron & Steel Co., 140 Mich. 401.

In this case the deceased was fourteen years old and was earning 75¢ per day. The father and mother testified that it cost 75¢ a day to feed and clothe and care for the boy. The testimony also showed that the father, who was working for the same employer as the deceased, made only $1.75 per day. A verdict of $7,487 was given.

It was held by the Supreme Court that this should be cut to $2,500. The Court said that $2,500 would give the parents an average of a little over $350.00 per year. 

Black v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 146 Mich. 568.

The deceased in this case was seven years old. It was shown at the trial that the boy was healthy, intelligent and obedient. The Court, in affirming the judgment of $1,500, said that the jurors had all been boys and that sufficient testimony had been offered to take the case to the jury and to support the verdict. 173

§ 79]  

Peklenk v. Isle Royale Copper Co., 187 Mich. 644.

The verdict in this case was for $750.00 for the death of a twelve year old boy. Evidence was offered to show that the father was in debt. The Supreme Court said that this was not proper, although it would have been proper to show in a general way the financial circumstances of the beneficiaries. 

Sceba v. Manistee Ry. Co., 189 Mich. 308.

This was an action for the death of a five year old girl. 

The verdict was for $71.00, the cost of the funeral. The lower court refused to permit the mother to answer the question as to whether the girl was kindly, tractable and obedient. The lower court also sustained the defendant's objection to other questions concerning the mother's estimate of the value of the child's services in comparison to the cost of support, and whether the value would increase with the age of the girl. The Supreme Court held that there was error in the lower court's refusal to permit this. testimony to be given. The Court said that it did not feel like holding that the damages awarded were inadequate as a matter of law, but that because of the errors there must be a reversal. 

Beach v. City of St. Joseph, 192 Mich. 296.

The deceased in this case was twenty years and six months old. She was single and living with her mother, contributing to her mother's support. She was earning $52.50 a month at the time of her death. The lower court gave a verdict of $400.00. The Supreme Court said that the measure of damages was limited to the earnings until the age of twenty-one, less the cost of support. The judgment of the lower court was reversed on other grounds. 174

[§ 

Elliott v. Detroit United Ry., 226 Mich. 92.

In this case a verdict of $7,500 was given for the death of a fifteen year old boy. The Supreme Court held that the verdict was excessive. The testimony given in the lower court showed that the boy was healthy and normal. 

In vacation time he earned money, and during the summer before his death he made $15.00 per week as a messenger boy. It was estimated that it cost $5.00 to $10.00 per week to support him.  "Assuming that he would contribute $10.00 per week for the next five years and four months until he reached his majority, computed on present value as is the rule, his contributions would be but a fraction of the amount awarded by the jury." 

Bade v. Nies, 239 Mich. 37.

The deceased in this case was six years old. held that a verdict of $5,150 was not excessive. 

Edgerton v. Lynch, 255 Mich. 456. 

It was

In this case the deceased was a three and a half year old boy. It was held that funeral expenses were part of the damages.

Sec. 80. Summary. 

In determining the damages in an action for the death of a minor, it is necessary to know what persons would take the deceased's personal property under the statute of distributions. It is then necessary to determine whether any of these persons have sustained any pecuniary injury as a result of the death of the minor. Inasmuch as the parents of a minor child would be beneficiaries and as they are entitled to the services of an unemancipated child until twenty-one years of age, they 175

§ 80] 

are usually the ones to sustain any pecuniary injury. As demonstrated in the Michigan cases the normal situation is the one where the parents are making the claim for pecuniary damages.

There are a number of situations which have not come up in the Michigan cases. For instance, there has not been a case involving the death of a minor who was emancipated at the time of his death. In the case of an emancipated minor it might be difficult to show any damages. Another situation which might present difficulty would be the instantaneous death of an orphan. The question here would probably arise as to who was entitled to the services of the child until the age of twentyone; whether that person, be it the state or someone else, could qualify as one sustaining pecuniary loss or injury as required in the Death Act.

Where the deceased is close to the age of twenty-one, is living with his parents and supporting or helping to support them, there is room for argument that the pecuniary injury should include amounts which the parents could reasonably be expected to enjoy after the deceased had become twenty-one years of age. The Michigan Supreme Court evidently has limited the recovery to the pecuniary loss up to the age of twenty-one. In Tiffany, Death by Wrongful Act, section 165, the following statement is made: "In accordance with the principle of these cases it is logically held in Arkansas, Maryland, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island that in an action for the death of a minor child of tender years, damages are limited to the loss of services during the child's minority, and that the chances of his surviving his parents and of his ability and willingness to assist them after that period should be excluded from consideration." 176

[§ 

In Sutherland on Damages, Vol. V, page 4931, the following statement is made: "In several states the damages for the death of a child have been limited to pecuniary benefits the parents had a legal right to claim from the child's services, and therefore the courts have confined the estimate to the period of minority."

Michigan is one of the states cited under this rule. It is noteworthy that no case can be found in Michigan where recovery has been allowed for pecuniary loss that might have occurred beyond the deceased's minority. 

Apparently the Michigan Supreme Court, by a negative attitude, has assumed the position of not permitting the parents to recover any more than they are legally entitled to, or in other words, the loss of earnings of the deceased less the cost of support up to the age of twentyone. On the other hand, it can be said that the Supreme 

Court has not in any well reasoned opinion denied the plaintiff a recovery for pecuniary loss in the majority period of the deceased's life, where there has been proof offered that the parents could have reasonably expected pecuniary benefits from the deceased after the deceased became of age. The case of Beach v. City of St. Joseph, cited above, where the deceased was twenty years, six months old, at the time of death and contributing to the support of her mother, is a very strong case for those who hold that the damages should be limited to the minority period of the deceased. Although there is no decision in Michigan which has discussed this question at length, the Michigan Court seems to be fairly definitely settled as shown by the Beach case. From the above cases the following general rules can be drawn. 

1. The measure of damages, where the deceased had parents and was unemancipated, would be the value of 177

§ 81] 

the loss of earnings of the minor until he would reach the age of twenty-one less the expense of caring for the child. 

2. The damages or pecuniary loss to the parents are special damages and must be alleged in the declaration, and some pecuniary loss must be proved to obtain a judgment. 

3. Where the child is of tender years and has not been working or earning anything, it is sufficient to put in proof of the general financial condition of the family, and the intelligence, health and inclinations of the child. If the family were poor, the damages of course would be much greater than if the family were wealthy. If the family were wealthy, it is probable that damages could not be proved in an action for the death of a child of tender years. The same would be true in an action for a child old enough to work but who was not working. 

4. In determining the damages the age of the deceased is important. If the deceased is close to the age of twenty-one, the damages would be small as the loss of earnings would be limited to a short period of time. 

5. In order to prove damages it must be shown that the person or persons, who have sustained pecuniary loss. by reason of the death of the child, would take personal property under the statute of distributions. 

6. It must be remembered that where an action is brought for the death of a very young child, who would not be able to earn anything for a number of years, the present value would be substantially reduced by reason of this.

Sec. 81. Death Actions for Adults. 

Hunn v. Railroad Company, 78 Mich. 513.

This was a death action for a twenty-seven year old The deceased was earning $900.00 per year. The man. 178

[§ widow testified that her husband's earnings were her only means of support. An attempt was made to introduce testimony showing that the present value of the amount of earnings during his expectancy was over $10,000. A judgment of $7,575 was given in the lower court, and the judgment was reversed but not on the amount of the verdict. The Supreme Court said that the lower court erred in admitting testimony showing the extent of the financial condition of the relatives and the encumbrance on the land. In commenting on the attempt to show the present value of the earnings during the expectancy, the Court said: "The question is not what he might have earned or saved if he had lived, but it is what she, as his wife, would have realized if his death had not occurred from the collision."

The Court also said that the instruction to allow merely nominal damages so far as the brother and sisters were concerned was correct, inasmuch as they had not sustained any pecuniary damages. 

Van Brunt v. Cincinnati, Jackson & Mackinaw Rd. Co., 78 

Mich. 530.

In this case the deceased was unmarried and twentytwo years of age, having no dependents. He had a father and a brother. The testimony showed that there was a doctor bill of $1.00 and a funeral bill of $60.00, but it was not shown that the father or brother paid for either of the bills. The plaintiff's attorney argued that the damages were for the jury to determine. The Supreme Court said that there could be no recovery as the damages had not been proved, and that damages would not be presumed. 13 179

§ 81] 

Richmond v. Rd. Co., 87 Mich. 374.

This was an action for the death of a thirty-two year old man. The evidence showed that he gave $7.00 per week to his mother for support and $2.00 per week to his sister. A verdict of $5,313 was held to be not excessive. 

In this case the defendant's attorney raised the question as to the proper distribution of the judgment after it was paid. The question was whether the amount of the judgment would be distributed among those, who would take personal property under the statute of distributions, in proportion to the amount they would ordinarily take under the statute. The Supreme Court said that it would consider this question when it was properly brought before it. 

Nelson v. Ry. Co., 104 Mich. 582.

This was an action for the death of a woman fifty-six years of age. The accident took place in Ohio, but the 

Ohio Statute at the time was similar to the Michigan Death Act. The deceased left a husband fifty-six years of age, and four children, two of them minors. She kept roomers and boarders, and the testimony showed that $100.00 per month was taken in. $30.00 was paid out for rent, and, of course, there was a substantial amount of expense for food and upkeep of the house. The only tangible evidence of pecuniary loss to the husband and children was for the board which was furnished them and clothing for the two children who were minors. A verdict of $7,000 was given and this was held to be excessive. 

The Supreme Court said: 

"It is not enough to prove the marriage, age and death, and then turn a jury loose upon a field of speculation to hunt for some basis for a verdict." 

The Court said that the compensation provided by the statute was strictly pecuniary and that there could be no 180

[§ compensation for grief, loss of companionship, wounded feelings or suffering, either of the deceased or of the beneficiaries. The Court also stated that the services must be proved and the value shown and stated that it was absurd to say under the facts that the husband and children sustained pecuniary loss of $7,000. 

Rouse v. Detroit Electric Ry., 128 Mich. 149.

A verdict of $5,550 was rendered in this case. The deceased left a widow and seven children. His expectancy was twenty-five years. The Supreme Court held that the lower court was in error in permitting the jury to consider damages to the children beyond their minority. 

"As to the children, no damages could be recovered for their support after they became of age. 

We do not pass on the question whether damages might be allowed for a dependent child after he becomes of age." 

Richardson v. Detroit Ry. Co., 176 Mich. 413.

In this case the deceased was single and thirty-seven years of age, being a school teacher. She made $60.00 per month and helped to support her father, who was seventy years of age and in bad health, and her mother, who was an invalid. The testimony showed that she contributed $40.00 per month during the school year and $15.00 to $20.00 in the other months. There was no testimony that the parents would have been a charge on the public if they had not had the help of their daughter. 

The Supreme Court said that the lower court was in error in permitting a recovery for the sister's pecuniary loss as at the time the statute of distributions did not make the sister a beneficiary. The Court held that the 181

§ 81] 

recovery for the pecuniary loss sustained by the parents was proper and said: "The fact, if it be a fact, that the plaintiff's decedent voluntarily assumed the performance of a duty which might be regarded as a legal obligation and made expenditures to a proper extent, might form a basis for a recovery in this action insofar as the father and mother are concerned." 

Ormsbee v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 197 Mich. 576.

This was an action for a sixty-nine year old man whose occupation was a ditch digger. His wife met instantaneous death with him. They left four adult children. Three of the children were married women in comfortable circumstances, and the other was a son who was married, supporting himself and wife. The testimony showed that at times the decedent brought eggs and chickens from his farm to two of the daughters. They valued his gift at $50.00 per year for each of them. There was a directed verdict for the defendant, and this was affirmed by the Supreme Court. The Court pointed out that the children of the decedent, being adults, were not legally entitled to support, and that this was a necessary prerequisite to pecuniary injuries under the statute. "It is equally clear that the occasional or even habitual donations by said decedent to one or more of his children of fruit, vegetables, eggs, or chickens, does not constitute such an assumption of a legal obligation as was held in the Richardson case to form a basis for a recovery." 

Sipes v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 231 Mich. 404. 

The decedent, twenty-four years old, left a widow twenty-one years of age and a child. He was earning slightly more than $60.00 per month. The defendant re- 182

[§ quested an instruction that the jury should consider the possibility of the widow's remarriage in fixing the pecuniary loss. This instruction was not given. It was held that this instruction should have been given. The 

Court also said that in the absence of evidence tending to show a reasonable prospect of larger earnings in the future, the jury should have based its finding of pecuniary loss upon his known earnings. The Court did say that the loss to the child may include expense for supplying such degree of nurture, and intellectual, moral and physical training as the parent was capable of giving. 

The verdict of $15,166 was called excessive. 

Following is a list of cases which do not add to the above cases on the law of damages in Death Actions for adults, but which do show the tendency of the Court in the matter of damages. 

Andrews v. Tamarack Mining Co., 114 Mich. 375.

This was a death action brought for a man who was earning $2.00 per day. A verdict of $12,000 was rendered. This was held to be excessive. The Supreme 

Court said that the interest on the verdict would amount to more than $2.50 per day, leaving the principal untouched. 

King v. Ann Arbor Rd. Co., 144 Mich. 65.

This was a death action for an assistant lighthouse keeper earning $450.00 per year and in line for promotion. He left a wife thirty-one years old and a seven months old child. He had an expectancy of thirty-five years. The verdict of $8,000 was reduced to $5,000. 

Little v. Bousfield & Co., 165 Mich. 654.

In this case the decedent's expectancy was twenty-one years.

The deceased at the time of death was in a 183

§ 82] 

diseased condition.

He contributed $22.50 to his wife each month. A verdict of $5,077 was reduced to $3,403. 

Wavle v. Michigan United Ry. Co., 170 Mich. 81.

This was an action for the death of a seventy-two year old farmer. He left a widow, and a claim was made that, inasmuch as the widow could support herself, she did not suffer much pecuniary loss. It was held by the Court that the fact that the widow could support herself made no difference. 

McDonnell v. Central Drug Co., 170 Mich. 291. 

Here a man forty-six years of age was killed. He had supported his family in the past and eleven months before his death he left his family in Flint, Michigan. He went to Detroit and worked as a porter for eleven months without contributing to his family. The verdict was for $6,268, but the Supreme Court cut this to $3,000. 

Meola v. Quincy Mining Co., 174 Mich. 305.

The verdict in this case was $5,040. The deceased contributed $25.00 every second month to his family. The amount of his contribution during his expectancy would not have amounted to more than $1,300. The verdict was held to be excessive. 

Tuttle v. Briscoe Manufacturing Co., 190 Mich. 22.

In this case the decedent was forty-two years of age. 

He was a married man earning $3,500 per year in a department store in Detroit. A verdict of $10,000 was held to be not excessive.

Sec. 82. Summary. 

In finding the amount of damages in an action for death of an adult it is, of course, necessary to make cer- 184

[§ tain that those who have suffered any pecuniary injury would take personal property from the deceased under the statute of distributions. It can clearly be seen that in some cases where an action is brought for the death of an adult it would be very difficult to prove any pecuniary injury to any of the heirs of the deceased. A number of typical situations are here given. 

1. A deceased without heirs or next of kin. In this situation there would be no damages as there would be no heir or next of kin to sustain pecuniary injury. 

2. The deceased, an old man or woman, who is a dependent. In this case there would be no damage as the deceased would have no dependents and would be supporting no one. The heirs could suffer no pecuniary loss. 

3. The deceased, a young single man not supporting anyone. In this type of case there would be no damage as the heirs could show no pecuniary loss. 

4. A young married man supporting a family. In this situation the damages would be heavy, if the deceased had a substantial earning power. 

5. The deceased, a housewife. In this situation it would be difficult to prove any pecuniary loss other than loss of services sustained by the husband, unless the wife helped to support the family as in the case of Nelson v. 

Railway Company, 104 Mich. 582, cited above.

From the above cases the following general rules can be given in actions for the wrongful death of adults. 

1. The measure of damages is the actual pecuniary injury sustained by those who would take personal property under the statute of distributions. 

2. In determining the amount of pecuniary injury, the expectancy of the deceased governs unless it is longer than the expectancy of the beneficiary. The expectancy of the beneficiary governs if it is shorter than that of the deceased. 185

§ 82] 

3. Although no Michigan case discusses the matter thoroughly, the amount of expenses incurred by the beneficiary in the way of contributions or support should be subtracted from the amount of contribution made by the deceased to the beneficiary. 

4. The pecuniary injury is not the amount of earnings of the deceased but the amount which the deceased contributed. In other words, the expenses of the deceased in supporting himself cannot be considered as pecuniary injury to a beneficiary. 

5. The pecuniary injury to minor children extends only during their minority. Where adult children survive the deceased, they cannot claim pecuniary injury unless the contributions for support are such as amount to an assumption of a legal obligation. 

6. Funeral expenses are a pecuniary injury if they are borne by the beneficiary. 

7. Services which constitute pecuniary injury should be proved and the value shown. 186

Sec. 83. Survival Actions for Minors. 

If the deceased minor survives an appreciable length of time, sufficient to bring the action within the Survival Statute, the measure of damages is entirely different from that found in the cases of instantaneous death. The difference should be great because the survival case is not supposed to be an action for death. It is a continuation of the action for personal injuries which would have existed if the injured person had not died. The 

Michigan decisions, which have resulted from actions under the Survival Statute for injuries causing death, are as follows: 

Love v. Detroit, Jackson & Chicago Rd. Co., 170 Mich. 1.

This was an action under the Survival Statute for a six year old boy. The child survived the accident eight hours. The verdict was $4500.00. Of this, $2000.00 was for pain and suffering. The judgment was affirmed. The 

Supreme Court said that from the nature of the case the damages could not be estimated with certainty, either as to pain, or as to future earnings after the age of 21, but that this did not prevent the award of damages. The fact that the child died before he became a wage earner 187

§ 83] 

would not prevent an inquiry as to the probable value of his services for the years ensuing his death. 

Swaczyk v. Detroit Edison Co., 207 Mich. 494.

In this case the deceased was a 13 year old boy, who lived one hour. The verdict of $6500 was reduced to $5000 by the Supreme Court.  "Conscious pain with attendant mental and physical distress for years, for which large verdicts have sometimes been sustained, are not involved here."

The Court also said that there was force to the contention that the verdict was beyond the fair measure of damages. 

Ignaszak v. McCray, 221 Mich. 10.

The deceased was a four year old boy. A verdict of $8000 was reduced to $5000. The Court cited cases in other states, indicating that the verdict was excessive, and pointed out that it had no means of knowing what portion of the verdict was for pain and suffering. 

Stone v. Sinclair Refining Co., 229 Mich. 103.

A verdict of $7380 was given, the deceased being a 7 year old girl, who was badly burned and survived four hours, being unconscious most of the time. The lower court, in the instruction, implied that the plaintiff might have recovered for "unconscious pain." The Supreme

Court ordered a new trial, saying that the instruction was not correct and evidently affected the verdict. 

Mulvihill v. Detroit United Ry., 231 Mich. 123.

This was a survival action for a 20 month old boy, who lived 40 hours after the accident. The verdict of $12,500 was reduced to $5000 by the Supreme Court. It 188

[§ was pointed out that it would have been 19 years before the child would have earned anything for himself. The 

Court said that no hard and fast rule could be laid down for computing damages in the case of young children. 

Stone v. Sinclair Refining Co., 235 Mich. 53.

The facts were given above in 229 Mich. 103. In the new trial a verdict of $6,125 was rendered. The jury awarded $2,000 for pain, and the rest for loss of earnings. The Supreme Court reduced the verdict to $5000, saying: "We are of the opinion, however, that the verdict as a whole was excessive under the trend of judicial opinion in similar survival cases involving actionable deaths of young dependent and unproductive children, where the technical distinction in cause and result under the death act and the survival act hinges on but a short intervening time between the palpable death-dealing accident and the resulting inevitable death with the question of conscious suffering at issue." 

Nicholas v. Maxwell Motor Corp., 237 Mich. 612.

The deceased was a boy 14 years old. He lived for 3 days. The testimony showed that he would have become a journeyman carpenter in four or five years, which would pay 90 cents to $1.00 per hour according to averages for the past four years. The boy at the time of death was an apprentice carpenter making $12.00 per week. He suffered pain during his survival. A verdict of $20,000 was cut to $15,000 by the Supreme Court. The 

Court said: "Loss of earnings would not accrue until he would have reached the age of 21. The plaintiff will have the use of the sum so allowed from the time of judgment until then, a period of four years." 189

§ 83] 

Oakes v. Van Zomeren, 255 Mich. 372.

The decedent was 7 years old. The boy survived 15 hours, being at least semi-conscious all but two hours. 

A $4500 judgment was affirmed, the Court saying: "Nothing short of a substantial sum can in good conscience be considered as fair compensation for the pain and suffering plaintiff's decedent must have endured."

The testimony showed that the boy was healthy and normally intelligent. 

Kinsler v. Simpson, 257 Mich. 7.

The decedent, a girl 17 months old, survived 20 minutes, not regaining consciousness. A verdict of $3000 was upheld, the Court saying: "The testimony covers the usual field relative to the health of plaintiff's decedent during her short life, the age and health of the parents, brothers and sisters, grandparents, etc. Also the station in life of the family is disclosed, including the occupation of the child's father." 

Sunday v. Wolverine Service Stations, 265 Mich. 19.

In this case a six year old boy was burned and lived nine hours. The judgment was reversed because of improper instructions. It should be noted that one Justice, in a dissenting opinion, commented on the award of $6000 for pain, saying that it should be reduced to $3000, leaving a judgment of $6000 in all. 

Janse v. Haywood, 270 Mich. 632.

This was a survival action for a 15 year old girl who lived for only a few minutes. A verdict of $6500 was rendered. In reversing the judgment, because of the in- 190

[§ jection of insurance into the case, the Court said that the influence on the jury was reflected in the amount of the verdict. 

See also Bos v. Gaudio, 267 Mich. 517.

Sec. 84. Summary. 

It is important to realize in these cases that, as the deceased would not have earned anything for himself until 21 years of age, the amount recovered would be affected substantially by this fact. Therefore, where there is an action for a one year old child, the judgment should be less than that given for a 9 year old child, other things being equal. The fact that the expectancy period beyond 21 is much more certain for a child 15 years old than for one two years old is also an important factor in determining damages.

The following general rules can be applied to actions under the Survival Statute for minors. 

1. The measure of damages is the pain and suffering up to the time of death plus loss of earnings beyond the age of 21. 

2. The loss of earnings must be figured according to present value. 

3. Where there is little or no pain and suffering, the recovery for an unproductive child of tender years is limited (if the decisions are to be followed) to about $5000. 

4. If the child has been earning money, a substantially greater recovery will be upheld, depending upon the indicated earning power of the minor. 

Sec. 85. Survival Actions for Adults. 

The measure of damages in survival actions for adults is about the same as that in survival actions for minors. 191

§ 85]  

However, the results of the actions are usually different. 

In a minor's suit the evidence as to earnings is ordinarily speculative. In the case of an adult the earning power, based upon past earnings, is generally fairly definite. 

The Michigan cases dealing with actions under the Survival Statute involving death of adults are given here in their chronological order. 

Kyes v. Valley Telephone Co., 132 Mich. 281.

The deceased was 39 years of age. He was conscious for about twenty-five hours before death. His earnings were $2.50 per day. A verdict of $5,000 was given and the judgment was affirmed.  "When an action survives, the representatives of the deceased are entitled to recover the same measure of damages that he could have recovered if he had lived to bring his suit to a successful issue." 

Olivier v. Houghton County Street Ry. Co., 134 Mich. 367.

In this case the deceased remained unconscious for fourteen hours up to the time of death. The defendant contended that there could be a recovery for only pain and suffering and loss of earnings up to the time of death. A verdict of $4.00 was appealed by the plaintiff, the lower court having followed the defendant's contention in instructing the jury. The Supreme Court reversed the lower court, saying: "An injured person may recover for loss of earnings for the period during which the evidence fairly shows that he would have lived but for the injury. 

This rule would apply to one who should live long enough to try his case, though he should die the following day. But defendant's contention would substitute another rule upon a second trial after his death should such trial become necessary. Such re- 192

[§ covery is based upon a probable prospective incapacity for a probable period. After death, such incapacity (and consequent loss) is made certain, where it was only probable before. The period alone remains uncertain." 

Olivier v. Houghton County Street Ry. Co., 138 Mich. 242.

This case was the new trial resulting from the above decision. A verdict of $7300 was rendered. The defendant contended that the expenses of the deceased for food, clothing and personal expenditures should be subtracted from the loss of earnings. The Supreme Court disagreed with the defendant.  "The action is to recover the damages which have resulted as a present loss to the injured party, in being deprived of a capacity to earn money, which capacity he had before the injury, and which he now has not."

The Court also said that it was none of the defendant's business how an injured party disposed of the money received in compensation for the injury, and consequently the fact that the person who was injured was dead and had no expenses made no difference. 

Davis v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 147 Mich. 479.

The lower court instructed the jury in this manner: "If you find for the plaintiff, you will render a verdict for all damages sustained in consequence of the injury to and the death of the young man. These will comprise a reasonable amount for any pain and suffering he endured from the time of the injury to his death, and, in addition, a reasonable amount for all sums that he would probably have earned during the years that he would probably have lived, but for the injury." 193

§ 85] 

The Supreme Court held that there was no error in this instruction. 

Stone v. Sinclair Refining Company, 229 Mich. 103.

A verdict of $7380 was given in this case where a woman was badly burned. At times she appeared to be conscious but most of the time was unconscious during the four hours of survival. The defendant complained of this instruction: "Consider and determine whether she was conscious or unconscious, because it is a matter of common experience and common observation that a person that is unconscious does not suffer as much pain as he or she does if entirely conscious." The Supreme 

Court said that in view of the size of the verdict the language constituted reversible error. 

Stone v. Sinclair Refining Company, 230 Mich. 472. 

For the facts in this case see 225 Mich. 344 and 229 

Mich. 103. The suit was brought under the Survival

Statute to recover for pain and suffering. The decedent, a woman, was badly burned and lived four hours. She suffered intense pain and was aware that she would die. 

The verdict was for $8000. The Supreme Court, in holding that the judgment should be reduced to $4000, said: "Assessment of damages for pain and suffering demands calm calculation, to some extent a heartless computation, and the feelings must be held in check, in order to arrive at a reasonable money award." 

Patton v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 236 Mich. 173. 

The decedent was 57 years of age and in good health.

He was working as a drayman. A verdict of $8560 was held to be not excessive. 194

[§ 

Siegel v. Detroit Cab Co., 246 Mich. 620.

In this case the deceased was engaged in the cartage business. He was 40 years old and in good health. His earnings were $50.00 per week. It was shown that he suffered pain. A verdict of $8000 was held to be not excessive. 

Collins v. Hull, 256 Mich. 507.

The decedent, a housewife 60 years of age, lived four days, during which she was conscious and suffered very great pain. A verdict of $4000 was upheld. 

Cooper v. Interstate Motor Freight Co., 264 Mich. 131.

The deceased was a partner in an electrical business. 

The testimony showed that each partner drew $40.00 per week as salary and that each withdrew $302.50 as profit in the past year. The Supreme Court held that it was error to admit evidence as to profits withdrawn from the business in the absence of an allocation of any part of these profits to capital investment. The court said it could not tell how the verdict was computed and said, citing another case: "Furthermore, the loss of profits in conducting a business involving the labor of others is not a necessary consequence of personal injury to the plaintiff. 

The extent of his recovery upon this ground would be what his services were worth in the conduct of such a business as he was engaged in.” 

Newell v. Ritter, 268 Mich. 405.

The decedent was 67 years of age. He was a prosperous farmer, strong and vigorous, and the owner of a 40 acre farm. The court said that it was difficult to estimate the probable earnings of a farmer. A $2500 judgment was upheld. 14 195

§ 86] 

Hanna v. McClave, 271 Mich. 133.

This was a survival action for a 76 year old man. The jury was instructed that burial expenses were part of the damages. In a dissenting opinion it was said that burial expenses were not part of the damages in survival actions. The majority opinion did not comment on this statement.

Sec. 86. Summary. 

The Michigan Supreme Court has, in a number of opinions, said that the Death Act created a new cause of action, while an action under the Survival Statute merely carried on an action already existing. Yet in defining the measure of damages in a survival action, the Court has virtually provided an action for death. In certain cases, it is true that the measure of damages would of necessity be the loss of earnings for the expectancy of the deceased. For instance, where a person died as a result of being hopelessly crippled, the damages would probably have been as great, so far as loss of earnings are concerned, if he had lived. However, in the situation where the decedent died from nervous shock, or from pneumonia or some other illness resulting from minor injuries, the decedent would not have lost his capacity to earn, if he had lived. Apparently there is no decision in 

Michigan in which the Court has been presented with this question and has thoroughly considered it. The Court has often said that in survival cases the recovery shall be the same as though the decedent had lived. If the decedent had lived in certain cases, he would have recovered from the nervous shock, or pneumonia, or his injuries, sufficiently, to earn as much, or nearly as much as before. 

If the court is to follow this argument out, it would seem that there should be a recovery for loss of earnings for a 196

[§ period of time during which the deceased would have lost his earnings had he lived. Of course the allowance for pain and suffering would be increased to allow for the pain which the deceased would have undergone had he lived. 

There is no question as to the measure of damages which is to be applied in an action under the Survival Statute as given by the Supreme Court. As the law now stands an action under the Survival Statute is virtually an action for death with a different measure of damages from that under the Death Act.

The following general rules can be worked out from the cases: 

1. The measure of damages includes pain and suffering up to the time of death, and loss of earnings during the expectancy of the deceased. 

2. If the deceased was unconscious up to the time of death, there is no recovery for pain and suffering. 

3. In the case of a housewife, not working outside her home, the damages would probably be restricted to pain and suffering. 197
