Sec. 87. Actions for Loss of Services. 

The right of a parent to recover for the loss of services of a child killed by wrongful act, or the right of a husband to recover for the loss of services of a wife, where there has been a survival, has not been determined in a well considered opinion by the Michigan Supreme Court. 

In an action under the Death Act the loss of services, sustained by a parent or a husband, is pecuniary injury. 

Consequently, where death is instantaneous there is no necessity for a separate action for loss of services. 

At common law, before the Death Acts or Survival Stat utes were passed, it seems to have been definitely decided that there was no right of action against a wrongdoer to recover for the loss of services caused by death. "The law has not become established indeed without vigorous dissent upon the part of able judges, but the common law rule may now be broadly stated to be that no civil action can be maintained against a person for causing the death of a human being." 

Tiffany's Death by Wrongful Act, 2nd Edition, p. 3. 

To get the history of the law in Michigan on the question it is necessary to carefully inspect the case of Hyatt v. Adams, decided in 1867. 198

MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS IN DEATH ACTIONS [§ 87 

Hyatt v. Adams, 16 Mich. 180.

This was a malpractice suit. The plaintiff's wife had died three days after an operation. A claim was made for loss of services, and a verdict of $2,000 was rendered. 

The evidence showed the services to be worth fifty cents per day. The Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decision, holding that there was no right to recover for loss of services, except for the three days preceding the death of the wife. The opinion gives the reasons for not allowing a recovery for the loss of services due to death.

It should be noted that at the time of this decision there was no Survival Statute applying to personal injury actions. 

Verlinde v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 165 Mich. 371.

This case was decided in 1911. The declaration contained one count, and sought to recover for loss of services of the deceased for 8 years until he would have become 21 years old. Damages under the Survival Statute were also alleged. The Supreme Court held that the defendant's objections to the declaration were well founded. 

"Independent of statute, the father could only recover for the loss of services accruing between the injury and death. No cause of action survived for loss of services which belonged to the father. And the father could not confer upon the administrator a cause of action for loss of services subsequent to death which he himself did not possess."'

The opinion indicated clearly that there could be no recovery for loss of services after death. The reasoning of the court in this case was approved in Lincoln v. Detroit & Mackinac Ry. Co., 179 Mich. 189. 199

§ 87]  

Kerns v. Lewis, 249 Mich. 27.

This was an action for the loss of services due to the death of the plaintiff's wife resulting from injuries. The deceased survived the injuries 6 months. Because of the length of the survival and the absence of comment by the Court on the question as to whether there could be a recovery for loss of services after death, this decision does not reverse the earlier Michigan decisions. 

Collins v. Hull, 256 Mich. 507.

This was an action under the Survival Statute for injuries resulting in the death of the plaintiff's decedent. 

The decedent was a housewife and lived for four days. 

The Court said that the decedent's husband was entitled to her services as a housekeeper and he alone could recover for them. Consequently there could be no recovery for loss of services in this action by the administrator. 

Scurlock v. Peglow, 263 Mich. 658. 

The plaintiff's wife was instantly killed in an accident and the plaintiff was seriously injured. He sued for his injuries and also for the loss of services of his wife. $3,000 of the amount of the verdict was for loss of services. The question as to whether it was proper to permit an action for loss of services by the plaintiff apparently was not raised. It should be noted that the death was instantaneous, and the husband could have recovered for pecuniary injury, which would have been loss of services, as beneficiary in an action under the Death Act.

From these cases it cannot be said definitely that where the question is raised properly, the Michigan Supreme 

Court would or would not permit a recovery for loss of services after death, where there has been a survival. 

To permit a recovery would, in the ordinary situation, virtually give a remedy under both the Death Act and 200

MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS IN DEATH ACTIONS [§ 88 the Survival Statute. For the damages under the Death 

Act would usually be loss of services where a minor child or a housewife were killed. To permit both a recovery by an administrator under the Survival Statute, and a recovery by a parent or husband for loss of services would shatter the effect of the jealously guarded principle in Michigan, that there cannot be a recovery under each statute for the death of one person. It would seem that the Survival Statute should not apply to an action for loss of services in the situation in question as the statute does not name such actions, and in addition it is generally understood that the Statute applies to prevent abatement of an action by death of a party. In the situation in question the party having the action is the husband or parent of the deceased. Death of the husband or parent would cut short the damages. Probably that is the reason the Survival Statute does not include loss of service actions by reference. Another sound reason for not allowing a recovery is that the Death Act alone provides for actions for wrongful death. Therefore, actions for the death of another should be grounded under the Death Act only in Michigan. Consequently, an action for the loss of services of a child or wife, who has survived injuries for some time, should be restricted to a recovery for loss of services up to the time of death and not beyond. Otherwise an action for death would be permitted not based upon the Death Act.

Sec. 88. Pleading. 

Where the plaintiff's declaration sets forth a cause of action under the Death Act, the statute should be referred to as the action is based upon a statute. See 1929

Compiled Laws 14129. 

In the case of Hurst v. Detroit City Ry., 84 Mich. 539, it was held that the plaintiff could not amend his decla- 201

§ 89] 

ration by inserting the Survival Statute as he had proceeded under the Death Act, and the amendment would introduce a new and different cause of action. 

However, it is proper to have two counts in the declaration, one under the Survival Statute and one under the Death Act. Where there is any doubt on the question of survival the declaration should be drawn in this manner. 

The plaintiff cannot be forced to make an election at the time of trial. The question of survival is for the jury unless the Court decides that the testimony does not present any question. See Carbary v. Detroit United Ry., 157 Mich. 683; Ely v. Detroit United Ry., 162 Mich. 287.

The two theories cannot be combined in one count as was held in Verlinde v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 165 Mich. 371.

For the rules of pleading as to damages the cases should be consulted. In alleging damages it is wise to be as specific as possible, especially in actions under the Death Act. The manner in which the beneficiaries will suffer pecuniary loss should be set forth in detail. The age and expectancy of the deceased should be given. The beneficiaries under the Death Act should be named and their ages given.

Sec. 89. Contributory Negligence of Beneficiary. 

In automobile accident cases it is not unusual to have a beneficiary guilty of negligence. For instance a minor child is riding with his father. The father is negligent and drives his car against another negligently driven automobile. The child is killed instantly. Suit is brought under the Death Act against the driver of the other car. 

Will the father's negligence bar a recovery by reason of the fact that he is a beneficiary? In Michigan, if the sole beneficiary is negligent, there can be no recovery. See 202

MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS IN DEATH ACTIONS [§ 90 

Feldman v. Detroit United Ry., 162 Mich. 486; Flintoff v. 

Muskegon Traction & Light Co., 208 Mich. 527.

If the negligent beneficiary is not the sole heir a recovery would probably be allowed in Michigan as indicated in the opinion in Love v. Detroit Rd. Co., 170 Mich. 

1. The weight of authority in the United States permits a recovery in such a situation. See 69 A. L. R. 478.

If the action is brought under the Survival Statute, negligence of the parent, as one who would benefit from a judgment, does not bar recovery. McCann v. City of Detroit, 234 Mich. 268.

Sec. 90. Effect of Defendant's Death Upon Death Action. 

Whether or not an action under the Death or Survival Statute survives the death of the defendant is an important question considering the number of automobile accidents where the wrongdoer is killed. As the Survival 

Statute applies not only to the death of a plaintiff but also to the death of a defendant, an action under the Survival Statute would surely survive where there has been any survival on the part of the defendant. 

The Michigan Supreme Court in the case of Ford v. 

Maney's Estate, 251 Mich. 461, considered this question and decided that if the tort-feasor lived any length of time, even only a few seconds, there was an action to survive. In this case the action was for injuries. The 

Court refused to pass upon the question as to whether there would have been any survival had the tort feasor been killed at the instant of injury.

The question is entirely different if the suit is brought under the Death Act. The overwhelming weight of authority in other states is that where an action lies under the Death Act and the defendant dies the action is abated. 

For a statement as to the general rule see 17 C. J. 1233. 203

§ 91]  

There is no decision in Michigan on the point. However, the Michigan Court would logically be forced to follow the majority rule. In Lincoln v. Railway Co., 179 Mich. 

189, it was held that the Death Act created a new right of action. The Death Act does not provide for a survival of the cause of action in case the wrongdoer dies. The Survival Statute does not mention actions for death. A few states have broad enough survival statutes to make the action survive. In Michigan it is quite obvious that the death of the wrongdoer at any time before judgment destroys the administrator's right under the Death Act.

Sec. 91. Other Miscellaneous Matters. 

The Death Act is considered substantive. If the wrong or injury is done in another state, the law of that state controls as to whether there is an action for death. All substantive matters are determined by the law of the state where the accident occurred, even though the death occurred in Michigan. See Petruska v. Korinek, 237 

Mich. 583.

The proper form of the verdict is indicated in the case of Jewell v. Rogers Township, 208 Mich. 318. The problem as to how the verdict is to be divided among the beneficiaries is outside the province of the jury. A special question may be submitted to the jury as to whether death was instantaneous. See Besonen v. Campbell, 243 

Mich. 209.

The right of action under the Death Act as well as that under the Survival Statute is considered an asset of the estate. This would be of importance where the decedent was instantly killed and left no other estate and there was a petition for appointment of administrator in the jurisdiction of the wrongdoer outside the county of the decedent's residence. Carbary v. Detroit United Ry., 157 

Mich. 683. 204

CHAPTER XVI PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE Sec. 92. Cases Having No Witnesses.

Sec. 92.

Cases Having No Witnesses. 

The presumption that the deceased exercised due care is indulged in because the mouth of the deceased is closed. 

He cannot describe his own actions. However, if there are witnesses, who can describe the actions of the deceased, it would seem that the presumption should not operate. So we read in the earlier cases the repeated statement that, in the absence of witnesses, the deceased is presumed to have exercised due care.

But a close examination of the many cases in Michigan, discussing this question, reveals a more complicated test than the absence or presence of witnesses in determining when the presumption operates. For instance, in the cases where there are no witnesses, the presumption may be relied upon entirely as declaring the decedent not negligent; it may be used only to send the case to the jury; or the presumption may not be relied upon at all. 

In the cases where there are witnesses we have an even more confused situation. Hence, in trying to determine 205

§ 92-a]  

the true test, the cases will be divided into two main groups. First, those in which there were no witnesses who saw the actions of the deceased. Second, those cases having witnesses.

Sec. 92-a. Presumption Relied Upon as to All of the 

Actions of the Decedent. 

Lincoln v. Detroit & Mackinac Ry. Co., 179 Mich. 189.

The decedent with three companions had rented one of defendant's boats and had gone for a boat ride. They were later found drowned, pieces of the boat being discovered indicating defective condition of the boat. It was held that the presumption could be relied upon, and the only question was the negligence of the defendant. It was said: "It should be borne in mind that there is no living witness to the drowning, and that decedent is not here to give his testimony. In the absence of such testimony the presumption is that he and his companions were in the exercise of due care, which presumption is sufficient to permit a recovery if negligence is shown on the part of the defendant." 

For the opinion on the second trial of the case see 197 Mich. 504, where a judgment for the plaintiff was reversed. 

Kruis v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 190 Mich. 105.

In this case a boy was electrocuted evidently while playing near a fence which was close to a third rail. The plaintiff's theory was that a loose wire was blown against the fence and the third rail. The court said: "In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, no person having seen the accident, it is presumed. 206

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 92-a that the plaintiff's decedent was free from any contributory negligence."

In this case several boys, who were playing at the scene of the accident, were in court under subpoena but did not testify. 

Clark v. Detroit & Mackinac Ry. Co., 197 Mich. 489.

This was another case of drowning while boat riding in a small boat, the facts being the same as the Lincoln case given above. The court said: "In any event, the presumption referred to is indulged only to relieve a plaintiff from an inference of negligence, and not to supply evidence of the negligence of a defendant.'

It was pointed out that the facts proved in this case were not those proved in the Lincoln case. The majority of the Court held that negligence had not been proved against the defendant, it being purely conjectural whether the loss of the boat and of the lives was the result of defendant's negligence. 

Clark v. Lawrence Baking Co., 240 Mich. 352.

The decedent was found lying on the highway. The defendant ran over him, thinking he was a blanket lying in the road. It was held that in the absence of witnesses the decedent was presumed to have exercised due care. 

Wilkins v. Bradford, 247 Mich. 157.

An eight year old boy was carrying milk along a trunk line highway. It was nearly dark. He was found dead, lying on the east side of the highway. The defendant had driven north on the road at about the time when the accident must have occurred. A mile north of the point where the boy was found, the defendant's car was in a 207

§ 92-b] 

slight accident. A south bound driver testified that he met no other vehicles, after passing defendant's car just before it struck the wagon, before he reached the boy. 

Milk was found on the defendant's radiator and also hair of the same color and texture as that of the decedent. 

There was a dent in the radiator about the size of the boy's head. There was no direct evidence of defendant's negligence. However, it was held that there was sufficient evidence to take the case to the jury. 66 'Assuming from the verdict that defendant's car struck decedent, and from the presumption of law that the decedent was in the exercise of due care, it is a legitimate inference, if not an inevitable conclusion, that defendant was guilty of one or more of the acts of negligence charged against him. 

The injury could not have occurred with both defendant and decedent exercising due care." 

Sec. 92-b. Presumption Relied Upon Only to Take Case to Jury. 

Adams v. Iron Cliffs Co., 78 Mich. 271.

The decedent was found dead under the wheels of a car on a train which had been standing for a long time and had just started. There were banks of snow on each side of the track. The plaintiff's theory was that the decedent was walking on the side of the snow bank, and had a hand against the car when the train started. 

It was held that it was a question of fact for the jury as to the plaintiff's contributory negligence. The Court said that the plaintiff had the right to go to the jury under his theory, if it did not amount to contributory negligence. "If there was, under the facts shown, a chance for different conclusions to be drawn by ordinarily can- 208

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 92-c did and intelligent men, it was a question to be determined by the jury and not by the court." 

Gilbert v. Ann Arbor Rd. Co., 161 Mich. 73.

The decedent caught his foot in the track. There were no witnesses. There was a question as to whether the defective condition was known to the defendant. The 

Court held that the plaintiff's contributory negligence was a question for the jury. 

Richardson v. Detroit & Mackinac Ry. Co., 176 Mich. 413.

A young woman, who had planned to take a train early in the morning, was found dead near the track and station platform. The plaintiff's theory was that she was near the track and was sucked in by a passing special train.

It was held that the question of the plaintiff's contributory negligence, especially in view of the presumption, was for the jury.

Sec. 92-c. Where Circumstances Show Decedent Was 

Negligent. 

Elrich v. Schwaderer, 251 Mich. 33.

The decedent drove his car into the rear of a concrete mixer which was standing on the highway. The collision occurred at night, and there were no eye witnesses of the actions of the decedent. In commenting on the presumption, the Court said that it was overcome by the physical facts, and held the decedent negligent as a matter of law. 

Pomeroy v. Dykema, 256 Mich. 100.

In the daytime the defendant was driving his car south on U. S. 31 in North Muskegon. There was a truck backed against the west curb which occupied practically all of 209

§ 93] 

the west half of the road. This compelled the defendant to drive on the east side of the road in passing the truck. 

He then turned back to the west side of the highway and at that point the decedent was struck. No witness saw the impact or the movement of the decedent from the curb. There was testimony that the door handle on the car was cracked.

It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the plaintiff could not rely upon the presumption as the fair and reasonable inferences from the proof were that the deceased had been negligent.

Tomczyk v. Detroit, Grand Haven & Milwaukee Ry., 267 

Mich. 474.

The decedent was killed while driving his car across a railway crossing. He had an unobstructed view of the approaching train for a long distance at any point within forty feet of the track.

It was held that the known facts showed that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law and the presumption did not apply.

Sec. 93. Summary of Cases Having No Witnesses. 

In this group of cases it is difficult to reconcile the decisions under groups 1 and 2. How can Clark v. Law rence Baking Company be reconciled with Richardson v. Detroit Ry. Co.? In each case the decedent was run over or struck. Yet in the Clark case the presumption was relied upon entirely, and the decedent was presumed to have exercised due care. In the Richardson case the presumption was only relied upon to send the question to the jury. It is significant that the cases under group 2 1 210

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 93 

15 are all railroad cases. This seems to indicate that when a person is killed by a train the chances for contributory negligence are so much greater than in other accidents that the presumption should not be relied upon in keeping the question from the jury. If the Supreme Court follows its recent holding in the Clark case, then it will hold in automobile cases, where the deceased was a pedestrian, that the presumption makes the deceased not negligent. This, of course, would be true only where there are no witnesses to any actions on the part of the deceased. The Clark case is a peculiar one as the deceased was lying helpless on the road when he was run over. It does not represent the usual pedestrian situation and, consequently, should not be given too much importance. The other cases under group 1 involved boys, who died under circumstances which indicated no negligence on their part.

The cases having no witnesses show that the presumption may not operate even though there are no witnesses. 

Circumstances seem to be the controlling factor. following general rules are suggested by these cases. The 

1. Where the circumstances are such that they suggest a theory of death which reasonable persons would agree did not amount to negligence, the presumption will be relied upon entirely. 

2. Where the circumstances are such that they suggest a theory of death upon which reasonable persons would disagree as amounting to negligence, the presumption will be relied upon only to take the question to the jury. 

3. Where the circumstances are such that, under ordinary conditions, they reasonably indicate the deceased was negligent as a matter of law, the presumption does not operate. 211

§ 94] 

 Sec. 94. Cases Having Witnesses. 

Sec. 94-a. Material Actions Witnessed. 

Mynning v. Detroit, Lansing & Northern Rd. Co., 64 

Mich. 93.

The decedent was killed while walking across a railway crossing. Witnesses testified as to the actions of the decedent in approaching and stepping onto the crossing. 

In holding him negligent it was said: "The presumption of law is that the person killed at a crossing did stop, and look and listen, and will prevail in the absence of direct testimony on the subject. But where there is affirmative, direct, and creditable testimony that the person injured went upon the track without stopping to look and listen, the presumption is rebutted and displaced." 

Underhill v. The Chicago & Grand Trunk Ry. Co., 81 

Mich. 43.

The plaintiff offered no proof of the actions of the decedent in crossing defendant's tracks. The defendant showed by the testimony of the fireman of the train that the decedent was negligent in her actions. 

The Court said that if there had been any conflict of testimony as to the actions of the decedent the case should have been submitted to the jury, but as there was no conflict and the testimony showed negligence as a matter of law, there was no question for the jury. 

Gates v. Beebe, 170 Mich. 107.

Defendant's automobile struck the decedent. There was conflicting testimony upon the question of contributory negligence. The lower court instructed the jury that, if the circumstances did not satisfy them that the 212

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 94-b deceased was guilty of negligence, the presumption applied.

In holding that the lower court was in error in giving this instruction, the Court said: "The court was in error in charging that such rule of presumption applied, and such charge was prejudicial to defendant. It added the weight of this presumption to the evidence in behalf of plaintiff, so that, if all the evidence of the attending circumstances did not satisfy them that plaintiff's decedent was guilty of negligence, its weight might have been decisive in his favor.” 

Russo v. City of Grand Rapids, 255 Mich. 474.

In this case the decedent, a pedestrian, was struck by defendant's truck. The Court held that the presumption was not involved. "When the facts surrounding an instant killing are fully disclosed by credible evidence, the facts control and the mentioned presumption is dormant." 

See also Fraser v. McArthur, 271 Mich. 622.

Sec. 94-b. Some of Material Actions Not Witnessed. 

Cinadar v. Detroit, Grand Haven & Milwaukee Ry. Co., 

193 Mich. 38.

The decedent, in a wagon, was killed while crossing railway tracks. His actions were witnessed up to the time he was twenty feet from the track but not after that. 

In holding that a question was presented for the jury, the Court implied that the presumption could be relied upon that the decedent looked before crossing, and at least created a question for the jury. 213

§ 94-b]  

Patterson v. Wagner, 204 Mich. 593.

The decedent, a man 59 years old, was struck by defendant's car while crossing Main street in Jackson from the south to the north on or near the crosswalk. The testimony was rather vague concerning the decedent's actions. There was no testimony as to whether he looked. 

It was almost dark and the defendant did not see him until just before the impact took place.

It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury; that it was for the jury to say whether, under the condition known or which should have been known to him, he exercised care in crossing. 

Gillett v. Michigan United Traction Co., 205 Mich. 410.

In this case the plaintiff testified that because of his injuries his mind was a blank as to what happened. Testimony showed that he turned his car from the curb and drove out onto the car tracks without stopping again. 

The plaintiff contended that he could rely on the presumption of due care as to observation as there was no evidence on that point.

Without holding that the presumption could be relied upon in such a situation, where the plaintiff had lost his memory, the Court affirmed the decision of the lower court, directing a verdict for the defendant. In this opinion the Court discussed the application of the presumption fully. "It will be seen that the real test in each case is whether or not the evidence tending to show contributory negligence, be it direct or circumstantial, is so conclusive that reasonable and unprejudiced minds could not fail to be convinced that decedent was careless. If there is room for reasonable doubt, the question must be submitted to the jury. And while the jury, in weighing the evidence, may not 214

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 94-b consider the presumption, yet if, uninfluenced by the presumption, they reach the conclusion that the evidence tending to show decedent's negligence is not entitled to credit and should be disregarded, the presumption may then be considered as remaining in force so far as may be necessary to establish the fact that the deceased exercised proper care in all respects not expressly established by the evidence." "The attempt to rebut the presumption having failed, it still remains in force so far as may be necessary to cover any particulars not touched on by the evidence."

In this case the Court held that it was clear that if the plaintiff had looked he would have realized the danger and he would have made some effort to avoid the collision. 

Arvo v. Delta Hardware Co., 231 Mich. 488.

The decedent, driving a wagon, made a turn in front of the defendant's approaching car. There was no testimony that the decedent looked or did not look or that he could have seen the car.

It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury and that under the presumption it must be presumed that the decedent looked. 

Petersen v. Lundin, 236 Mich. 590.

The decedent was crossing a street in Menominee and was on a crosswalk when hit by defendant's car. The defendant was the only witness. He did not see the decedent until he was in front of his car. 

It was held that the evidence presented a case for the jury. "In the absence of testimony showing the actions of Mr. Petersen as he approached the path of the 215

§ 94-b] 

oncoming automobile, the law permitted the presumption of due care on his part to carry the issue to the jury. This being true, the court was not in error in instructing the jury that they should assume 

Mr. Petersen saw the automobile." 

Hinchey v. J. P. Burroughs & Son, 240 Mich. 273.

In this case no one saw the decedent's movements until he was within one foot of the defendant's truck. He was crossing a city street in the middle of the block on a dark night.

A judgment for the defendant was reversed and a new trial ordered. The Court said that up to the time the decedent was seen he was presumed to have exercised due care. 

Fenn v. Mills, 243 Mich. 634.

The decedent, while walking from the north to the south curb, was struck by defendant's east bound car. 

The defendant was the only eye witness. He first saw the decedent when the latter was about six feet in front of the car, walking with his head down and his back to the car. The plaintiff, on appeal, contended that the decedent was presumed to have been free from negligence, and the question of contributory negligence should not have been submitted to the jury. 

It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury; that the decedent's conduct in crossing the street in front of the car and the judgment he used was for the jury to determine. 

Richardson v. Williams, 249 Mich. 350.

The decedent, while crossing a highway at noon, was struck by an auto. There was conflicting testimony. The highway was 18 feet wide, and decedent had an unob- 216

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 94-b structed view for one-half mile. He was struck after going 14 feet.

The Court said that the jury should have been instructed that the decedent's acts must be judged as though he had seen the car. "When the presumption is permissible, its function is only provisional; it serves, if at all, alone, and never in company with evidence, and, therefore, cannot be weighed in the scale with or against evidence. The presumption is not evidence at all, but only a rule relative to procedure." 

Billingsley v. Gulick, 252 Mich. 235.

The defendant testified that the decedent was crossing the highway 25 feet ahead of the car, without looking at the car.

The lower court instructed the jury that, to overcome the presumption, the defendant's testimony must show that he saw the deceased a sufficient time in advance so that he might have controlled his car. 

It was held that this was an improper instruction; that if the jury believed the defendant's testimony the decedent was negligent. 

Gembolis v. Rydeski, 258 Mich. 521.

The decedent was struck, at night, by the defendant's car on a country road. The defendant did not see him before the impact.

It was held that the decedent was presumed to have exercised due care and that contributory negligence was not a question for the jury.

For railway crossing cases where the deceased was held negligent as a matter of law, see Kwiotkowski v. Grand 

Trunk Ry. Co., 70 Mich. 549; Baker v. Delano, 191 Mich. 204. 217

§ 95] 

 Sec. 95. Summary of Cases Where There Are Witnesses. 

It is not difficult to understand the decisions in the cases where the material actions of the deceased are witnessed. 

The rule undoubtedly is that where there is direct, positive and credible testimony, uncontradicted, as to negligent acts of the decedent, there should be a directed verdict for the defendant.

The difficulty comes in considering the operation of the presumption as to actions which are not witnessed. In the case of Hinchey v. Burroughs, the court said that the decedent was presumed to have exercised due care up to the time he was first seen. It was not necessary for the court to hold this, and it might be explained away as an unfortunate dictum. Certainly the other pedestrian cases do not go this far. If the Supreme Court held to such a doctrine, it would be necessary for them in many cases to hold the decedent free of any negligence, if the decedent was very close to the car or in front of the car when first seen.

In the cases where the issue of contributory negligence is left to the jury, the presumption still operates to some extent. Thus, if the jury finds that there is no negligence on the part of the decedent from the testimony it may fall back on the presumption to fill up the gaps not covered by the testimony. It is difficult to reconcile some of these cases. For instance, the language used in Petersen v.

Lundin does not fit in with what the court says in Fenn v. 

Mills. In the first case the presumption is relied upon as to observation. In the second case the court seems to forget about the presumption.

The cases in this group seem to indicate that the court will in the future follow these rules, where part of the decedent's actions are not witnessed. 218

PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE CARE [§ 95 

1. The presumption will not be relied upon entirely in freeing the deceased of negligence. In other words, the jury will decide on contributory negligence. (For exception see Gembolis v. Rydeski.) 

2. As to the question of observation the presumption will operate, and it will be presumed that the decedent looked. If the car was visible he will be presumed to have seen it. 

3. The presumption will not operate as to the care exercised by the decedent after he has made his observation. This will be a question for the jury to decide based upon the other testimony and circumstances. 

It appears that in cases where part of the actions are observed and part are not the court will rely upon the presumption as to the major duties of the decedent such as observation and stopping. As to the exercise of judgment once the observation has been made, the court will leave the question to the jury with proper instructions. 

Of course, if the circumstances are such as to indicate clearly that the deceased was negligent, there will be a directed verdict for the defendant. 219
