Sec. 120. Summary-Imputed Negligence. 

Sec. 121. Joint Enterprise. 

Sec. 122. Summary-Joint Enterprise. 

Michigan is one of the few states having a so-called ownership statute. The statute has been amended a number of times since the original act was passed. This chapter deals with the important cases in which the Supreme Court has interpreted the statute. Not only the liability of owners, but the liability of others, is considered in this chapter.

Michigan law on imputed negligence is distinctly contrary to the overwhelming weight of authority in the other states. The ownership statute virtually imputes the negligence of the driver to the owner in certain situations. Consequently, the doctrine of imputed negligence, which imputes the negligence of the driver to the occupant in certain situations, is covered in this chapter. 

Joint enterprise in automobile cases is also considered, as it is closely related to imputed negligence. 

Sec. 96. Liability of Owner. 

Section 4648, Compiled Laws of 1929, sets up the statutory liability of an owner of an automobile. It reads as follows: 

"CIVIL ACTIONS. Nothing herein contained shall be construed to abridge the right of any person to prosecute a civil action for damages for injuries to either person or property resulting from a violation 221

§ 97] 

of any of the provisions of this act by the owner or operator of a motor vehicle, his agent or servant. 

The owner of a motor vehicle shall be liable for any injury occasioned by the negligent operation of such motor vehicle whether such negligence consists of a violation of the provisions of the statutes of the state or in the failure to observe such ordinary care in such operation as the rules of the common law require. 

The owner shall not be liable, however, unless said motor vehicle is being driven with his or her express or implied consent or knowledge. It shall be presumed that such motor vehicle is being driven with the knowledge and consent of the owner if it is driven at the time of said injury by his or her father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, or other immediate member of the family:"

Section 4632 (c), Compiled Laws of 1929, defines "owner" as including "any person, firm, association or corporation owning or renting a motor vehicle or having the exclusive use thereof, under a lease or otherwise, for a period greater than thirty days."

Sec. 97. Constitutionality of Act. 

Daugherty v. Thomas, 174 Mich. 371.

In this case, Thomas, the owner of the automobile, left it at a repair shop for repairs. One of the employees of the repair shop took the car out to test it in company with another employee and, while so testing it, ran into and injured the plaintiff Daugherty.

It should be noted that the lower court rendered judgment for the plaintiff and Thomas appealed. The case was tried under Section 10 of Act No. 318, Public Acts of 

1909. The Court said subdivision 3 of this section of the 

Act was unconstitutional as not a necessary exercise of 222

[§ the police power and a plain violation of the provisions of the Constitution as the taking of property "without due process of law." The statute above only provided that "the owner shall not be so liable in case such motor vehicle should have been stolen."  "Had this provision of the statute been followed by language indicating that the owner shall not be liable in case the automobile or other motor vehicle was taken or used in violation of Act No. 33 of the 

Public Acts of 1909, the infirmity would have been cured." 

Act No. 33, Public Acts of 1909, prohibited the unau thorized taking or using of automobiles without intent to steal the same by drivers or caretakers thereof. Of course, after this decision, the statute was amended so as to provide liability only in case the car was used with the consent or knowledge of the owner. 

Hawkins v. Ermatinger, 211 Mich. 578.

In this case the defendant's automobile was driven by his minor son. The defendant had issued orders to the garage not to allow his son to have the automobile except on written order. The defendant had instructed his son to the same effect. Section 4825, Compiled Laws of 1915, was questioned as unconstitutional. The Court held that the enactment of the statute by the Legislature was a valid exercise of the police power. Consequently, the legislature may, in exercise of police power, impose a liability on the owner of an automobile for damage due to its negligent operation by a member of his family who is using it without his permission and contrary to his orders. 

Bowerman v. Sheehan, 242 Mich. 95.

The same question arose in this case as in Hawkins v. 

Ermatinger. The Court sustained the constitutionality 223

§ 98] 

of Section 4825, Compiled Laws of 1915, by a five to three decision.  "This law should be sustained as a valid exercise of the police power upon the broad principle that he who owns property, in its nature a dangerous instrumentality when recklessly operated, will not be permitted to suffer it to be handled by members of his immediate family, over whom he has full control, in such a negligent manner as to inflict injury upon another without responding in damages therefor." 

Rogers v. Kuhnreich, 247 Mich. 204. 

Who is a member of "immediate family"?

In this case the defendant's nephew, who roomed in an apartment occupied by defendant and his estranged wife and paid her rent for his room, was not a member of defendant's family within the meaning of Section 4825, Compiled Laws of 1915, creating a conclusive presumption that when the automobile was being driven by member of family, it was by the owner's consent, rendering him liable for injuries negligently inflicted. 

In this case it should be noted that the statute at that time provided that where an automobile was operated by an immediate member of the family, the owner was conclusively presumed to have given consent. The statute as it now exists does not contain the word "conclusive." 

Sec. 98. Owner Liable When Car Loaned. 

Stapleton v. Independent Brewing Co., 198 Mich. 170.

In this case, the Independent Brewing Company loaned a truck to another corporation whose employee was driving it at the time that the plaintiff was injured. The 

Court held it was within the police power of the state to enact the statute (Section 4825, Compiled Laws of 1915) 

224

[§ and that there was no violation of constitutional rights in depriving a person of property without due process of law. The present statute safeguards the right of persons using the streets and does not unreasonably infringe the rights of those able to own automobiles.

Sec. 99. Joint Owner. 

Mittelstadt v. Kelly, 202 Mich. 525. 

One Ira J. Kelly and his father, George Kelly, owned an automobile jointly. The son, Ira J. Kelly, while driving the automobile on his own business, negligently injured the plaintiff. The Court held that the father, George Kelly, as joint owner, was not liable.  "It is not evident that the legislature intended to make each part owner of a car liable for the consequences of the negligent operation of it by a co-owner or his agent or employee. In the first place, the foundation for such a rule does not exist, since a part owner of an automobile may not choose the agents or employees of the other owner nor control possession of the car by the co-owner. In the second place, the language of the law, fairly interpreted, does not evidence a purpose to visit upon an owner the consequences of negligence committed by persons whose custody and possession of the car he may not and cannot control. In the third place, it may be said that it is at least doubtful whether the legislative power extends to visiting upon the citizen consequences of tortious actions which he cannot prevent or control."

Sec. 100. Presumption of Consent. 

Transcontinental Insurance Co. v. Berens, 254 Mich. 613. 

In this case it was held that to overcome the presumption created by Section 4648, Compiled Laws of 1929, that 225

§ 101] 

the son was driving his father's truck with his knowledge and consent, the evidence had to be direct, positive and credible. In this case under the evidence, it was properly left to the jury. See also, Karl v. Gary, 255 Mich. 621. 

Barnum v. Berk, 256 Mich. 363.

In this case, the car was owned by the defendant Carl Berk and driven by his nephew, Ventre Berk. The Court held that it was a question for the jury to determine whether or not the car was being driven with the consent of the defendant Carl Berk. Of course, that consent might be either express or implied. It should be noted that under certain circumstances, the jury might find that the owner had given implied consent to drive the car. In close questions, of course, this matter is submitted to the jury.

Sec. 101. Implied Consent-Question for Jury. 

Lidtka v. Wagner, 253 Mich. 379. 

Wagner Brothers operated a garage in Kalamazoo owning an automobile they desired to sell. Lawrence, their salesman, drove the car to Battle Creek and left it with one Badger who had a prospect for it. Badger introduced Lawrence to John Eagy who took the car and drove it and then returned it to Badger's garage. Next day, John Eagy and his father returned to the Badger garage and the salesman in charge told them to take the car and try it. John Eagy drove the car from the garage but then permitted his father to drive when accident happened in juring plaintiff. The Court held: 

"It is well settled that it is not necessary a particular driver must be known to the owner of the car and his driving assented to by the other, (Kerns v. Lewis, 226

[§ 16 

246 Mich. 423). There was sufficient evidence to take the case to the jury on implied consent as to Wagner Brothers." 

Scott v. Wallace, 251 Mich. 28.

Herrig was a brother-in-law of defendant Wallace, who had just been married nine days before the accident, to Herrig's sister. The testimony showed that four or five times before the accident, Wallace suggested that Herrig drive Wallace's car. Wallace gave the key of the car to his wife who sent Herrig to have the battery changed.

Wallace claimed that he especially told his wife that she alone might drive the car. The Court held, following 

Kerns v. Lewis, 246 Mich. 423, that the controlling question was whether the car was being driven with the owner's express or implied consent. The circumstances in the case together with the testimony made it a case for the jury to determine whether the car was being driven with the owner's express or implied consent. The accident in this case happened December 1, 1928. It should be noted that Section 4825, Compiled Laws of 1915, had been amended by Act No. 56, Public Acts of 1927. No claim was made here that Herrig was a member of defendant's immediate family. 

Kerns v. Lewis, 246 Mich. 423.

Defendant was an automobile dealer and had a sales manager by the name of Clinton. Clinton loaned one of the defendant's cars to one John F. Pentkowski who in turn permitted his brother to drive. While so driving, the brother, Walter Pentkowski, injured the plaintiff's intestate. The question arose as to whether or not the defendant gave consent under these circumstances to the driving of his car. The Court said, page 425: "Does the essential consent mentioned in the statute relate to the driver or to the vehicle 'being 227

§ 102] 

driven'? The statute makes the owner liable if the 'motor vehicle is being driven with his or her express or implied consent or knowledge,' and we cannot read into it the restriction that the particular driver must be known by and his driving consented to by the owner. The statute may be drastic, but we cannot render it less so by any permissible construction." 

Sec. 102. Owner-Certificate of Title. 

Endres v. Mara-Rickenbacker Co., 243 Mich. 5.

In this case an automobile dealer who sold a car, loaned license plates to the buyer and delivered possession to the buyer without delivering a certificate of title as required by Act No. 16, Public Acts of 1923, amending Act No. 46, 

Public Acts of 1921, was held liable as owner, under Act 

No. 287, Public Acts of 1925, Section 11, for the negligence of the buyer in driving the car, since the sale was void. 

Scarborough v. Detroit Operating Co., 256 Mich. 173.

The Court held that a purchaser having the exclusive use of an automobile under a conditional sales contract was the "owner" within the meaning of Section 4658, Compiled Laws of 1929, requiring the seller to transfer to the purchaser a certificate of title, although the purchaser agreed to keep the car in the seller's garage. Furthermore, such a conditional sales contract was void for the seller did not transfer to the purchaser a certificate of title as required by said Section 4658. 

Bos v. Holleman De Weerd Auto Co., 246 Mich. 578.

The sale of an automobile without delivery to the purchaser of a certificate of title was void under Act No. 16, Public Acts of 1923. Since there was no consideration, the purchaser was allowed to recover the money paid with interest. 228

[§ 

Kelly v. Lofts, 253 Mich. 552.

Under Section 4660, Compiled Laws of 1929, where the legal ownership of an automobile had passed to the buyer, the Court held that the car could not be returned to the seller without a certificate of title being executed and delivered. 

Schomberg v. Bayly, 259 Mich. 135.

In this case a certificate of title was delivered to the automobile buyer before the accident, in which he was involved, occurred. The buyer's title was perfected as regards liability for said accident, although the delivery thereof was not within ten days after the delivery of the automobile, as required by Sections 4660 to 4665, Compiled Laws of 1929.  "If the sale of the motor vehicle is otherwise effected, title thereto passes and sale becomes fully consummated upon delivery of certificate of title properly executed notwithstanding such delivery is belated." 

Kruse v. Carey, 259 Mich. 157. 

When does title pass?

The Court held in this case that the title to a motor vehicle passes on delivery of a properly executed assignment of certificate of title, notwithstanding there was a delay in forwarding such certificate to the secretary of state. 

Kimber v. Eding, 262 Mich. 670.

It was held that a title to a motor vehicle passed from the seller to the purchaser when the former delivered to the latter an assignment of the certificate of title and not before and, therefore, the purchaser who had not received an assignment of title was not the owner, although he was 229

§ 103] 

in possession of the car.

The Court construed Section 

4660, Compiled Laws of 1929.

In this case, the dealer who took in a second-hand automobile as part of the purchase price of a new one but who had not received an assignment of title at the time it was involved in an accident while being driven by an employee but not on the owner's business, was not the "owner" and therefore was not liable under the statute for the driver's negligence.

Sec. 103. Liability of Owner Knowingly Lending Car to 

Reckless Driver.

The owner of an automobile is liable for the negligence of the borrower where the owner lends it knowing that the borrower is incompetent, reckless and a careless driver, and likely to cause injuries to others in its use.

This is true although the declaration did not allege that the driver was the agent or servant of the owner engaged in his business at the time of the accident. 

Note: Kimber v. Eding, 262 Mich. 670. The Court held that the dealer was not the owner. In Tanis v. Eding, 265 Mich. 95, the dealer was held liable as an owner on a different theory. It should be noted that in Tanis v. 

Eding, the dealer had possession of the car and one of his employees was using it although he did not have a certificate of title.

Sec. 104. Summary-Liability of Owner. 

The ownership statute makes the owner liable for the negligent acts of the driver of his car if it is used with his consent. The following rules are suggested by the cases. 

1. A joint owner, who is not using the car at the time of the accident, it being used by the other joint owner, is not liable, (Mittelstadt v. Kelly). 230

[§ 2. Consent means consent to the car being driven, and not to the particular driver operating the car, (Kerns v. Lewis). 

3. Where an immediate member of the owner's family was driving, the presumption can be overcome only by direct, positive and credible evidence. 

4. To transfer ownership, it is necessary to deliver the certificate of title to the transferee. Otherwise, the sale may be void and the transferor may be liable as owner.

Sec. 105. Liability of Employer. 

Croff v. DeVries, 253 Mich. 180.

DeVries had purchased a second-hand automobile and had given a chattel mortgage thereon which had been assigned to the General Motors Acceptance Corporation. 

When all but $5.00 had been paid, a representative of the 

Acceptance Corporation called and they agreed that DeVries would take the car to a certain garage and leave it there until the $5.00 was paid. On the way to the garage, an accident happened injuring plaintiff. The trial court directed a verdict for the General Motors 

Acceptance Corporation. The Supreme Court said that to warrant it in reversing the judgment, it would have to find from the testimony that DeVries was acting as a servant or agent of the Acceptance Corporation at the time of the accident. The court felt that DeVries did not surrender possession of the car at his home to the agent of the Acceptance Corporation and therefore he did not drive it as an agent of the Corporation. Under this decision, of course, there can be no liability of an employer when a person driving the car is not his agent and the car is not owned by the corporation. Of course, there was no 231

§ 106] 

testimony in this case that the defendant DeVries was doing anything for the Acceptance Corporation to bring him in as an agent or doing work for that Corporation. 

Sec. 106. Implied Authority That Agent Is Working in the Course of Employment. 

Emery v. Ford, 234 Mich. 11.

Plaintiff and one of defendant's employees was supposed to gather up ballot boxes throughout the state of Michigan. The defendant's agent who had general charge of the matter testified that when plaintiff's principal and defendant's agent agreed on collecting the ballot boxes, nothing was agreed relative to transportation, or even thought of. The Court held that under these circumstances, there was implied authority for those in charge of the details of the work to obtain such means of transportation as they thought best served the undertaking, including the use of automobiles.  "In the law of agency it is a fundamental principle that every delegation of power carries with it authority to do all things that are reasonably necessary or proper to efficiently carry into effect the power conferred, unless it be a thing especially forbidden, and as to torts against third parties, even doing a forbidden thing is not always the test, if the agent is acting within the scope of his employment.' 

The testimony in the case supports the theory that the plaintiff and defendant's agent at the time of the accident were acting in their respective employers' business. 232

[§ 

Sec. 107. Deviation from Route by Servant. 

Murphy v. Kuhartz, 244 Mich. 54.

The Michigan Court in this case cited the case of 

Garesse v. Lowe, 41 Cal. App. 715, where the Court said: "If the servant takes his master's machine for a junketing or business trip of his own, the trip is not complete when he reaches a point miles away from the place where the machine ought to be; the servant is upon his own trip until his return to the point of departure, or to a point, where in the performance of his duty he should be."

In the present case, the Court held the servant had resumed his employment when the accident happened saying: "When he reached this route at a point less distant than the last place of delivery, he had completed the trip which he had taken on his own business and had reentered the employment of his master." 

Gorman v. Jaffa, 248 Mich. 557.

In an action for personal injuries against an automobile sales company where it appears that the automobile was placed in the service department of defendant's garage and left in reverse gear, that his bookkeeper obtained permission from the manager to go to lunch and that in starting it, backed against the plaintiff, an invitee of the defendant, causing serious injuries, the trial court properly refused to direct a verdict in favor of the defendant on the ground that the driver was not at the time of the accident engaged in any work for the defendant 233

§ 108] 

and that the operation of the car was not in the course of his employment. The Supreme Court said: 

"We think the trial court properly submitted the disputed question of fact to the jury."

Sec. 108. Implied Consent or Knowledge of Employer. 

Kerns v. Lewis, 249 Mich. 27.

The sales manager of an automobile sales company gave a customer a car to use while the customer's car was being repaired. The customer injured plaintiff's wife negligently. The evidence showed that the defendant himself, the owner of the sales company, had loaned a car to a customer and the custom was established that dealers under similar circumstances loaned cars to customers. The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff. 

The court held that Clinton, the sales manager, had authority to loan the car so that when the accident occurred, it was being driven with defendant's "implied consent or knowledge" and that defendant was liable under Section 29 Act No. 56, Public Acts 1927. At page 

30 the Court said: "Implied authority is to be gathered from facts and circumstances, and is usually a question for the jury. When one invests another with general authority and discretion, and it is exercised in due course and furtherance of the principal's business, the latter is not relieved from the consequences of a mistake of judgment of the agent, either as to the extent of his authority or the manner of exercising it, as against third persons, nor is the authority to be limited to the principal's unexpressed intention.' 

Sec. 109. Presumption-How Overturned. 

Wehling v. Linder, 248 Mich. 241. 

One Quisenberry, a friend of one of defendant's employees, without authority took defendant's truck to de- 234

[§ liver certain goods of defendant. An accident happened injuring plaintiff. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff but on defendant's motion, the trial court entered a judgment non obstante veredicto. The Supreme 

Court sustained the trial judge saying: "One who is driving a motor vehicle incident to the owner's business is presumed to be duly authorized so to drive the vehicle; but it is the established law in this State that such a presumption prevails in favor of the litigant relying thereon only so long as that phase of the case is not covered by testimony to the contrary. (Cases cited omitted.) If the testimony opposed to the presumption is clear, positive and uncontradicted, it becomes the duty of the trial judge to direct a verdict if the issue is a controlling one in the case.' 99 In this case it was uncontradicted that Quisenberry was not an employee of the defendant or that he had permission, express or implied, to drive the defendant's car or that the defendant had any knowledge that Quisenberry was driving the car.

Sec. 110. Servant Acting Contrary to Instructions. 

Chajnacki v. Dougherty, 254 Mich. 296.

Defendant's driver, contrary to instructions, invited the plaintiff to ride on a truck. As the plaintiff attempted to get on the truck, it moved forward and the plaintiff fell causing injury to himself. The trial judge directed a verdict for the defendant. The Supreme Court said: "It is well settled that a master is not liable for the negligent acts of his servant unless at the time the servant is acting within the scope of his employment or within his actual authority. In inviting the plaintiff to ride, the driver of the truck was not act- 235

§ 111] 

ing within the scope of his employment. His act was not only unauthorized but was contrary to the express instructions of his employer.". 

Sec. 111. The Test as to Whether the Relationship of Agent, Servant or Independent Contractor Exists. 

Marchand v. Russell, 257 Mich. 96.

The defendant Russell owned an automobile which he used for transportation in calling upon dealers of defendant Detroit Electric Company. At the time the plaintiff was injured, one Ray Zerbel, a customer of the company, was operating Russell's car although Russell was in the car. Russell was paid a weekly salary which included expenses, also a commission if his sales exceeded a certain amount. Was Russell a servant, agent or independent contractor? The Court lays down the rule as follows: 

"It has been many times said that the right to control, not only as to the result to be accomplished, but also as to the means to be used, is decisive of the relation existing. Actual interference with the control need not be shown if the right to exercise it exists." 

The Court points out that the facts in this line of cases are never the same. In this particular case, however, the relation of master and servant existed at the time of the accident.

The general rule quoted with approval by the Michigan 

Supreme Court in Zoltowski v. Ternes Coal & Lumber 

Co., 214 Mich. 231, following the citation from 26 Cyc. p. 1546, is as follows: "An independent contractor is one who, carrying on an independent business, contracts to do a piece of work according to his own methods, and without being subject to the control of his employer as to the 236

[§ means by which the result is to be accomplished, but only as to the result of the work. Generally the circumstances which go to show one to be an independent contractor, while separately they may not be conclusive, are the independent nature of his business, the existence of a contract for the performance of a specified piece of work, the agreement to pay a fixed price for the work, the employment of assistants by the employees who are under his control, the furnishing by him of the necessary materials, and his right to control the work while it is in progress except as to results."

This quotation also appears with approval in Hanisko v. Fitzpatrick Brothers, 232 Mich. 593, where many cases are cited in its support. 

Sec. 112. No Implied Consent Where Servant Is on His Own Business. 

Anderson v. Schust Co., 262 Mich. 236. 

Defendant's car was driven by Merle J. Bowman who worked for the defendant in Grand Rapids. Edward J. 

Rohring had charge of the defendant's agency there. 

He had been instructed to use defendant's cars only in the company's business. On the day of the accident 

Rohring told Bowman he could take the car to drive to Pinconning. The proof showed that Bowman was using the car for his own business and pleasure. There was a directed verdict for the defendant. The Supreme Court affirmed this decision. The important question was whether defendant's automobile was driven with its implied consent or knowledge.  "An assent may only be implied if Bowman's act was against the instructions of defendant and if Bowman was acting within the apparent scope of his authority." 237

§ 113] 

Here, however, the servant was on his own business and not furthering the master's interest, nor did the master receive any benefit of the servant's act. 

Sec. 113. Servant Acting Contrary to Employer's Instructions but Following Course of Conduct Sanctioned by Employer. 

Breger v. Feigenson Brothers Co., 264 Mich. 37.

In this case, the servant, contrary to the employer's instructions, picked up a boy to carry him on a truck. 

The boy previously had ridden on the truck and had aided the servant in doing his work. The boy was injured. The testimony showed that it might be inferred from the circumstances that the servant, although acting contrary to the general instructions of the employer, yet was following a course of conduct sanctioned by the employer. The verdict and judgment for the plaintiff in this case was sustained by the Supreme Court on the theory that where the servant committed a tortious act in the course of his employment, the employer may be held liable even though ignorant of such tortious act and the servant in committing it, exceeded his authority and disobeyed the employer's express instructions. 

In a case of this kind, a question of fact would always be involved and the testimony would have to show certain facts from which it could be inferred that the employer had sanctioned the general conduct of the servant at the time of the injury.

Sec. 114. Employee Acting Against Specific Instructions and Not in the Course of His Employment.

Hooks v. Western and Southern Life Insurance Co., 268 

Mich. 421.

The employer, an insurance company, was held not liable for injuries caused by negligent use of automobile 238

[§ owned and operated by employee who was on his way home to lunch from duties as house to house canvasser at the time of the accident on day during which the employees doing such work were instructed not to use the car and at time of day during which such work was forbidden. The employee at the time of the accident was acting against instructions of the employer and not in the course of his employment.

Sec. 115. Independent Contractor. 

Whether or not the relationship of master and servant exists or whether that of an independent contractor is sometimes difficult to ascertain. The Michigan Supreme 

Court has stated that "an abstract definition of what constitutes an independent contractor is useful in the test of whether the relation in a case is such or that of an employer but is seldom decisive for each case has its own facts and the facts call for applicable law." Denis v. 

Sinclair Lumber and Fuel Company, 242 Mich. 91.

As a general rule, however, it can be said "that the relation of master and servant does not exist where the person employed is in the exercise of a distinct, independent employment and not under the immediate control, direction, or supervision of the employer." 

McBride v. Jerry Madden Shingle Co., 173 Mich. 251.

A ready test seems to be as to whether or not the employer has the right to control, whether in fact it is exercised or not. In some cases, it appears that the employer reserved the right of control and exercised it in such a manner as to create a master and servant relationship. For such a case, see Cooper v. Interstate Motor 

Freight Co., 264 Mich. 131.

For a history of the Michigan cases, see the following: 

DeForrest v. Wright, 2 Mich. 368; Lenderink v. Village of Rockford, 135 Mich. 531; Burns v. Michigan Paint Co., 239

§ 116] 

wwww 

152 Mich. 613; McBride v. Jerry Madden Shingle Co., 173 Mich. 248; Gall v. Detroit Journal Co., 191 Mich. 405; 

Van Simaeys v. George R. Cook Co., 201 Mich. 540; Lynn v. Roberts, 257 Mich. 116; Cooper v. Interstate Motor 

Freight Co., 264 Mich. 131; Hazard v. Great Central Co., 270 Mich. 60. 

Sec. 116. Bailments.

Under modern conditions in large cities, automobiles are parked during certain hours on parking lots. When the owner of an automobile thus parks his car, the re lationship of bailor and bailee arises. Act No. 391, Pub lic Acts of 1919, being Compiled Laws of 1929 Section 4796 and following, imposes certain obligations upon the part of an automobile owner and enables the owner to make out a prima facie case against the bailee. 

In the case of General Exchange Insurance Corpo ration v. Service Parking Grounds, Inc., 254 Mich. 1, the insurance company which had insured a certain car which had been stolen from a parking lot, attempted to recover from the parking lot on the subrogation clause in its insurance policy. The parking lot in defense claimed that the automobile had been stolen. The Court in this case pointed out, however, that the burden was on the parking lot not only to show that the car was stolen but that theft took place without any negligence on its part. The above statute referred to was so construed and the word 'damage" was so construed as to cover the total loss of an automobile. Thus a bailee can be held responsible for the loss of property which it negligently cares for. 

For a case in which the garage delivered a car to the wrong person and the one not holding the claim slip, see the case of Crowley v. Detroit Garages, Inc., 259 Mich. 

170. Because of the fact that the garage did not return 240

[§ 117-b the automobile to its owner at the time he demanded it on presentation of his storage ticket as a result of the negligence of one of its own employees in delivering the car to a stranger, the Court held that a conversion had been committed and that the owner of the car was entitled to the value of the car at the time it was converted. 

Preferred Automobile Insurance Company v. Grand 

Rapids Garages, Inc., 258 Mich. 32. This case points out the distinction between a contract for the personal service of a chauffeur and the bailment of an automobile. 

In this case the garage owner furnished a chauffeur to drive an automobile to another city and return. On the return trip, the owner's car was damaged and he claimed that inasmuch as Sections 4795 to 4800, Compiled Laws of 1929, provided that proof of damage of an automobile while in a garage owner's custody was prima facie evidence of negligence, he could recover for damage caused to his automobile. However, the Court pointed out that there was no bailment in this case but only a contract for the personal service of the chauffeur.

Sec. 117. Liability of Relatives. 

Sec. 117-a. Children Against Parents. 

Elias v. Collins, 237 Mich. 175.

At common law, a minor may not sue his parent in tort. There is no statute in Michigan abrogating this law and, consequently, a child cannot recover from its parent in a tort action. This rule, of course, is based on sound public policy.

Sec. 117-b. Wife Against Husband. 

Harvey v. Harvey, 239 Mich. 142.

A wife cannot recover at common law against her husband for a personal tort. This rule has not been abro- 241

§ 117-c]  

gated by statute in Michigan, and consequently, the common law rule prevails. This is true since the married women's act, being Section 12357, Compiled Laws of 1915, only provided that when a cause of action shall accrue to or arise against any married woman, she may sue or be sued in the same manner as if she were sole. It does not confer a right of action against her husband for injuries. Of course, the reverse of this is also true that a husband would have no cause of action against his wife for personal tort.

Sec. 117-c. Wife's Cause of Action Against Owner Where Husband Is Driving. 

Riser v. Riser, 240 Mich. 402.

In this case the husband of the plaintiff was driving his father's automobile. The wife attempted to recover from her father-in-law. The Court held that inasmuch as a wife could not recover from her husband, she could not recover from the owner because the wife would have to show that the proximate cause of her injuries was the neglect of her husband, the driver.

Sec. 118. Summary-Liability of Others. 

Where there is a Master and Servant, or Principal and

Agent relationship between the owner and driver, the ownership statute does not broaden the liability of the owner. If he is not liable as Master or as Principal, he is not liable as owner. See Loux v. Harris, 226 Mich. 315.

The Court in this case said that where a Master and 

Servant relationship existed, the ownership statute did not apply and could not be relied upon to make the Master liable in a situation in which he would not be liable except for the statute. 242

[§ 119-c 

In an automobile case, a question sometimes arises as to whether the owner of a truck is an independent contractor or a servant acting under the control of another. 

There are a large number of questions involved, the final analysis being whether the owner of the truck has control over the means and methods of the work to be accomplished. 

If an action is contemplated against a parking lot owner or garage, the statutes should be consulted and also ordinances regulating such defendants. 

An unemancipated minor has no action against his parent as a result of negligently driving an automobile. 

A spouse cannot sue the husband or wife for injuries received in an accident, or the owner where the car was driven by the husband or wife.

Sec. 119. Imputed Negligence. 

The general rule in Michigan is that the negligence of the driver of an automobile is imputed to the occupant. 

See Colborne v. D. U. R., 177 Mich. 139. The following are exceptions to the general rule in which there is no imputed negligence to the occupant of an automobile : 

Sec. 119-a. Fellow Servants. 

In the case of fellow servants. See McKernan v. Detroit Citizens' Ry. Co., 138 Mich. 519; Skvarce v. Sales 

Necessity, Inc., 267 Mich. 540.

Sec. 119-b. Common Carriers. 

See Galloway v. D. U. R., 168 Mich. 343; Rogers v. 

Weber, 235 Mich. 180.

Sec. 119-c. Minors. 

See Donlin v. D. U. R., 198 Mich. 327; Block v. Ann 

Arbor Rd. Co., 202 Mich. 341. 17 243

§ 119-d] 

 Sec. 119-d. Servant Where Master Is Driving. 

See Robertson v. United Fuel & Supply Co., 218 Mich. 

271 where the Court said at page 277: "Upon consideration of the cases bearing upon the question, we hold the negligence of the master in driving is not as a matter of law imputable to the servant riding with the master in the course of his employment. Circumstances may be such, however, by way of participation of the servant in the driving or degree of care exercised as to constitute the negligence of the master as well as the negligence of the servant riding with him." 

Sec. 119-e. Private Conveyance for Hire. 

See Rogers v. Weber, 235 Mich. 180; Lachow v. Kimmick, 263 Mich. 1. 

Wojewoda v. City of Detroit, 264 Mich. 277.

In this case a workman contributed a certain sum of money to a fellow workman for transportation to and from work. The court permitted the jury to determine whether or not the plaintiff was a passenger for hire. 

If he was a passenger for hire, of course, the driver's negligence was not imputed to him. Testimony showed that a definite sum of money was paid for transportation and that this was a method of contributing to the cost of gasoline consumed and was a matter of courtesy but it was also shown that the money would not have to be used for the purchase of gasoline. 

See also Caswell v. New York Central Railroad, 263

Mich. 18. In this case the legal allowance of mileage to a drain commissioner for driving his automobile was not considered the hiring of a car and, consequently, the pas- 244

[§ senger was a gratuitous passenger and the driver's negligence was imputed to him.  "Mileage is a well-established method, widely used in public and private business, of reimbursing an officer or employee for the expense necessarily sustained by him in traveling to perform his duties. It is merely a substitute for actual expenses, and, theoretically, covers only the cost of transportation of the individual officer or employee, and the rate is set upon that basis unless otherwise indicated by circumstances. It involves no control of the car by the superior officer or employer, nor does it change the driver's relation or liability to anyone who might ride with him." 

Also, see Johnson v. Mack, 263 Mich. 10.

Sec. 120. Summary-Imputed Negligence. 

In Michigan, if an adult occupant of an automobile sues the driver of the other car involved in the accident, he must prove that his own driver was not negligent before he can recover. The negligence of the driver is imputed to the occupant in the usual situation. The following rules may be safely stated: 

1. Negligence is not imputed to a minor occupant. 

2. If the vehicle is being used by a common carrier, such as a taxicab, the negligence is not imputed to the passenger. 

3. There is no imputation of negligence where the car is being used by a private carrier, although it would seem that in this situation there is more reason for imputing the negligence that in any other, as was suggested in one opinion in Lachow v. Kimmick. 

4. A servant riding with his master would not be barred from recovering because of the master's negligence. 245

§ 121] 

5. A servant riding with a fellow servant, especially if performing a separate duty, can recover in spite of his driver's negligence.

Sec. 121. Joint Enterprise. 

When the occupants of an automobile join together in a "joint enterprise," the negligence of the driver is imputed to the other occupants of the car. See Hanser v. 

Youngs, 212 Mich. 508; Farthing v. Hepinstall, 243 Mich. 

380 and Frisorger v. Shepse, 251 Mich. 121. 

What constitutes a "joint enterprise"? The Court in 

Farthing v. Hepinstall, 243 Mich. 380, at page 382, defines it as follows: "To constitute a joint enterprise between a passenger and the driver of an automobile within the meaning of the law of negligence, there must be such a community of interest in its operation as to give each an equal right of control. There must be a common responsibility for its negligent operation, and there can be no common responsibility unless there is a common right of control. It must be held that the driver is acting as the agent of the other members of the enterprise. The rule of joint enterprise in negligence cases is founded on the law of principal and agent. On no other theory could the negligence of the driver be imputable to a passenger. 

Being parties to the same enterprise, they are assumed to have common control and possession of the machine. Otherwise, each could not be charged with the negligence of the other.”

In Johnson v. Mack, 263 Mich. 10, where the owner and driver of an automobile acting as a private carrier was conveying fellow employees to work when the accident occurred in which a driver collided with the rear of a 246

[§ truck injuring plaintiff, the Court stated that the plaintiff was not involved in a joint enterprise because the plaintiff had no control whatever over the car in which he was riding. The element of control, of course, is essential in proving a joint enterprise.

In Frisorger v. Shepse, the plaintiff was not permitted to recover from the driver of the car in which the plaintiff was riding because the plaintiff and defendant were on a joint enterprise.

Sec. 122. Summary-Joint Enterprise. 

The test of a joint enterprise is whether there is an equal right to control. If the driver of the car is also the owner, there would be less chance to prove a joint enterprise than where the car is borrowed. 

The law developed in Frisorger v. Shepse is contrary to the overwhelming weight of authority. In other states the plaintiff may recover from the driver in spite of joint enterprise. The negligence is imputed only where suit is brought against the driver of another car involved in the accident, but in Michigan the member of a joint enterprise cannot recover from the driver of the car or another member. 247

CHAPTER XVIII SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE Sec. 123. Subsequent or Discovered Negligence. 

Sec. 124. Summary-Subsequent or Discovered Negligence. 

Sec. 123. Subsequent or Discovered Negligence. 

In the whole field of negligence law in Michigan, pertaining to automobiles, there is probably no greater confusion than is found in the decisions involving the question of subsequent or discovered negligence. The cases which are considered in this chapter have been chosen because the opinions mark the changes in the Court's interpretation of the doctrine, as well as the gradual development of the law on the subject. The very early decisions are not given as it would not serve any good purpose to go into them, and because the opinions which are set forth discuss the old decisions. 

At first the Court treated the question of subsequent negligence largely from the standpoint of proximate cause. Then the words gross negligence began to appear in the decisions. It is interesting to note that in a number of opinions the phrase "last clear chance" is used synonymously with subsequent or discovered negligence. 

The cases are given in their chronological order. 

Fike v. Pere Marquette Rd. Co., 174 Mich. 167.

The plaintiff claimed that, in driving a wagon across the defendant's tracks, the horses were frightened and the wheels became cramped so that he could not move the 248

SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE [§ 123 

wagon; that the engineer was looking directly at the wagon and was traveling slow enough to have stopped. 

The case was submitted to the jury upon the theory of subsequent negligence.

It was held that the evidence presented a question of subsequent negligence. The opinion has these quotations from other cases. "It is true that the contributory negligence of the plaintiff does not prevent recovery in a case where the defendant, who knows, or ought by the exercise of the most ordinary care to know, of the precedent negligence of the plaintiff, by his subsequent negligence does plaintiff an injury." "In all of these cases the negligence of the defendants occurred when there was a condition of danger, and it may be said that it was unimportant how such antecedent condition arose, or whether it was due to the negligent act of the plaintiff or not. The defendant's wrong being a want of ordinary care, which care would have prevented the accident notwithstanding plaintiff's antecedent negligence, it was responsible for it, and plaintiff's antecedent negligence being at most a remote cause, and there being no other negligence on the part of the plaintiff, he might recover. It has in some cases been said that his negligence might be said to be a remote, and not the proximate cause." "The cases do not attempt to define these acts as gross negligence but place the right of recovery upon the ground that the proximate cause of the injury is the act of the defendant."

This opinion unquestionably shows the court's attitude to be that the doctrine was principally one of proximate cause. The negligence of the plaintiff must have been antecedent and must have constituted only a remote cause. 249

§ 123] 

King v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 176 Mich. 645.

The plaintiff stopped his car on defendant's tracks and left his motor running. He turned and watched the young man, who was with him, close his garage doors. 

His car was struck by defendant's street car. The motorman had an unobstructed view for 340 feet, and the testimony showed that the auto was standing on the track for one-half minute.

It was held by the majority of the Court that the case presented a question of subsequent or discovered negligence. The Court said that the motorman, if he was exercising due care, could have seen the dangerous situation of the plaintiff in time to avoid the collision. Three judges in a minority opinion held that the plaintiff could have driven off the track in a second's time, and said that the original act of negligence continued until the catastrophe happened. The minority opinion also stated that there was no proof that the motorman had knowledge of the dangerous situation. It should be noted that in the dissenting opinion the words "last chance" are used.

In this case the Court adopted the rule of law that it was not necessary that the peril of the plaintiff was actually discovered, but only that by the exercise of due care it should have been discovered. 

Huff v. Michigan United Traction Co., 186 Mich. 88.

The plaintiff was driving his car north on Charleton street in Battle Creek. It was his intention to turn west on Marshall street after he had crossed the defendant's tracks. He testified that he entered the intersection slowly and saw the interurban car 250 feet west. He turned his car to the right, but the defendant's car, which 250

SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE 

[§ 123 was traveling 30 to 35 miles per hour, struck the rear corner of his car.  "We have carefully examined the authorities cited and relied upon by the defendant and are of the opinion that the question whether the defendant's agent, the motorman, should have discovered from the actions and situation of plaintiff his peril, and should have, but did not, take ordinary precaution to avert that peril, was one for the determination of the jury, under all the circumstances disclosed by the record in this case."

The Court seems to have gone rather far in applying the doctrine to the facts in this case as it was an intersection accident in which the defendant's motorman could not have had much time to see the negligence of the plaintiff and react. 

Walter v. Detroit, Jackson & Chicago Ry. Co., 191 Mich. 181. 

In this case the Court said: "It is clear that in the instant case the alleged negligence of the defendant's motorman intervened between the scaring of the plaintiff's horse by the automobile and the injury, and must therefore be said to have been properly denominated the cause of the accident."

It should be noted that in this case the court talks about gross negligence and erroneously cites the opinion in Fike v. Railroad Company, 174 Mich. 167, as approving the rule as to gross negligence. By referring to pp. 207-8 of that decision it will be seen that the court did not adopt the rules given in appellant's brief but merely made an unnecessary reference to one of the rules. Why the court thought that it was necessary to 251

§ 123] 

mention gross negligence in connection with the discovered negligence doctrine is difficult to understand. 

Simon v. Detroit United Ry., 196 Mich. 586.

In this case the plaintiff, who was driving his auto across defendant's track, tried to rely upon the doctrine of discovered negligence. "Gross negligence may be defined as the intentional failure to perform a manifest duty, in wanton, wilful, or reckless disregard of the consequences, as affecting the life or property of another. It also implies a thoughtless disregard of consequences, without the exercise of any effort to prevent or avoid them."

Under this definition of gross negligence it would be necessary to prove that the defendant had some actual knowledge of the dangerous situation of the plaintiff. 

But in the decisions prior to this case the Court repeatedly said that, if the defendant by exercising due care would have known of plaintiff's perilous position, the doctrine of subsequent negligence would apply. 

Krouse v. Southern Michigan Ry. Co., 215 Mich. 139.

The plaintiff's car stalled on the defendant's track when the defendant's car was 1000 feet away and approaching at a speed of 15 to 20 miles per hour. The decedent did not get out of the automobile before the collision although the driver did.

In holding that this did not present a question of discovered negligence, the Court said: "There is a vast difference between negligently getting in a place of danger without ability to remove therefrom and remaining in such a place after the danger is apparent and there is opportunity open 252

SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE [$ 123 

to avoid injury and a way to escape pointed out.

The principle which controls where the danger is discovered applies to plaintiff's decedent as well as the defendant. Under the evidence, and the most favorable view thereof, the proximate and efficient cause of the accident involved the concurrent negligence of plaintiff's decedent and defendant, unbroken by any efficient supervening cause."

Here the Court squarely refuses to apply the doctrine because the plaintiff was negligent up to the time of injury. It unequivocally lays down the rule that concurrent negligence on the part of the plaintiff prevented him from relying on the doctrine. 

Apps v. Walters, 216 Mich. 17.

This was a pedestrian case in which the plaintiff ran across the street and was struck near the curb by defendant's car.  "Conceding defendant was guilty of negligence, we find the contributory negligence of plaintiff was not only antecedent but continuing and actively concurrent until the accident happened, being both a remote cause and as efficient a proximate cause as any negligence of defendant. . . . In other words, if plaintiff's active contemporaneous negligence was a concurring proximate cause, the doctrine of gross or subsequent negligence did not apply.”

In this case the Court seems to go very far in refusing to allow the doctrine to be applied. The reason given is concurrent negligence. 

Gibbard v. Cursan, 225 Mich. 311. 

The plaintiff's intestate, a girl 13 years old, was struck by defendant's truck while walking on a paved country 253

§ 123] 

highway in the afternoon. The girl was walking north with other girls, and the testimony showed that the truck driver did not sound his horn until close to the decedent and that he had a clear view of the girl when 80 rods south of her.

It was held that the testimony presented a question as to wilful or wanton misconduct. The lower court did not submit the case to the jury under the discovered negligence theory. The Supreme Court said that this was proper as the negligence of the girl, if any, in stepping to the left, was concurrent negligence.

This opinion points out the difference between wilful and wanton misconduct and ordinary negligence. Gross negligence is classed with subsequent negligence or last clear chance. A plaintiff concurrently negligent with the defendant could not recover under the discovered negligence theory or if the defendant was merely grossly negligent. But if the defendant was guilty of wilful or wanton misconduct, the plaintiff's concurrent negligence would not bar recovery. However, the Court admitted that the term gross negligence is sometimes used erroneously to define wilful and wanton misconduct. In other words, the Court looked upon gross negligence as another phrase for discovered or subsequent negligence and something which should not be used synonymously with wilful and wanton misconduct. 

Gross negligence, when correctly used, according to the Michigan Supreme Court, is the same as subsequent or discovered negligence or last clear chance. Sometimes it is incorrectly used to define wilful or wanton misconduct. The Court as it stood at the time of this decision would say that the opinion in Simon v. Detroit 

United Ry. given above gave an incorrect definition of gross negligence in connection with a question of subsequent or discovered negligence. 254

SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE [§ 123 

Jones v. Armstrong, 231 Mich. 637.

The plaintiff walked across a 55 foot street diagonally and was struck near the far side by defendant's car, which was coming up to the plaintiff from the rear. The plaintiff contended that the doctrine of last clear chance applied.

It was held by a divided Court that the doctrine of last clear chance did not apply. The Court said that there was nothing in the record to indicate that the driver of the car did not suppose the plaintiff would stop for a moment, or if he did not do so that he would quicken his pace.

This case is important because it shows the Court's attitude toward the application of the theory of discovered negligence to pedestrian cases. It naturally would be easier to find concurrent negligence in a pedestrian case than where a car becomes stalled on railway tracks or the plaintiff by his negligence gets into an inextricable position. 

Johnson v. Grand Trunk Rd. Co., 246 Mich. 52.

The plaintiff was struck by a backing train while standing on the track. There was no train employee on the rear end of the train. 

It was held that there was no proof of wilful or wanton misconduct, and that the last clear chance doctrine was not applicable. The following allegation was in the declaration: "negligently failed to warn the plaintiff of the approach of its engine, after plaintiff's position of peril became or by exercise of reasonable care should have become known." In commenting on this allegation the 

Court said: "This allegation is one commonly spoken of as subsequent or after-discovered negligence and involves the doctrine of "last clear chance" 255

§ 123] 

While courts have somewhat differed as to its application when the evidence showed that the acts of the plaintiff, relied upon as establishing contributory negligence continued until the time of the accident, and such negligence was therefore concurrent with the subsequent negligence of the defendant, we are not called upon in this case to consider that question." 

Siegel v. Detroit Cab Co., 246 Mich. 620.

The plaintiff's decedent was struck by defendant's cab while crossing a 50 foot city street. There was proof that the cab was on the wrong side of the street when it struck the decedent. The defendant's driver testified that he saw the decedent start from the curb 18 to 20 feet in front of his car; that the cab was going 12 or 13 miles per hour and he could stop it at this speed in 10 feet. The plaintiff produced two witnesses who testified that the cab could have been stopped in two feet.

It was held that the testimony presented a question as to discovered negligence.

In this decision the Court seems to have gone very far in applying the doctrine at least under the defendant's testimony. It is difficult to reconcile this case with Apps v. Walters given above. 

Harrison v. Eastern Michigan Motor Bus Co., 257 Mich. 329.

In this case the plaintiff's car was driven to the left side of the road to pass traffic. The driver could not get ahead of the line of cars and tried to get back into the line of traffic but his car was struck by the defendant's approaching bus.

In holding that this did not present a question of subsequent negligence, the Court said: “. . . but it is true that one who by his own negligence gets into a perilous position by reason of which 256

SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE [§ 123 

he is injured and his negligence continues to and contributes to his injury, cannot recover."

Once again the Court refused to apply the doctrine because of concurrent negligence. 

Spencer v. City of Detroit, 257 Mich. 601.

The plaintiff's decedent, driving east on a narrow street, drove onto the car track to pass a parked automobile and before he could get off was struck by defendant's street car.

It was held that this did not present a case of subsequent negligence because the decedent was concurrently negligent. "The negligence of plaintiff's decedent continued until the instant of the impact, because he continued to drive his automobile forward and in the direction in which it collided with the street car. It was a proximate cause of the accident itself." 

Smarinski v. Markowitz, 265 Mich. 412.

In this case the plaintiff's decedent started across the street at a crosswalk when the signal light was in his favor. While crossing the light changed and the defendant drove his car onto the crosswalk, striking the decedent. The defendant contended that the decedent's negligence was concurrent with that of the defendant and that therefore the doctrine of subsequent negligence did not apply.

The Court held that the evidence presented an issue of subsequent negligence and said: "Counsel for defendant cites cases from other jurisdictions upon the question of concurrent negligence. In this jurisdiction, where we apply the rule of subsequent negligence, there is no room for the doctrine of continuing or concurring negligence." 257

§ 123] 

This statement by the Court may mean a revolutionary change regarding concurrent negligence. By going back to the case of Johnson v. Grand Trunk Rd. Co., given above, we see the only premonition that the Court might change its rule on this point. But since that decision there have been several in which the Court defeated the plaintiff because of concurrent negligence. The facts seemingly were strong enough to submit the question of subsequent negligence to the jury without changing the rule of concurrent negligence. The plaintiff was in a perilous situation and was observed by the defendant. 

If the plaintiff was concurrently negligent, the case might have been submitted to the jury on the question of wilful and wanton misconduct. 

Beckman v. Baraga Township, 271 Mich. 195.

The decedent was driving a truck with a load of logs. 

The width of the load was in violation of the statute, being more than 96 inches. A school bus struck the logs near a narrow bridge. It was claimed that the plaintiff should recover on the theory of subsequent negligence as the bus driver should have seen that the decedent's truck was out of control. It was held that there could be no recovery under the subsequent negligence theory as the decedent's negligence carried him up to the point of collision. 

Hale v. Cooper, 271 Mich. 348.

The plaintiff's car, after passing another car, started to skid and came to a practical stop almost off the road. 

The driver then accelerated his motor, and the car whipped around so that it was struck by the defendant's car. It was held that this was not a case of subsequent negligence as the plaintiff's driver was guilty of negligence up to the time of the accident. 258

Sec. 124. Summary. 

In Michigan the phrases Subsequent Negligence, Discovered Negligence, Last Clear Chance and Gross Negligence are synonymous. Disregarding the recent decision of Smarinski v. Markowitz, the following rules are suggested by the cases. 

1. Before the theory can be relied upon the plaintiff must be guilty of negligence which has placed him in a perilous situation visible to the defendant. 

2. This negligence must be antecedent. That is, it must not be concurrent or continuing up to the time of the injury. (Exception Smarinski v. Markowitz.) 

3. The defendant from the time he discovers or should have discovered the perilous position of the plaintiff must be able, by the exercise of due care, to avoid the injury. 18 259

§ 124] 

This doctrine of discovered negligence is entirely dif ferent from wilful or wanton misconduct which excuses contributory negligence even though concurrent. Thus, if a pedestrian is seen by the defendant auto driver negligently walking across the road with every indication that he will continue to be negligent and the driver, with plenty of time to stop, runs him down, we might have a case of wilful and wanton misconduct which would permit the plaintiff to recover, regardless of his negligence up to the time of the injury. On the other hand, if the driver was not looking ahead and did not see the pedestrian, he would have no knowledge of a dangerous situation and would not be guilty of wilful and wanton misconduct. The concurrent negligence of the pedestrian would prevent the application of the theory of subsequent negligence.

The case of Smarinski v. Markowitz cannot be reconciled with the other decisions. There is no basis for this decision in the Michigan cases in which the question of concurrent negligence has been involved. 260

Sec. 125.
