Sec. 137.

Garnishment. 

The ground covered in this chapter is only that which particularly applies to an automobile case. Unusual matters of procedure are dealt with for the most part, it being assumed that the ordinary rules of procedure are well known, or are covered in other books on procedure. 

In considering action in courts, justice court jurisdiction is not discussed, because of the variety of courts in Michigan having jurisdiction similar to that of the justice courts. A discussion concerning statutes of limitation is included in this chapter as some of the statutes are so worded as to determine the procedure to be taken. 

In addition, before determining in what court the suit should be brought, the plaintiff's attorney must first decide that the action has not been barred. The procedural questions are considered in groups. First, matters before trial. Second, trial procedure. Third, procedure after trial. 261

§ 125] 

 Sec. 125. Statutes of Limitation. 

The period of time in which actions to recover damages for injuries to person or property must be brought is three years from the time the action accrued. However there are a number of exceptions to the statute found in section 13976 of Compiled Laws 1929. The statute does not run against a minor or an insane person as provided in section 13978. If the defendant is out of the state when the action accrues, or goes outside the state for a period in excess of two months, the statute does not run while he is out of the state as provided in section 13980.

Section 13981 is important because it is applicable to death or survival actions and to actions against a defendant who dies. If either party dies, either before the period runs or within 30 days after it runs, the action may be commenced or the claim may be proved against the estate at any time within two years after granting letters testamentary or of administration. But the action must be brought within three years after the period would ordinarily have run. In the case of Szydelko v. 

Smith's Estate, 259 Michigan 519, the Court held that the two year period started to run from the time when the general administrator was appointed and not from the appointment of the special administrator. The two year extension applies to claims filed against an estate which is important as it conflicts with the statute requiring claims against the estate to be filed within the period of time set by the probate court.

Section 13983 lends itself especially to the so-called hit and run case. If the defendant fraudulently conceals the cause of such action, the action may be started within two years after the cause of action is discovered though the three year period had run. 262

PROCEDURE 

[§ 126 

Sec. 126. Action in Federal Court. 

There are a number of situations, involving automobile cases, over which a federal court has jurisdiction. For instance, if a resident and citizen of Ohio, while driving his car in Michigan, has an accident with a resident and citizen of Michigan, it probably will not be necessary for the Michigan resident to start his suit in Ohio. He could probably get service on the Ohio resident in the federal court in Michigan by serving him by mail under the Michigan Non-Resident Act, section 4790. In a recent 

Pennsylvania case, O'Donnell v. Slade, decided late in 

1933, the state non-resident service act was made applicable to a federal court action. The Michigan Non-Resident Act was amended in 1935 to apply to non-resident owners as well as operators. The amendment took effect on May 28, 1935. See Public Acts 1935, No. 110. Before the amendment the statute did not apply to a non-resident owner who was not operating the car. See Brown v. Cleveland Tractor Co., 265 Mich. 475, and Flynn v. 

Kramer, 271 Mich. 500.

The most common method followed in getting within federal court jurisdiction is the appointment of an alien or citizen of another state than that of the defendant to act as guardian for a minor or as administrator in a death or survival action. It has been generally assumed that this practice gives the federal court jurisdiction. 

However, the procedure has been questioned. The United 

States Judicial Code (United States Code Annotated, 

Title 28, Section 80) has this provision. "If in any suit commenced in a district court, or removed from a State court to a district court of the United States, it shall appear to the satisfaction of the said district court, at any time after such suit has been brought or removed thereto, that such suit does not really and substantially 263

§ 126] 

involve a dispute or controversy properly within the jurisdiction of said district court, or that the parties to said suit have been improperly or collusively made or joined, either as plaintiffs or defendants, for the purpose of creating a case cognizable or removable under this chapter, the said district court shall proceed no further therein, but shall dismiss the suit or remand it to the court from which it was removed, as justice may require, and shall make such order as to costs as shall be just. 

The case of Cerri v. Akron-Peoples' Telephone Co., 219 

Fed. 285, involved this section of the Code. The defendant contended that the administrator had no interest in the case and had been appointed solely for the purpose of getting within the jurisdiction of the federal court. The 

Court dismissed the case on the ground of collusion. The opinion in this case should be consulted for the procedure followed by the defendant, and a discussion of the cases in point. The case of City of Detroit v. Blanchfield, 13

Fed. (2d) 13, if carefully studied, will not be offered as opposed to the Cerri case. The Court pointed out that the defendant had not proved fraud or collusion and indicated that it thought the question should have been raised before the trial was in progress. It should also be noted that the case of Mecom v. Fitzsimmons Co., 284

U. S. 183, is not in point as the alleged fraudulent appointment of the administrator was made to keep the case out of the federal court, and not to get into it. 

Consequently, the language of the Code did not apply to that case.

On June 8, 1935, Act No. 240 of the 1935 Public Acts of Michigan became effective. This Act provides that "no person shall hereafter be deemed suitable and competent to administer the estate of a deceased person, as executor or administrator thereof, or of a minor or in- 264

PROCEDURE 

[§ 127 competent person, as guardian thereof, who is not a resident of this state and a citizen of the United States." 

Sec. 127. Claims in Probate Court. 

When the defendant is killed in the accident or dies before suit is started, a question arises as to whether an action can properly be started in the circuit court or some other court without filing the claim with the commissioners on claims in the probate court. The confusion is due to the seeming conflict between two statutes. Section 15688 of Compiled Laws 1929 provides that when commissioners are appointed no action shall be commenced against the executor or administrator, with certain exceptions, until the expiration of the time limited by the court for the payment of debts. Section 13981, which was considered under the heading Statutes of Limitations in this chapter, provides that after the death of the defendant an action may be commenced against the administrator or the claim may be proved as a debt against the estate, as the case may be. The words "as the case may be" might mean that where commissioners are appointed the claim is to be presented to them. Certainly, where commissioners have been appointed, the safe procedure would be to present the claims in probate court and not to run the risk of starting an action in the circuit court, and have it dismissed.

Frequently the defendant dies intestate without property to distribute. His heirs do not have an administrator appointed. Can the plaintiff secure the appointment of an administrator for the purpose of presenting his claim for damages or starting a suit? The answer seems to be that, if the deceased was a resident of Michigan, the plaintiff, as a creditor, may secure the appointment of an administrator in the county where the de- 265

§ 128] 

cedent resided. If the deceased was not a resident of 

Michigan, the appointment may be secured in the county where the deceased has left an estate. If the deceased carried insurance on his automobile, protecting him against the claim of the plaintiff, his estate would be in the county where his administrator could sue the insurance company. For a ruling on this point, the case of 

Olson v. Preferred Automobile Insurance Co., 259 Mich. 

612, should be read. It should be carefully noted that in this decision the fact that there was a judgment against the deceased in a certain county, resulting from the accident, did not create an estate in that county as the insurance company could not be sued in that county. 

Sec. 128. Action in Circuit Court. 

Section 13997 of Compiled Laws 1929 provides that, with certain exceptions, all tort actions shall be commenced in the county where one of the parties resides. 

Section 14090 provides that when the suit is brought in the county where the defendant, or one of the defendants, resides the process may be served anywhere within the state. As a result when the suit is started in the county where the plaintiff resides, the defendant not residing in that county, the service of process must be in that county. 

If suit is commenced in the county where the defendant resides, he may be served any place in the state. 

In automobile cases resulting from automobile accidents it not infrequently happens that the plaintiff and defendant are non-residents of the state. Before the so-called non-resident service act was passed, a question might have been raised as to the jurisdiction of a circuit court in this state in this situation, neither party being a resident. Now section 4790, as amended, Public Acts 

1935, No. 110, would permit the plaintiff to start suit in 266

PROCEDURE 

[§ 129 Michigan and secure proper service on the defendant by registered mail.

When suit is started against more than one defendant and service must be made outside the county on part of the defendants, the defendant in the county where the suit is started should be served and a proper return made before an attempt is made to serve the other defendant outside the county. For the proper procedure see Engel v. Smith, 200 Mich. 395. 

Sec. 129.

Procedure Before Trial. 

Michigan Court Rule 41, Section 2, provides that in an action for damages for injuries to person a physical examination by the defendant's doctor may be ordered in advance of the trial.

Rule 41 also provides that, on application and hearing, the court in its discretion may order the taking of the deposition of the opposite party. It should be noted that the 1931 rule was changed and made more general as to the scope of the deposition. The case of Fisher v. Smith, 259 Mich. 279, decided that after summons was served on the defendant and before the declaration was filed, the plaintiff could take the deposition of the defendant in a tort action. The 1931 rule is discussed in Vincent v. Van 

Blooys, 263 Mich. 312. In the case of Bartenbach v. 

Smith, 268 Mich. 653, the Supreme Court said that the trial court might very properly have excluded from the scope of the discovery matters which were obviously within the knowledge of the plaintiff. The Court said that the purpose of the rule was to shorten trials and not to harass the defendant or to virtually force him to two trials instead of one.

Rule 42, Section 2, provides that any party, by notice in writing, not later than 10 days before trial, may call 267

§ 130] 

on any other party to admit any specific fact or facts mentioned in such notice.

Rule 40 provides for the production and discovery of books, papers and documents in certain situations for the purpose of pleading or the trial of the case. In Gemsa v. Dorner, 256 Mich. 195, the Court said that an order for the production of books for the purpose of preparing for trial should not be granted unless it is shown that the information could not be obtained at the trial of the case by a subpoena duces tecum. In the case of Layton v. 

Cregan & Mallory Co., 263 Mich. 30, the defendant in its answer denied ownership of the automobile, consent to the operation and denied that the driver was an employee. The plaintiff under Rule 40 secured an order requiring the defendant to produce its insurance policy on the car and the correspondence between the defendant and the insurance company in relation to the accident. It was held that the order was proper as the information could not be obtained by subpoena duces tecum, the defendant having its office in Auburn, Indiana. The Court said that a deposition could have been taken under Rule 41, but it would have been more expensive and inconvenient for both parties. See also Detroit Bar Association v. American Life Ins. Co., 264 Mich. 495.

Sec. 130. Examination of Jury. 

There is probably no more troublesome a question in the trial of an automobile case than the extent to which the plaintiff's attorney may go in examining the jury regarding their connection with insurance companies. In 

Link v. Fahey, 200 Mich. 308, the plaintiff was permitted to ask each juror if he was a member of a certain mutual company. In Stehouwer v. Lewis, 249 Mich. 76, the 

Supreme Court said that the bringing up of insurance in 268

PROCEDURE 

[§ 130 a case was a dangerous practice and too frequently increased the amount of the verdict. In this case the defendant was permitted to testify that he had no insurance on the ground that the plaintiff had questioned the jury as to their interest in insurance companies. 

In Holman v. Cole, 242 Mich. 402, the insurance company was a foreign corporation. In examining the jury the plaintiff's attorney asked each juror if he was a stockholder in that company, naming it. The Court, in holding that this constituted reversible error, said that the purpose of the attorney was evidently to prejudice the jury. It was pointed out that, if information was wanted, the jurors could have been asked if any of them were stockholders in any corporation, and, if they were, they could have been asked as to the kind of corporation. 

In the case of Harker v. Bushouse, 254 Mich. 187, the suggestion made in the Holman case is again made even though the company involved was a mutual. The opinion suggests to trial judges this procedure in examining a jury. The judge should first inform the jury that some drivers are insured and some are not; that he asks the question which he is about to put to them in all negligence cases; that he does not know whether the defendant was insured; that the law does not permit any further reference to the subject during the trial of a case, but that the plaintiff has a right to know whether any members of the jury are officers, employees, or stockholders in any insurance company or members of any mutual insurance company. If, after asking the question, the answer is in the negative, the question is disposed of. The Supreme 

Court said that such action on the part of the trial court should result in further exclusion of all reference to insurance under penalty of a reversal of the case. To make this method effective the court should do all of the ques- 269

§ 131]  

tioning and the procedure should be carefully explained before the examination to the attorneys. The plaintiff's attorney should be warned that he is not to make any requests before the jury for further questions by the court on this subject. Otherwise the purpose of the procedure would be frustrated.

The Michigan Supreme Court, in the case of Monison v. McCoy, 266 Mich. 693, seems to have restricted the right of the plaintiff's attorney in his examination. The jury was asked if any of them were insured in a certain mutual company, were agents of the company or knew anyone connected with the company. Timely objection was made to each question. This statement appears in the opinion. "This case was not against an insurance company. 

No insurance company was a party to the record. 

If the case directly involved an insurance company some of the questions might be proper as bearing upon the interest of the jurors and possibly to develop reasons for peremptory challenges; but upon the record the question of insurance was not involved. We think the persistent interrogation of witnesses in relation to insurance and a particular insurance company brings this case fairly within the prior decisions of this court and constituted prejudicial error." 

See also Janse v. Haywood, 270 Mich. 632.

Sec. 131. Opening Statement. 

The evidence in a case is not limited to matters mentioned in the opening statement of counsel for the plaintiff. The declaration, rather than the opening statement, controls. See Perry v. Hannagan, 257 Mich. 120. However, if the opening statement does not set forth facts 270

PROCEDURE 

[§ 133 which would at least make out a question for the jury, the defendant may secure a directed verdict at the close of the opening statement. In Gifford v. Dice, 269 Mich. 293, the defendant, at the close of plaintiff's opening statement, made a motion for a directed verdict. The court directed a verdict, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision. Consequently, the plaintiff's attorney should know the theory of his case, and in his opening statement set forth in general what facts will be proved.

Sec. 132. Re-opening Case and Non-Suit. 

In Deyo v. Detroit Creamery Co., 257 Mich. 77, the trial court had permitted the plaintiff to recall two of his witnesses to give additional testimony after he had rested and prior to the introduction of testimony on behalf of the defendant. The Supreme Court said that this was discretionary with the court.

In Oestrike v. Neifert, 267 Mich. 462, it was held that there was no reversible error in permitting the plaintiff to introduce further evidence after he had closed his case and the defendant had moved for a directed verdict. 

The plaintiff in an automobile case not infrequently is unable to prove essential facts in his case and finds it advisable to submit to a non-suit. Section 14335 of Compiled Laws 1929 provides that, after the defendant shall have entered upon his defense in open court, the plaintiff shall not be allowed to discontinue his suit or submit to a non-suit without the consent of the defendant.

Sec. 133. Motion for Directed Verdict- 

("Empson Act').

The motion for a directed verdict is common at the close of the plaintiff's case in automobile cases. Section 

14531 of Compiled Laws 1929 gives either party the right 271

§ 133] 

to ask for a directed verdict before the case is submitted to the jury and gives the trial judge the right to reserve his decision. If the decision is reserved, the court may hear arguments after the verdict is given and before the judgment is entered, and order a judgment entered, notwithstanding the verdict, for the party who made the motion. In fact it is not necessary for the court to state on the record that he is reserving his decision. See Day v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 218 Mich. 215. After the verdict is rendered, the party, who has made the motion which has been reserved, should have entry of judgment stayed until the court has given its final decision. It should be noted that under section 14532 the Supreme Court may order a new trial in certain situations even though the lower court has erroneously acted on the motion to set aside the verdict. The so-called Empson Act was passed to permit the court to get the jury's verdict so that new trials could be avoided. However, there may be other errors in the case which require a new trial. 

It is sometimes argued that in a trial without a jury the defendant cannot make a motion for a judgment at the close of the plaintiff's case and then go on with his case. Section 14307 seems to permit the defendant to make his motion without resting his case.

Where the defendant makes a motion at the close of the plaintiff's case and the court reserves its decision, the defendant's testimony cannot be relied upon in the final decision of the court. Quite often the plaintiff fails to prove a case, but the defendant's witnesses may give sufficient evidence to make out a question of fact. In spite of this, the court must decide the case solely on the testimony given up to the time the motion was made at the close of the plaintiff's case. Snyder v. Johnson, 264 

Mich. 286. 272

PROCEDURE 

[§ 135 

Sec. 134. Special Questions. 

The statute providing for special questions is found in section 14290 of Compiled Laws 1929. In connection with this statute, Rule 37, Section 7, of Court Rules 1933 should be studied. Special questions are sometimes very useful to parties in an automobile case. In Pajalich v. Ford 

Motor Co., 267 Mich. 418, the Court said that under Court

Rule 37 all essential issues of fact should be submitted to the jury. But if essential facts are not covered in the questions, the court may make a finding as to such facts. 

Consequently, if the questions do not cover all of the material facts, the court may act as a jury and make a finding which may require a judgment against the party favored by the jury.

Sec. 135. Instructions. 

The Supreme Court of Michigan has indicated in recent decisions that the appellant has but little chance to secure a reversal for the failure of the trial court to instruct on a certain point, unless the appellant requested such an instruction. In Ogland v. Detroit Edison Co., 261 Mich. 583, the defendant contended that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court instructed the jury that the question of contributory negligence was not in the case. No request for an instruction on contributory negligence was submitted either before or after the charge. It was held that, as the defendant did not request a charge, no error was committed. Another reason given was that the defendant made no claim that there was a question of fact as to contributory negligence. 

Consequently, in the trial of an automobile case, it is advisable for each side to request instructions covering all of the material issues in the case. 273

§ 135] 

In Geglio v. Huizenga, 261 Mich. 512, the defendant's attorney in his opening statement said that the question to be decided was whether the defendant's automobile was on the wrong side of the road. The court in its instructions restricted the case to this question. The defendant on appeal claimed that there were other questions involved. It was held that, as no request was made for instructions and as the court followed the theory submitted by each attorney in his opening statement, no error was committed.

Often a request is made for an instruction based upon certain evidence which is in conflict with other evidence. 

In Thomson v. Brandt, 249 Mich. 127, it was held that if the trial court stated the law in his general charge, it was not necessary for him to comment upon any particular testimony. In Nickels v. Hallen, 247 Mich. 291, the court was in error in instructing the jury, in a pedestrian case, that a driver should have his car under such control that he can, if necessary, stop soon enough to avoid an accident. In Simmons v. Petersen, 207 Mich. 509, it was reversible error for the court to instruct that the driver of an automobile should, after he has discovered the danger, do everything possible to prevent an accident. 

In cases involving claims for permanent injuries, where no evidence has been introduced that the injuries are permanent, the defendant should request a specific instruction that there can be no recovery for permanent injuries. In Main v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 207 Mich. 

473, the court's instruction, that the jury should give a verdict covering pain and suffering for such time as the jury found the plaintiff would suffer from headaches, was held to be erroneous as there was no evidence of the permanency of the headaches. 

Court Rule 37, Section 9, provides that the failure to instruct on any point of law shall not be ground for set- 274

PROCEDURE 

[§ 137 19 ting aside the verdict unless such instruction was requested.

Sec. 136. Certifying Judgment to Probate Court. 

In the case of Hoban v. Equitable & Central Trust Co., 259 Mich. 586, a judgment was rendered against the estate of Charles Ryder. Ryder had a policy of insurance on his automobile. After the accident he died, and the suit against his estate, growing out of the accident, followed. After the judgment was rendered a garnishment action was brought, and a writ of garnishment was served on the insurance company. It was held that under section 15689 Compiled Laws 1929, the judgment in the circuit court should have been certified to the probate court. The judgment against the insurance company in the lower court was reversed. Therefore, when a judgment on an automobile case is rendered against an administrator, the original defendant having died, the judgment should be certified to the probate court. If further proceedings are necessary, the plaintiff may secure an assignment from the administrator and then sue the insurance company, if the original defendant was covered by insurance. 

Sec. 137.

Garnishment. 

After a judgment is obtained against the defendant on an automobile case, the proper procedure to collect on the judgment from an insurance company, with whom the defendant was insured, is to serve a writ of garnishment on the insurance company. This is done because of the theory that after the judgment was rendered the insurance company became liable to the judgment debtor for the amount of the judgment up to the policy limits. See 

Barney v. Preferred Automobile Insurance Exchange, 

240 Mich. 199.

In the usual type of automobile policy the 275

§ 137] 

company now becomes liable when the judgment is rendered and is not appealed. Kipkey v. Casualty Association, 255 Mich. 408; Rogers v. Youngs, 256 Mich. 213.

In a garnishment proceeding the judgment creditor of course is in no better position than the judgment debtor so far as the defenses of the insurance company are concerned. See Kidd v. Minnesota Atlantic Transit Co., 261

Mich. 31. A policy release obtained by the insurance company may be held void as to the judgment creditor because of inadequate consideration, and as a fraud on creditor. Iden v. Huber, 259 Mich. 3. 276

Sec. 148. Proper Parties Defendant. 

The Statutes and Court Rules in Michigan relative to pleading are so concise, and the rulings of the courts are generally so liberal, that only a small amount of space is given over to the subject of pleading. Pleading in death and survival actions has been discussed in the chapters covering those actions. Also in the chapter on Damages, questions of pleading in connection with damages are covered to some extent.

The subject of Parties is closely connected with that of Pleading and consequently is discussed briefly in this chapter. Some phases of the subject of Parties are indirectly commented on in the chapter on Procedure. 

Sec. 138. Pleading Statutes and Ordinances. 

Section 14129, Compiled Laws 1929, provides that when any action is based upon the provisions of any statute, or city or village ordinance, it shall be sufficient for 277

§ 138] 

the plaintiff, without setting forth the special matter, to aver that said action arose by virtue of the provisions of such statute or ordinance by reference to the same. Consequently, where the cause of action is based upon a statute and not upon the common law, reference should be made to the statute or ordinance giving rise to the cause of action, and it should be alleged that the action is based upon the statute or ordinance. It is not necessary to set forth the statute in the declaration. For example, if the action is to recover for damages by reason of wrongful death under the Death Statute, the action is based not on the common law but on the Death Statute, and it should be referred to. With the exception of the action for wrongful death, most of the actions arising out of an automobile accident would be based upon the common law, and, consequently, it would not be necessary to refer to any statute.

It is quite common in declarations based upon automobile cases to set up the statute, the violation of which constitutes negligence according to the claims of the plaintiff. This is surplusage as the court takes judicial notice of these state statutes. See Anderson v. Matt, 223

Mich. 534, in which it was held that the court took judicial notice of the motor vehicle speed statute; and, although the declaration did not refer to such statute, the plaintiff could rely upon it.

Although the plaintiff does not have to set forth the statutes or even refer to them, he must set forth a city or village ordinance if he wants to rely upon the violation of such ordinance as proof of negligence on the part of the defendant. See Yeoman v. Muskegon Traction & Lighting Company, 214 Mich. 68. The reason given for this is that the common law declaration will not support proof of a duty created by an ordinance unless the defendant is 278

[§ given notice thereof. In the case of Kellstrom v. City of 

Detroit, 249 Mich. 431, plaintiff was relying upon the defendant not stopping for a stop street. The plaintiff had failed to set up the ordinance in his declaration. At the time of trial the plaintiff asked to be given the right of amendment, and this was granted, but the declaration was not formally amended. The Supreme Court said that if there had not been any formal amendment it would permit the plaintiff to amend in the Supreme Court. Even though the plaintiff has not set up the ordinance in his declaration or referred to it, he may rely upon it to free himself from contributory negligence. In the case of 

Putnam v. Detroit United Ry., 164 Mich. 342, the plaintiff had not pleaded the ordinance but, at the time of trial, introduced it for the purpose of showing that the plaintiff had a right to anticipate that the speed of the defendant's car would not exceed a certain maximum rate set by the ordinance. The Supreme Court held that the ordinance could be admitted in evidence without pleading where the sole purpose of its admission was to acquit the plaintiff of contributory negligence.

Sec. 139. Alleging Duty. 

Michigan Court Rule No. 82, as set forth in the 1931 rule, provided that pleading substantially similar to the forms appended to the rule would be deemed suitable and sufficient in all cases where applicable forms were attached to the rule, and it should be noted that in the forms for declaration in negligence cases no duties were alleged. 

In the case of Jolman v. Alberts, 186 Mich. 643, the Court held that the failure to allege duty was not fatal. The 

Court said that the rules of pleading required an allegation in the declaration of the duty the defendant owed to the plaintiff on the particular occasion in question. The 279

§ 140] 

Court, however, went on to say that this rule had been somewhat modified on several occasions by holding that, where the facts were set forth in the declaration in such a manner that the duty could be implied, it was not necessary to set forth the duty. In Niedzinski v. Coryell, 215 

Mich. 498, the declaration did not contain any allegations of duty. The plaintiff contended that he had followed one of the forms attached to the court rules. The Supreme Court held that the declaration was sufficient and said that it thought no one would be misled by the declaration or would fail to understand that the negligence charged as the cause of the accident was the failure of the defendant to observe due care and to comply with the laws of the road when passing the plaintiff in the same direction. From the decisions in these two cases and the above mentioned forms attached to the court rules, it would seem well settled in this State that it is not necessary to allege duties where the allegations of negligence would imply the duty. In an automobile case the allegations of negligence would seem to necessarily imply duty. 

Sec. 140. Pleading Discovered or Subsequent 

Negligence.

If the plaintiff desires to proceed upon a theory of discovered negligence or subsequent negligence, he should put the proper allegations covering the theory in his declaration. In Smith v. Grand Rapids Railway Company, 240 Mich. 637, it was held that where a suit was not planted or tried on the claim of discovered negligence, the plaintiff could not rely upon it. In Kerns v. Lewis, 246 Mich. 423, the plaintiff alleged due care, denied negligence on his part and alleged negligence on the part of the defendant. The Supreme Court said that under these allegations an issue of discovered negligence was not 280

[§ raised. The Supreme Court said that the instruction of the lower court injected the Last Clear Chance Doctrine, which could not arise except there be such an issue presented by the plaintiff in confession of his own negligence. 

In the case of Sabol v. Chicago & Northwestern Railway 

Company, 255 Mich. 548, the defendant claimed that the declaration did not allege wilful misconduct. The Supreme Court said that no objection was made in the trial court of the insufficiency of the declaration in that regard. 

The Court said, however, that there was no merit to the objection as the declaration alleged facts which amounted to wilful misconduct. It was held in Hook v. Solomon, 194 Mich. 517, that the plaintiff could recover for ordinary negligence although the declaration characterized the negligence as wilful and wanton. In Weitzel v. Detroit United Railway, 186 Mich. 7, the Court said that, although subsequent or discovered negligence ought to be alleged in plaintiff's pleading, if an objection was not presented to the lower court, it would not be considered fatal or an error, and an amendment would be permitted upon a new trial. For proper pleading of this theory, see pleadings used in cases listed in chapter on Subsequent or 

Discovered Negligence. 

Sec. 141.

Damages. 

In an action to recover for personal injuries, it is advisable to allege in detail the nature of the injuries sustained and the resulting damages therefrom. Special damages must, of course, be alleged. See Gleason v. 

Lowe, 232 Mich. 300, where the Court held that, in the absence of the allegation of special damages, the plaintiff could not put in evidence as to the amount he had paid for labor on his farm while he was unable to work on the farm. In Markoff v. Detroit United Railway, 169 Mich. 281

§ 142] 

37, it was held that the plaintiff should have been permitted to give testimony concerning an injury to his heart where it was alleged that he had received permanent injury to his head, the base of his brain, and general allegations as to injuries and bruises, resulting in faintness and dizzy spells. In the case of Ralph v. Gies Gear Company, 164 Mich. 44, there was no allegation that the plaintiff's general health had been injured. However, there were allegations as to serious injuries, and the Court held that the testimony should have been admitted as to the effect of the injuries upon the general health of the plaintiff, although the declaration did not allege such injury. Such damage as loss of earnings, loss of profits, expenses incurred, or injury to earning capacity should certainly be alleged. As stated before, it is advisable to set forth the damages in detail as much as is possible; and if, while the case is pending, new injuries appear or additional damage is sustained, an amendment to the declarations should be sought.

Sec. 142. Sufficiency of Allegations. 

It is not sufficient that a general allegation be made that the defendant is negligent. It should be alleged in what particular way the defendant was negligent. It is advisable in pleading the negligence of the defendant to set forth in a simple way the negligent act of the defendant. 

See Thomas v. City of Detroit, 263 Mich. 166, where it was held that the plaintiff had not alleged any negligent acts on the part of the defendant, and, consequently, the declaration was defective. Sometimes an allegation of general negligence is held to include a specific act. For instance, in the case of Kuchcinski v. Curtis, 251 Mich. 

210, it was held that, where there was an allegation that the driver of the truck was negligent in failing to have it 282

[§ under control, it was broad enough to admit evidence showing that the brakes of the truck were defective. 

Sec. 143. Variance. 

The subject of variance in pleading in connection with automobile cases is not important in Michigan under the broad rule of amendment and, also, because of the lenient attitude of the Court where the question of variance arises. For instance, in the case of Formiller v. Detroit 

United Ry., 164 Mich. 653, it was held that there was not a fatal variance under the declaration, charging that after plaintiff stepped on the lower step of the car the defendant's servant suddenly started the car forward and threw him off, when the testimony showed that the car had started in the usual way and as he was stepping on the second step, it suddenly increased the speed and threw him to the ground. However, in Gibbs v. Dayton, 166

Mich. 263, where the declaration charged that the decedent was proceeding in a northerly direction along the east side of the street, it was held that proof that the decedent was riding in a southwesterly direction was at variance with the declaration. In this case the declaration alleged a head-on collision, whereas the proof showed that the decedent was crossing the street. However, the Court said that the variance might be corrected by an amendment. 

Sec. 144.

Amendments. 

It is entirely within the discretion of the Court to allow or disallow amendments to a declaration. See Kerr v. 

City of Detroit, 255 Mich. 446. In this case the rule is laid down for an amendment. The same evidence must support both the original and the amended declaration, and there must be the same measure of damages appli- 283

§ 145] 

cable to both. In this particular case the amendment was not allowed as it would have required new evidence to show that the defendant discovered the plaintiff in a position of danger. If, at the time the amendment is asked, the Statute of Limitations has run and the amendment would constitute a new cause of action, it will, of course, not be permitted. Also, see case of Volay v. Williams, 258 Mich. 184, for amendment of declaration.

Sec. 145. 

Answers. 

Rule 23 of the Michigan Court Rules, Section 2, requires the defendant, in his answer, to set forth the substance of the matters which will be relied upon to support each denial. This requirement virtually compels the defendant to set forth the facts of his defense, at least in substance. 

Rule 24 requires that new matter set forth in the answer shall be answered by a reply. 

Sec. 146.

Cross-Declaration. 

Section 14142 of Compiled Laws, 1929, provides that the defendant, in an action to recover damages for any injury to person or property, may, at the time of filing and serving his plea, serve a cross-declaration against the plaintiff for damages or injuries to his person or property arising out of the occurrence forming the basis of the plaintiff's case. It should be noted that it is not compulsory for the defendant to file a cross-declaration if he wants to make a claim against the plaintiff and that he has the right to proceed against the plaintiff on a separate suit. 

Sec. 147. Real Party in Interest. 

The Real Party in Interest Statute in Michigan, Section 14010, Compiled Laws of 1929, for many years has required that every action shall be prosecuted in the name 284

[§ of the real party in interest. Up to 1929, when the statute was amended, permitting an insurance company to join with a policy holder in a suit to recover for personal injuries and property damage, there was much confusion in Michigan as to the proper party plaintiff where an insurance company had paid for part of the loss and was an interested party.

As the result of an automobile accident, the owner of the car is often compensated either in whole or in part for the damage to his car by an insurance company. 

Prior to the amendment in 1929 there was a question as to how the case should be sued where an attempt was made to recover for the property damage or for the property damage plus injuries sustained by the owner of the car.

Sometimes suit was started in the name of the owner of the car although he had no interest in the case, it being claimed by the plaintiff that he was acting as a trustee for the insurance company. Suits were started by joining the insurance company with the plaintiff, it being claimed that there was no splitting of the cause of action as the defendant was not being subjected to more than one lawsuit. 

Suits were also started in the name of the insurance company alone, the company having taken an assignment of the whole cause of action from the owner of the automobile. The cases giving rise to the confusion in the law on this point will not be considered. The leading cases are 

The Continental Insurance Co. v. Loud & Sons Lumber 

Co., 93 Mich. 139; Everhard v. Dodge Bros., 202 Mich. 48; 

Grubaugh v. Simon Murphy Co., 209 Mich. 551; Barak v. 

Detroit Apartments Co., 232 Mich. 59; Cox v. D. U. R., 234 Mich. 597; Heck v. Henne, 238 Mich. 198; Cox v. 

D. U. R., 238 Mich. 527; McPeake v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 242 Mich. 676. 285

§ 147] 

In the case of Copeland v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 249

Mich. 115, the plaintiff had received part payment on a fire loss from the insurance company. Suit was started in the name of the plaintiff, the policyholder, only. After a verdict was rendered for all of the damages, the insurance company was added as a party plaintiff with the consent of the defendant. The Supreme Court said that this was error, but, inasmuch as the defendant had waived the error, it would not reverse the decision. The Supreme 

Court pointed out that the real party in interest statute was amended in 1929 to permit the insurance company to be joined with the policyholder in such an action. The 

Court admitted that an uncertainty had arisen as to the proper procedure before the amendment of the statute. 

In the case of Worth v. Wagner, 255 Mich. 433, the policyholder joined with the insurance company in a case against the defendant for personal injuries and property damage loss. The defendant contended that they were separate causes of action and that the amended statute only applied to a property damage loss. The Supreme

Court held that the case was properly sued and that the purpose of the statute was to cover just such a situation and avoid a multiplicity of suits. In Solomon v. Ryder, 257 Mich. 193, the plaintiff had sustained personal injuries in an automobile accident, and her car was damaged. 

She was paid for the damage to her car by her insurance company and sued in her own name, alleging that she was acting as a trustee for the insurance company to the extent of the property damage. The defendant moved to dismiss the case on the ground that the action was not brought in the name of the real party in interest, and the plaintiff and the insurance company waived all claims for damages for loss of the car, and the court permitted the case to proceed. The Supreme Court said that, had the 286

[§ plaintiff stood upon the declaration, it would have been the duty of the court to have dismissed the action. However, the waiver by the plaintiff and the representative of the insurance company of the claim for the loss of the car made the completeness of the action single in purpose and the plaintiff the only party in interest. It can be seen from these cases that the confusion which was in existence before the statute was amended has not been completely avoided. There is considerable law in Michigan to support the contention that, if a policyholder has not made an assignment of his claim or has the legal title to the cause of action, he is the real party in interest even though part of the proceeds of the judgment would go back to the insurance company. Consequently, if a policyholder is injured in an accident and makes no assignment of the property damage claim, it could be argued that he has the legal title to the cause of action and is the sole party in interest. If the insurance company, before suit was started, made an assignment of its claim back to the policyholder, and the policyholder sued in his own name, a question would arise as to whether he was the real party in interest so far as the property damage was concerned. The safe way to proceed is to join the insurance company with the policyholder.

Where a husband and wife are joint owners of an automobile and are in the automobile when an accident occurs and are both injured, a question would arise as to the proper manner in bringing a suit to cover their property damage and their personal injuries. For such a situation, see case of Tuttle v. Everhot Heater Co., 264 Mich. 

60. The accident in this case occurred in New York State, and the law of that state controlled. However, in the opinion it is stated by the Michigan Court that in Michigan damages for injuries to person and property as a re- 287

§ 148] 

sult of a single tort give rise to but a single cause of action. It would therefore seem that in such a situation where the accident occurred in Michigan there could be only two suits-one for the husband and one for the wife, and in each suit the plaintiff would have to sue for his share of the damage to property. This is assuming that the property would not be held by the husband and wife by entireties but would be held jointly. 

The wife is a proper party plaintiff to recover for loss of earnings even though she has no assignment from her husband. See Werner v. Wegusen, 252 Mich. 41.

Sec. 148. Proper Parties Defendant. 

Where suit is to be brought on a charge of negligence against the driver of an automobile, it is advisable to make the owner of the automobile a defendant as well as the driver. It is also possible that, in addition to the driver and owner, an individual or corporation was using the automobile at the time of the accident and would be liable for the negligent acts of the driver. If such is the case, this individual or corporation should be made a party defendant along with the driver and the owner. 

There is also a possibility of showing that one who is not an owner or an employer is liable because he permitted a known reckless driver to operate the car.

Where there are two cars involved and a charge of negligence is to be made against each driver, and the plaintiff was not an occupant of either car, the normal procedure is to sue the two drivers and the owner and possibly other liable parties in one action. 288
