Miscellaneous Cases. 

Sec. 168. Res Ipsa Loquitur. 

No attempt is made in this chapter to consider all of the questions of evidence which might arise in a trial of an automobile case. There are many decisions, however, which are peculiar to the automobile case. Rules of law are found in these decisions applicable to the introduction of evidence concerning the operation of a motor vehicle, the charges of negligence, and the claims as to injuries. 

Cases of this nature are considered in this chapter. 

There are also several statutes, dealing with evidence, which are constantly being relied upon in the trial 289

§ 149] 

of an automobile case. Section 4788, Compiled Laws 1929, makes the driver of the car in the rear prima facie guilty of negligence where the ordinary type of rear end collision takes place. Section 4796 makes garage keepers prima facie guilty of negligence where damage is done to cars in their care. Section 14221 makes a personal injury action an exception under the statute preventing one spouse from testifying for or against the other. Section 

4722 prohibits the use of a police report of a motor vehicle accident in a court action. Other statutes are considered under headings.

Sec. 149. Matters Equally Within Knowledge of 

Deceased.

Section 14219, Compiled Laws 1929, provides that when a suit is prosecuted or defended by a personal representative of a deceased person, the opposite party, if examined as a witness in his own behalf, shall not be permitted to testify at all to matters which, if true, must have been equally within the knowledge of the deceased. If the opposite party is a corporation, the prohibition applies to an officer or agent of the corporation. If a corporation is prosecuting or defending a claim and the only officer or agent, who had certain information, is dead, the opposite party is not permitted to testify as to that information. 

This provision also applies if the person, though not dead, has been adjudged to be and still is insane or mentally incompetent at the time of trial.

This statute is often involved in automobile cases because of the large number of death actions. It not infrequently happens that the defendant dies as a result of the accident and hence his personal representative may invoke the statute.

The important decisions affecting automobile cases are as follows: 

290

EVIDENCE 

[$ 149 

Noonan v. Volek, 246 Mich. 377.

This was a survival action. The defendant, driving an automobile, approached the decedent's milk wagon from the rear and collided with the wagon. The defendant was not permitted to testify, in the lower court, that he sounded his horn on the ground that it was a fact equally within the knowledge of the deceased.

It was held that the trial court was in error in excluding this testimony. It was a question of fact for the jury whether the horn, if sounded, was heard by the deceased.

"The statute applies to actions of tort prosecuted by the heirs, representatives, or legatees of a deceased to recover damages under the survival act. The fact that other persons witnessed the accident and testified to matters equally within the knowledge of the deceased did not lift the bar or waive the protection of the statute. While such is the rule, its application, in tort actions, is fraught with difficulty in determining what knowledge the deceased had of a particular event, for the bar is not up until it affirmatively appears that the fact, if true, was known to the deceased."

The Court said that whether the facts were equally within the knowledge of the deceased could not be inferred. The jury should have been instructed that it should not give the testimony the same consideration, if it found it was equally within the knowledge of the deceased. "The burden of showing that the fact, if true, was equally within the knowledge of the deceased rests with one invoking the prohibition of the statute." 

Rock v. Gannon Grocery Company, 246 Mich. 545.

In this case, a survival action, the decedent was riding with her husband and others in an automobile driven by 20 291

§ 149] 

Theodore Nault. The husband and a son testified as to how the accident occurred. They said that the defendant's truck was driven toward their car and onto the wrong side of the road, striking it. The lower court did not permit the defendant to testify. 

It was held that the testimony should have been permitted as the plaintiff had called the husband and son of the decedent to testify fully as to circumstances claimed to have been equally within the knowledge of the deceased. 

"The statute is a shield and not a sword. Death having sealed the lips of one, the statute closes the lips of the other, except in contradiction of testimony given by witnesses having a pecuniary interest in the recovery. The statute recognizes a condition occasioned by death and establishes equality between the living in interest, but does not permit the living, in behalf of their pecuniary interest, to advance a sword from behind the shield and forbid its parry. It has long been held that the statute may be waived. It is manifestly unfair to permit those having a pecuniary interest in the suit to testify to matters equally within the knowledge of the deceased and to deny the opposite party the right to contradict or be heard with reference to such testimony."

It should be noted that the Court pointed out that, even if there had been no waiver, the lower court should have submitted the question, of whether the deceased had equal knowledge, to the jury, and that that fact should not have been inferred. 

Miner v. Scholton, 250 Mich. 645.

The plaintiff's car came in contact with the defendant's truck driven by Scholton who was also a defendant. Before trial Scholton died. At the trial the question was 292

EVIDENCE 

[§ 149 which vehicle was on the wrong side of the highway at the time of impact. The plaintiff was asked this question. "Did your truck and the truck coming from the opposite direction there have a collision?" The affirmative answer was stricken as equally within the knowledge of the de ceased Scholton. The Supreme Court said: 

"Assuming that it was a question for the jury whether Scholton knew the location of plaintiff's truck with reference to the center of the highway, the question, nevertheless, included the fact of collision, which was obviously within the knowledge of Scholton, and rendered the answer inadmissible." 

Olmsted v. Sober, 251 Mich. 688.

This was a survival action resulting from an accident in which a pedestrian was injured. A cardboard had been substituted for the lower part of the windshield of the defendant's truck. The defendant driver was permitted to testify that it in no way interfered with his vision. 

He also testified, over objection, to certain other facts, which the plaintiff urged were equally within the knowledge of the deceased. The trial court instructed the jury to disregard any testimony which it found was equally within the knowledge of the deceased. 

It was held that the testimony was properly admitted as it did not appear at the time or thereafter during the trial that the fact, if true, was known to the deceased. 

Billingsley v. Gulick, 256 Mich. 606.

At the first trial the defendants were sworn and testified. No objection was made by the plaintiff. The witnesses were cross-examined. At the second trial the plaintiff objected to their testimony. 

The Court held that the plaintiff, by failing to object to the competency of the defendants and electing to cross- 293

§ 149] 

examine them on the first trial, waived her right to object in a subsequent trial. 

Loucks v. Fox, 261 Mich. 338.

This was an action under the Death Act. The only witness to give a coherent, clear statement as to how the accident occurred was the defendant, who was rigidly crossexamined by the plaintiff. No objection was made to the testimony.

It was held that the admission of the testimony was not error. The Court said that the plaintiff could not withhold his objections and cross-examine the defendant and thus take his chances on favorable testimony, and then maintain that such testimony was improperly admitted. 

Caswell v. Smith's Estate, 263 Mich. 390.

The plaintiff brought suit against the decedent's estate on an alleged oral contract for services. The wife of the plaintiff was permitted to give testimony concerning the alleged contract.

It was held that the wife's testimony was not admissible as she was an opposite party in interest although not an opposite party of record. 

Lapachin v. Standard Oil Company, 268 Mich. 477.

The plaintiff, a pedestrian, was struck by the defendant's car. The driver of the car was dead at the time of the trial. The defendant contended that the plaintiff's testimony as to what part of his body was struck by the car, what part of his body struck the ground, where he was lying on the pavement, and that the right front fender of the car hit him was not admissible because it was equally within the knowledge of the deceased. The Supreme Court said: 294

EVIDENCE 

[§ 150 "The difficulty in this case is to know which, if any, of this testimony was known to the deceased driver. 

The testimony was admissible unless the facts asserted, if true, were equally within the knowledge of the driver. We may not infer. The burden is upon the one invoking the prohibition of the statute." 

The Court found no reversible error. 

Hanna v. McClave, 271 Mich. 133.

It was held in this case that the lower court was in error in not permitting the defendant to testify as to the southerly point that the decedent pedestrian reached and whether there was anything in his position that indicated there was any danger of an impact. 

Sec. 150.

Summary. 

Although the statute says that the opposite party shall not be admitted to testify, the objection must be made by the party desiring to rely upon the statute. If the opposite party testifies and is cross-examined, no objection being made, the testimony stands. (Loucks v. Fox.) If once admitted, the testimony cannot be barred at a subsequent trial. (Billingsley v. Gulick.) If the personal representative calls a witness to testify as to certain facts, and the witness is a beneficiary of the estate, the opposite party may testify as to such facts. (Rock v. 

Gannon Grocery Co.) If the right is not waived and a timely objection is made, the burden is on the party, invoking the prohibition of the statute, to show that the facts were equally within the knowledge of the deceased. 

(Lapachin v. Standard Oil Company.) The situation may be such as to present a question for the jury as to whether the deceased had knowledge of the facts. (Noonan v. 

Volek.) It should be noted that a witness may be barred 295

§ 151] 

from giving testimony though not a party, if the witness has sufficient interest in the outcome of the case. (Caswell v. Smith's Estate.)

Sec. 151. Physician-Patient Privilege. 

Information obtained by a physician in attending a patient, which is necessary to enable him to prescribe for the patient, is privileged under section 14216, Compiled Laws 1929. This statute also provides that if the patient brings an action for personal injuries and produces any physician as a witness, who has treated him for such injuries, he waives the privilege as to all other physicians who may have treated him for such injuries. 

These rules are suggested by the cases following. The privilege must be claimed before the physician testifies or it is waived. If the plaintiff uses a physician as a witness to testify concerning the nature of the injuries, he cannot object to the defendant calling other doctors who attended the plaintiff. The information which is privileged is only that which is necessary to enable the physician to treat the injuries. 

Briesenmeister v. Knights of Pythias, 81 Mich. 525.

In this case it was held that the privilege must be claimed before the testimony is admitted or it ceases to be a privilege.

La Count v. Von Platen Fox Company, 243 Mich. 250. 

The plaintiff called a physician to show the nature of his injury. The defendant called two physicians who had attended the plaintiff before the claimed injury to show that the alleged injury was a chronic trouble of long standing.

It was held the testimony of the physicians was competent. 296

EVIDENCE 

[§ 152 

Perry v. Hannagan, 257 Mich. 120.

The plaintiff in this case called the physician who had given the defendant first aid after the accident, and the physician testified that he noticed the odor of liquor on the defendant's breath.

It was held that the testimony was not privileged. 

Sec. 152. Cross-Examination of Opposite Party or 

Agent.

Section 14220 of Compiled Laws 1929 provides that either party may call the opposite party or his agent and cross-examine him as though he were called by the opposite party. The party so calling and examining such witness shall not be bound to accept such answers as true. At first glance it would seem that the party, calling the opposite party under the statute, would not be bound by the testimony of the witness. However, it must be remembered that the right is the same as the right to cross-examine when the witness is called by the opposite party.

The following cases are the important ones involving an interpretation of the statute. If employees or agents of the defendant are called by the plaintiff, they are not made the defendant's witnesses. The plaintiff is bound by the testimony unless it is contradicted. The defendant may ask the witness leading questions. In order to rely upon the statute the plaintiff should announce that he is calling the defendant under the statute before he begins his questioning. The plaintiff may ask the witness any questions material to his case. The credibility of the witness may be attacked during the examination. 

Jones v. Pere Marquette Rd. Co., 168 Mich. 1.

The plaintiff called a number of the defendant's employees as witnesses under the statute. The plaintiff 297

§ 152] 

insisted that the witnesses were not the plaintiff's but the defendant's witnesses.  "This Act allows such witnesses to be cross-examined and contradicted by the party calling them. 

The provision that such calling shall not interfere with their right to contradict or deny the truth of their statements conferred no new right. The act does not give the right to make them the witnesses of the adversary of the party calling them." 

Johnson v. Union Carbide Co., 169 Mich. 651.

The plaintiff assigned error because the court permitted a witness, in the employ of the defendant and called by the plaintiff for cross-examination under the statute, to be cross-examined and asked leading questions by the defendant.

No error was committed according to the Supreme Court. 

Aphoresmenos v. McIntosh, 189 Mich. 680.

Plaintiff's counsel called the defendant for cross-examination. After giving testimony at length upon material issues, which testimony was not contradicted, the plaintiff's counsel contended that the plaintiff was not bound by it. The Court said: "Testimony developed in this manner may be contradicted and overcome by other testimony, but its effect cannot be destroyed or put aside by mere assertion. Defendant's testimony so developed stood in no different position in the case than it would had it been called out by cross-examination after he had taken the stand in his own behalf." 

Walter v. Detroit, Jackson & Chicago Ry. Co., 191 Mich. 181.

The plaintiff served a subpoena on the defendant's motorman. He put him on the witness stand and, after 298

EVIDENCE 

[§ 152 asking a few preliminary questions, the plaintiff's attorney announced that the witness was called under the statute. The defendant asserted that the plaintiff had waived his right to call the witness under the statute.

It was held that there had been no waiver as the questions which had been asked at the time the announcement was made were preliminary and the main facts had not been gone into. 

Waller v. Sloan, 225 Mich. 600.

It was held in this case that the plaintiff could prove his case by calling and cross-examining the defendant. "The so-called 'orthodox rule' extending the right of cross-examination to all points material to issues involved, and not limiting it to matters brought out on direct-examination, has ever prevailed in this State." 

Kuitula v. Abbott, 229 Mich. 84.

The plaintiff called the defendant under the statute. 

He testified that he was not driving faster than 14 miles per hour. He was then asked in what distance he could stop his car going at that rate of speed. The lower court did not allow the defendant to answer.

It was held that the answer should have been permitted. “It is true that the statute does not give the plaintiff the right to call the opposite party for the purpose of inquiring into his defense, but this question related to a matter that was part of the plaintiff's The question was material to the plaintiff's case and should have been answered." case. 

Swank v. Croff, 245 Mich. 657.

In this case it was held that the plaintiff was bound by the testimony of the defendants called under the statute 299

§ 153] 

except in so far as such testimony was disputed. The 

Court said that the plaintiff could not select isolated portions of the testimony and claim a force and effect for it which the whole testimony did not warrant. 

Miller v. Beasley, 255 Mich. 15.

In this case the plaintiff, having called the defendant under the statute, asked the witness if he had not been guilty of a named act of immorality the night before. 

It was held that the credibility of the defendant was a point material to the issues involved and was proper on cross-examination under the statute.

Kovich v. Church & Church, Inc., 267 Mich. 640. 

In this case the Court said: "The purpose of this statute is to permit the calling as a witness of the opposite party or his agent or employee with the same privileges of cross-examination and contradiction as though such witness had been called by the opposite party."

The cases dealing with questions of evidence peculiar to the automobile case will be dealt with under topical heads. The questions are not considered exhaustively. 

Only the decisions of the Michigan Supreme Court on any particular question are given.

Sec. 153. Proof of Ownership. 

Theisen v. Detroit Taxicab Co., 200 Mich. 136.

The plaintiff's son testified that he telephoned the defendant company. A man answered and said that he was the manager; that the company owned the cab and the driver had reported the accident.

It was held that this testimony was admissible and made out a prima facie case as to ownership. 17 300

EVIDENCE 

[§ 153 

Hatter v. Dodge Bros., 202 Mich. 97.

This suit was against the defendant as owner of the automobile involved in an accident. The license number was proved and testimony was offered showing the number was registered in the name of the defendant. The name "Dodge Bros." was on the side of the car. The driver, after the accident, admitted that he worked for 

Dodge Bros.

It was held that this testimony was sufficient to prove ownership and that the possession and use of the car raised a presumption that the car was used with the owner's consent. 

Jones v. Detroit Taxicab Co., 218 Mich. 673.

To prove that the defendant owned the automobile the plaintiff introduced a certified copy from the Secretary of State of the issue of license plates, bearing the number in question, to the defendant.

It was held that this was prima facie proof of ownership. Also see Pratt v. Detroit Taxicab Co., 225 Mich. 147. 

Belleville v. Ingram, 230 Mich. 462.

Testimony was given by the plaintiff's attorney that he called upon the defendants and they admitted that they owned the car involved in the accident. 

It was held that this presented a question for the jury as to ownership. 

McAvon v. Brightmoor Transit Co., 245 Mich. 44. 

To prove ownership the plaintiff offered a certificate by the Secretary of State that the car bearing a certain number was in the name of the defendant. 

It was held that this was not admissible as it was not a transcript of a public record. Had a copy of the applica- 301

§ 154] 

tion for plates been certified by the Secretary of State, it would have been prima facie evidence of ownership.

It should be pointed out here that the certificate should recite that up to the date of the accident there had been no transfer of ownership. In case of a number of transfers in one year it might be advisable to offer certified copies of the titles showing the order of transfer. 

Sec. 154. Proof of Speed. 

Harnau v. Haight, 189 Mich. 600.

The witness, a railroad engineer, saw the car travel a distance of 20 feet. He thought that it was going 30 miles per hour from the sound of the engine. He estimated its speed as 20 miles per hour from his sight of it. 

It was held that he was competent to testify as to the car's speed. 

Wright v. Crane, 142 Mich. 508.

The witness testified that he first saw the car when it was but 20 feet away and coming toward him.

It was held that the witness was not in a position to judge the speed of the car coming directly toward him and only 20 feet away. 

Faulkner v. Payne, 191 Mich. 263.

A witness, who had driven horses all of her life, had ridden in autos and trains and testified that she knew something about the speed of trains and that she saw the car approaching for a sufficient distance to judge its speed, was held competent to testify as to speed. 

Jones v. Detroit Taxicab Co., 218 Mich. 673.

A witness, who saw the cab travel 40 feet, and had ridden in wagons and autos, and had watched speedometers, was held competent to testify as to speed. 302

EVIDENCE 

[§ 155 

Hinderer v. Ann Arbor Railroad Co., 237 Mich. 232.

It was held in this case that the plaintiff could not testify as to the speed of a train, having seen it for the first time only two feet away. 66 ‘An estimate of speed based simply on an opinion of the force of impact is not evidence of speed." 

Zylstra v. Graham, 244 Mich. 319.

A witness who had driven a car for five years and who saw the defendant's car 50 feet away was held competent to testify as to speed. 

Stehouwer v. Lewis, 249 Mich. 76.

A witness, who saw the car 200 feet from the scene of the accident pass in front of him, was held competent, though he had never driven a car, having ridden in automobiles and watched speedometers. The Court said that the witness need not qualify as an expert provided he is fully questioned so that the jury can give proper weight to the questions. 

Sec. 155.

Evidence as to Marks. 

Anderson v. Lynch, 232 Mich. 276.

In this case the main question was which car was on the wrong side of the highway. A witness testified that he could see marks left by the wheels of the bus and the Ford car and that the marks from the bus wheels were traced back from the bus to the place of the accident, the left wheel being one and one-half feet over the center line.

It was held that this testimony was admissible. 

Gembolis v. Rydeski, 258 Mich. 521.

A question was raised in this case as to whether the plaintiff was walking on the pavement or the shoulder. 303

§ 155] 

A witness was allowed to testify that, five hours after the accident, he found glass in a certain spot. A police officer had testified that one hour after the accident he had found glass on the pavement and shoulder. There was other testimony indicating liability on the part of the defendant.

The Court held that in view of the evidence given the admission of what the witness saw five hours after the accident was not reversible error. 

Billingsley v. Gulick, 252 Mich. 235.

Testimony as to the position of certain articles of the deceased pedestrian the morning after the accident was held to be not admissible without proof that there had been no change in position. 

Miner v. Scholton, 250 Mich. 645.

In this case there were no eye witnesses of the accident. The plaintiff tried to prove his case by showing the defendant's truck was on the wrong side of the road as indicated by the marks on the highway. Testimony was offered as to the marks left by the wheels of each vehicle. However, there was no testimony as to the point where the impact occurred.

It was held that, even though part of the marks left by the wheels of defendant's truck were on the wrong side of the highway, there was no proof of negligence as the accident might have occurred in one of several ways. "Where testimony goes no further than to indicate that several conditions may have been present which could have caused an accident, but fails to show that one was actually present, it is pure conjecture to hold it the cause." 

Also see Peters v. Wurzburg, 267 Mich. 45. 304

EVIDENCE 

[§ 156 

Sec. 156. Position of Cars. 

Prove v. Interstate Stages, 250 Mich. 478.

The accident occurred on an 18 foot concrete road. A truck was stopped headed east on the south half of the highway. The plaintiff, east bound, claimed that he stopped behind this truck and that his car was struck by the west bound bus. After the accident the plaintiff's car faced north with the right side almost touching the rear end of the truck. 

Three justices held that the position of the plaintiff's car disproved his theory and said that it would have been impossible for the bus to have been on the wrong side and the plaintiff's car to come to a stop where it did. 

Five justices held with the plaintiff, saying this: "Automobile accidents and collisions are attended by strange, unexpected and apparently incredible results, which seem to defy commonly known laws of physics and their effects." 

Loucks v. Fox, 261 Mich. 338.

In this case there was a dispute as to which car was on the wrong side of the road just before the collision occurred. The defendant testified that he turned to the left to avoid the other car which was approaching on the defendant's side of the road. The right side of the defendant's car struck the left side of the other car. The defendant's auto left the road but the other car remained on the traveled portion of the highway. 

The Court said that at the most the physical facts lead to conjecture. It was pointed out that it could be argued that the final position of the plaintiff's car on the road indicated it was on the wrong side just before the collision, as otherwise it would have been pushed off the road. 305

§ 157] 

 Sec. 157. Photographs. 

Amedeo v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 215 Mich. 37.

In this case the Court held that it was within the discretion of the trial court to permit a photograph of the deceased to be introduced for the purpose of showing the decedent's physical appearance. 

Bade v. Nies, 239 Mich. 37.

While the mother of the deceased was testifying, she was shown a photograph of the deceased. 

It was held that the photograph had no place in the trial but, as there was no dramatic scene resulting, there was no reversible error. 

Martin Parry Corp. v. Berner, 259 Mich. 621.

Photographs of the scene of the accident taken the day after were introduced. Witnesses testified that they presented a fair picture of the situation. 

This evidence was held admissible. Its weight as to whether the defendant's car was on the right side of the road was for the jury. 

Peters v. Wurzburg, 267 Mich. 45.

During the trial the jury visited the scene of the accident. Photographs were shown by the defendant, who claimed that they proved that the plaintiff should have seen the defendant coming over the hill in time to avoid the accident.

The Supreme Court said that it would not substitute the photographs for the jury's conclusions.

Sec. 158. Res Gestae. 

Jolman v. Alberts, 192 Mich. 25.

The plaintiff testified that the defendant said he would pay for the repair of the buggy, making the statement 306

EVIDENCE 

[§ 158 21 almost immediately after the accident. The defendant contended that this was a compromise offer and was not admissible. 

It was held that the testimony was admissible as res gestae. 

Link v. Fahey, 200 Mich. 308.

A witness was permitted to testify that 15 to 20 minutes after the accident the driver of the defendant's car said that he was to blame.

It was held that there was no error as the admission did not influence the jury. 

Hyatt v. Leonard Storage Co., 196 Mich. 337.

A witness testified as to statements made by the driver of the defendant's truck one half hour after the accident. 

It was held that this was not admissible. It was not spontaneous and consequently was not res gestae. 

Wald v. Packard Motor Car Co., 204 Mich. 147.

Ten minutes after the accident the driver of the defendant's car told a police officer that he worked for the defendant. It was held that this was admissible. 

See Metcalf v. Peerless Laundry & Dye Co., 215 Mich. 601. 

Phinney v. Detroit United Ry., 232 Mich. 399.

A witness was not permitted to testify as to what the defendant's motorman said ten minutes after the accident and after he had telephoned his superior officer. 

McAvon v. Brightmoor Transit Co., 245 Mich. 44.

In this case it was held that a witness could not testify as to a statement made by defendant's driver immediately after the accident in answer to a question as to who 307

§ 159] 

was the owner. The Court explained that the statement was not related to the cause of the accident and was not res gestae. In addition, the declarations of an agent were not admissible to show agency although the agent's testimony was. 

Martin Parry Corp. v. Berner, 259 Mich. 621.

A witness testified that immediately after the accident the driver of plaintiff's car was placed in his car and he kept saying that there weren't any lights. One of the main issues was whether the defendant had lights on his car. 

It was held that this testimony was admissible although the defendant was not present.

Sec. 159. Admissions Against Interest. 

Ward v. De Young, 210 Mich. 67.

A witness, in testifying as to certain admissions made by the defendant, mentioned insurance. 

It was held that it was part of the defendant's statement and, as there was no evident intention to inject insurance into the case, there was no error. 

Donker v. Powers, 230 Mich. 237.

In this case the Court discusses the question of the silence of the defendant when statements are made in his presence. If one would ordinarily reply, but silence is maintained, it may amount to an admission. 

Sec. 160. Adjusters. 

Musliner v. Detroit United Ry., 197 Mich. 409.

An adjuster for the defendant was put on the stand to testify concerning a statement which he had taken from 308

EVIDENCE 

[§ 161 the plaintiff. The Court said that the plaintiff could cross-examine to show the purpose in making the statement as favorable to the defendant as possible. 

Morris v. Montgomery, 229 Mich. 509.

In this case it was held that the error, in permitting the plaintiff to testify that an insurance adjuster was present when he talked to the defendant, was cured by the instruction. 

Rosenberg v. Mageda, 251 Mich. 696.

Here the plaintiff was given the right to explain circumstances under which she signed a statement for the adjuster of an insurance company. It was also held that the statement taken by the adjuster was not substantive evidence but was to be considered only as bearing on the credibility of the witness.

Sec. 161. Credibility. 

Van Goosen v. Barlum, 214 Mich. 595.

In this case the defendant was cross-examined as to the number of times he had been arrested and convicted. 

The Court said that this was proper as bearing on his credibility. 

Niedzinski v. Coryell, 215 Mich. 498.

The lower court permitted the plaintiff to show that the defendant had been convicted of crimes on different occasions without showing the records. 

It was held that this was proper as bearing on credibility even though each crime was driving a car too fast. 

It should be noted that section 14218 of Compiled Laws 1929 provides that a conviction of a crime may be shown to affect the credibility of a witness. Where the convic- 309

§ 162] 

tion is for the violation of an ordinance the statute would not apply as such a violation is not a crime. Therefore, in an automobile case where an attempt is made to show a conviction resulting from a violation of some motor vehicle law, it is important to know whether the charge was a violation of an ordinance or a state statute. 

Sec. 162. Proof of Property Damage. 

Stephens v. Hamtramck Bottling Works, 224 Mich. 156. 

The plaintiff's car was repaired by a service company, the bill being paid. The plaintiff testified as to the nature of the damage. An estimator from the service company testified that the charges were reasonable for the items shown on the repair bill. 

It was held that this evidence was sufficient to send the case to the jury. 

Kavanagh v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 244 Mich. 391. 

In this case the Court said that the plaintiff, who testified as to the purchase price of his car, was competent to testify as to the value of the car at the time of the fire. 

Sec. 163. Exclamations of Pain. 

Simmons v. Petersen, 207 Mich. 508.

The daughter of the plaintiff was permitted to testify that her father was in pain because he screamed and his exclamations were that he was in awful pain. 

Stinson v. Payne, 231 Mich. 158.

The plaintiff's brother testified as to his actions and exclamations of pain one month after the accident and before suit was started.

It was held that this was admissible. 310

EVIDENCE 

[$ 165 

Layton v. Cregan & Mallory, Inc., 265 Mich. 574.

In this case it was held that testimony of exclamations of pain made by the plaintiff under circumstances negativing spontaneity was not admissible. 

See same case 269 Mich. 574.

Sec. 164. Examination by Physician for Trial. 

Marshall v. Wabash Railroad Co., 171 Mich. 180.

The plaintiff was a physician. A doctor made an examination of the plaintiff before the trial for the purpose of giving testimony. He testified as to the responses of the plaintiff to a number of tests. The defendant objected on the ground that the actions and responses of the plaintiff could be controlled. Some of the actions could be controlled. The witness, though warned, did not restrict his testimony. 

A new trial was ordered. 

Layton v. Cregan & Mallory Co., 269 Mich. 574.

The plaintiff had a doctor examine him for the purpose of testifying at the trial. The doctor got the history from the plaintiff and testified that in his opinion the condition of the plaintiff might have been caused by the accident. He admitted that this was based upon the history given by the plaintiff.

It was held that this testimony invaded the province of the jury. The Court said that the witness was not treating the plaintiff. The purpose of the examination removed the ordinary safeguards and tempted the plaintiff to exaggerate.

Sec. 165. Proof of Expectancy. 

Morse v. Detroit, Grand Haven & Milwaukee Ry., 168 

Mich. 99.

This was a survival action for the death of a 27 month old child. The plaintiff, against objection, was permitted 311

§ 166] 

to introduce the mortality table for the purpose of showing the probability of life on the part of the child after arriving at the age of 21 years.

The admission of the mortality table was held to be reversible error. The table gave no expectancy of life for any age under 10 years. The Court said that it was the duty of the jury to estimate the expectancy from the age of 27 months and not 10 years. The Court recognized the fact that infant mortality was great compared to children of 10 years. 

Love v. Detroit, Jackson & Chicago Rd., 170 Mich. 1.

In this case the Court permitted the age of grandparents and other ancestors of a child under six years to be shown as bearing upon the expectancy of the child. 

Pilch v. Yellow Taxicab Co., 225 Mich. 484.

There was testimony that the plaintiff had sustained permanent injuries. The Court said that mortality tables were admissible. 

See Adelsperger v. City of Detroit, 248 Mich. 399. 

Sec. 166. Custom. 

Imus v. Ann Arbor Rd. Co., 172 Mich. 292.

Boys had been using a hill for coasting for several winters. The defendant knew this and protected the boys by sending one of the trainmen to the crossing with a lantern.

The Court said that the plaintiff had a right to rely on custom and therefore he was not negligent as a matter of law. 312

Sec. 167. Miscellaneous Cases. 

Vezina v. Shermer, 198 Mich. 757.

It was held in this case that the witness could say whether the driver appeared to have his car under control. 

Zuidema v. Bekkering, 256 Mich. 327.

The defendant testified as to details of driving and then was asked if he did all that he could to avert the accident. It was held that his answer to this question was admissible. 

Gardiner v. Studebaker Corp., 204 Mich. 313.

The plaintiff called the defendant's driver under the statute. His testimony showed no negligence on his part. 

In a statement to the prosecutor he had not mentioned a dump wagon; whereas, in his testimony he said the girl ran from behind a dump wagon. The plaintiff contended that the jury had a right to disbelieve the witness. 

"The difficulty with counsel's contention and its availability to work a reversal of the case lies in the fact that there is no evidence in the case, either direct or circumstantial, that the accident happened in any other way than as testified by this witness." 

Tuttle v. Briscoe Co., 190 Mich. 22. 

Witnesses testified that they heard no horn signal.

It was held that there was no legal testimony that a signal was not given. 

Also see Lambert v. Minneapolis Ry. Co., 209 Mich. 

107, and Moreau v. Grandmaison, 220 Mich. 238. 313

Werney v. Reid, 219 Mich. 257.

The defendant was permitted to testify that he had driven a car for nine years and never had an accident. 

Alt v. Konkle, 237 Mich. 264.

In this case the Court said that the fact that the medical bills were paid was some evidence that they were reasonable. 

Mills v. Michigan Electric Ry. Co., 237 Mich. 393.

During the trial the defendant tried to show that the plaintiff had assigned his claim to an insurance company but did not offer written evidence of an assignment. 

It was held that the lower court was not in error in refusing to permit the defendant to cross-examine the plaintiff to show the assignment as a motion to dismiss should have been made by the defendant. 

Cawood v. Earl Paige & Co., 239 Mich. 485.

It was held in this case that the defendant had no right to inquire as to the plaintiff's accident insurance. 

Siegel v. Detroit Cab Co., 246 Mich. 620.

The plaintiff was permitted to introduce testimony of a witness who had made tests with a car similar to the defendant's that it could be stopped in two feet at 12 miles per hour. ، ، This was held admissible. Evidently the defense slipped" in this case, failing to bring out the fact that a car travels several feet even at a slow rate of speed before the driver can react and get his brake applied. 

Morris v. Montgomery, 229 Mich. 509.

In this case it was held that a witness who had driven several makes of cars about 50,000 miles, and who drove 314

EVIDENCE 

[§ 168 defendant's car immediately after the accident, could testify within what distance, with the automobile going 15 to 18 miles per hour, it would have been possible to stop or turn to pass where the plaintiff lay in the road. 

Shannon v. Township of Jamestown, 251 Mich. 597.

The Court said, in this case, that the defendant could produce proof as to the odor of intoxicating liquor on the breath of the plaintiff's driver. 

Van Dyke v. Knoll, 262 Mich. 644.

The plaintiff testified that on the day following the accident the defendant told her that he was covered by insurance. The trial judge allowed the answer to stand on the ground that it might have some bearing upon the question of liability. This testimony was held prejudicial. 

Beattie v. Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co., 265 Mich. 108.

Where the witness testifies as to part of plaintiff's statement as to how the accident happened on crossexamination, it is error to exclude the rest of the statement on re-direct examination. 

For cases on hypothetical questions see Bishop v.

Sec. 168. Res Ipsa Loquitur. 

The Michigan Supreme Court has often said that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur does not exist in Michigan. 

The mere fact that an accident occurs is not sufficient to raise an issue for the jury. The burden of proof is upon the plaintiff. But an examination of some of the cases reveals the fact that the Michigan Court sometimes does all but invoke the doctrine in name. 315

§ 168] 

A few of the leading cases in which the Court has permitted the plaintiff to recover on circumstantial evidence are given in detail. 

Bayer v. Grocholski, 196 Mich. 325.

An action was brought against the defendant for injuries received as a result of the breaking of a scaffolding. 

The scaffold had held three men for two hours. When a fourth man was set to work upon it, it broke. 

It was held that this evidence presented a question for the jury. The Court said that the testimony tended to prove much more than an accident. 

Burghardt v. Detroit United Ry., 206 Mich. 545.

A trolley pole fell and struck the plaintiff as he was passing the car.  "This court has not adopted the rule res ipsa loquitur; we have uniformly held that the happening of the accident alone is not evidence of negligence; and we have as uniformly held that negligence may be established by circumstantial evidence, and that where the circumstances are such as to take the case out of the realm of conjecture and within the field of legitimate inferences from established facts, that at least a prima facie case is made."

The Court said that if the pole was properly secured it would not have fallen from the socket and that a proper inspection would readily disclose whether it was securely fastened. It was held that a question for the jury had been raised. 

Fuller v. Magatti, 231 Mich. 213.

The defendant testified that he parked his car on a grade, cramping the wheels against the curb, setting the 316

EVIDENCE 

[§ 168 brake and putting the gear in reverse. The plaintiff was struck by the defendant's car at a point 400 feet below the parking place. The defendant claimed that the accident occurred 25 to 30 minutes after he had parked his car. A witness testified that after the accident the brake was not set and the gear was in neutral. A witness testified that he heard the defendant say that the next time he would see that the wheels were cramped to the curb. 

It was held that a case for the jury was made out, especially in view of testimony that the accident might have occurred within five minutes after the car was parked. 

Wilkins v. Bradford, 247 Mich. 157. 

An 8 year old boy was found dead near the edge of the highway. There was evidence that the defendant's car had struck the boy but no evidence as to how the accident happened and no direct evidence of negligence.

It was held that a jury question was presented. The 

Court said that the jury could draw legitimate inferences from established facts and to do so was not to speculate or guess the facts. 

Also see Eaton v. Consumer Power Co., 256 Mich. 549, and Durfey v. Milligan, 265 Mich. 98. 317

CHAPTER XXII DAMAGES Sec. 169. Excessive Verdicts. 

Sec. 170. 

Sustained Verdicts.

Sec. 176.

Miscellaneous Cases. 

Often the most important part of a personal injury action is the question of what the damages amount to. 

Consequently, a number of Michigan decisions are considered in this chapter, because they are examples of cases, which are constantly being tried, involving certain questions of damages. Although this field of law is extensive, the subject of damages is not given much space due to the fact that much of the Michigan law is in line with the weight of authority and the law of damages has been thoroughly covered in a number of works. 

The Michigan law of damages in Death and Survival actions has been covered in other chapters. This leaves actions for personal injuries, loss of services, and property damage. A number of cases are given under the heading "Sustained Verdicts." In reading these cases it must be remembered that they have not been chosen because the amounts of the verdicts represent the average verdict for the injuries sustained. The cases were selected as showing what the Supreme Court considers is not excessive for certain types of injuries. There is also 318

DAMAGES 

[§ 169 a group of cases under the heading "Excessive Verdicts" which have been selected because they are examples of types of injuries. The decisions under the other headings were chosen because they are leading cases. The opinions and holdings speak for themselves. Therefore no further comment is necessary. 

Sec. 169. Excessive Verdicts. 

Grubaugh v. Simon J. Murphy Co., 209 Mich. 551.

The plaintiff's medical expenses were $1,735.00. He had a laceration from the left corner of his mouth to his ear, completely through the cheek. The alveolar process was torn out, and also nine upper teeth. The left arm was broken. Both clavicles were fractured. The arm was set five times, and there was testimony that the plaintiff would never recover the use of it. There was also testimony as to other injuries. The verdict of $18,000 was held to be excessive. It should be noted that the Court also held that the plaintiff's attorney had gone too far in injecting the insurance angle into the case. 

Amsdill v. Detroit Motorbus Co., 233 Mich. 150.

The plaintiff, a married woman, was given a verdict of $25,000. The Supreme Court said that the amount was excessive and ordered a new trial unless the plaintiff accepted $15,000. The Court commented upon the fact that there was no claim for loss of earnings. 

Olah v. Katz, 234 Mich. 112. 

A boy, four years old, injured his eye so that it eventually was removed after several operations. A year later the child died from scarlet fever not connected with the accident. An action was brought to recover for pain and 319

§ 169] 

suffering. The Supreme Court reduced the verdict of $5,000 to $3,000. 

Newell v. Detroit, Toledo & Ironton Rd. Co., 235 Mich. 687. 

The plaintiff was 24 years old, being a boiler maker and ship fitter by trade. He was receiving $5.00 per day when injured. He lost one eye but was offered work by the defendant at the same wage. He was not incapacitated to follow his trade, but he refrained from entering it again for fear of losing the other eye. The verdict of $25,000 was reduced to $15,000. 

Palmer v. Security Trust Co., 242 Mich. 163.

In this case a verdict of $74,000 was held excessive. 

The plaintiff was 38 years old. He lost the use of his hands for all practical purposes. He could not button his clothes, lace his shoes or lift any weight. The plaintiff contended that a dollar would buy only one-half of the commodities it would have commanded several years before. The Court said that it would pay no attention to such an argument as applied to loss of earnings and scant consideration as applied to compensation for pain and suffering. The Court also pointed out that the sum awarded, placed at interest at five per cent, would bring an income about equal to the earnings of the plaintiff at the time of the accident. Thus the sum would be left intact at the end of the life expectancy. 

McLean v. American Ry. Express Co., 243 Mich. 113.

A verdict of $16,000 was cut to $3,500 by the trial court, and the reduction was approved. The plaintiff was a carpenter. He worked at his trade for twelve weeks between the date of the accident, December 21, 1926, and the trial date, July 1, 1927. Soon after the accident he went 320

DAMAGES 

[§ 169 to Virginia where he remained for nine weeks. There was medical testimony tending to support his claim of permanent injury to his spine. This was met by the testimony of three doctors, called by the defendant, who were experts in spinal troubles, and who testified from examinations and X-rays that they found no external evidence of injury and no apparent cause of the suffering the plaintiff claimed to be enduring. 

Kanieski v. Castantini, 243 Mich. 454.

A verdict of $13,615 was held to be excessive and was reduced to $10,000. The testimony was meager as to the extent of the pain and suffering. The medical expense was $160. The plaintiff's condition was improving at the time of the trial. His physician testified that the partial paralysis of the arm and leg might be permanent to the extent of 30 or 40 per cent finally. This paralysis was due to a lesion of the spinal cord. It was shown that the result might be caused by hemorrhage, by a tumor or by syphilis. 

Leary v. Fisher, 248 Mich. 574.

In this case the jury brought a verdict for $15,000. 

From an order, granting a new trial unless the plaintiff agreed to a judgment of $5,000, both parties appealed. 

The plaintiff received a fracture of each leg, the right leg being permanently injured, causing permanent partial disability. The right leg had 50 per cent of its normal flection at the knee and but 25 per cent at the ankle. It was held that the trial court had not abused its discretion. 

Flynn v. Kramer, 271 Mich. 500.

The plaintiff lost an eye. His left frontal bone was crushed. His left knee cap was destroyed with a resulting impairment of the use of the leg. He was permanently 321

§ 170] 

disfigured and had much pain and suffering. The plaintiff was 51 years old and was employed as a hoisting engineer at a salary of $55 per week. He was laid up and away from work for two and a half months. His earning capacity apparently was unimpaired. It was held that the verdict of $25,000 was excessive and should be reduced to $10,000. 

Sec. 170. Sustained Verdicts. 

Johnson v. City of Bay City, 164 Mich. 251.

A girl five years old lost two fingers and a part of a third, and the palm of the same hand was badly scarred from a burn. A verdict of $7,500 was held to be not excessive. 

Guy v. Cincinnati Northern Rd. Co., 198 Mich. 140.

The plaintiff lost his left arm just below the shoulder and his right arm at the wrist. He also had a fractured jaw. A $35,000 verdict was held to be not excessive. 

Faulkner v. Parish Mfg. Co., 201 Mich. 182.

A verdict of $9,800 was affirmed in this decision. The plaintiff, 39 years old, was a skilled mechanic earning $25.00 per week. His pecuniary loss at the time of the trial was $2,100. He had a fractured thigh bone, which resulted in an infection. He was in the hospital for over nine months. The injured leg was two inches shorter than the other. 

Rathbone v. Detroit United Ry., 203 Mich. 695. 

At the time of the plaintiff's injury he was 77 years old. At the time of the last trial he was 84 years old.

He sustained a fracture of both bones in one leg and a fracture of two ribs. At the time of the first trial he had 322

DAMAGES 

[§ 170 2 made a good recovery and was earning money to some extent. He was then 79 years old. The plaintiff had earned over $900.00 per year up to the time of injury. 

On the first trial a verdict of $6,000 was called excessive by the Supreme Court. The last trial resulted in a $11,000 verdict which was affirmed. The Court explained that the plaintiff had lived beyond his expectancy period and had demonstrated his right to recover for pain and suffering endured at least up to the date of the last trial. The 

Court also justified the second verdict because of the question of earnings and the time which had elapsed since the accident. 

Fishleigh v. Detroit United Ry., 205 Mich. 145.

A verdict of $23,000 was upheld in this case. The expenses at the time of the trial amounted to $2200. The plaintiff since the accident had dropped from 150 pounds to 98½ pounds. During fourteen months she had been in bed, suffering constantly. As the result of the accident she was permanently crippled. She was 29 years old and employed as a saleslady at the time of the accident and at the time of the trial, 22 months later, she was a helpless cripple. 

Wilson v. Detroit United Ry., 208 Mich. 411.

The plaintiff at the time of the accident had a tubercular knee and a hernia. There was testimony that he was able to do his work up to the time of the accident. 

He was 39 years old and made $91.00 per month. There was testimony that the injury to his knee aggravated the tubercular condition, and with his other injuries, rendered him permanently unfit to continue as a wage earner. The loss of earnings was $2500. A verdict of $6000 was sustained. 323

§ 170] 

Bruman v. Yellow Taxicab Co., 220 Mich. 41.

The plaintiff, 18 years old, received a broken collar bone and other injuries when struck by an automobile. 

She had been a stenographer, and she testified that because of her nervous condition and trouble with the fingers of her right hand she had to give up stenographic work and secure employment as a saleswoman. Other witnesses testified that the injuries caused a radical change in her manner, temperament and physical appearance. She had scars on her body and a small one above the eye. A verdict of $7,500 was upheld. 

Kurtz v. Detroit United Ry., 221 Mich. 82.

In this case a verdict of $17,166 was held not excessive. 

The plaintiff, 31 years old, was earning about $6,000 per year and was made a permanent cripple by the accident. 

He had one leg amputated. His loss of earnings and other expenses at the time of trial amounted to $5,000. He was then earning only $40 per week. 

King v. Neller, 228 Mich. 15.

The plaintiff, a married woman, was injured on March 18, 1922, receiving a fractured pelvis, fractured lumbar vertebra, shock and internal injuries. At the time of the trial, February, 1923, she was well on the way toward recovery, although she was still suffering pain. There was no claim for expenses or loss of earnings. A verdict of $6,275 was upheld. 

Sutzer v. Allen, 236 Mich. 1.

The plaintiff showed that she was incapacitated for work for nearly eight weeks. She lost almost $300.00 in wages. Her pecuniary loss was $554.00. A scar was left on her wrist and one over her eye. She testified that she suffered considerably. A verdict of $1500 was sustained. 324

DAMAGES 

[§ 170 

Cawood v. Earl Paige Co., 239 Mich. 485.

In this case a verdict of $22,000 was upheld. The plaintiff was 41 years old. The upper part of the fibula was broken. The muscles were shrunken so that he had a lateral motion to the knee which made walking impossible without a brace. Medical expense amounted to $1000 and there was $2500 in lost earnings at the time of the trial. 

Ballance v. Dunnington, 246 Mich. 36.

A verdict of $16,000 in this case was sustained. The plaintiff, 42 years old, and earning $135 per month as a truck driver, lost his leg seven inches below the knee five months after the accident. He testified to extreme pain during this time. 

Sebring v. Mawby, 251 Mich. 628.

The plaintiff was given a verdict of $4490 of which $4,000 was for pain and suffering. The plaintiff was 59 years old and suffered a concussion of the brain, a fracture of the hip, and an injury to the kidney zone. She was in a cast for eight weeks and at the trial, six months later, she was able to move about to a limited extent by means of crutches. The verdict was upheld.

Defenbaugh v. Inter-State Motor Freight Corp., 254 Mich. 

180.

A verdict of $35,000 was sustained in this case. The plaintiff was 21 years old and was preparing to enter the law profession. He was in excellent physical and mental condition. After the accident he was unconscious for 30 days. The injuries caused a partial paralysis of his right side, impaired his speech, sight and hearing and rendered him incapable of physical or mental effort. 

There was testimony that this condition would be perma- 325

§ 170] 

nent and that the injuries brought about a complete change in his personality and mentality. 

Sabol v. Chicago & North Western Ry. Co., 255 Mich. 548.

At the time of the accident the plaintiff was 23 years old. He was earning $25.00 a week. He was totally and permanently disabled. About one-fourth of his body was covered with scars which were painful. A verdict of $18,000 was upheld. 

Garber v. Stone, 259 Mich. 607.

A judgment of $3,000 in this case was upheld. The plaintiff was a physician, engaged in practice. His collar bone and two of his ribs were broken. He was in bed for three weeks. He testified that his earnings were $60 per day. The trial court allowed $1125 for pain and suffering in addition to $1500 for loss of earnings and $375 for expenses. 

Geglio v. Huizenga, 261 Mich. 512.

The plaintiff, a woman, had both bones in her left forearm broken into several small fragments. She had a number of bruises and abrasions about the face and body. 

Her arm was put in a cast. There was a pussy discharge from one of her legs which was injured. A verdict of $3,000 was upheld in view of her suffering and condition at the time of the trial. 

Bachand v. Rosemurgy, 261 Mich. 519.

In this case a verdict of $35,000 was upheld. The plaintiff, 20 years of age, sustained serious injuries causing a complete paralysis of the lower bowel. There was a fracture of the second lumbar vertebra and a complete tearing of the spinal cord. The leg muscles were atro- 326

DAMAGES 

[§ 171 phied. He was totally and permanently disabled. The present worth of medical expenses and loss of earnings was estimated to be above the amount of the verdict. 

Watrous v. Conor, 266 Mich. 397.

The plaintiff's ribs were fractured and her shoulder and elbow injured. She suffered a ruptured vein in her leg, resulting in a gangrenous condition which left a long irregular scar about eight inches in length. Seventeen months after the accident the leg was still swollen. A $5,000 verdict was upheld.

Sec. 171. Future Damages. 

Amanta v. Michigan Central Rd. Co., 177 Mich. 280.

The plaintiff lost his right arm and left leg in an accident. It was claimed that since the accident he had been practically unable to do any work. The defendant contended that there was no evidence to show that the plaintiff was likely to suffer pain in the future. The court permitted the jury to award damages for future pain.

In answer to the defendant's contention, the Supreme Court said that the physical condition of the plaintiff was a complete answer and was sufficient evidence of future pain and humiliation. 

Main v. Grand Rapids Ry. Co., 207 Mich. 473.

The plaintiff received a slight scar on her face. She testified that after the accident her head ached. There was no testimony as to the permanency of the injuries. 

A verdict of $1500 was given. The scar at the time of the trial, four months after the accident, was a half inch in length, and the testimony was that it would fade to a white line almost imperceptible, except on close inspection. A new trial was ordered, error being found in the 327

§ 171]  

instructions on damages. The Court said that the instruction should have confined the jury's consideration to such damages as were proximately shown by the evidence with reasonable certainty to have resulted from the injury. "Only such future damages can be recovered as the evidence makes reasonably certain will necessarily result from the injury sustained." 

Milks v. Tritten, 258 Mich. 236.

The plaintiff suffered a broken leg, a broken nose, loosened teeth, a misplaced jaw bone and other injuries. 

At the trial he testified that his leg pained him and his jaw hurt when he ate. The defendant contended that the court submitted some elements of compensation which were not covered by the declaration. No objection was made to the testimony. No request to limit recovery was made. A verdict of $3,500 was upheld. The Court said that the trial court was not in error in permitting the jury to consider compensation for future pain and suffering, as pain from broken bones does not cease in an instant. 

Peters v. Wurzburg, 267 Mich. 45.

In this case the declaration contained an allegation of permanent injuries. Future pain and suffering were not alleged. There was testimony that the plaintiff was still suffering at the time of the trial. The court instructed the jury that it might consider the question of damage for future pain and suffering, though there was no evidence offered that the plaintiff would undergo pain in the future. The Court said that there was no error as the reasonable effect of the permanent injury was future pain. 328

DAMAGES 

[§ 172 

Sec. 172. Loss of Services. 

Burns v. Township of Van Buren, 218 Mich. 44.

This was an action for expenses and loss of services caused by injuries to the plaintiff's wife. A verdict of $800 was upheld. The medical expenses amounted to $300. There was testimony that the wife received permanent injuries which made her less efficient as a housewife. 

Pratt v. Detroit Taxicab & Transfer Co., 225 Mich. 147.

The plaintiff brought this action to recover for the loss of services of his boy, six years old, who was injured, resulting in probable loss of eyesight. The medical bills amounted to $225. Testimony was given that the parents had a minor son making $17.50 per week and expected to set the injured boy to work when he became 16 years old. A verdict of $2,225 was upheld. 

Kerns v. Lewis, 249 Mich. 27.

This was an action for loss of services of the plaintiff's wife and for expenses in caring for her. The jury allowed the plaintiff $500 for his own services in caring for his wife. He estimated that he spent six months away from his work while caring for his wife. It was held that the worth of his lost time was a proper element of his damage. 

Werner v. Wegusen, 252 Mich. 41.

In this case it was held that a wife could recover for loss of earnings in business due to personal injuries without alleging or proving an assignment from her husband. 

Mulder v. Achterhof, 258 Mich. 190.

This was an action to recover for loss of services caused by injury to a 16 year old boy. During the vaca- 329

§ 173] 

tion period he earned $6 per week. The jury awarded less than $1000 for loss of services. The verdict was sustained. It was held that where the child lives, the cost of support is not to be subtracted in arriving at the amount of the damages. 

Solomon v. Blakeslee, 263 Mich. 176.

A $2,000 verdict was rendered in this case for damage to the plaintiff's automobile, expenses caused by his wife's injuries and for loss of services. It was held that the verdict was not excessive.

Sec. 173. Miscarriage and Sterility. 

Nevala v. City of Ironwood, 232 Mich. 316.

At the time of the accident the plaintiff was pregnant. 

She claimed that because of her injuries she feared a miscarriage and worried over the possibility that the child might be deformed. There was no miscarriage or deformity. It was held that the plaintiff's apprehension of miscarriage or deformity of the child was not a subject for consideration of the jury. See 102 Mich. 624. 

Ford v. Nicol, 261 Mich. 307.

The plaintiff claimed that, without injury to her sexual organs, the injuries she received rendered her sterile.

The jury awarded her $2500 for her injuries and $5000 compensation for inability to bear children. The accident occurred in October, 1927. In October, 1930 she had chronic tumors of the womb, not caused by the accident, which rendered her permanently sterile. She was 39 years old at the time of the accident and had one child, eight months old. Her physician testified that she had no cuts or bruises, but she complained of pain in her neck which he attributed to torn ligaments. He testified that 330

DAMAGES 

[§ 175 it was his opinion that up to the time that she acquired the tumors she was sterile as a result of her nervous condition due to the accident. It was held that the sterility was too remote and speculative, considering the nature of the injuries, to warrant the verdict rendered. 

Sec. 174. Nervous Shock. 

Goldman v. Detroit United Ry., 200 Mich. 543.

The plaintiff was a passenger in a street car. When the car was struck by another street car and was derailed, the plaintiff who was sitting in the middle of the car found herself on the rear end of the car. She was taken home where she fainted and was put to bed. The doctor found no marked symptoms, but later she developed highly nervous symptoms which resulted in permanent injury to her health according to the plaintiff's claim. It was held that there was sufficient evidence for the jury to conclude that the plaintiff's injuries, even though not immediately visible upon the surface of the body, and which developed at a future date, were due to the violent collision. The Court said that it still followed the rule laid down in Nelson v. Crawford, 122 Mich. 466, that fright alone, unaccompanied by physical injury, was not a basis for damages.

Sec. 175. Present Worth. 

Seabury v. Detroit United Ry., 194 Mich. 423.

In this case it was shown that the plaintiff had an expectancy of over 26 years. The plaintiff's attorney was sworn as a witness and testified that the present worth of $26 paid at the rate of $1 per year for 26 years would be $16.37. It was held that there was no error in admitting this testimony. 331

§ 176] 

Present worth is determined by dividing the loss of the first year by 1.05; the loss of the second year by 1.10 and so on. For each additional year five-hundredths is added to the divisor. The amounts are added and the total represents the present worth. 

Nagi v. Detroit United Ry., 231 Mich. 452.

The plaintiff, 33 years old, earning $190 per month, sustained serious injuries. Both arms were broken and one leg crushed, resulting in a stiff knee. The upper part of his nose was crushed, causing a deformity. The upper jaw was broken and he lost some teeth. He was forced to use crutches for 16 months and a cane for 6 months.

The actual monetary loss up to the time of the trial was $6460. Because of the failure of the court to instruct as to present value, the verdict was reduced from $30,000 to $21,000. 

Newell v. Detroit, Toledo & Ironton Rd. Co., 235 Mich. 687.

In this case a verdict of $25,000 was held to be excessive, the Court saying this: "Had the amount of this verdict been placed at interest at six per cent, the income would probably equal his earnings through the years of his expectancy and at his death the principal sum would remain intact. This is not permissible.' 

Sec. 176. Miscellaneous Cases. 

Ralph v. Gies-Gear Co., 164 Mich. 44.

A verdict of $100 was appealed by the plaintiff on the ground that it was inadequate. There was testimony that much of the pain suffered by the plaintiff was due to his own neglect in caring for the injury. The Court said 332

DAMAGES 

[§ 176 that, if the jury believed this testimony, it might account for the small verdict. For this reason the verdict was not inadequate. 

Rouse v. Michigan United Ry. Co., 164 Mich. 475.

In this case the plaintiff was injured on March 8, 1907. 

The plaintiff testified at the first trial on April 23, 1908. 

The defendant contended that at the second trial the damages should be confined to period ending April 23, 1908. It was held that there could be a recovery for damages sustained subsequent to the first trial. 

Pawlicki v. Detroit United Ry., 191 Mich. 536. Six 

The plaintiff was 65 years old when injured. months before the injury he gave up his work in a shoe factory at $12 per week and came to Detroit, intending to open a shoe store. He was waiting and looking for a place of business when he was injured. It was held that there was no error in permitting him to testify as to his wages as a shoe maker as it was a guide to his earning capacity and was not too remote. It was not error to permit the jury to consider his former rate of wages as an element of damages. 

Osmalowski v. Deyman, 249 Mich. 586.

This was an action for damage done to plaintiff's automobile in a collision. The plaintiff had purchased his car six weeks before the collision and had paid $650 for it. As a result of the collision it was a complete wreck, and it was given to a junk dealer. A judgment of $625 was upheld. 

Evans v. City of Detroit, 255 Mich. 381.

In this case there was a verdict of no cause of action, evidently based upon the ground that the plaintiff had 333

§ 176] 

not been injured in the accident. The Supreme Court sustained the verdict, even assuming that there was liability. 

Cosgrove v. Thomas, 257 Mich. 376.

This action included a claim for disfigurement suffered by a 10 year old girl. There was testimony that the nose could be put in the same condition as before the accident for from $150 to $400. The court instructed the jury in such a manner that they could have given a verdict for permanent disfigurement and the cost of the operation. 

It was held that, unless the plaintiff filed a remittitur in the sum of $400, a new trial would be ordered. The Court said that the lower court was in error in submitting both permanent disfigurement and the cost of the operation to correct the disfigurement, as elements of damage. 

Parker v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 261 Mich. 293.

In this case the trial judge, in assessing the damages, said that he was governed by the hospital and medical expense among other things. The plaintiff was in the hospital for three months. But no evidence was put into the record on expenses incurred in the hospital or by doctor's treatment. The Supreme Court ordered a new trial, saying that the amount of the judgment indicated the allowance of a considerable sum for such expenses. 

Sima v. Wright, 268 Mich. 352.

The trial court submitted to the jury, as elements of damage, pecuniary loss, loss of time and impairment of earning capacity. While there was testimony that for a time the plaintiff was incapacitated from conducting his business as a tailor, there was no evidence of the worth of his services nor of pecuniary loss. A new trial was ordered because of this error. 334

APPENDIX IMPORTANT MOTOR VEHICLE STATUTES IN MICHIGAN (Section Numbers Refer to Michigan 1929 Compiled Laws.) § 4632 SECTION 1. Definitions. (a) The term "motor ve hicle" as used in this act shall include all vehicles impelled on the public highways of this state, by mechanical power except traction engines, road rollers, such vehicles as run only on rails or tracks, fire trucks and apparatus owned by any person, firm or private corporation and used for fire protection, and motor vehicles owned and operated by the federal government. 

Motor vehicles owned and operated by the state of Michigan, or any municipality thereof, shall be designated by proper signs showing in which department or institution of said state or municipality such motor vehicles are employed, and such department, institution or municipality shall obtain license plates annually from the secretary of state upon applications furnished by him, the cost of same in no case to exceed fifty cents per pair. Tractors operated on the public highways under their own power shall not be exempted under the provisions of this subdivision except those that are used exclusively in agriculture. (b) The term "chauffeur" shall mean any person operating a motor vehicle for hire, or as the employe of the owner thereof. (c) The term "owner" shall include any person, firm, association or corporation owning or renting a motor vehicle or having the exclusive use thereof, under a lease or otherwise, for a period greater than thirty days. 335

APPENDIX 

(d) The term "public highway" shall include any public street, alley, public place or highway as defined by the general laws of this state. (e) The term "motorcycle" shall include all motor vehicles of bicycle or tricycle type operated by motive power. (f) The term "trailer" shall include all vehicles drawn by a motor vehicle. When a trailer is drawn by a motor vehicle having no load capacity the rate for commercial vehicles shall apply to both. (g) The term "county jail" referred to in section twentyeight of this act shall be construed to mean the county jail of any county where the violation of any of the provisions of this act shall occur, and the Detroit house of correction shall be construed to mean the institution of that name located in the city of Detroit, this state. 

§ 4648 SEC. 29. Civil actions. Nothing herein contained shall be construed to abridge the right of any person to prosecute a civil action for damages for injuries to either person or property resulting from a violation of any of the provisions of this act by the owner or operator of a motor vehicle, his agent or servant. The owner of a motor vehicle shall be liable for any injury occasioned by the negligent operation of such motor vehicle whether such negligence consists of a violation of the provisions of the statutes of the state or in the failure to observe such ordinary care in such operation as the rules of the common law require. The owner shall not be liable, however, unless said motor vehicle is being driven with his or her express or implied consent or knowledge. It shall be presumed that such motor vehicle is being driven with the knowledge and consent of the owner if it is driven at the time of said injury by his or her father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, or other immediate member of the family: Provided, however, That no person, transported by the owner or operator of a motor vehicle as his guest without payment for such transportation shall have a cause of action for damages against such owner or operator for injury, death or loss, in case of 336

APPENDIX 

accident, unless such accident shall have been caused by the gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct of the owner or operator of such motor vehicle and unless such gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct contributed to the injury, death or loss for which the action is brought. 

Act No. 65, P. A. 1931, amending Sec. 4660. 

Transfer of ownership; duties of holder of certificate, purchaser and secretary of state; licensed dealer; when issued to next of kin. SEC. 3. In the event of the sale or other transfer after October one, nineteen hundred twenty-one, of the ownership of a motor vehicle for which a certain certificate of title has been issued as aforesaid, the holder of such certificate shall endorse on the back of same an assignment thereof with warranty of title in the form printed thereon with a statement of all liens or encumbrances on said motor vehicle, sworn to before a notary public or some other person authorized by law to take acknowledgments, and deliver the same to the purchaser or transferee at the time of the delivery to him of such motor vehicle, which shall show the payment or satisfaction of any mortgage or lien as shown on the original title. The purchaser or transferee, unless such person is a dealer licensed under section fourteen of this act, shall within ten days thereafter present such certificate, assigned as aforesaid, to the secretary of state, accompanied by a fee of one dollar, whereupon a new certificate of title shall be issued to the assignee: 

Provided, however, If such person shall, in such manner and form as the secretary of state prescribes, authorize and direct the delivery of the certificate of title to some other designated person, firm or corporation, delivery shall be made accordingly. It shall be the duty of the secretary of state, in all certificates of title hereafter issued, to provide suitable space for such authorization. Said licensed dealer shall on selling or otherwise disposing of said motor vehicle, execute and deliver to the purchaser thereof an affidavit of conveyance or assignment in such form as the secretary of state shall prescribe, 337

APPENDIX 

to which shall be attached the assigned certificate of title received by such dealer. It shall also be the duty of such licensed dealer to notify the secretary of state on forms provided by the department of state of any used car held for sale for a period greater than thirty days, such signed form to become part of the transfer record filed by the department of state. 

The purchaser of said motor vehicle shall within ten days from purchase of such motor vehicle, apply for and receive from the secretary of state a certificate of title. Said certificate, when so assigned and returned to the secretary of state, together with any subsequent assignments or reissues thereof, shall be retained by the secretary of state and appropriately filed and indexed for a period of six years: Provided, When the ownership of any motor vehicle shall pass by operation of law, the person owning such motor vehicle, may, upon furnishing satisfactory proof to the secretary of state of such ownership, procure a title to said motor vehicle regardless of whether a certificate of title has ever been issued. In event of the death of an owner of not more than one motor vehicle, not exceeding in value five hundred dollars who does not leave other property necessitating the procuring of letters of administration or letters testamentary as is required in section one of chapter fifty-three of the judicature act of nineteen hundred fifteen, being section fifteen thousand five hundred eighty-five of the compiled laws of nineteen hundred twenty-nine, the surviving husband or wife or next of kin in the order named in section two of said chapter, being section fifteen thousand five hundred eighty-six of the compiled laws of nineteen hundred twenty-nine, may make application for title, after first having furnished the secretary of state proper proof of the death of the registered owner, attaching thereto an affidavit setting forth the fact that said applicant is the surviving husband or wife or next of kin and upon proper petition, the secretary of state shall furnish applicant with a certificate of title.
