Speed of vehicles; limits, powers of local authorities and state highway commissioner, signs. SEC. 5. Restrictions as to speed. (a) Any person driving a vehicle on a highway shall drive the same at a careful and prudent speed not greater than nor less than is reasonable and proper, having due regard to the traffic, surface and width of the highway and of any other condition then existing, and no person shall drive any vehicle upon a highway at a speed greater than will permit him to bring it to a stop within the assured clear distance ahead. (b) Subject to the provisions of subdivision (a) of this section and except in those instances where a lower speed is specified in this act, it shall be prima facie lawful for the driver of a vehicle to drive the same at a speed not exceeding the following, but in any case when such speed would be unsafe it shall not be lawful:

Fifteen miles an hour on all highways in a business district as defined herein;

Twenty miles an hour in a residence district, as defined herein, and in public parks unless a different speed is fixed by local authorities and duly posted.

It shall be prima facie unlawful for any person to exceed any of the foregoing speed limitations, except as provided in subdivision (c) of this section. In every charge of violation of this section the complaint, also the summons or notice to appear, shall specify the speed at which the defendant is alleged to have driven, also the speed which this section declares shall 342

APPENDIX 

be prima facie lawful at the time and place of such alleged violation. (c) Local authorities in their respective jurisdictions are hereby authorized in their discretion to increase the speed which shall be prima facie lawful upon through highways at the entrance to which vehicles are by ordinance of such local authorities required to stop before entering or crossing such through highways: Provided, That the state highway commissioner is hereby authorized in his discretion to increase the speed which shall be prima facie lawful upon all through trunk line highways outside of business districts under the jurisdiction of such local authorities. A written copy of such authorization or determination shall be filed in the office of the county clerk of the county or counties where such highway is located and a certified copy thereof shall be prima facie evidence in all courts of the issuance of such authorization or determination. Local authorities shall place and maintain upon all through highways upon which the permissible speed is increased adequate signs giving notice of such special regulations and shall also place and maintain upon each and every highway intersecting any said through highway, appropriate stop signs which shall be illuminated at night or so placed as to be illuminated by the headlights of an approaching vehicle or by street lights: Provided, however, That whenever the state highway commissioner shall increase the speed upon any trunk line highway as herein provided, the state highway department shall place and maintain upon all such highways adequate signs giving notice of such permissible speed as fixed by said state highway commissioner. 

§ 4703 SEC. 11. Drive on right side of highway. 

Upon all highways of sufficient width except upon one way streets the driver of a vehicle shall drive the same upon the right half of the highway and shall drive a slow moving vehicle as closely as possible to the right hand edge or curb of such highway, unless it is impracticable to travel on such side of the highway and except when overtaking and passing an- 343

APPENDIX 

other vehicle subject to the limitations applicable in overtaking and passing set forth in sections thirteen and fourteen of this act. 

§ 4704 SEC. 12. Keep to the right in crossing intersections or railroads.

In crossing an intersection of highways or the intersection of a highway by a railroad right of way, the driver of the vehicle shall at all times cause such vehicle to travel on the right half of the highway unless such right half is obstructed or impassable. 

§ 4705 SEC. 13. Meeting of vehicles. 

Drivers of vehicles proceeding in opposite directions shall pass each other to the right, each giving to the other at least one-half of the main traveled portion of the roadway as nearly as possible. 

§ 4706 SEC. 14. Overtaking a vehicle. 

(a) The driver of any vehicle overtaking another vehicle proceeding in the same direction shall pass at a safe distance to the left thereof, and shall not again drive to the right side of the highway until safely clear of such overtaken vehicle. (b) The driver of an overtaking motor vehicle not within a business or residence district as herein defined shall give audible warning with his horn or other warning device before passing or attempting to pass a vehicle proceeding in the same direction. 

§ 4707 SEC. 15. Limitations on privilege of overtaking and passing. (a) The driver of a vehicle shall not drive to the left side of the center line of a highway in overtaking and passing another vehicle proceeding in the same direction unless such left side is clearly visible and is free of oncoming traffic for a sufficient distance ahead to permit such overtaking and passing to be made in safety. 344

APPENDIX 

(b) The driver of a vehicle shall not overtake and pass another vehicle proceeding in the same direction upon a grade or upon a curve in the highway unless the driver's view along the highway is sufficient to insure safety. (c) The driver of a vehicle shall not overtake and pass any other vehicle proceeding in the same direction at any steam or electric railway grade crossing nor at any intersection of highways unless permitted so to do by a traffic or police officer: § 4708 SEC. 16. Driver to give way to overtaking vehicle.

The driver of a vehicle upon a highway about to be overtaken and passed by another vehicle approaching from the rear shall give way to the right in favor of the overtaking vehicle on suitable and audible signal being given by the driver of the overtaking vehicle, and shall not increase the speed of his vehicle until completely passed by the overtaking vehicle. 

§ 4709 SEC. 17. Following too closely. 

(a) The driver of a motor vehicle shall not follow another vehicle more closely than is reasonable and prudent, having due regard to the speed of such vehicle and the traffic upon and condition of the highway. (b) The driver of any motor truck when traveling upon a highway outside of a business or residence district shall not follow another motor truck within one hundred feet, but this shall not be construed to prevent one motor truck overtaking and passing another. This rule shall also apply to two or more motor vehicles being delivered from one point to another: 

Provided, That no truck or combination of motor vehicles having a length over all of fifty feet shall follow within one thousand feet of each other except when overtaking and passing each other. 

§ 4710 SEC. 18. Turning at intersections. 

(a) Except as otherwise provided in this section, the driver of a vehicle intending to turn to the right at an intersection 345

APPENDIX 

shall approach such intersection in the lane for traffic nearest to the right hand side of the highway, and in turning shall keep as closely as practicable to the right hand curb or edge of the highway, and when intending to turn to the left shall approach such intersection in the lane for traffic to the right of and nearest to the center line of the highway and in turning shall pass beyond the center of the intersection, passing as closely as practicable to the right thereof before turning such vehicle to the left.

For the purpose of this section, the center of the intersection shall mean the meeting point of the medial lines of the highways intersecting one another. (b) Local authorities in their respective jurisdictions may modify the foregoing method of turning at intersections by clearly indicating by buttons, markers or other direction signs within an intersection the course to be followed by vehicles turning thereat, and it shall be unlawful for any driver to fail to turn in a manner as so directed when such direction signs are installed by local authorities. 

§ 4711 SEC. 19. Signals on starting, stopping or turning. 

(a) The driver of any vehicle upon a highway before starting, stopping or turning from a direct line shall first see that such movement can be made in safety and shall give a signal as required in this section. (b) The signal herein required shall be given either by means of the hand and arm in the manner herein specified, or by a mechanical or electrical signal device which conveys an intelligible signal or warning to another driver approaching from the rear.

Whenever the signal is given by means of the hand and arm, the driver shall indicate his intention to start, stop, or turn by extending the hand and arm horizontally from and beyond the left side of the vehicle. 

§ 4712 SEC. 20. Right of way. 

When two vehicles enter an intersection at approximately the same time, the driver of the vehicle on the left shall yield 346

APPENDIX 

the right of way to the vehicle on the right except as otherwise provided in section twenty-one. The driver of any vehicle traveling at an unlawful speed shall forfeit any right of way which he might otherwise have hereunder. 

§ 4713 SEC. 21. Exceptions to the right of way rule. 

(a) The driver of a vehicle entering a public highway from a private drive shall come to a full stop before entering such highway. (b) The driver of a vehicle upon a highway shall yield the right of way to ambulances, police and fire department vehicles when the latter are operated upon official business and the drivers thereof sound audible signal by bell, siren or exhaust whistle. This provision shall not operate to relieve the driver of a police or fire department vehicle from the duty to drive with due regard for the safety of all persons using the highway nor shall it protect the driver of any such vehicle from the consequence of an arbitrary exercise of such right of way. (c) The state highway commissioner and local authorities are authorized to designate through traffic highways and streets in accordance with section twenty-three of this act. 

The driver of a vehicle entering such highways and streets shall yield the right of way to all vehicles approaching on such highways and streets. (d) All motor vehicles forming a funeral procession when going to any place of burial shall have the right of way over all other vehicles except fire apparatus, ambulances and police patrol vehicles, at any street or highway intersection within this state: Provided, That each vehicle in such funeral procession shall have displayed on the front thereof a flag which shall be white in color, and upon which shall be printed, stamped or stained a purple cross. Any person passing through a funeral procession of motor vehicles designated as aforesaid with a vehicle of any kind, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof shall be punished in accordance with section fifty-three of title six hereof. 347

SEC. 26. Stopping on highway. 

It shall be unlawful to park a vehicle on the beaten track or paved surface of any highway outside the limits of any village or city. $ 4722 dent. (a) 

SEC. 30. Duty to stop and report in event of acci 

The driver of any vehicle involved in an accident resulting in injury or death of any person shall immediately stop such vehicle at the scene of such accident and any person violating this provision shall upon conviction be punished as provided in section fifty-six of this act. (b) The driver of any vehicle involved in an accident resulting in damage to property shall immediately stop such 348

APPENDIX 

vehicle at the scene of such accident and any person violating this provision shall upon conviction be punished as provided in section fifty-three-a of this act. (c) The driver of any vehicle involved in any accident resulting in injury or death to any person or damage to property shall also give his name, address, and the registration number of his vehicle, also the name and address of the owner, and exhibit his operator's or chauffeur's license to the person struck or the driver or occupants of any vehicle collided with and shall render to any person injured in such accident reasonable assistance including the carrying of such person to a physician or surgeon for medical or surgical treatment if it is apparent that such treatment is necessary or is requested by the injured person. (d) The driver of every motor vehicle involved in an accident resulting in a vehicle or vehicles becoming so disabled as to be incapable of being propelled in the usual manner, or resulting in personal injury or death of any person shall report such accident to the nearest or most convenient police station or police officer within forty-eight hours after such accident. 

The officer receiving such report shall forthwith forward the same to the commissioner of public safety on forms to be prescribed by him. Such report shall not be available for use in any court action, but it shall be for the purpose of furnishing statistical information as to the number and cause of accidents. 

§ 4731 SEC. 39. Brakes. 

Every motor vehicle when operated on a highway shall be equipped with brakes adequate to control the movement of and to stop and to hold such vehicle, including two separate means of applying the brakes, each of which shall be effective to apply the brakes to at least two wheels and so constructed that no part which is liable to failure shall be common to the two, except that a motorcycle need be equipped with only one .brake.

Adequate brakes shall consist of a service brake capable of stopping the vehicle within a distance of forty feet from a 349

APPENDIX 

speed of twenty miles an hour on a dry, smooth, hard surface road free from any loose material; and an emergency brake capable of holding the vehicle on any grade which it can ascend. 

Act No. 64, P. A. 1931, amending Sec. 4736. 

SEC. 44. Require Lighting Equipment on Motor Vehicles. 

(a) When Vehicles Must Be Equipped. 

Every vehicle upon a highway within this state during the period from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise and at any other time when there is not sufficient light to render clearly discernible any person on the highway at a distance of two hundred feet ahead shall be equipped with lighted front and rear lamps as in this section respectively required for different classes of vehicles and subject to exemption with reference to lights on parked vehicles as declared in section forty-eight. 

(b) Headlamps on Motor Vehicles. 

Every motor vehicle other than a motorcycle, roadroller, road machinery, or farm tractor shall be equipped with two headlamps at the front and on opposite sides of the motor vehicle, which headlamps shall comply with the requirements and limitations set forth in section forty-six or forty-seven. 

(c) Headlamps on Motorcycles. 

Every motorcycle shall be equipped with at least one and not more than two headlamps which shall comply with the requirements and limitations set forth in section forty-six or section forty-seven. (d) Rear Lamps.

Every motor vehicle and every trailer or semi-trailer which is being drawn at the end of a train of vehicles shall carry at the rear a lamp of a type which exhibits a red light plainly visible under normal atmospheric conditions from a distance of five hundred feet to the rear of such vehicle and so con-. structed and placed that the number plate carried on the rear of such vehicle shall under like conditions be so illuminated by 350

APPENDIX 

a white light as to be read from a distance of fifty feet to the rear of such vehicle. 

(e) Warning Lights. 

All trucks weighing more than two tons and all tractors, trailers and buses operated on the public highways except within the limits of incorporated cities and villages, shall display in the front and in the rear three green warning lights or three green reflex reflectors of sufficient candlepower to be plainly visible at a distance of not less than two hundred feet: 

Provided, however, That motor vehicles equipped with acetylene headlights shall be deemed to have complied with the provisions of this act, anything to the contrary notwithstanding, when such headlights are fitted with six inch bright spherical mirrors, five-eighths foot burners and clear plane glass fronts, and such vehicle displays a green or amber reflecting device on the extreme left front corner of the body thereof, and a reflecting device on the rear thereof in the same manner as is hereby provided for reflecting devices upon other trucks, trailers, buses and other commercial vehicles. Nothing herein contained shall be considered as prohibiting the use of acetylene lighting systems on motor vehicles. The warning lights must be mounted parallel to the axles of the truck, tractor, trailer or bus and the lights shall be so placed as to be not more than nor less than six inches apart. The front warning lights shall be mounted at the top of the windshield and in no manner obscured by any part of the truck, tractor, trailer or bus. 

The rear warning lights shall be mounted at the extreme rear of the truck, tractor, trailer or bus, where the visibility of same is in no manner obscured. (f) Reflex Reflectors.

Every motor vehicle having a width in excess of eighty inches, upon any highway within this state during the period from one-half hour after sunset to one-half hour before sunrise, shall be equipped on the rear with a reflex reflector which, when opposed by the main beam from properly adjusted headlamps on all overtaking motor vehicles, shall reflect a red light of such intensity as to be visible to the driver behind 351

APPENDIX 

the opposing headlights from a distance of three hundred feet when one vehicle is directly behind the other and from a distance of fifty feet when the vehicles are at an angle of twenty degrees to one another. (g) Lamps on Bicycles. 

Every bicycle shall be equipped with a lighted white lamp on the front thereof visible under normal atmospheric conditions from a distance of at least three hundred feet in front of such bicycle and shall also be equipped with a reflex mirror reflector or lamp on the rear exhibiting a red light visible under like conditions from a distance of at least two hundred feet to the rear of such bicycle. 

(h) Lights on Other Vehicles. 

All vehicles not heretofore in this section required to be equipped with special lighted lamps shall carry one or more lights, lamps or lanterns displaying a white light, visible under normal atmospheric conditions from a distance of not less than five hundred feet to the front of such vehicle and displaying a reflex reflector or red light visible under like conditions from a distance of not less than three hundred feet to the rear of such vehicle. 

Act No. 59, P. A. 1931, amending Sec. 4738. 

SEC. 46. Requirements as to head lamps and auxiliary driv ing lamps. (a) The head lamps and auxiliary driving lamps of motor vehicles shall be so constructed, arranged, adjusted and used that, except as provided in subsection (c) of this section, they will at all times mentioned in section forty-four and under normal atmospheric conditions and on a level road produce a driving light sufficient to render clearly discernible a person two hundred feet ahead, except when approaching an oncoming vehicle when it shall be sufficient to render clearly discernible a person seventy-five feet ahead. (b) Head lamps and auxiliary driving lamps shall be so aimed and used upon approaching an oncoming vehicle that 352

APPENDIX 

they do not project a glaring or dazzling light into the eyes of the approaching driver. Such lamps shall be deemed to comply with this provision prohibiting glaring and dazzling lights if substantially none of the main bright portion of the beam used in approaching an oncoming car is directed to the left of the vertical plane through the axis of the left head lamp and parallel to the longitudinal axis of the vehicle and above the horizontal plane passing through the lamp centers parallel to the level road upon which the loaded vehicle stands, and in no case higher than forty-two inches, seventy-five feet ahead of the vehicle. (c) Whenever a motor vehicle is being operated upon a highway or a portion thereof, which is sufficiently lighted to reveal a person on the highway at a distance of two hundred feet ahead of the vehicle it shall be permissible to dim the head lamps or to tilt or depress the beams downward or to substitute therefor the light from an auxiliary driving lamp or pair of such lamps, subject to the restrictions as to glaring and dazzling lights set forth in the foregoing subsection: Provided, That at all times required in section forty-four at least two lights shall be displayed on the front of and on opposite sides of every moving motor vehicle other than a motorcycle, road roller, road machinery or farm tractor. 

§ 4740 SEC. 48. Lights on parked vehicles. 

Whenever a vehicle is parked or stopped upon a highway whether attended or unattended during the times mentioned. in section forty-four there shall be displayed upon the left side of such vehicle one or more lamps projecting a white light visible under normal atmospheric conditions from a distance of two hundred feet to the front of such vehicle and projecting a red light visible under like conditions from a distance of two hundred feet to the rear, except that local authorities may provide by ordinance that no lights need be displayed upon any such vehicle when parked in accordance with local ordinances upon a highway where there is sufficient light to reveal any 353

APPENDIX 

person within a distance of two hundred feet upon such highway. 

§ 4788 Prima facie evidence of negligence. SECTION 1. In any action, in any court in this state when it is shown, by competent evidence, that a vehicle traveling in a certain direction, overtook and struck the rear end of another vehicle proceeding in the same direction, or lawfully standing upon any highway within this state, the driver or operator of such first mentioned vehicle shall be deemed prima facie guilty of negligence. 

This act shall apply, in appropriate cases, to the owner of such first mentioned vehicle and to the employer of its driver or operator. 

§ 4789 Absence of lights. SEC. 2. This act may not be invoked by the owner of any vehicle, the rear of which was struck under the circumstances above mentioned, if the accident occurred between one hour after sunset and one hour before sunrise and the vehicle so struck did not, at the time, have a lighted lamp or lantern reasonably visible to the drivers of vehicles approaching from the rear. § 4796 Garage keeper; prima facie evidence of negligence.

SECTION 1. Whenever any damage shall be done to any motor vehicle while in the possession or under the care, custody or control of the owner, his agent or servant, or the keeper of any public garage or other establishment where such vehicle shall have been accepted for hire or gain, proof of such damage shall be prima facie evidence that such damage was the result of the negligent act of such owner or keeper of the place where such vehicle was stored. § 4797 Same; prima facie evidence of conversion. SEc. 2.

If any integral part, appliance or equipment, any spare tire fastened to such motor vehicle or any part, appliance or equipment locked in or to such vehicle shall be removed or shall disappear therefrom while such vehicle is so held, proof of 354

APPENDIX 

such removal or disappearance shall be prima facie evidence of conversion by the owner or keeper of the garage or other establishment where such vehicle was so held. 

§ 4798 Examination of vehicle and notice of loss. SEC. 3. 

The provisions of this act shall not apply unless the owner of a motor vehicle so placed in any public garage or other establishment as herein provided, shall examine the same before leaving such garage or other establishment or the grounds or street immediately adjacent thereto, and, upon discovery of any loss or damage, forthwith notify the owner or keeper of such garage or other establishment of the loss or damage claimed. § 4799 Forms for statement of condition, owner's refusal to sign bar to recovery of damages. SEC. 4. The owner or keeper of any such garage or other establishment may provide blank forms upon which a description of the condition of any motor vehicle when so left in his care, may be noted; and when so provided and properly filled out in duplicate, he may require the owner of such motor vehicle to sign the same before leaving such vehicle. And if such a signed description is made, the owner or keeper of the garage or other establishment shall deliver a copy thereof to the owner of the vehicle. Refusal by the owner of such vehicle to sign such form shall be a bar to recovery under this act.

NON-RESIDENT SERVICE ACT 

Act No. 110, P. A. 1935, amending Sec. 4790, and Sec. 4791.

SECTION 1. From and after the effective date of this act, the operation by a non-resident of a motor vehicle upon a public highway of this state, or the operation on a public highway in this state of a motor vehicle owned by a non-resident if so operated with his consent, express or implied, shall be deemed equivalent to an appointment by such non-resident of the secretary of state to be his true and lawful attorney, upon whom may be served the summons in any action against him, growing out of any accident or collision in which such non-resident may be involved while operating a motor vehicle on such a public highway, or in which such motor vehicle may be involved while being so operated on such a highway. Such operation shall be deemed a signification of his agreement that any such summons against him which is so served shall have the same legal force and validity as if served on him personally within this state. Service of such summons shall be made by leaving a copy thereof with the secretary of state, or his deputy, who shall keep a record of each such process and the day and hour of service, and such service shall be sufficient service upon such non-resident, provided that notice of such service and a copy of the summons are forthwith either served upon the defendant personally by the sheriff or constable of the county in which he resides or sent by registered mail by the plaintiff or his attorney to the defendant: And provided further, That if personal service of such notice and copy of summons be had upon the defendant, the officer making the service shall so certify in his return which shall be filed with the court having jurisdiction of said cause, or if service be made by registered 356

APPENDIX 

mail, then the plaintiff or his attorney shall make an affidavit showing that he has made service of the notice and summons upon the defendant by registered mail as herein provided and the affiant shall attach thereto a true copy of the summons and notice so served and the registry receipt of the defendant and shall file the affidavit and attached papers with the court having jurisdiction of said cause. The court in which the action is pending may order such extension of time as may be necessary to afford the defendant reasonable opportunity to defend the action.

SEC. 2. The court shall include as taxable costs, in addition to other legal costs, against the plaintiff in case the defendant shall prevail in such suit, the actual traveling expenses of the defendant from his residence to the place of trial and return, not to exceed the sum of one hundred dollars.

ADMINISTRATORS' AND GUARDIANS' QUALIFICATIONS Act No. 240, P. A. 1935. 

SECTION 1. It is hereby declared to be the public policy of this state to require that all persons acting in a representative capacity under appointment of a probate court, as executors or administrators of estates of deceased persons or as guardians of the estates of minors or incompetent persons, shall at all times be amenable to process issued out of the courts of this state, and to that end no person shall hereafter be deemed suitable and competent to administer the estate of a deceased person, as executor or administrator thereof, or of a minor or incompetent person, as guardian thereof, who is not a resident of this state and a citizen of the United States: Provided, That in the discretion of the probate court, the widow or husband, or if there be no widow or husband, then the next of kin of such deceased, minor or incompetent person, shall be deemed suitable and competent to discharge such trust: Provided further, That nothing herein shall be construed to limit the powers 357

APPENDIX 

of any bank or trust company authorized to do business in this state, or to limit the power of the court in such appointment. 

SEC. 2. The probate court in which the estate of a deceased person, minor or incompetent person is being probated or administered shall, on its own motion upon learning the facts, or on motion, remove any executor, administrator or guardian hereafter appointed who is not a suitable and competent person to discharge the trust, as provided in section one hereof. 

Motion for such removal may be made at any time during administration of such an estate by any person interested in the estate or indebted, or claimed to be indebted thereto, or having in his, her or its possession assets, or claimed assets, thereof. 

SEC. 3. Upon removal of any executor or administrator hereunder, the probate court shall, unless request shall be made within thirty days thereafter for the appointment of some other suitable and competent person as such executor or administrator, grant administration of the estate affected to the public administrator for the state. 

SEC. 4. So much of section two of chapter fifty-three of act number three hundred fourteen of the public acts of nineteen hundred fifteen, being section fifteen thousand five hundred eighty-six of the compiled laws of nineteen hundred twentynine, as is inconsistent with the provisions of this act, and all other acts and parts of acts inconsistent with the provisions of this act, are hereby repealed. 358

Frye v. Brinker, 272 Mich. 339. 

Plaintiff's decedent, while crossing Woodward Avenue in Detroit, was struck by defendant's car which was driven north on the east side of the street. The only eyewitnesses were the defendants. Their testimony was uncontradicted that the deceased came suddenly from the car tracks, and appeared to stumble into the path of the automobile when it was within two feet of him. 

There was a verdict for the defendant. In affirming the judgment for the defendant, the Court said that the evidence negatived negligence of the defendant, and established, as the proximate cause of the accident, the want of reasonable care on the part of plaintiff's decedent. 

Buchel v. Williams, 273 Mich. 132.

Defendant was driving her car north on North Grand River Avenue in Lansing at night. She failed to stop for West Grand River, a stop intersection, and drove 1

81] 

across the intersection at a speed of 20 to 30 miles per hour. She saw plaintiff's decedent 25 to 30 feet away and three feet from the east curb. She blew her horn, swerved to the left and applied her brakes, but the right front of the car struck the decedent. The testimony showed that the decedent was struck three and a third seconds after the car passed the stop sign. The jury found for the defendant. The judgment was vacated and a new trial was ordered because of erroneous instructions. The Court said that the absence of other traffic and defendant's testimony that she saw decedent 

25 to 30 feet away made inapplicable the portions of the charge pertaining to a situation where one steps into a street in front of or very close to an approaching car. 

The Court also said that defendant's failure to stop bore directly upon defendant's negligence and decedent's contributory negligence. 

Lagassee v. Quick, 273 Mich. 295.

Plaintiff testified that she was crossing the street from the east to the west side. When she was near the center of the street she heard a horn signal and jumped back, being struck at a point three feet east of the center of the highway. The defendant, who was driving south, testified that he slowed his car to a speed of five to ten miles per hour and allowed plaintiff to cross the center of the street. He turned to the left to pass behind her, sounding his horn. She turned toward the car, jumped back and was struck. Judgment for the plaintiff was reversed and a new trial was ordered. The lower Court instructed the jury that under Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4703, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1571, the driver of a vehicle was required to keep as near the right curb as practicable. The Supreme Court held that this was error 2

SUPPLEMENT 

[§1 as there was no other traffic. The Court said that the defendant was entitled to an instruction on emergency if the emergency was caused wholly by the plaintiff. The 

Court felt that plaintiff's and defendant's negligence was a question for the jury to decide. 

Guina v. Harrod, 275 Mich. 393.

Plaintiff was walking west across Hamilton Avenue at an intersection in Detroit. When in the center of the street she saw a car 40 feet away going south on the southbound car track. It slowed and stopped, and she proceeded westerly but was struck by defendant's car which passed to the right of the stopped automobile. 

Defendant said that he was behind the other car and thought the driver was about to make a left turn. However, the driver had given no signal. Judgment for the plaintiff by the lower Court without a jury was affirmed. 

The Court said that the defendant violated an ordinance. 

Plaintiff was excused for not seeing defendant's car because it was closely following the other automobile. 

Brodie v. City of Detroit, 275 Mich. 626.

In this case the direction of a verdict for the defendant was upheld. A 10-foot traffic lane had been marked across John R. Street in Detroit at the entrance to Grace

Hospital. Plaintiff alighted from a southbound bus which stopped by a parked car. This put the left side of the bus close to the center of the street. Plaintiff walked around the front of the bus to go east to the hospital and was struck by another southbound bus which cleared the other bus by about a foot. Plaintiff did not look to the north. It was held that the place of the accident was not an intersection; that the bus driver had a right to pass to the left of the other bus, and that the plaintiff had a legal duty to look to the north, and that 3

§1] 

he could have seen through the windows of the standing bus. Consequently, plaintiff was guilty of negligence. 

Krukowski v. Englehardt, 276 Mich. 136.

Plaintiff testified that at night she was walking south across the intersection on the east crosswalk. She looked to the west when in the center of the street and seeing no car approaching, she continued and was five feet from the south curb line when struck. The defendant said he drove south, stopped in the center of the intersection and then turned left. When he was a few feet from the crosswalk, he saw plaintiff running with her head down, and she ran into the path of the car. The case was submitted to the jury which decided for the plaintiff. In affirming the judgment for the plaintiff, the Court said. that one was not necessarily required to look back for the approach of vehicles, and the question of contributory negligence was for the jury. 

Walker v. McGraw, 279 Mich. 97.

In this case the defendant was driving north at night on U. S. 2 through an unincorporated village when his car struck a pedestrian, who was walking in an easterly direction across the 48-foot highway. Plaintiff's decedent was walking behind his wife and a boy. They had seen the car about a mile south before they started across. 

No horn was sounded and the car traveled 250 to 300 feet after the impact. It was held that a question of fact was made out. The Court said that there was no rule of law requiring a pedestrian to rivet his eyes on an automobile. 

It was pointed out that the decedent saw the car but either misjudged its speed or the distance. 

Arndt v. Grayewski, 279 Mich. 224.

This was a suit for the death of a pedestrian. The accident occurred at night on Warren Avenue in Detroit

SUPPLEMENT 

[$1 at a point where the street was 72 to 80 feet wide with street car track in the center. The defendant testified that he was driving 20 to 23 miles per hour 10 to 15 feet back of another eastbound car. Neither he nor his companion saw the pedestrian before the impact, which occurred immediately after the car ahead had swerved to the right. The driver of the car ahead did not testify. 

His statement to the police that the pedestrian ran into the path of the car was introduced as evidence. Testimony showed the front of the car struck the woman. 

After a verdict for the plaintiff, the lower Court entered judgment for the defendant. In reversing the lower 

Court the Supreme Court said that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant in driving too close to the car ahead and in watching the speedometer instead of the highway. The question of contributory negligence was for the jury as the defendant did not see the pedestrian until she was in the path of the car and practically at the time of impact. The Court said that the statement of the driver of the car ahead showed that the pedestrian had stopped. The remainder of the statement that she then ran into the path of defendant's car was a question for the jury as this man was hardly in a position to see such an act, having just passed the pedestrian. 

Young v. Martinich, 279 Mich. 267.

Plaintiff was diagonally crossing a street in a village, walking in a northerly direction. He testified that he looked twice each way and saw lights of a car 1300 to 1400 feet east. He thought he could get across safely, did not look again and was struck by the car which was traveling 40 to 45 miles per hour, the impact occurring just as he was at the north edge of the street. The lower

§1] 

Court directed a verdict for the defendant which was affirmed. The Court said this: "Did his mistaken sense of safety, so easily corrected by the exercise of ordinary care, present an issue of fact for the jury? To so hold would subordinate the reasonable rule of duty to that of predetermination. It was plaintiff's duty, not only to take a view of traffic upon the street before attempting to cross, but, when he reached the center of the street and was about to enter the pathway of the car he knew was approaching, to make observation thereof while crossing and adapt his movements to accord with his own safety." 

Moore v. Noorthoek, 280 Mich. 431.

Plaintiff was walking west across a 42-foot street in Grand Rapids. When in the center she looked north and saw defendant's car 160 feet away coming south. She formed no judgment as to its speed. As she stepped over the westerly rail of the westerly track she was hit. 

There was a Grand Rapids ordinance requiring the operator of a car to yield the right of way to a pedestrian crossing on a crosswalk. The Court in holding that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law stressed the fact that the accident occurred in a business district; that the plaintiff made an observation just before she was hit, and made a dash to get away from the car. 

Davis v. Belmont Creamery Co., 281 Mich. 165. 

Plaintiff testified that at 1:30 a. m. he started to cross

Oakland Avenue in Detroit in a westerly direction at a point 40 feet north of the intersection. He claimed that the defendant's truck made a turn at the intersection when he was in the middle of the street and then struck 6.

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 1 him. A police officer testified that he saw the truck making a left turn to go north and at that time he saw the plaintiff crawling across the street and that the truck did not strike the plaintiff. No mud was knocked off the truck. Blood was traced to a pool of blood between parked cars at the east side of the street. The Supreme 

Court said that plaintiff's story was highly improbable and ordered a new trial on the ground that the verdict was contrary to the great weight of the evidence. 

Burton v. Yellow & Checker Cab Co., 283 Mich. 384. 

Plaintiff was attempting to cross Saginaw Street in

Flint at a point between intersections and in a business district. Saginaw Street was 60 feet wide. The westerly street car rail was 20 feet from the west curb. Before · leaving the west curb plaintiff saw defendants' cab 250 to 300 feet north. He stepped out into the street and made another observation from a point in line with the east side of a parked car. The cab was 180 feet away.

He testified that the cab did not appear to be traveling fast and he believed that he had time to cross the street. 

He continued east and looked to the north when he was at the westerly rail. He saw the cab but 30 feet away and approaching at a rapid speed. He became confused and started to run but was struck. In holding that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law the court said: "He had a right to assume that the driver thereof would obey the law and not operate his car at an excessive and unlawful rate of speed."

There was evidence that the cab was going 40 miles per hour. The Court said that plaintiff suddenly found himself in a perilous situation.

$1] 

Rentz v. Anhut, 284 Mich. 695.

Plaintiff's decedent, a pedestrian, was struck while on Livernois Avenue in Detroit. Defendant and an occupant of his car testified that they were going north when the decedent appeared in front of the car. Several witnesses testified that they saw the decedent standing on the yellow line in the center of the street just before the impact. The trial Court directed a verdict for the defendant. This was reversed and a new trial ordered. 

It was held that the testimony of the witnesses raised the question as to whether the decedent was standing in the center of the street when struck. 

Carter v. C. F. Smith Co., 285 Mich. 621.

Plaintiff testified that he was crossing Linwood Avenue in Detroit. He looked to the south and saw that the signal light one half block away was red for north and south traffic. There was no car coming north. He then left the east curb and walked to the center of the street without again looking to the south. While standing in the center of the street he was struck by defendant's truck. The trial Court entered judgment for the defendant notwithstanding the verdict. It was held that this was error. 

The judgment was reversed and a new trial was ordered. 

Plaintiff had contended that the verdict was inadequate. 

The Court said that had the statement of the driver of defendant's truck been admitted, as it should have been, the verdict might not have been the same. 

Haley v. Grosse Ile Rapid Transit Co., 290 Mich. 373. 

Plaintiff's decedent, walking south across West Jefferson Avenue in Detroit, was struck by defendant's bus which was traveling west, the impact occurring about two feet south of the northerly rail of the west bound street car track. Plaintiff's only witness testified that the bus

SUPPLEMENT 

[$1 was being driven at a speed of 35 to 40 miles per hour.

The decedent came out into the street when the bus was 150 feet away. He was seen to look in the direction of the bus. He continued to walk until struck by the front of the bus near the right edge. The decedent was attempting to cross the street in the middle of the block. 

The bus did not slow down or change its course. It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. 

Gayden v. Arabais, 292 Mich. 651.

The plaintiff alighted from an eastbound street car on Warren Avenue in Detroit. She walked behind the street car to go to the north curb, 22 feet from the north rail. Plaintiff saw defendant's westbound automobile 

115 feet away. Watching the car while walking, she realized that it was coming faster than the ordinary speed when she was 10 feet from the curb. She walked faster but the car was turned toward the curb and she was hit by the left front of the automobile. There was testimony that the car was being driven at a speed of 35 miles an hour. It was held that the question of contributory negligence was for the jury. 

Peck v. Hampel, 293 Mich. 252.

Plaintiff's declaration alleged that the decedent was crossing the intersection in the City of Big Rapids from the northwest to the southeast corner. This was in violation of an ordinance. Plaintiff produced no testimony as to the actions of the decedent. The defendant driver did not testify and there were no other eyewitnesses. The trial Court directed a verdict for the defendant on the ground that plaintiff failed to prove that decedent was free from contributory negligence. It was held that the defendant was an eyewitness to the accident and that plaintiff could not rely upon the presump-

$1] 

tion of due care. The Court also said that the decedent was in a place he should not have been, and was violating the ordinance which was evidence of negligence. 

Maloney v. Moore, 293 Mich. 428.

Plaintiff testified that she was crossing Woodward Avenue in Detroit in an easterly direction. When at the east edge of the cars parked at the west curb, she observed that there was no traffic for two blocks north. She started across and when 3 or 4 feet west of the southbound car tracks she ceased looking straight ahead and looked to the south. After taking two or three steps she was struck by defendant's taxicab, which had made a U-turn to go south on Woodward Avenue. It was held that a question of fact was made out on plaintiff's testimony. 

Poundstone v. Niles Creamery, 293 Mich. 455.

The jury disagreed and defendant made a motion for a judgment. The trial judge denied the motion and defendant appealed. It was held that defendant was entitled to a judgment because there was no evidence of negligence on the part of defendant. Defendant was driving a truck along a street in Niles at a speed of 12 to 15 miles per hour and 5 to 7 feet from the curb. Defendant was looking straight ahead when two hands came up against the right window and smashed the glass. The decedent was found lying on the street 3 feet from the curb. 

Eagan v. Edwards, 294 Mich. 260. 

Plaintiff, at night, was walking in a westerly direction across North Saginaw Street in Flint when he was struck by defendant's northbound automobile. Plaintiff testified that he left the east curb when he saw the car 250 feet away. He again saw it when it was 130 feet away. 10

SUPPLEMENT 

[$1 He continued walking and when he looked south again, the car was on him and struck him before he reached the east rail of the street car track. Defendant did not see plaintiff before the impact which damaged the front of the car. The lower Court, sitting without a jury, gave plaintiff a judgment which was affirmed. 

Straub v. Andrews, 295 Mich. 129. 

Plaintiff's decedent was first seen standing 12 to 4 feet east of the center line of Jefferson Avenue in Ecorse. The street was 90 feet in width having 5 lanes for traffic on each side. The testimony indicated that he was facing in a northwesterly direction. There was testimony that immediately prior to the accident the northbound traffic lane just east of the center line was free of traffic; that defendant, traveling in this lane, passed several cars and struck the decedent who was standing. Defendant did not see decedent until he was 4 to 6 feet away. It was held that the trial Court did not err in not finding decedent guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law. 

Shank v. Luckner, 296 Mich. 705.

Plaintiff was attempting to cross a 60-foot street in 

Benton Harbor at night. He started north and continued to look to the west until 2 feet out from the parked cars. 

He saw nothing approaching. He looked to the right and proceeded 4 feet further. A car was approaching from the east. While waiting he again looked to the west and saw nothing coming. After waiting for the westbound car to pass he took a step to the north and was struck by defendant's eastbound auto. Plaintiff's theory was that defendant's car was not lighted and was exceeding the speed limit. It was held that there was a jury question because of the observation made by the plaintiff. 11

MICHIGAN AUTOMOBILE Law 

Agranowitz v. Levine, 298 Mich. 18.

Plaintiff, a woman 73 years old, was walking in a westerly direction across Fourteenth Avenue in Detroit. 

Defendant was driving his car north behind car No. 2. 

No. 2 car was behind car No. 1. Plaintiff's counsel admitted that his client was negligent in walking into the path of car No. 1, and stopping when the car was 8 to 10 feet from her. Cars No. 1 and 2 were stopped and the defendant's car struck the rear of car No. 2, forcing it into car No. 1, which was shoved against the plaintiff. 

The jury brought in a verdict for the defendant. It was held that this instruction was proper. "Was it an unavoidable accident owing to circumstances then pending upon the situation at that particular moment? How did all these parties act one towards the other?"

It was also held that there was no error in the failure to instruct that the jury could draw an inference unfavorable to the defendant because of his failure to testify. The Court said that there was no showing of subsequent negligence. 

Covert v. Randall, 298 Mich. 38. 

Plaintiff's decedent, while attempting to cross Warren

Avenue in Detroit, walking in a northerly direction on a crosswalk, was struck by defendant's eastbound automobile. An eyewitness testified that the decedent, who was a deaf mute, walked 12 feet from the south curb before he was struck; that just prior to the moment decedent started, defendant's car was about a block and a half to the west. In holding that a question of fact was presented, the Court pointed out the fact that a car traveling 60 miles per hour would take 5 seconds to traverse the distance of a block and a half. The accident occurred in a business district. 12

SUPPLEMENT 

[81 "With a car almost a block and a half away, a pedestrian would have a right to assume that the driver would obey the law and thus allow him ample time to cross the street or at least to proceed sufficiently to the north so as to reach a place of safety." 

Delfosse v. Bresnahan, 305 Mich. 621.

Plaintiff's decedent was killed while crossing a street in Menominee. There were no eyewitnesses. Several witnesses testified that defendant admitted that he did not see the pedestrian. Defendant made a report to the chief of police, but it was excluded as privileged. 

The chief of police testified as to blood marks on the street and the damage to the front of defendant's car. 

The defendant did not testify. There was a verdict for plaintiff. It was held that a question of fact was made out. The Court said that the condition of decedent's body and the damage to defendant's car indicated very rapid speed of the car. There being no witnesses, the 

Court found that the presumption arose that decedent was free from negligence. 

Moldenhauer v. Smith, 311 Mich. 265.

Plaintiff was crossing East Genessee Avenue in Saginaw on the west crosswalk in a northerly direction. She paused in the center of the street. and observed defendant's car 75 feet to the east. She then walked rapidly toward the north curb believing she could continue in safety. As she was about to reach the northerly curb she observed the car near her and attempted to run and jump out of the way but was struck. Plaintiff testified that she continued to observe the car. The car was turned to the left to avoid the accident. There was an ordinance giving pedestrians on a crosswalk the right of way. The jury brought in a verdict of no cause for action. On appeal the plaintiff claimed errors in in- 13

$

structions. The Court held that the plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 2. Summary of Cases (Crossing City Street). 

The recent decisions in this type of case have not made any material change in the law. All of the cases cannot be reconciled. The decisions are so numerous that they are broken down into subdivisions in this summary. The Index should be consulted for a more detailed treatment. 

Where pedestrian is dead-If the pedestrian stepped into the path of the car when it was close, and there is evidence of such fact, the plaintiff will have difficulty avoiding a directed verdict. On the other hand, if the decedent was first seen when in the path of the car, the defendant will have difficulty in obtaining a directed verdict. It must be remembered that in the absence of testimony as to the decedent's actions, the plaintiff may rely upon the presumption of due care. (305 Mich. 621.) 

Other death cases are 272 Mich. 339; 279 Mich. 224; 

284 Mich. 695; 293 Mich. 252; 293 Mich. 455; 295 Mich. 129. 

Negligence in walking into path of car-Usually, where the pedestrian moves into the path of a car which is being operated at a reasonable speed, without change of course, on the right side of the street, and which is plainly visible, he is negligent as a matter of law. For such decisions, see 272 Mich. 339; 275 Mich. 626; 279 

Mich. 267; 290 Mich. 373; 311 Mich. 265. Even though the car is operated at an excessive speed, the pedestrian may be negligent. However, there are some decisions which cannot be reconciled with this rule. 14

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 2 

Where the automobile is operated at an excessive speed-Usually, if the speed is excessive to a sufficient degree, the pedestrian's negligence is a question for the jury. Otherwise, he may be negligent as a matter of law. 280 Mich. 431; 283 Mich. 384; 290 Mich. 373; 

292 Mich. 651; 296 Mich. 705; 298 Mich. 38; 305 Mich. 621.

Excuse for stepping into path of car-In the following cases the speed of the car or some other reason was sufficient reason to make the pedestrian's negligence a question of fact. 273 Mich. 132; 275 Mich. 393; 280 

Mich. 431; 283 Mich. 384; 294 Mich. 260; 296 Mich. 705; 

298 Mich. 38. 

Ordinance giving pedestrian right of way—A number of cities in Michigan have an ordinance giving a pedestrian on a crosswalk the right of way. This does not give the pedestrian a right to proceed without observation, or freedom from negligence in walking into the path of a car. 280 Mich. 431; 311 Mich. 265.

Duty to look when reaching the center of street-The pedestrian has the duty to make observation to his right when he reaches the center of the street. 279 Mich. 267. 

When on a crosswalk there is no duty to look back for a car making a turn across the crosswalk. (276 Mich. 

136.) There is no duty on the part of a pedestrian to rivet his eyes on a car. (279 Mich. 97.) The car driver may be négligent in driving too close to the car ahead. (279 Mich. 224.) If the car driver is forced to drive to the left of the center of the street, the pedestrian may be negligent in stepping into the path of the car. (275 Mich. 626.) The pedestrian may not be negligent in not seeing a car which has just made a U-turn. (293 Mich. 428.) 15

§3]  Sec. 3. Children Cases. 

Moore v. Cook, 275 Mich. 578.

The plaintiff, nine years old, was walking in an easterly direction across a street ten to fifteen feet north of an intersection. The defendant was driving a car north on 14th Street, a heavily traveled thoroughfare in Detroit, with headlights lighted. The plaintiff testified that she looked to the south when in the middle of the street and there were no cars approaching. She never saw the car which was being driven on the proper side of the street. 

The decision of the lower Court that the girl was negligent as a matter of law was affirmed. 

Brinker v. Tobin, 278 Mich. 42.

Defendant was driving her car in a northerly direction on a street in the city of Escanaba in the daytime. She saw two small girls standing on the east side of the street looking toward the north. She sounded her horn, and when her car was three feet west of the plaintiff and one foot south, the girl ran into the path of the car. The girl testified that she looked and saw no car, and did not hear the horn signal. The testimony showed the girl to be seven years and seven months old, and that she knew it was dangerous to go out into the road without looking. The decision of the lower court holding the girl negligent as a matter of law was affirmed. Plaintiff contended that a child of the age of the injured girl should not be held negligent as a matter of law. 

Bird v. Meade, 281 Mich. 114. 

Plaintiff's decedent, a 12-year-old girl, ran from behind a wagon out onto a trunk line highway into the path of defendant's car. The lower Court directed a verdict for defendant and the judgment was affirmed. 16

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 3 

Guscinski v. Kenzie, 282 Mich. 204.

A 5-year-old boy came on to a parking lot and sat down near the side of a building. The defendant who had been repairing his car testified that he got into the car, looked into the rear view mirror and along the left side and saw no one. He backed a car length and the rear wheel struck the boy. The Court gave a general instruction. Judgment for the defendant was affirmed. The Court emphasized the fact that the accident did not occur on a public highway and not on defendant's property. 

Clemens v. City of Sault Ste. Marie, 289 Mich. 254. 

Plaintiff, a boy 8 years and 3 months old, chased a small parachute into the street. He saw defendant's car about a block away and thought he had time to retrieve the parachute. When he had gone 15 or 18 feet he was struck. The car was going 45 to 50 miles per hour. The legal rate was 25 miles per hour. In holding that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, the Court said: "We think the rule sustained by the weight of authority is that the question of contributory negligence of a boy of the age of plaintiff under the circumstances of this case was a question of fact for the jury." 

Dedo v. Skinner, 296 Mich. 299.

Plaintiff was a week under 7 years of age. She was attempting to cross Lowell Street in Ironwood in a business section. She left the west curb near the middle of the block and testified that she looked to the north and south but saw no car. Defendant did not see the plaintiff before the impact. There was testimony that defendant was driving her car at a speed of 30 miles per hour in a southerly direction on a comparatively narrow busi- 17

§3] 

ness street. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Chadwick v. Kempf, 300 Mich. 402. 

The plaintiff, a 9-year-old girl, looked both ways be fore leaving the curb and saw only one car, more than a block away. She ran across the street without looking again and was struck when she had nearly reached the curb. Defendant's car made skid marks of 106 feet as observed by a police officer, indicating a speed of 35 or 40 miles per hour. It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Colvaruso's Guardian v. Stroh Brewery Co., 301 Mich. 245. 

Plaintiff was just under 4 years of age. Defendant's truck was being operated in an easterly direction on a city street at a speed of 7 miles per hour. Plaintiff's witnesses saw two children cross the street from north to south before plaintiff tried to do likewise and it was claimed that defendant's driver was negligent in not seeing these children. It was held that as a matter of law the plaintiff could not be guilty of negligence; that there was no negligence on the part of defendant's driver as he performed his duty as to the plaintiff. The 

Court pointed out the physical facts, indicating the boy had run into the side of the truck; also that the street was only 26 feet wide and with parked cars on each side the driving space was but 14 feet. The truck was 9 feet wide and the construction gave the driver no opportunity to see the boy unless he was some distance in front of the truck. Defendant's driver was the only witness who saw the plaintiff just before he was struck. The Court said the witnesses who testified that they saw plaintiff in an almost stationary position in the path of the truck did not see the boy at the time of the impact. 18

Ackerman v. Advance Petroleum Transport, Inc., 304 

Mich. 96.

Plaintiff's decedent, a normal boy slightly over 8 years old, was killed when he collided with the right side of defendant's truck which was being driven in an easterly direction on a street in Bay City at a speed of 10 miles per hour. The boy was last seen running in a northerly direction on the east sidewalk 10 feet south of the south curb, and he was looking back to the south. 

Defendant's driver saw the boy running but did not blow his horn. The Court held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of defendant, but that the boy was negligent as a matter of law. It was also held that a question of fact was not presented on the theory of wilful and wanton misconduct. 

Morris v. Radley, 306 Mich. 689.

Defendant was driving a truck in a westerly direction on a 20-foot black-top road at a speed of 45 to 50 miles per hour. A child 4 years, 9 months old, ran into the highway from a driveway which entered the road from the north. Defendant did not see the child until she was on the road, although he had a clear view of the driveway. The Court held that there was a question of fact as to defendant's negligence and said that had defendant been reasonably alert and observant, he probably might have prevented the accident. 

Sec. 4. Contributory Negligence Age. 

Tyler v. Weed, 285 Mich. 460.

In this case it was held that a child 6 years, 8 months old, could be guilty of negligence as a matter of fact. 

See opinion in this case for thorough discussion of the question. 19

$5] 

Morris v. Radley, 306 Mich. 689.

In this case it was held that a child 4 years, 9 months old, could not be guilty of negligence. 

See Brinker v. Tobin, 278 Mich. 42; Clemens v. City of Sault Ste. Marie, 289 Mich. 254; Ackerman v. Advance Petroleum Transport, Inc., 304 Mich. 96.

Sec. 5. Summary of Children Cases. 

It seems well settled now that a child may be negligent as a matter of fact if close to the age of 7 years. (285 

Mich. 460.) A child 7 years may be negligent as a matter of law. (278 Mich. 42.) A child as young as 4 years, 9 months could not be guilty of negligence. (306 Mich. 689.) 

If an average child 7 years of age or over runs into the path of a car or walks into the car without seeing it, he may be negligent as a matter of law. (275 Mich. 

578; 278 Mich. 42; 281 Mich. 114; 304 Mich. 96.)

When a child too young to be negligent runs into the street, a driver may not be negligent. (301 Mich. 245.)

Where the car is being operated at an excessive speed, the child's negligence is usually a question of fact. (289 

Mich. 254; 296 Mich. 299; 300 Mich. 402; 306 Mich. 689.)

The driver of a car on private property does not have as great a duty to look for children as on a public highway. (282 Mich. 204.)

Sec. 6. Country Highway Cases. 

Hanna v. McClave, 273 Mich. 571.

The decedent in this case was walking in a southerly direction across a highway. The defendant driving east testified that as the decedent entered the pathway of the car, he swerved the car to the left, but the decedent stepped back and was struck. It was held that the failure 20

SUPPLEMENT 

[86 of the defendant to stop, his rate of speed with the decedent in full view, and the want of warning of his approach, were all proper questions for the jury. 

Funk v. Tessin, 275 Mich. 312.

The plaintiff testified that she was on the shoulder of the highway when struck by defendant's car which was being driven in the same direction at night. The defendant claimed that his car never left the pavement and that an approaching car had just passed him when he saw a pedestrian six feet ahead of his car on the pavement. 

Defendant at no time saw the plaintiff who was walking with the other pedestrian. It was held that there was a question of fact as to plaintiff's contributory negligence. 

Plaintiff had admitted to a police officer that she was walking on the pavement when struck. The Court said that the proof was overwhelming that the accident occurred on the pavement and that there was ample proof that the plaintiff stepped onto the pavement in the path of defendant's car. The Court went to some length in considering proper instructions in this type of case. The verdict for the defendant and judgment were affirmed. 

The Court said that in passing on plaintiff's contributory negligence it was necessary for the trial Court to submit the case both on the theory that the plaintiff was off the pavement when struck, and on the theory that she was. on the paved portion of the highway. 

Lucy v. Dowd, 276 Mich. 289. 

Plaintiff's decedent attempted to cross the Dixie Highway in a southerly direction. The road was 40 feet wide. 

At the north edge of the pavement the decedent's companion stopped, but the decedent continued walking onto the highway and was struck when about in the center by the defendant's car which was westbound. Witnesses testified that although it was dark there were no lights 21

§6]  

on the car until just before the impact. The testimony did not show whether or not the decedent looked for traffic. It was held that decedent's contributory negligence was a question for the jury. The Court said that the testimony of one witness on cross-examination indicated that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law, but his testimony on direct negatived such a conclusion. 

Mullaney v. Woodruff, 280 Mich. 66.

The defendant was driving his car in an easterly direction at night on a highway 20 feet wide in the village of Melvin. A car ahead had slowed down and was practically stopped. When 200 to 250 feet back of this car, defendant turned his car to the left to pass it. About this time decedent, who had been walking in an easterly direction on the north shoulder, started to cross the highway, the stopped car being directly in front of him. The testimony showed that as the decedent reached the center of the highway he jumped back eight feet and was struck when two feet from the north edge of the pavement. The jury found each party negligent. The defendant relied upon the theory that the decedent was negligent in stepping back into the path of the car. It was held that the testimony presented a question of fact. 

Bird v. Meade, 281 Mich. 114. 

Plaintiff's decedent, a girl 12 years old, ran from behind a wagon in a northerly direction into the path of defendant's westbound car. The accident occurred in the country on a trunk line highway. The lower Court directed a verdict for the defendant, and the judgment was affirmed. 

Brown v. Lilli, 281 Mich. 170.

Plaintiff alighted from the right side of an automobile which was stopped just north of a trunk line highway. 22

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 6 She testified that she walked to the front of the car and after allowing a westbound car to pass, she looked to the right and left and seeing no car she took a few steps onto the road when she saw defendant's car to her left, 40 to 50 feet away. She attempted to escape the car but was not successful. It was undisputed that she had a clear view for 1215 feet. The Court held plaintiff negligent as a matter of law, and said that if she looked and failed to see that which was plainly visible, she was held in point of law to have seen it. 

Anderson v. Bliss, 281 Mich. 323.

The decedent was standing at the east side of a truck which was headed south and which was mostly on the west shoulder, there being three feet of the truck on the highway. The defendant testified that he was driving north and when 150 feet from the decedent he saw him standing by the truck and did not see him again until at the time of impact, although the accident occurred in the daytime. There was testimony that the decedent walked in a northeasterly direction with his head down and was struck. It was held that the decedent was negligent in walking from a place of safety into the path of the truck when he had a clear view of it. 

Pearce v. Rodell, 283 Mich. 19.

Plaintiff claimed that he was walking on the shoulder of the road at night and was struck from behind by defendant's car. Defendant contended that plaintiff was on the pavement.  "Even though plaintiff was walking upon the right-hand side of the pavement, as the plaintiff claims, so that he was struck by the right-hand fender and headlight of defendant's automobile, still it was a question for the jury whether or not plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence. 23

cas 

6] "The trial Court further charged the jury that if they found plaintiff at the time of his injury was walking upon the berm, and not upon the paved portion of the highway, then he was in the exercise of ordinary care and caution and was not guilty of contributory negligence. This part of the charge was proper. 

Fors v. LaFreniere, 284 Mich. 5. 

Plaintiff's decedent was killed on highway U. S. 2 near

Crystal Falls at night. The only witnesses to the accident were the defendants. They were driving through a fog and did not see the decedent until they saw a couple of hands which seemed to come toward the side of the car. The car was being driven in an easterly direction, and after the accident the decedent was lying 7 or 8 feet south of the pavement. The headlight was broken, the right front fender was damaged, and the windshield was cracked.

The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed by an evenly divided court. Four justices held that the damage to the car and other physical facts refuted defendants' theory that the pedestrian walked into the side of the car. They also decided that the decedent's contributory negligence was a question of fact for the jury, including the decedent's degree of intoxication and the possibility that the effect of the liquor had worn off. 

Four justices held that whether the decedent stumbled into the car from the side of the road, or whether he paid no attention to the oncoming car was not shown by the record but in either event there was a failure to use ordinary care. 

Holmes v. Merson, 285 Mich. 136.

In this case the decedent was walking in a westerly direction. There was testimony that he was near the 24

SUPPLEMENT [§ 6 west edge of the road when struck by defendants' northbound car. It was held that a question of fact was pre- 'sented as there was testimony showing that defendants' car was on the wrong side of the road. 

Kemp v. Aldrich, 286 Mich. 591.

Plaintiff, in a snowstorm, was walking through a cut in the snow which was only 6 or 7 feet wide. There were no paths alongside the highway opened up for pedestrians. She did not see any lights or hear any horn and was struck by defendant's truck which was approaching her. It was held that the question of negligence on the part of the plaintiff and defendant was for the jury. 

Rohrkemper v. Bodenmiller, 287 Mich. 311. 

Deceased and her companion, at night, were walking in a northerly direction along the westerly side of the highway. Defendant, driving north and while passing a northbound car, struck deceased. The pavement was 16 feet wide with a shoulder of 4 to 6 feet. Defendant did not see the decedent until he was 5 feet from her. The case was tried without a jury. The trial judge found that the decedent was negligent. An evenly divided court affirmed judgment for the defendant. Four justices held that there was a question as to whether the decedent should have noticed the approach from the rear of defendant's car. Four justices held that the presumption of due care operated as there was no eyewitness who saw what the decedent did, and no testimony of negligence. 

Herzberg v. Knight, 289 Mich. 29.

Plaintiff was driving his cattle south on a north and south gravel highway. Defendant was operating his automobile in a northerly direction. Plaintiff testified 25

§ 6]  

​that the road was free of cattle and that the car struck him at the west edge of the road off the gravel. Defendant claimed that the cows occupied the east side of the road, and that when he drove to the west side to avoid the cattle, plaintiff ran after one of the cows, which struck the front of the car, and ran into the automobile. 

The court reversed the judgment for the plaintiff and ordered a new trial because of improper instructions. 

The trial Court gave an emergency instruction. It was held that such instruction was wholly foreign to any claim or issue in the case. An instruction, that because an automobile is a dangerous instrumentality and a collision between a car and a pedestrian would not endanger the car, the jury should consider such in measuring the duty of the driver, was called improper. 

Haight v. Fox, 291 Mich. 601. 

Plaintiff was crossing a 32-foot gravel road. Before crossing he looked to the north and saw a car 35 or 40 rods distant. Walking in an easterly direction he testified that he was past the center of the road when he saw the car 10 feet away. He was one or two feet beyond the center when struck. Defendant testified that the impact occurred on the west half of the road. There were skid marks on the west half and after the accident the car was in the west ditch, and the plaintiff was lying east of the center of the road. It was held that the question of plaintiff's contributory negligence was for the jury. 

Sweet v. Sturgis, 292 Mich. 323.

Plaintiff testified that defendant's car was 400 to 425 feet away and he thought that he could cross the pavement in front of it. He took two or three steps, con- 26

[$6 cluded he could not get across, and started to retrace his steps when defendant's automobile struck him. There was no proof as to the speed of defendant's car. In holding plaintiff negligent as a matter of law, the court said: "Plaintiff could not indefinitely await the prospective accident, and he had ample time to avoid injury while the automobile of the defendant was traveling 400 feet." 

Ebel v. Bruzewski, 296 Mich. 654.

Plaintiff had been involved in an accident and was standing close to the rear of his car being interrogated by a police officer, when he was struck by defendant's automobile. The Court said that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, and the evidence warranted a finding that he was not guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of fact. 

Dokey v. Carpenter, 300 Mich. 648.

This accident occurred just outside the city limits of 

Kalamazoo on U. S. 12A. Defendant was driving in a westerly direction on the four-lane highway. Plaintiff was crossing from the south to the north. When he reached the center of the highway he looked to the east and saw nothing. From then on he kept looking to the right but saw nothing. He was struck when he had reached the most northerly lane by the right side of defendant's car which had been driven past a westbound car 300 feet from the point of impact and then into the most northerly lane. The Court held that a question of fact was presented as to plaintiff's negligence. If plaintiff had seen defendant's car he might have been justified in believing that defendant would not swerve back to the right until he had passed the pedestrian. 27

Jacobson v. Carlson, 302 Mich. 448.

A question was raised concerning the constitutionality of Act No. 318, Pub. Acts 1939, Section 4726-1, Mich. 

Stat. Ann. 1941 Cum. Supp., Section 9.1594(1), which makes it unlawful to walk on the main traveled portion of a highway where sidewalks are provided; where not provided, pedestrians, when practicable, shall walk on the left side facing traffic. The Court held the amendment constitutional. See this case for instruction concerning this statute. 

Beers v. Arnot, 308 Mich. 604.

Plaintiff alighted from a truck which was stopped headed west on the north half of a black-top road. After making an observation to the west he walked to the rear of the truck on the north side, and then walked behind the truck in a southerly direction across the highway. At a point near the left rear corner of the truck the plaintiff looked to the west and saw no càr. When he reached the south edge of the black-top he noticed defendant's eastbound car and he lunged forward and was on the shoulder when struck. Plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that had plaintiff made a proper observation when in the middle of the highway, he would have seen the car. 

Malone v. Vining, 313 Mich. 315.

Defendant was driving east on Nine Mile Road in Macomb County. The 20-foot pavement was blocked on the south side by a machine where men were working. Defendant drove past this machine, being on the north side of the road. She then turned her car back to the south side and as she was completing the turn, the left front of the car struck the pedestrian at a point 2 or 3 feet south of the center of the highway. The pedestrian testified that while standing on the north side of the pave- 28
