[§ 7 ment he saw the defendant's car approaching, but could not say how far away it was, and he did not judge its speed. He did not make any further observation. In holding the plaintiff negligent as a matter of law, the 

Court said that he left a place of safety and without making proper observation walked into a zone of danger. 

Sec. 7. Summary of Country Highway Cases. 

In this type of case there is often a dispute as to whether the plaintiff was on the shoulder or the traveled portion of the highway. (For proper instructions in such a case, see 275 Mich. 312; 283 Mich. 19.) 

Pub. Acts 1939, No. 318, Section 34a, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1594(1), provides that where sidewalks are not provided, pedestrians shall walk on the left side of the highway, when practicable, facing traffic which passes nearest. Where sidewalks are provided it shall be unlawful to walk upon the main traveled portion of the highway. This statute raises the question as to whether a pedestrian is negligent as a matter of law in walking on the right side of the highway, or if there are sidewalks, in walking on any part of the highway. In 302 

Mich. 448, the Court speaks of usable sidewalks and seems to imply that a violation of the statute would defeat recovery.

In certain situations the pedestrian's negligence is a question for the jury although he walks into the path of the car. (276 Mich. 289; 285 Mich. 136; 286 Mich. 

591; 291 Mich. 601; 300 Mich. 648.) 

Usually, in country highway cases, the pedestrian is negligent in walking into the path of the car. (281 

Mich. 114; 281 Mich. 170; 281 Mich. 323; 292 Mich. 323.)

In 308 Mich. 604, the pedestrian was held negligent although he had reached the shoulder of the road when he was struck. 29

§ 8] 

Where the pedestrian is standing close to the rear of his car after an accident and is struck, his negligence is usually a question of fact. (296 Mich. 654.) 

Where the pedestrian is dead, there may be a recovery for lack of evidence as to his negligence. (284 Mich. 5.) 

However, see 287 Mich. 311.

Sec. 8. Backing Car. 

Jenkins v. Bentley, 277 Mich. 81.

In this case an 11-year-old boy was leaning against a tree 27 inches from the curb. The defendant in turning his truck in the street backed over the curb against the boy. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. The 

Court said that the law imposed upon the defendant a duty to ascertain that the way was clear before backing. 

There was no legal duty to anticipate that the truck would be backed over the curb. 

Guscinski v. Kenzie, 282 Mich. 204.

In this case a 5-year-old boy was injured when defendant backed his car on a parking lot. Defendant testified that he looked in his mirror and along the left side of his car and saw no one. The rear wheel struck the boy's head. In affirming the judgment for the defendant, the 

Court said that the accident did not occur on a public highway or on defendant's property. 

Dubeau v. Bordeau, 291 Mich. 418.

Plaintiff was walking north on the east crosswalk at an intersection in Saginaw. Defendant drove south, and after making a right turn, backed across the intersection striking plaintiff when she was north of the center of the street. After a verdict for the defendant, plaintiff appealed, claiming error in the instructions. It was held 30

Wai SUPPLEMENT DI 

[$9 that plaintiff was not entitled to an instruction on sudden emergency. The Court in affirming the judgment for the defendant said that there was no prejudicial error, although the instructions touched upon matters not involved. 

Schultz v. Frost, 294 Mich. 457.

Plaintiff testified that she waited until the traffic signal changed in her favor and then stepped from the curb. 

Upon seeing the taxicab backing toward her she tried to get back to the curb but was struck. It was held that a question of fact was presented concerning contributory negligence. 

In re Estate of Miller, 300 Mich. 703.

Plaintiff, a child, was injured when the car was backed by Sherman Miller, who was delivering mail. The accident occurred in the street. It was held that there was not competent evidence of the negligence of Miller. There was no testimony as to what observation was made by 

Miller; nor was there any evidence that Miller knew children were hanging on the rear bumper.

Sec. 9. Summary of Backing Car Cases. 

Where the vehicle is backed over the curb, the pedestrian is not bound to anticipate such act and the driver has the duty to ascertain that the way was clear. (277 

Mich. 81.)

A pedestrian may be negligent in not avoiding a car backing across a crosswalk. (294 Mich. 457.) 

If the driver is dead, the plaintiff's case may fail because of lack of proof of negligence as to observation and knowledge of children on the rear bumper. (300 

Mich. 703.) 31

Sec. 10. Car on Wrong Side of Street. 

Hanna v. McClave, 271 Mich. 133.

The deceased was attempting to cross a highway in a southerly direction. When the decedent had gone four or five feet onto the 18-foot pavement, the witness heard the squeal of brakes and saw the decedent step back. 

The defendant's car, traveling east at a speed of 30 to 40 miles an hour, left a mark one foot and two inches north of the center line. It was held that the decedent was not negligent as a matter of law, because he was at all times on the north half of the road.  "This should have been a place of safety for him as to the danger from automobiles traveling in an easterly direction." 

Warwick v. Blackney, 272 Mich. 231.

Plaintiff and his wife were walking south on the east side of the highway which was crowded with cars going to the Harmsworth boat race. Defendant's car was being driven south on the left side of the road with other cars ahead. Defendant sounded his horn and plaintiff stepped aside. There was no evidence that the car left the pavement. There was evidence that the plaintiff came in contact with the side of the car which was moving slowly. The jury disagreed and a judgment was entered for the defendant. This judgment was affirmed. The 

Court said that defendant was not negligent in driving on the left side of the road as he could not turn to the right because of the congestion ahead and around him. 

There was no other evidence of negligence. 

Campbell v. Brown, 276 Mich. 449.

In holding that plaintiff's contributory negligence was a question for the jury, the Court said that the plaintiff 32

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 10 was not required as a matter of law to continue to look, after passing the center of a highway, for cars running on the wrong side. 

Greene v. Richer, 278 Mich. 1.

The defendant's car was driven on the left-hand side of a street to pass another car and struck the plaintiff's decedent. Defendant introduced testimony to show that the plaintiff's decedent was intoxicated. It was held that even though the decedent was intoxicated there was no showing that such intoxication was a contributing cause. of the accident. 

Ehlers v. Barbeau, 291 Mich. 528.

Plaintiff was crossing from the north to the south side of the street. He testified that he stopped north of the center of the street to allow two eastbound cars to pass, and that the second car turned out to pass the first, crossing the center line and striking the plaintiff. Defendant contended that the damage on the car and the absence of injury to plaintiff's legs and body proved conclusively that the plaintiff walked into the side of the car. The 

Court found that the testimony and physical facts amply sustained plaintiff's claims. There was some evidence of damage to the headlight and front fender. 

Dewey v. Perkins, 295 Mich. 611.

Plaintiff was attempting to cross West Michigan Avenue in Battle Creek. She testified that she walked in a southerly direction to a point 2 feet north of the center of the street where she was struck by defendant's eastbound automobile. Plaintiff's two witnesses and defendant's disinterested witness contradicted plaintiff and testified that she did step across the center line and that defendant's car was not on the wrong side of the street. It was 33

§11] 

held that the verdict for the plaintiff was against the great weight of the evidence, and a new trial was ordered. 

Wallace v. Kramer, 296 Mich. 680.

Plaintiff was walking north across East Warren Avenue in Detroit and had not reached the center of the street when he was struck by defendant Kramer's westbound automobile. There was testimony that defendant 

LeGro was driving from 40 to 65 miles per hour, and that in passing Kramer, his car cut off Kramer's view and caused Kramer to apply his brakes, his car skidding 92 I feet into the plaintiff. It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of each defendant. 

Plaintiff testified that it was a business district. The 

Court said that in figuring business frontage, only that part of the land contiguous to the highway which is available for buildings should be included. The proof was not specific as to the frontage of 300 feet. It was held that the Court properly allowed the jury to determine whether it was a business or residential district. 

Burnash v. Compton, 298 Mich. 70.

Plaintiff was walking in a westerly direction across a 26-foot street in Flint and had reached a point 2 feet east of the center when he was struck by defendant's southbound car. It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 11. Summary of Wrong Side of Street Cases. 

The recent cases in this type of case clearly demonstrate that it is difficult to prove negligence on the part of the pedestrian, if the car is on the wrong side of the 34

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 12 street without reason. Ordinarily there is no duty to look for cars running on the wrong side of the street. (276 Mich. 449.) Where there is a congested condition of traffic the driver may not be negligent in operating his car on the wrong side. (272 Mich. 231.) Although the pedestrian testifies that the car was on the wrong side, the verdict for the plaintiff may be against the great weight of the evidence. (295 Mich. 611.)

Sec. 12. Traffic Signal Cases. 

Manley v. Potts, 286 Mich. 671. 

The plaintiff after taking 5 or 6 steps from the west side of Woodward Avenue was struck by defendant's taxicab. Plaintiff started to cross Woodward Avenue with the green traffic signal, and after the accident was lying 20 feet south of the southwest corner of Woodward and Canfield. There was no testimony concerning the operation of the cab. The Court reversed judgment, holding that no proof of negligence on the part of the defendant had been offered. "If defendant was negligent, the burden of presenting the necessary proof thereof rested upon plaintiff, and its absence was not to be supplied by a guess of the jury." 

DeJager v. Vandenberg, 288 Mich. 136.

The plaintiff started across a city street on a crosswalk, the traffic signal light being green for him. When he reached the center of the street the light changed. 

The plaintiff, with a case of beer on his right shoulder, stopped in the center of the street. He looked to his right but because of a standing car could see only 11 35

§ 12] 

or 12 feet. Without again looking he walked in front of this car and into the left side of defendant's automobile which was passing the standing car and was entering the intersection on a green light. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law.  "He did not see defendant's car until the front of it passed by him and then his momentum carried him against the side thereof near the double doors. 

He knew the light had changed and he was in the pathway of vehicles, but took no care. Defendant's car did not run him down; he heedlessly walked against the car."

The Court said that if defendant violated the law that did not send plaintiff's contributory negligence to the jury. 

Beaulieu v. City of Detroit, 293 Mich. 364. 

Plaintiff's decedent, a man 79 years of age, started across Woodward Avenue in Detroit under the protection of a green light. He was walking in a westerly direction. The light changed before he reached the first rail of the northbound track, and he continued, deflecting his course from the crosswalk in a northerly direction. 

He was struck by a northbound street car. 

The jury brought in a verdict for the defendant. Plaintiff appealed claiming error in the instructions and the refusal to instruct as requested. Witness testified that the pedestrian could have safely stopped before reaching the car track. The judgment for defendant was affirmed. 

The Court said: 

"Under the evidence it is apparent that plaintiff's decedent, after the light changed and released the traffic going north and while he was in the path thereof, proceeded with his head down and without 36

SUPPLEMENT 

[$ 12 looking in the direction of the released traffic, and walked into the front corner of a street car." 

Neesley v. Lord, 297 Mich. 163. 

Plaintiff was attempting to cross Third Avenue on the south side of West Grand Boulevard in Detroit. She testified that when stepping from the southeast corner she looked at the traffic light on the northeast corner and it was red for north and south traffic. After taking two or three steps she heard motors starting and she started to run. She imagined that she was at least in front of defendant's car at that moment. On cross-examination she admitted that she did not know exactly where she was when the car started. It was held that her negligence was a question of fact. The court said that if the testimony of a witness on direct examination conflicts with that on cross-examination, it is for the jury to decide when, if at all, he testified truthfully, provided that the subsequent testimony is not given for the purpose of correcting or explaining the former testimony. The position of the traffic light on the southwest corner made it necessary for plaintiff to look north. 

Sloan v. Ambrose, 300 Mich. 188.

Plaintiff testified that when she left the curb to cross the street the signal light was green for her. She did not make any further observation. She was walking in a southerly direction on the east crosswalk and was struck by defendant's westbound automobile. The light changed when plaintiff approached the center of the street. Plaintiff was found negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that one starting to cross a street under the protection of a traffic light is still required to observe the change, if any, and to employ reasonable care in proceeding into the path of released traffic. The 37

§ 13]  

drivers of released traffic must observe pedestrians caught by change of light and exercise reasonable care to avoid striking them.

Sec. 13. Summary of Traffic Signal Cases. 

Pub. Acts 1939, No. 318, Section 8, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1568, governs the rights of a pedestrian where traffic is regulated by signal lights. 

Where light changes when pedestrian reaches middle of street-If the light changes against the pedestrian when he reaches the middle of the street, he has the duty to look for traffic coming from his right. (288 Mich. 136.) 

Where light changes before pedestrian reaches middle of street-In this situation the pedestrian may be negligent in not making proper observation to the left. (293 

Mich. 364; 300 Mich. 188.) But the question of negligence of the pedestrian may be for the jury. (297 Mich. 163.)

Defendant attempted to turn out of the rut but was unable to do so and ran into the plaintiff. Judgment for defendant was affirmed. The Court held that the question of plaintiff's contributory negligence was one of fact. 38

Decal for CHAPTER II INTERSECTION CASES Sec. 15. Usual City Intersection. 

Thompson v. Michigan Cab Co., 279 Mich. 370.

Plaintiff was driving south on a street in Lansing at night. He stopped at the intersection and looked to the left and saw no car coming. He then drove into the intersection and saw defendant's cab 150 feet away to the left. Because of the icy condition of the street he could not stop or speed up his car enough to avoid the accident. 

It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law for not seeing the cab sooner even though he could have seen farther to the east had he stopped two to three feet further south. Neither street was a stop street, but slow signs were posted on each side of the intersection. The Court said that other testimony made contributory negligence a question of fact. 

Alexander v. Sanders, 279 Mich. 465.

This case was tried without a jury. Plaintiff was driving south on a street in Lansing at 20 miles per hour. 

When one-half block from the intersection plaintiff saw defendant's car a block west of the intersection. Plaintiff was at the north side of the intersection when defendant was 50 feet west of the intersection. Defendant's car struck plaintiff's car when its front end was almost even with the south side of the intersection. Judgment for the defendant was affirmed. The Court said that there was evidence from which the trial court could make the findings it did. 

Knight v. Merignac, 281 Mich. 684.

Plaintiff was driving south in the daytime on a city street. Defendant was driving west. 

When 40 feet from 39

§ 15] 

the intersection, plaintiff looked to the left and saw no car coming. When near the center of the intersection, plaintiff first saw defendant's car two or three car lengths away. The Court said that the defendant was clearly guilty of negligence in driving 25 to 30 miles per hour and in failing to give plaintiff the right of way, plaintiff having entered the intersection first. Plaintiff when 40 feet north of the intersection had a clear view of the other street 160 feet east of the intersection. She traveled 60 feet at 15 miles per hour from this point.

When entering the intersection defendant must have been 40 feet away without any indication of slackening his speed. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law for failing to make proper observations. The 

Court said that she was chargeable with seeing what could have been seen. 

Wells v. Oliver, 283 Mich. 168.

At night plaintiff was driving east on a street in Saginaw. When 30 feet from the intersection he looked south and saw no car approaching within a distance of 200 feet, the limit of his vision. After looking to the left he entered the intersection at a speed of 17 miles per hour and looking to the right he saw defendants' car 80 feet away and approaching at a high speed. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. "If, as plaintiffs claim, their view to the right, from the point before entering the intersection, was restricted then Mr. Wells was guilty of negligence in not taking another look to his right when the view was enlarged and before proceeding to the center of the intersection."

The Court said that plaintiff was bound to observe traffic from his right while crossing the street. Had ho 40

Each car was traveling 20 miles per hour. The left front of plaintiff's car struck the right side of defendant's auto. When 30 feet east of the intersection plaintiff's decedent could see 143 feet south on Stanton. It was held that plaintiff's decedent was guilty of contributory negligence, even assuming that he entered the intersection first. "It is apparent that when plaintiff's decedent entered the intersection, the defendant was at, or almost to, the intersection without showing any indication of coming to a stop."

Plaintiff was driving east on Federal Avenue in 

Saginaw. Defendant was going north on Second Street. 

Plaintiff entered the intersection at a speed of 8 miles per hour and could have stopped almost instantly. She saw defendant's car 300 feet away and coming at a speed of 45 to 50 miles per hour. Plaintiff did not attempt to stop or increase her speed and the collision occurred in the middle of the 30-foot street. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. 

Ashworth v. City of Detroit, 293 Mich. 397.

Plaintiff at night was driving west on Cherry Street in Detroit and stopped about 20 feet east of the east curb of Trumbull which was 54 feet wide. She drove ahead about 8 feet and stopped again. She could see 150 feet south on Trumbull and noted that there was no traffic north. Plaintiff then started across Trumbull without looking again and her car was struck by a northbound street car. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. By mathematical calculation the Court came to the conclusion that plaintiff could not safely rely upon her last observation. 

Stephens v. Koprowski, 295 Mich. 213.

Plaintiff's car was being driven north on a street in Grand Rapids. Because of an obstructing building the driver did not see defendant's car until he was 20 to 25 feet from the intersection. Defendant was 75 feet from the center of the intersection and driving east. Defendant turned his car to the left side of the street and plaintiff's car was struck on the left side in the northeast quarter of the intersection. Plaintiff's driver testified that when he first saw defendant he was driving 15 miles per hour and thought he could cross safely. It was held 43

§ 15] 

that plaintiff's driver was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that he was not bound to assume that defendant would change his course and swerve to the left. 

Sexton v. Niewoonder, 296 Mich. 443.

Plaintiff was driving east on a residential street in Kalamazoo. Defendant was driving south. This was a blind intersection. Plaintiff first saw defendant's car when it was 150 feet from the intersection and noticed that it was slowing down. Plaintiff started to cross the intersection at a speed of 12 to 15 miles per hour. She next saw defendant's car 6 feet from the point of impact.

It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Saunders v. Berger, 297 Mich. 199.

Defendant was driving south on College Street in 

Battle Creek. He made a left turn, cutting the corner to Champion Street where College Street ended, and plaintiff operating a motorcycle in a westerly direction collided with the car. Plaintiff was proceeding at a speed of 18 to 20 miles per hour. His view was cut off by parked cars. When plaintiff was 24 feet from defendant's car and 17 feet from the point of impact he saw defendant's auto at the north curb line. Because defendant was cutting the corner, plaintiff claimed that he was faced with an emergency. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court pointed out the fact that plaintiff did not retard his speed in approaching the intersection and would not have been able to avert a collision had defendant not cut the corner. 

Saunders v. Joseph, 300 Mich. 479.

Plaintiff was driving his car north on a residential street in Flint. When he was 50 feet from the inter- 44

wl SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 15 section he saw defendant's car 100 to 150 feet east of the intersection going 30 to 40 miles per hour. When he reached the center of the intersection defendant was 

50 feet away. Plaintiff's car was north of the intersection when it was struck. The impact was north of the intersection. In holding that plaintiff was, not negligent as a matter of law, the Court said that plaintiff was not required to assume that defendant would turn to the right. 

Ayers v. Andary, 301 Mich. 418.

Plaintiff was driving in an easterly direction on a street in Lansing. He slowed down to 15 miles per hour and as he reached the intersection he noticed defendant's car 125 to 150 feet south of the intersection. Upon making a second observation to his right just before the collision, plaintiff saw the other car 30 to 35 feet away coming at a high rate of speed. The plaintiff was held to have been negligent as a matter of law.  "Obviously the first observation made by plaintiff's driver of defendant's car amounted to no more than a fleeting glance of the oncoming car without forming any judgment whatever as to the rate of speed at which it was approaching."

The Court said that a proper observation must include some judgment of the approximate speed. 

Shotwell v. Bultman, 303 Mich. 193.

Plaintiff was driving his car in an easterly direction on a street 66 feet wide. When he was 75 feet west of the center of the intersection of Silver Avenue, which was 60 feet wide, he saw a car coming north one short block away. Plaintiff slowed down from 18 to 15 miles per hour. When he was practically through the inter- 45

997 section he looked again and saw defendant's car coming very fast and turning towards him. This car struck the rear corner of plaintiff's car. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law, the Court saying that where the view is open, observation must be made. and maintained. 

Francis v. Rumsey, 303 Mich. 526.

Plaintiff was driving his car in a westerly direction on a street in the City of Holland. Defendant was driving south. The plaintiff, when 53 feet east of the center of the intersection, saw defendant's truck 150 feet north, and formed no judgment as to its speed. He did not look to his right again until his car was two-thirds across the intersection, when he saw the truck at the crosswalk. He then pulled to the left and was hit on the right rear fender. The Court found that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the testimony and the physical facts clearly established that plaintiff was negligent because he failed to observe the speed of defendant's truck and failed to make further observation to ascertain if he could cross safely. 

Afman v. Kraker, 305 Mich. 504.

Plaintiff was driving east on a residential street in the City of Holland. He testified that when 65 to 75 feet west of the intersection he looked to the north and saw no car approaching. A house obstructed his view of defendant's car. He then looked to the south, and when 35 or 40 feet west of the intersection he again looked to the north and saw defendant's car 50 or 60 feet north of the intersection. Plaintiff had been driving 

20 miles per hour. He increased his speed, relying on the right of way, and the cars met at the center of the intersection. Plaintiff was held guilty of negligence. 46

Wimmer v. Colman, 307 Mich. 413.

Plaintiff was driving west on a dirt street and defendant was proceeding south on a dirt street. When 70 feet east of the intersection plaintiff observed defendant car 250 to 300 feet north of the intersection. When 5 to 10 feet from the intersection defendant's car was observed 125 to 150 feet north of the intersection. Plaintiff drove across the intersection at the same speed of 20 miles per hour without making any further observation, and the rear end of the car was 3 to 5 feet west of the traveled portion of the north and south street when it was struck. Plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law for not properly observing and heeding the distance and speed of the approaching car. 

Waling v. City of Detroit, 308 Mich. 163.

Plaintiff's decedent was driving west on Schoolcraft in Detroit before daylight. He approached the intersection at 20 to 25 miles per hour. The collision occurred in the northwest corner of the intersection when the northbound bus struck the left side of the car. There was testimony that the bus was being driven on the left side of the street at a speed of 30 to 35 miles per hour, and that the decedent's car was about to leave the intersection when struck. It was held that decedent's negligence was a question for the jury. The instruction as to the right of way was approved.

Sec. 16. Summary of City Intersection Cases. 

The decisions in this group in recent years have increased the duties of drivers at the ordinary city inter- 47.

§ 16] 

section.

The cases have been subdivided according to duties. The Index should be consulted for a more detailed treatment of intersection cases.

The fact that plaintiff's car is on the right, or reaches the intersection first, is not sufficient to make out a question of fact. Neither can plaintiff get to a jury by showing that the defendant's car was moving at a very excessive speed. Something more than this must be shown. 

For decisions holding a driver negligent as a matter of law where the defendant's car was on the right, see 279 

Mich. 465; 283 Mich. 168; 286 Mich. 635; 291 Mich. 697; 

293 Mich. 370; 301 Mich. 418; 303 Mich. 193; 303 Mich. 

526; 307 Mich. 413. For similar decisions where the party is negligent although his car is on the right, see 

281 Mich. 684; 283 Mich. 524; 305 Mich. 504. The following duties have been put upon drivers by the listed decisions: 

1. Duty to look when entering intersection. 281 

Mich. 684; 283 Mich. 524; 286 Mich. 635. 

2. Duty to look after entering intersection. 283 

Mich. 168; 291 Mich. 697; 293 Mich. 397. 

3. Duty to continue to observe. 301 Mich. 418; 303 

Mich. 193; 303 Mich. 526. 

4. Duty to observe and stop although on right if collision is imminent. 281 Mich. 684; 283 Mich. 524; 

286 Mich. 635. 

5. Duty not to drive into path of fast moving car. 

281 Mich. 684; 283 Mich. 168; 286 Mich. 635; 291 Mich. 

697; 293 Mich. 370; 301 Mich. 418; 303 Mich. 193; 307 

Mich. 413. 

6. Duty not to drive too slowly. 286 Mich. 635.

The fact that the plaintiff's car is almost clear of the intersection does not free him of negligence. 291 Mich. 

697; 303 Mich. 193; 307 Mich. 413. 48

Although the defendant may have turned his car to the left of the center of the street, the Court may recognize that such act was a frantic effort to avoid plaintiff's car, and plaintiff may be negligent as a matter of law.

From the cases in this group, it is clear that a driver of a car is under such a weight of duties in crossing an uncontrolled city intersection that he will have difficulty getting to a jury.

Faustman v. Hewitt, 274 Mich. 458.

Plaintiff, who did not testify, was driving south on a gravel road and defendant was driving east on a gravel road. At the close of plaintiff's case the only testimony as to the accident was that the defendant's car was damaged on the front end and was at the southeast corner of the intersection, while plaintiff's car was damaged on the right side and was in the south ditch east of the intersection. There was some testimony of skid marks starting west of the center of the north and south road. Defendant moved for a directed verdict at the close of plaintiff's case. It was held that plaintiff's driver was negligent as a matter of law. Hekman Biscuit Co. v. Commercial Credit Co., 291 Mich. 156. 

Plaintiff's car was being driven south and collided with a westbound automobile at an intersection in the country. Neither driver could see the other until his car reached the intersection. Plaintiff's driver admitted a speed of 25 miles per hour in entering the intersection.

The case was tried without a jury and a judgment was entered for the defendant. This was affirmed, the Court holding that the finding of negligence on the part of plaintiff's driver was amply supported by the evidence. 

Stuck v. Tice, 291 Mich. 486.

Plaintiff's car was going north on a gravel road in the country. Defendant was driving in an easterly direction. The view of each driver was unobstructed.

As it approached the intersection the truck appeared to slow down either for the purpose of stopping or making a turn. For this reason plaintiff's car was driven through the intersection without slackening of speed. Defendant, after slowing down, picked up speed and the collision occurred several feet north of the center of the east and west road. It was held the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law.

Rathburn v. Riedel, 291 Mich. 652.

Plaintiff was a mail carrier, and was driving east on a 30-foot gravel road. Defendant was traveling south on the same type of road. Plaintiff's view was obstructed. 

He slowed from a speed of 45 to 30 miles per hour, and when 4 to 6 feet from the west edge of the intersection he looked to the north. When he entered the intersection he observed defendant's car, 50 feet to the north, slowing up, and believing defendant was stopping, plaintiff continued. Defendant turned to the left and the collision occurred. The majority of the Court held that a question of fact was made out. Taylor v. Williamson, 298 Mich. 251.

Plaintiff's car was being driven north on a macadam road. When 110 to 130 feet south of the intersection of a gravel road, the driver looked to the west and saw no automobile. Strong v. Kittenger, 300 Mich. 126.

Plaintiff was driving north and defendant east. Plaintiff testified that when he was 50 to 75 feet from the intersection he saw defendant's car 150 to 200 feet from the intersection and noticed that it started to slow down. 

He believed it was going to stop and give him the right of way. Plaintiff continued to observe defendant's car, and, when at the intersection realized it was not stopping. It was then too late to avoid the collision. It was held that this testimony made out a question of fact.

Beecher Road. Neither highway was preferred. Plaintiff's driver testified that he stopped 15 feet south of the intersection and looked in both directions. Plaintiff could have stopped in 20 feet, but he increased his speed and the collision occurred in the center of the intersection. Plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 18. Summary of Country Intersection Cases. 

The numerous recent decisions have placed a heavy duty on the driver of a car at an uncontrolled country intersection. The plaintiff in the usual case is unable to escape a directed verdict. 

1. Where the view is obstructed until the driver is close to the intersection, he must have his car under such control that he can stop before reaching the path of the 57

§ 19] 

other car, if a collision is imminent. 288 Mich. 126; 288 

Mich. 498; 289 Mich. 301; 291 Mich. 156; 295 Mich. 54; 

309 Mich. 89. The court will not accept plaintiff's estimate of the distance of defendant's car from the intersection, if it does not square with the physical facts. 288 

Mich. 186; 289 Mich. 301. 

2. Where the view is unobstructed there is a duty to continue to observe. 288 Mich. 186; 298 Mich. 251; however, in 306 Mich. 500, plaintiff's negligence was a question for the jury, although there was not further observation. Even if plaintiff continues to observe, he is negligent if the danger of a collision is imminent. He cannot take a chance. 275 Mich. 22; 285 Mich. 593. 

3. If plaintiff's car is on the right and defendant slows down in approaching the intersection, plaintiff may not be negligent in proceeding across the intersection. 291 Mich. 486; 291 Mich. 652; 300 Mich. 126. The latter case cannot be reconciled with the other decisions in this group, as the plaintiff was driving too fast to avoid a collision when he first made his observation. 

Where there is insufficient proof, plaintiff's case may fail. 274 Mich. 376; 274 Mich. 458.

Although one highway is paved and the other is gravel, and carries much more traffic, it is not superior to the other. The duties of the driver on the heavier traveled road are not lessened when crossing the other road. 298 

Mich. 251.

Sec. 19. Duties of Drivers Crossing Stop Highways. 

Leader v. Straver, 278 Mich. 234.

This case was tried without a jury. Plaintiff's car was being driven north on Twelfth Street, a stop street in Detroit, and struck the right side of defendant's car which was driven east on Chicago Boulevard. Plaintiff's 58

SUPPLEMENT 

[$ 19 driver testified that he saw two cars standing at the west edge of the intersection but did not see defendant's caruntil just before the impact. In affirming the judgment for the plaintiff the Court said that it was not against the preponderance of the evidence.  "The purpose of a stop street is to afford traffic on it a preference. It is the duty of one arriving at such street not only to stop but so to remain until a reasonable opportunity to proceed appears. . 

When Leader saw the standing cars he was close enough to the intersection to justify a reasonable belief that they would not proceed until he had crossed, especially because there was another car immediately ahead of him." 

Ault v. Kuiper, 279 Mich. 1.

Plaintiff's car was going south on a trunk line highway, 20 feet in width, at a speed of 40 miles per hour. Defendant approached the intersection at a speed of 25 miles per hour and failed to stop. It was held that the defendant was clearly guilty of negligence in violating the statute and that plaintiff's negligence was a question of fact for the jury. Defendant claimed the lower Court was in error in instructing that plaintiff's driver had a right to assume that vehicles approaching the trunk line road would come to a complete stop before crossing. The instruction was held proper. 

Pulford v. Mouw, 279 Mich. 376.

In this case it was held that defendant was guilty of negligence in failing to stop for a stop street in the city of Royal Oak. 

DeCoopman v. Hammond, 279 Mich. 619. 

Plaintiff at 2:30 a. m. was attempting to cross the northbound traffic lanes of Woodward Avenue on Twelve Mile 59

§19] 

Road. He stopped in the center of the parkway, and look, ing to the south saw the lights of defendant's car 600 to 

900 feet away. Thinking he had time to cross he drove out into the northbound lanes and was struck. He did not see the defendant's car again until just before the impact. On holding plaintiff negligent as a matter of law the Court said that the plaintiff drove slowly into the path of the car without paying any further attention to its approach. "The ordinary prudent man needs no prodding to awaken to the fact that such failure to watch a known approaching danger in the nighttime, with ability, had he done so, to have avoided the collision, was want of reasonable care."

Although the defendant was restricted to a speed limit of 45 miles per hour, the court said that excessive speed was no excuse for the plaintiff's want of reasonable care. 

It was nighttime and plaintiff could but guess at the location and speed of defendant's car when it was first seen. 

Lodato v. Campbell, 284 Mich. 217.

Plaintiff stopped his car on Inkster Road at the north edge of Grand River Avenue, a super-highway, 40 feet in width on each side of a parkway. He saw defendant's car 500 feet to his left. He testified that he could not judge its speed and thought he could get across safely. 

When about half way across the westbound lanes he saw the defendant's car again when it was 20 feet away. The pavement was icy. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law.  "Plaintiff's thought that he could cross ahead of the approaching car did not relieve him from testing the accuracy thereof by subsequent observation of the known rapidly changing condition upon the icy roads." 60

[§ 19 

Wallace v. Rosenfeld, 285 Mich. 204.

Plaintiff's car was driven east and was stopped about 8 feet from the edge of U. S. 31, a four-lane highway. 

The driver looked to the north, being able to see 700 to 800 feet, and saw no car coming. He started out into the highway and when the front of the car was in the third lane the rear of the car was struck by defendant's southbound car. Plaintiff's driver first saw the defendant's car when it was 30 or 40 feet away and coming at a speed of 70 or 80 miles per hour. It was held by a majority of the Court that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that as plaintiff's car entered U. S. 31 the defendant was approximately 

528 feet away, and that while the driver was charged with the knowledge of having seen what was plainly there to be seen, reasonable minds might differ upon the question of contributory negligence. 

Cramer v. Brictson, 286 Mich. 224.

Plaintiff, driving on a dirt road in an easterly direction, came up to M-14, a trunk line highway, which was 24 feet in width. He testified that when he was at the west edge of M-14 he could see 1,000 feet to the south and he saw no car approaching. As he crossed to center of the highwa he looked to the south again and saw defendant's car 6 or 8 feet away traveling 60 miles per hour.

Plaintiff was found negligent as a matter of law. The court found that defendant's car must have been within 500 feet of the intersection when plaintiff was at the west edge of the highway, and that plaintiff either did not look or did not see the defendant's car which was plainly within his vision. 

Carey v. DeRose, 286 Mich. 321. 

Plaintiff's driver drove up to a trunk line highway and stopped. She had a view to the right of 1175 feet. 61

§ 19] 

She saw no car approaching. She started in low gear and proceeded a distance of 60 feet when her car was struck by defendant's automobile, which she did not see, and which came from her right. She was held guilty of negligence as a matter of law.  "Had Mrs. Carey looked while crossing the intersection it is manifest that she would have seen the approaching car in ample time to have avoided the collision." 

Rodgers v. Blandon, 294 Mich. 699.

Plaintiff was in a car which was driven east on Stimson Avenue in Detroit. The driver testified that he stopped for Second Boulevard. He saw a Ford car onehalf block south which was followed by a taxicab, and started across the boulevard. When his car reached the middle of Second Boulevard he saw the Ford car 50 or 60 feet away and the taxicab behind it in the lane just east of the center lane. Rodgers continued across the boulevard at a speed of 10 miles per hour and his car was struck by the taxicab on the rear right wheel. This evidence showed that the taxicab had been turned to the right of the Ford and had passed it. It was held that the question of Rodgers' negligence was for the jury.

The Court said that it was negligence as a matter of law for a vehicle approaching another from the rear to pass it at an intersection or on the right-hand side. Defendant contended that the statute did not apply as lanes had been marked on the boulevard. 

Hubbard v. Canavare, 295 Mich. 499.

Plaintiff's car was driven north onto highway U. S. 2 at a speed of 10 miles per hour. The stop sign had been removed. The driver was looking for the main highway but did not know that he had reached it. Defendant's 62

Defendant was in a speed zone of 20 miles per hour and his car struck plaintiff's automobile on the left rear at the center of the pavement. In holding the plaintiff negligent as a matter of law, the court said that the physical facts showed that defendant's car, with lights burning, was within plaintiff's view at a point where he could have stopped in a place of safety. 

Schuckert v. Berdan Bread Co., 298 Mich. 379.

Plaintiff's car was driven across trunk line M-24 in

In holding him negligent as a matter of law, the Court said that he should have made further observation to the south. The skid marks and the location of the cars were consistent with the testimony that the collision occurred in the east lane. 

Gallagher v. Walter, 299 Mich. 69.

Plaintiff's car was driven in a westerly direction on Ten Mile Road in Oakland County. In crossing Orchard 

Lake Road, a through highway, plaintiff's driver slowed down but did not stop. There was a stop sign 125 feet east of the intersection. Defendant's southbound automobile came in contact with plaintiff's car at a point east of the center of the highway according to plaintiff. 

This was denied by defendant. After a verdict for defendant plaintiff appealed, claiming error in the charge of the court concerning plaintiff's duty to make observa- 63

§ 19] 

tion and see defendant's car approaching before driving onto the highway. It was held that there was no error; also that it was not necessary to prove that the stop sign was legally erected, as the record indicated that all parties considered Orchard Lake Road as a through highway. 

Wilson v. Corwin, 299 Mich. 494.

Plaintiff was driving south and stopped 5 feet from the north edge of M-89. She made an observation to the east, and not seeing any car, she drove onto M-89 and was about to turn east when she saw defendant's car coming over the hill 55 to 70 miles per hour. Plaintiff claimed that her car was on the south side of the highway at the time of impact. Defendant claimed that plaintiff did not stop and that the impact occurred on the north side of the highway. In affirming the judgment for defendant, the Court said that plaintiff could have seen to the east for more than 400 feet; that the finding of glass after the accident was not at all persuasive as to the exact point where the cars came together. 

Heckler v. Laing, 300 Mich. 139.

Plaintiff's decedent was driving alone in a westerly direction, and while crossing U. S. 2 came into collision with the defendant's northbound car. Plaintiff presented testimony that defendant was driving on the wrong side of the road at a speed of 60 to 65 miles per hour, which was in excess of the speed limit of 25 miles per hour. 

There was testimony that the decedent stopped for U. S. 

2 and that the collision occurred on the west side of the intersection. There was no testimony as to what observation was made by the decedent. He could have seen 

500 or 600 feet south. It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. 64

[§ 19 

People v. Silver, 302 Mich. 359.

It was held that where a street or highway is divided by a parkway, there are not two intersections. 

See Nicewander v. Diamond, 302 Mich. 239. 

Boyce v. Shtukas, 306 Mich. 467.

Plaintiff was in an automobile which was being driven in a westerly direction on Mapier Avenue south of Benton Harbor. Defendant's car was driven south on Colfax Avenue, a through highway. The plaintiff testified that he had no memory of the facts. The driver of each car died as a result of injuries. Mrs. Hardke, in plaintiff's car, was the sole survivor able to testify concerning the accident. She testified that her husband stopped his car before entering the intersection and looked to the north. She heard the sound of a motor, which grew louder, and looked to the north, but there were no lights visible. They started across and were struck by defendant's car. Witnesses testified that defendant was driving 60 to 65 miles per hour without lights. Plaintiff had remarked that the sound of the motor must be coming from a car. This remark was heard by the driver. The trial judge without a jury found for the plaintiff and judgment was affirmed. 

Carrothers v. French, 309 Mich. 340. 

Plaintiff was driving in an easterly direction on U. S. 

12. Defendant was driving in a northwesterly direction on Ann Arbor Trail. The defendant stopped at the through highway and, looking to the west, saw a car 750 feet away. He proceeded across without making further observation and did not see plaintiff's car until it was in front of him. Plaintiff had passed the car, observed by defendant, at a point 600 feet from the intersection. The impact occurred 3 feet from the north 65

§ 19] 

edge of the highway. It was held that the defendant was negligent as a matter of law and that the verdict of no cause as to each claim was supported by the evidence. 

DiMatteo v. Smith, 309 Mich. 640.

Plaintiff's decedent was crossing Meyers Road in Detroit, traveling west. Plaintiff's witness testified that the decedent was driving at a speed of one-half mile per hour across Meyers, which is 40 feet wide. The car appeared to stop at the middle of the intersection but was struck west of the center of Meyers. When the decedent's car was just west of the center line, defendant's car was half a block or less away. The decedent was held negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that one cannot enter an intersection and see a rapidly approaching car nearing him and then just slow down. 

LaCaeyse v. Roe, 310 Mich. 591.

Plaintiff was driving on U. S. 31A, a two-lane highway, and was crossing U. S. 31, a four-lane highway. 

Plaintiff testified that he stopped before entering U. S. 

31, as he was required to do by reason of a stop sign. 

He could see half a mile to the left. He saw a car 300 or 400 feet away coming from his left. He started to cross and was entering the fourth lane when the collision occurred. Defendant was driving 55 or 60 miles per hour in spite of a "Slow Down-Intersection" sign and turned to the left of the center of the highway, leaving skid marks of 165 feet. Plaintiff made no observation to the left after starting to cross. The Court, in holding that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law, quoted the lower court's conclusion that the fact that the defendant's frantic effort to avoid plaintiff's car put the impact beyond the center of the highway did not save the plaintiff. 66

[§ 20 

Waskelis v. Continental Baking Co., 310 Mich. 649.

Plaintiff was driving west on Canfield Avenue in Detroit at night. He stopped his car at a stop sign 10 to 15 feet east of Trumbull Avenue, which was 40 to 50 feet in width, with two sets of streetcar tracks. He looked to the south and saw the lights of a truck 150 feet away and traveling midway between the curb and the car tracks. 

He did not estimate the speed of the truck. He proceeded into the intersection, and when the front half of his car was over the most westerly rail, he saw the truck 20 to 30 feet to his left and then was struck at the left center of the car. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. 

Ann Arbor Construction Co. v. Russ, 312 Mich. 527.

Plaintiff's truck was being driven south across the four eastbound lanes of Ecorse Road, a through highway. As he started up an incline to cross the road, plaintiff saw defendant's truck 900 to 1000 feet to the west. 

He gained a speed of 4 miles per hour. Although he saw defendant's truck approaching at all times, he did not stop, although he could have stopped within 10 feet. 

Defendant continued rapidly without slackening speed in the second lane from the south and then turned into the first lane where the impact occurred. The Court found that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. 

Sec. 20. Summary of Cases Involving Duties of Drivers Crossing Stop Highways. 

The decisions in this group of cases, handed down in the last 10 years, have increased the plaintiff's burden in making out a question of fact. Now a driver is usually negligent as a matter of law in driving onto a stop highway and coming into collision with a car on that highway. 67

§ 20] 

1. Failure to stop before entering the stop highway will usually make recovery impossible. 279 Mich. 1; 279 

Mich. 376; 299 Mich. 69. 

2. It is the duty of a driver not only to stop, but to remain stopped until a reasonable opportunity to proceed appears. 278 Mich. 234. 

3. There is a duty to make observation while crossing the highway. 279 Mich. 619; 284 Mich. 217; 286 

Mich. 224; 286 Mich. 321; 298 Mich. 379; 299 Mich. 69; 

309 Mich. 340; 312 Mich. 527.

Although the defendant, on the stop highway, is on the wrong side of the road, the plaintiff crossing the highway is usually negligent. 299 Mich. 494; 300 Mich. 

139; 310 Mich. 591; 310 Mich. 649. In the latter case the Court emphasized the fact that the defendant turned his car to the left of the center in a frantic effort to avoid a collision.

For two decisions making the question of driver's negligence a question for the jury, see 294 Mich. 699.

Defendant turned from one marked lane to another just before collision. 285 Mich. 204. It is difficult to reconcile this decision with the others in this group of cases. 

Where the parties in the record considered the highway a through highway, it is not necessary to prove that the stop sign was legally erected. 299 Mich. 69. Also see 284 Mich. 88, for case involving evidence necessary to prove a through highway.

Where there is no stop sign, the driver may be negligent as a matter of law. 295 Mich. 499. Where the plaintiff is crossing a trunk line highway and there is no stop sign, there is a question concerning his duties. and the duties of the driver on the trunk line highway. 

See 299 Mich. 69. In considering 284 Mich. 88, the Record and Briefs should be consulted to get the true picture of the facts. Also, it must be remembered that the 68

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 21 statute involved in that case has been changed. See

Summary, Sec. 22. 

Where a highway or street is divided by a parkway, there are not two intersections. 302 Mich. 359. This bears on the question of the duty to stop at the parkway. 

Where there is no testimony concerning the observation of the driver, because of death, he may be held negligent as a matter of law. 300 Mich. 139; 306 Mich. 467; 

309 Mich, 640.

Sec. 21. Duties of a Driver on a Stop Highway. 

Leitch v. Getz, 275 Mich. 645.

Defendant was driving east at 45 miles per hour on a trunk line highway in the daytime. He saw plaintiff's car off the pavement at the south side and just starting north when 60 to 70 feet from the car. Plaintiff stopped his car blocking the eastbound lane and defendant turned to the left to pass in front of him. However, plaintiff started ahead and in turning to the right, defendant's car skidded on the damp pavement into the left rear wheel of plaintiff's car. It was held that the defendant was not negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that there was no rule making a speed of 45 miles per hour negligence where visibility was restricted to 500 feet, nor was there a rule requiring a driver on a trunk line highway to keep his car under such control that he could stop within 70 feet. 

Holloway v. Nassar, 276 Mich. 212. 

State trunk line highway M-71 ran north from Durand for two miles and then turned west. From the intersection at the turn a road ran north and a road continued east. Plaintiff was driving north. When at the intersection he saw defendant's car, which was traveling east, 69

§ 21] 

slacken speed as it approached the intersection. Thinking defendant was intending to turn right and stay on the trunk line road, plaintiff continued north and was struck after he had crossed the center of the intersection. 

It was held that the question of plaintiff's negligence was for the jury. 

Marciniak v. Sundeen, 278 Mich. 407.

This case was tried without a jury. Plaintiff's decedent was driving a car south on Hoover. Road. Defendant, driving east on Ten Mile Road, failed to stop for a stop sign and struck plaintiff's car. Each driver had a clear view of the other. The occupants of decedent's car testified that when their car was 75 feet from the intersection, defendant's car was 150 feet from the center of the intersection and that neither car changed its speed. The lower 

Court found negligence on the part of the decedent on the ground that the defendant's car was approaching at a high rate of speed according to the plaintiff's testimony. On affirming this judgment the Court said: "Plaintiff's decedent had a right to assume that defendant would obey the statute requiring him to come to a full stop before entering Hoover Road, a through highway, but notwithstanding the fact that Marciniak had the right of way, he was not entitled to proceed heedlessly and without taking any precaution for the safety of himself and others riding in his automobile."

The Court assumed that the lower Court found the decedent negligent as a matter of fact and not as a matter of law. 

Silkworth v. Fitzgerald, 279 Mich. 349.

Plaintiff was driving east on a stop street in Battle Creek and claimed that defendant going south on a cross 70

wrdd SUPPLEMENT 

[$ 21 street, failed to stop, striking her car. The trial court instructed the jury on right of way quoting Section 20 

of the Motor Vehicle Law, Comp. Laws 1929, Section 

4712, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1580, which gave the driver on the right the right of way unless driving at an unlawful rate of speed. It was held that this was error, as Section 21 of the Motor Vehicle Law, Comp. Laws 1929, 

Section 4713, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1581, provided that a driver entering a stop street should yield the right of way to vehicles on the stop street. The Court said that 

Section 21 applied and not Section 20 and consequently the plaintiff did not necessarily forfeit her right of way. 

Pulford v. Mouw, 279 Mich. 376.

Plaintiff's decedent was driving south on a stop street in Royal Oak 20 to 25 miles per hour. The defendant drove into the intersection at a speed of 30 to 35 miles per hour. The view was unobstructed for 100 feet. The only witnesses were in a car behind decedent's automobile. It was held that the decedent was not negligent as a matter of law, and that sufficient facts were presented to make out a question of fact regarding decedent's contributory negligence. 

Arnold v. Krug, 279 Mich. 702.

This was an action resulting from the death of a 17-year-old girl who was an occupant of a car which was driven into a trunk line highway colliding with defendant's truck. The truck was traveling east at 45 miles per hour when the plaintiff's car was driven into the highway from the south without stopping and made a short left turn into the path of the truck. A high embankment made this a blind corner.. The road south of the highway was rarely used. Judgment for plaintiff was re- 71

§ 21] 

versed on the ground that there was no evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant.  "The driver is entitled to assume that those approaching it (trunk line highway) will obey the law and stop. He is not obliged to have his car under such control at each intersecting road that he may stop at once and avoid collision with persons who may illegally come into his path."

It was pointed out that to have avoided the collision the defendant would have had to slacken his speed so that he could have stopped well within 30 feet. The Court refused to impose such a duty on a driver on a trunk line highway. 

Dramis v. Dunbar, 280 Mich. 300. 

At 3:30 a. m. plaintiff was driving east on Grand River

Avenue, a stop street in Detroit. When 40 to 50 feet from Livernois Avenue he slowed down to 10 to 15 miles per hour and looked north, being able to see 30 to 40 feet up Livernois. He saw no traffic and increasing his speed he drove into the intersection without again looking to the left and was struck by defendant's southbound truck which was traveling 35 miles per hour. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. However, the Court said: "On the other hand it cannot be said that Dramis was free from negligence as a matter of law. It is a well known fact that early in the morning, when traffic is light, drivers are not so heedful of stop signs as in the daytime. Dramis had an open road ahead. It is not difficult to quickly shift gaze from side to side. The fact that he did not see the truck until the moment of collision suggests an inattention which forbids holding him guiltless of negligence in law. In our opinion, the record presents an issue of fact for the jury.' 72

Potter v. Felician Sisters Home, 281 Mich. 101.

The car in which plaintiff's decedent was riding was traveling north on a through highway. The only testimony offered was that of an eyewitness, a gas station attendant. He testified that each car was traveling 35 miles per hour and that plaintiff's car swerved to the right just before the collision. Defendant's car, eastbound, failed to stop for the through highway. It was held that plaintiff had raised an issue of fact concerning contributory negligence, and it was a question for the jury. 

Knaggs v. Lewis, 287 Mich. 431.

Defendant was driving a police car west on Kercheval Street in Detroit in answer to a burglary alarm. The plaintiff, a minor, was in a car which was driven into the path of the police car at the intersection of Fischer Avenue. Kercheval was a stop street. The trial judge, without a jury, found for the defendant, and the judgment was affirmed. 

Rhoades v. Finn, 288 Mich. 262.

Plaintiff was driving west on a through traffic highway. Defendant was driving north and was required to stop at the intersection. When plaintiff was 200 feet from the intersection she saw defendant's car slowing down and paid no further attention to it. It was held that the trial Court was not in error in charging the jury that the plaintiff was guilty of negligence if she attempted to cross at the intersection when the circumstances indicated that the other party was not going to stop. 

Holley v. Farley, 289 Mich. 676.

Plaintiff's car was being driven west on M-60, a trunk line highway, and was struck by defendant's automobile, 73

§ 21] 

which was going south on M-78, a trunk line highway. 

Defendant had a stop sign, but failed to stop, entering the intersection at a speed of 45 miles per hour. Plaintiff's driver when 150 feet from the intersection looked to the right but his view was obstructed. He did not again look to the right until warned by one of his passengers just before the collision. Plaintiff's witness, a passenger, observed defendant's car when it was 125 feet from the center of the intersection. It was held that plaintiff's driver was negligent as a matter of law, as he had the same view as the passenger, and he failed to take advantage of it until too late.  "Under repeated decisions of this court the right of way has attached the duty of making observation. of existing conditions and possible precautionary action thereunder.'

It should be noted that plaintiff had no stop sign on M-60.

The lower Court found that the defendant was not negligent as he was close enough to the intersection to justify a reasonable belief that the other driver would not proceed until he had crossed the intersection. The Court also found that defendant was not negligent in relying upon the plaintiff's car stopping. 

Judgment for the defendant was affirmed. 74

Rife v. Colestock, 297 Mich. 194.

Plaintiff was driving his car in a southwesterly direction on Greenwood Avenue, a through street in the City of Jackson. Plaintiff then looked toward the east and did not look to the west again. Defendant approached from the west and did not stop for Greenwood Avenue. 

Plaintiff's wife saw defendant slow down upon approaching the stop sign. It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Breker v. Rosema, 301 Mich. 685.

Plaintiff's car was being driven in an easterly direction on M-50 and, when nearly across the intersection of M-114, was struck by defendant's northbound car, which did not stop as required by the stop sign. It was held that plaintiff's contributory negligence was a question for the jury. Each car was traveling between 35 and 40 miles per hour and arrived at the intersection at about the same time. The Court pointed out the fact that it was dark and, therefore, more difficult for the plaintiff to determine the speed of defendant's car. He might have had good reason to believe that defendant would stop. 76

Perhaska v. Silberg, 302 Mich. 47.

Plaintiff was driving west on a street in Ironwood. 

Defendant was driving south at a speed of 15 to 20 miles per hour. He slowed down for the intersection, but did not heed the stop sign, making a left turn. The collision occurred in the southeast quarter of the intersection as plaintiff turned his car to the left when he was 30 feet from the intersection. At that point plaintiff was driving only 10 miles per hour and he observed that defendant was not stopping. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law. The Court said that the emergency instruction should not have been given.

Plaintiff knew he was approaching a dangerous intersection. The Court said that it was common knowledge that with good brakes a car could be stopped in less than 45 feet when traveling less than 10 miles per hour. 

Plaintiff was 45 feet from the center of the intersection when he knew defendant was not stopping. 

Stabler v. Copeland, 304 Mich. 1.

Plaintiff's decedent, a minor, was in an automobile which was driven east on Fullerton Avenue in Detroit across Schaefer Highway at a speed of 30 miles per hour. The defendant was driving north on Schaefer, a through street. The defendant, when 40 to 60 feet south of Fullerton, saw the lights of a car, 250 to 300 feet west of the intersection. He crossed railroad tracks and observed a tractor and trailer traveling west and a car on Schaefer coming from the north. Plaintiff's car collided with defendant's automobile in the northeast quarter of the intersection after defendant had slowed down to a speed of 15 miles per hour. The jury rendered a verdict for the defendant, which was affirmed. The Court said that there were circumstances which, standing alone, would indicate that defendant was negligent as a matter 77

§ 21] 

of law. However, taking into consideration the railway crossing, the other cars approaching the intersection, and the fact that defendant's car had cleared the south half of Fullerton, the Court decided that a question of fact was presented. 

Seymour v. Carr, 307 Mich. 109.

Plaintiff was driving north on Southfield Road, a through street in Detroit. Defendant, driving east on

Outer Drive, failed to stop for Southfield and drove across the southbound lanes at a slow speed and did not see plaintiff's car until he had entered the northbound lane. Plaintiff was driving at a speed of at least 40 miles an hour. His view of defendant's car was blocked by parked cars. The testimony showed that Outer Drive carried heavy traffic. The speed limit in this district was 45 miles per hour. Plaintiff contended that there was no evidence of negligence on his part. The judgment for the defendant was affirmed. The Court found that plaintiff's contributory negligence was a question for the jury, as was the question of proximate cause in defendant's failure to stop. 

Slivensky v. Wayne, 307 Mich. 443. 

Plaintiff was driving north on highway U. S. 27. According to plaintiff's testimony a cornfield obstructed his vision until he reached the cross road. 

The trial judge with a jury found that this was true. It was held that a question of fact was presented and the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 78

Sec. 22. Summary of Cases Involving Duties of a Driver on a Stop Highway. 

The recent decisions in this group have not altered the law concerning the duties of a driver on a stop highway. In the great majority of the cases the question as to whether the driver is negligent is a question of fact. 

Although the driver on the through highway has the right of way, he is not entitled to proceed without taking precautions. 278 Mich. 407; 280 Mich. 300. It should be noted that in several of the decisions the driver on the through highway was found negligent as a matter of fact, although the other car did not stop. 278 Mich. 

407; 307 Mich. 109.

The driver on the through highway may be negligent as a matter of law, if proper observation will warn the driver that the other car is not stopping. 289 Mich. 676; 

302 Mich. 47. 

Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4713, par. (c), Mich. Stat. 

Ann., Section 9.1581, par. (c), provides that the driver of a vehicle entering a through highway or street shall yield the right of way to all vehicles approaching on such highways. It was held in 279 Mich. 349 that a driver on a through street did not necessarily forfeit the right of way because of unlawful speed and by reason of Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4712, Mich. Stat. Ann.,

Section 9.1580. 

For the duty to drive at a certain speed, see 275 Mich. 

645. At a blind intersection the driver on the through highway is not required to reduce his speed so that he can avoid a collision with persons who illegally come into his path. 279 Mich. 702.

Where a car is approaching the plaintiff on a through highway and leaves the road at a right angle turn to continue on another highway, the question of plaintiff's 79

§ 23] 

negligence would probably be for the jury. 276 Mich. 212. 

Where two trunk line highways intersect, the state highway commissioner and the commissioner of the state police, acting jointly, shall determine which traffic, if any, shall be given preference. See Pub. Acts 1939, No. 318, Section 21, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1581. 

This is supposed to correct the situation which existed in Shoniker v. English, 254 Mich. 76. This statute (e) requires all vehicles approaching the intersection of a state trunk line highway to come to a full stop. The state highway commissioner is required to erect stop signs. This raises the question as to the duty of a driver to stop where there is no stop sign, and the right of the driver on the state trunk line highway to rely upon the car stopping. See 284 Mich. 88, remembering that the statute has been changed to some extent since that decision. See comment in Summary, Sec. 20, concerning evidence necessary to prove that highway is a through or trunk line highway.

City of Lansing v. Hathaway, 280 Mich. 87.

In the daytime a fire truck in the City of Lansing was being driven through a red traffic signal at an intersection in response to a fire alarm. The defendant driving through the intersection under the protection of a green light struck the fire truck. A warning was being sounded from the fire truck but defendant claimed that a rainstorm prevented him from hearing the warning or seeing the fire truck. A judgment for the defendant was affirmed. 80

Sec. 29. Running Off Highway. 

Crowley v. Upleger, 273 Mich. 541.

In a trial without a jury plaintiff claimed that defendant while driving on a gravel road lost control of his car and, becoming angry, swore at it and turned the steering wheel abruptly to the left, applied the brakes, and the car turned over. Defendant denied this, testifying that he tried to regain control of the car. Judgment for the defendant was affirmed. 

Holmes v. Wesler, 274 Mich. 655.

Defendant in attempting to make a gradual curve at a speed of 70 to 75 miles per hour lost control of his car and almost instantly thereafter the car struck a telephone pole. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Keilitz v. Elley, 276 Mich. 701.

Defendant who was not acquainted with the road was driving 62 miles per hour at night approaching a railroad 81

§ 29] 

crossing and a curve. An oecupant warned him to slow down for the crossing but he said that he could handle it. 

The car left the curve after going up in the air when it struck the crossing. The Court said that a showing of excessive speed was not enough and held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Riley v. Walters, 277 Mich. 620.

Defendant attempted to drive round a curve at a speed of 65 to 70 miles per hour. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Breckinridge v. Arms, 279 Mich. 384.

While the car was rounding a curve defendant removed his right hand from the wheel and reached down to fix the rubber covering on the accelerator. He bent his head under the cowl and the car traveled one thousand feet while he had his head under the cowl until just before it struck a tree. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Godley v. Mueller, 280 Mich. 203.

Defendant drove round a gradual curve at a speed of 90 to 100 miles per hour on a 30-foot pavement. After traversing 700 feet of the curve, the car left the pavement and went 187 feet before stopping. No protests were made. In holding that there was no evidence of gross negligence, the Court said that there was no positive evidence that the speed of the car caused it to leave the road. 

Olszewski v. Dibrizio, 281 Mich. 423.

The plaintiff testified that while turning out to pass a car defendant took both hands from the steering wheel to light a cigarette, and the car went in. a ditch. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 82

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 29 

Pawlicki v. Faulkerson, 285 Mich. 141.

Defendant, on an icy road, drove 35 to 40 miles per hour. The car skidded many times and defendant was asked to reduce his speed which he did not do. The car skidded on a curve and the accident happened. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Thayer v. Thayer, 286 Mich. 273.

The defendant, before getting into his car, had a chill and did not feel well. Later while driving he remarked that he wished his granddaughter were with them as no one else in the car could drive. While trying to turn at a corner he was seized with cramps. Not being able to move the steering wheel the car went into a ditch. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. The 

Court said that defendant was not put on notice that he would lose control of the car. 

Thompson v. Ross, 292 Mich. 450.

Plaintiff was a guest of defendant who was driving the automobile on a cement highway which was wet and icy. Plaintiff's testimony was that when the car was 20 rods from the sharp curve the driver was warned of the turn ahead. The car was driven at a speed of 50 miles per hour and when the brakes were applied the car struck the curb injuring plaintiff. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Sherman v. David, 293 Mich. 489. 

Defendant to whom passengers had given warning of a bad curve and protests as to speed was not guilty of gross negligence in driving at a speed of 50 to 75 miles per hour until 100 feet from the curve where brakes were applied. wwww 83

§ 30] 

Bushie v. Johnson, 296 Mich. 8.

There was testimony that the driver was warned of speed on the curves. He was cautioned to drive slower.

He would slow down and then after a few miles go fast again. One occupant, who had a suit pending, testified that the defendant drove 60 to 70 miles an hour and sort of zigzagged, and said, "Watch me give them a scare."

This was denied. After coming out of an S curve the car left the pavement and struck a tree. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. Three justices dissented. 

Coppin v. Lippy, 299 Mich. 586.

Plaintiff testified that defendant drove at a speed of 

45 or 50 miles per hour on a road covered with snow.

Several times the car skidded onto the shoulder of the highway. Plaintiff asked defendant to slow down on account of poor visibility, but he stated that he could see. 

The car went off the pavement and struck a culvert. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Sec. 30. Car on Wrong Side of Road. 

Raby v. Dodge, 279 Mich. 626,

Defendant's car went onto the wrong side of the highway striking another car. Defendant could not give any reason for the car skidding, although it was drizzling at the time the accident occurred. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. 

Case v. Klute, 283 Mich. 581.

Defendant was driving on a super-highway four lanes in width, at a speed of 50 miles per hour. When 200 feet from an approaching truck defendant's car swerved to. the left into the truck. Plaintiff's decedent was killed.

Bielawski v. Nicks, 290 Mich. 401.

The question in this case was whether defendant was guilty of such wanton misconduct that his liability to plaintiff survived his subsequent discharge in bankruptcy.
