Sec. 33. Failure to Stop Within Assured Clear Distance. 

Sherman v. Yarger, 272 Mich. 644.

While driving on a winding gravel road in a park a tree loomed up in the center of the road, and defendant skidded into it. Plaintiff had objected to the speed and there was testimony that defendant had said he would get one of the occupants, who had climbed onto the tire cover, off in some way. Judgment for the defendant on a directed verdict was affirmed. The Court said that the defendant had not driven over the road before. 

Fink v. Dasier, 273 Mich. 416. 

Defendant was driving 70 miles per hour at night.

His car overtook and collided with an automobile being driven 35 miles per hour. Plaintiff testified that he saw the tail-light of the car ahead when they were 300 feet from it. Defendant testified that he did not see it until he was 15 to 20 feet from the car. In holding that there was no evidence of gross negligence, the Court said: 86

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 33 BesThe collision occurred within a fraction of a second after the car ahead was observed and under circumstances which constituted ordinary negligence but which negative the presence of wilful or wanton misconduct or gross negligence on the part of defendant. Because of defendant's ordinary negligence he was suddenly and unexpectedly confronted with an emergency.

The accident happened instantly. It was unavoidable after defendant became aware of the impending danger." 

Schlacter v. Harbin, 273 Mich. 465.

Plaintiff was standing on the running board on the right side of defendant's roadster. Three persons beside the defendant were on the front seat. The pavement was slippery and a mist limited visibility to 15 or 20 feet.

Defendant had to work his windshield wiper by hand. 

The plaintiff protested against the speed of 40 miles per hour within the city limits of Pontiac. Defendant testified that he did not see the parked car which he grazed. 

In holding that there was no evidence of gross negligence the Court said that defendant believed he had his car under control and the accident resulted from his failure to see the parked car. The accident was not caused by the skidding which provoked the previous cautions to be careful. 

Quinlan v. Wells, 291 Mich. 214.

Plaintiff, in this guest case, pleaded that defendant drove his automobile at a high and dangerous rate of speed in a snowstorm. The defendant answered that he drove into the rear end of a truck, the tail light of which was obscured by a sander. Defendant moved for a directed verdict upon the pleadings and the court granted the motion. Judgment for the defendant was affirmed. 87

§ 34] 

The Court said that the proximate cause of the accident was defendant's failure to see the truck, and this was only ordinary negligence.

Sec. 34. Defendant Driving While Intoxicated. 

See Bonnici v. Kindsvater, 275 Mich. 304. 

Bielawski v. Nicks, 290 Mich. 401.

It was claimed that shortly after the accident defendant admitted that he had taken a drink some time before. 

The testimony of all of the witnesses indicated that defendant was not intoxicated. The Court said that even intoxication is not necessarily indicative of wilful and malicious misconduct.

Sec. 34-a (New). Interference by Occupant. 

Ladrig v. Renike, 312 Mich. 277.

The defendant, in spite of protests by the plaintiff, continued to permit the occupant of the front seat to put his hand on the steering wheel. The car was driven at a moderate rate of speed, and when 25 feet from the approaching car, the occupant deliberately turned the steering wheel and caused the car to go across the center line into a collision. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence. The Court said that a driver is not required at his peril to comply with the demands of his guest passenger, nor does noncompliance in and of itself constitute evidence of gross negligence.

Sec. 35. Defendant Asleep When Accident Occurred. 

Perkins v. Roberts, 272 Mich. 545.

Defendant feeling drowsy stopped his car, got out and walked about, smoked a cigarette and feeling refreshed continued driving. He testified that he fell asleep without warning and awakened to find his car on the wrong side of the road, and just about to collide with an ap- 88

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 35 proaching car. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence, and the Court said: "A driver overcome by sleep is not guilty of wanton or wilful misconduct unless it appears that he continued to drive in reckless disregard of premonitory symptoms. 

Also see Malicote v. DeBondt, 281 Mich. 650. 

Wismer v. Marx, 289 Mich. 38.

Plaintiff as a guest started on a trip with defendant at 2 a. m. Plaintiff claimed that a short time before the accident defendant fell asleep at the wheel and that an accident was averted by her arousing him. It was claimed that by continuing to drive and falling asleep again, which resulted in the accident, he was guilty of gross negligence. Defendant had worked from 3 p. m. to 11 p. m. She testified that on the first occasion when he fell asleep and was awakened by plaintiff's shout, she suggested that if he was sleepy to let her drive or park the car and take a nap. He answered that he was not then sleepy, and that if he got sleepy he would stop and park. Plaintiff believed him. The accident occurred 3 or 4 miles further along. It was held that there was no evidence of gross negligence.  "Judging from the driver's expressed state of mind relative to his ability to continue to drive and plaintiff's acquiescence therein it cannot be found that his further driving constituted a conscious and reckless disregard of consequences to plaintiff..The case stands apart from instances where danger was recognized by a guest, called to the attention of the driver, protest made, request for discontinuance or right to leave the vehicle refused, and the anticipated result by reason of the continued recklessness of the driver has been realized, and a wilful and wanton disregard of consequences can be found." 89

Nasser v. Kalush, 298 Mich. 133.

In this guest case, the question was whether the de fendant was grossly negligent in falling asleep at the wheel. It was held that he was not. No circumstances were shown which would cause a reasonably prudent person to anticipate falling asleep.

Sec. 37. Cases in Which Plaintiff Recovered. 

Schneider v. Draper, 276 Mich. 259.

The defendant was driving high school students to a football practice in Saginaw. There were four in the car and two boys on the right running board. Defendant zigzagged his car from curb to curb at a speed of 45 miles per hour. He was headed for a pole and did not turn until 15 feet away which was too late. The weight of the boys on the running board made the tire scrape the fender and interfered with the steering. In holding that there was evidence of gross negligence the Court said: "While Draper's actual intention whether to dislodge or frighten the boys on the running board or otherwise, would bear upon his intention and its .wantonness, plaintiff was not obliged to point out what was actually in his mind.” "But if Draper drove his car at a speed of 45 miles per hour, more than twice the legal limit, dodged close to a parked car, zigzagged back and forth across the street and ran directly at the pole and closer than he ought to in the course of careful driving be- 90

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 37 fore he attempted to turn, and if he did all these things intentionally, his conduct justified a finding that he was guilty of wilful and wanton misconduct if, indeed, it would not so convict him as matter of law." 

Lucas v. Lindner, 276 Mich. 704.

Defendant's car had gone off the road at a right angled turn. Plaintiff refused to go on with defendant until he promised to drive slower. On the return trip plaintiff warned defendant that they were approaching a right angled turn. Defendant continued to drive at a speed of 

45 to 50 miles per hour over a hill and ran off the road at the curve which was 150 feet beyond. The road was slippery and soft. In a five to three decision it was held that there was evidence of gross negligence. 

Wolfe v. Marks, 277 Mich. 154.

Plaintiff testified that while the car was traveling 50 miles per hour she smelled a strong odor of burning rubber and the defendant said it was the boot in the tire. 

Against the protests of the occupants the defendant increased his speed instead of stopping and a rear tire blew out, upsetting the car. The blowout was where the boot was in the tire. In holding that this testimony created an issue of fact as to gross negligence the Court said: "Whether friction of a boot in a rear tire would occasion an odor perceptible to passengers in the car, under a speed of 50 miles per hour, was a question of fact for the jury." "Defendant knew he had a boot in the left rear tire; his attention was called to the burning rubber; he sensed that it was occasioned by the boot; he was requested to have it looked to, or to slow speed, or 91

§ 

let the plaintiff and her husband out, and his driving at a high rate of speed under such circumstances was in reckless disregard of easily apprehended consequences and constituted wilful and wanton misconduct." 

Thomas v. Parsons, 278 Mich. 276.

The defendant drove his car on a gravel road 50 to 60 miles per hour over a bridge which caused the car to bound to the side of the road. He approached a second bridge 70 to 75 miles per hour and bounded to the side again. The occupants asked him to slow down. The road became narrow and rough. The car jumped over the road and nearly went into a ditch. Defendant waited until he was within 100 feet of a car ahead and then swung to the left and lost control of his car. Defendant after the accident said that he was trying to scare the passengers in his car and the car ahead. In holding that there was evidence of gross negligence the Court emphasized the roughness of the road, the continued negligence, and the mental attitude of the defendant. 

Malicote v. DeBondt, 281 Mich. 650.

The defendant went to sleep while driving. He refused to allow the plaintiff to get out of the car and after driving a few blocks he fell asleep again and the car struck a safety zone post. The Court said that there was evidence of gross negligence, citing Manser v. Eder, 263 

Mich. 107.

Sec. 38. Doctrine of Assumed Risk. 

Schneider v. Draper, 276 Mich. 259.

In commenting on the question of assumed risk, the 

Court said: "It is not necessary to determine whether the boys on the running board assumed the risk of Draper's ordinary negligence. No authorities are cited nor reasons advanced to indicate that guests, licensees or even trespassers assume the risk of wilful and wanton misconduct toward them after their presence is discovered." 

Sec. 39. 

Whether Plaintiff Is a Guest. 

Riley v. Walters, 277 Mich. 620.

In this case the Court held that plaintiff was a guest, saying that the young men were skylarking trying to find a friend, and that although defendant had asked plaintiff to get back into the car to help find the friend, he was still a guest. 

Langford v. Rogers, 278 Mich. 310.

It was held in this case that the plaintiff's decedent was a guest of the defendant although he was riding on a toboggan towed by defendant's automobile.  "So long as the party transported accepts the hospitality of the owner or driver, or is carried or 95

§ 39] 

transported by reason of an implied invitation of such owner or operator of the motor vehicle, as in this case, for his own entertainment, pleasure and enjoyment, without compensating the owner of the vehicle, he is a guest within the meaning of the statute." 

Pietrantonio v. Tonn's Estate, 278 Mich. 535.

It was plaintiff's claim that the defendant was demonstrating the car to him for the purpose of selling it to the plaintiff and that the guest statute did not apply. Judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 

Ravey v. Healy, 279 Mich. 323.

Defendant ordered plaintiff to get off the running board of his car. She hid herself from his sight but stayed on. The Court said that she was not a guest. It was held that there was no evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. It was held that there was no duty on the part of the defendant to make sure that plaintiff was not on the running board. 

Cardinal v. Reinecke, 280 Mich. 15.

Plaintiff operated a school of beauty culture. Defendant's daughter, a graduate of the school, had a possible opening at Harbor Beach. Defendant asked plaintiff to go with her daughter. It was held that plaintiff was not a guest. She went on the trip not of her own volition but to render a service to the defendant and her daughter. 

Peronto v. Cootware, 281 Mich. 664.

Plaintiff was the mother of Clarence and Leslie Cootware. Clarence asked Leslie to drive their mother to his home to care for his sick wife and to tell her that she 96

[$ 39 would be paid for services. On the trip she was injured.

It was held that plaintiff was not a guest as she was not making the trip for her own pleasure but in order to render a service to Clarence. Judgment against Leslie was affirmed. 

Plaintiff's decedent was an instructor in a 4-H Club supervised by defendant. There was testimony that defendant was driving plaintiff back to her home from the camp, and that the transportation was part of the consideration of the contract of hire. It was held that a question of fact was raised as to whether plaintiff was a guest. Judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 

Thomas v. Currier Lumber Co., 283 Mich. 134.

In this case plaintiff was contemplating buying material from the defendant. He was riding with defendant's salesman to defendant's place of business to discuss terms when the accident occurred. In holding that the plaintiff was not a guest, the Court said: "It would not be necessary, in holding that plaintiff was not a gratuitous guest passenger, to find that a cash payment was made by him for his transportation. It is sufficient if a benefit accrued by reason of such transportation." 

Steudle v. Yellow & Checker Cab & Transfer Co., 287 

Mich. 1.

In this case the question was whether plaintiff was a passenger for hire in a taxicab or was a guest. It was held that the evidence presented a question of fact for the jury. 

See Salewsky v. Wright, 291 Mich. 587; Wood v. Merchants Ins. Co., 291 Mich. 573. 97

§ 39] 

Brown v. Wood, 293 Mich. 148.

Plaintiff, a minor occupant of defendant's automobile, paid to defendant, also a minor, 75 cents per week for riding with him to school. It was found that defendant was guilty of ordinary negligence. In the declaration it was alleged that the injured minor was a passenger for hire. It was held that plaintiff could not recover. The 

Court said that the infant's contract was voidable, and as a general rule if the tort with which an infant is charged is so connected with his contract that a commission of a tort constitutes a breach of. the contract, then since the infant is not liable upon the contract, he cannot be liable for his tort. The tort could not be separated from the contractual relationship. Through his guardian at the trial the minor defendant disaffirmed any contract of carrying for hire. 

In re Harper's Estate, 294 Mich. 453.

Defendant and plaintiff were close friends. Defendant agreed to accompany plaintiff to a football game if plaintiff would help with the driving on a trip the next day.

The accident occurred the next day while defendant was driving. It was held that plaintiff was a guest. The 

Court said: "The proffer of assistance in driving was only a friendly gesture, and the sociability element was the dominant, if not sole, thought." 

Guiney v. Osborn, 295 Mich. 559.

The question here was whether plaintiff was a passenger for hire. Defendant drove the decedent from Trenton to Detroit occasionally. The decedent purchased gasoline and sometimes gave defendant gifts. It was held that there was no contract for hire.  98

[§ 39 "Gratuitous purchase of gasoline did not constitute the transportation one for hire or change the relation from that of gratuitous guests." 

Bushouse v. Brom, 297 Mich. 616. 

Defendant and her mother, contemplating a motor trip to Florida, invited plaintiff, a friend, to go with them. 

Up to the time of the accident plaintiff had paid slightly more than one-third of the expenses. Nothing definite had been decided as to the percentage which she would contribute. It was held that the plaintiff was a guest. 

The Court said that friendship and social relation motivated the undertaking. 

Shpakow v. Brown, 300 Mich. 678.

This case was tried without a jury. There was a question as to whether plaintiff accompanied defendant to give him advice concerning the value of a horse. The trial judge decided for the defendant. This judgment was affirmed, and the Court said that in the absence of a finding of fact, it must be assumed that every finding of fact was made which was necessary to support the judgment. There was sufficient evidence to support the finding that plaintiff was a guest. 

Baker v. Costello, 300 Mich. 686. 

Plaintiff was riding with defendant when injured. The declaration alleged ordinary negligence and that plaintiff was not a guest. This was denied by defendant's answer. Plaintiff offered no proof that plaintiff was not a guest. Defendant produced no proof. A verdict directed for defendant. This was affirmed. The

Everett v. Burg, 301 Mich. 734.

Six fellow employees arranged for daily transportation to their place of employment. By agreement each was to use his car for one week. One of the occupants was killed in an accident. The sole question was whether decedent was a guest, a passenger for hire, or engaged in a joint enterprise. It was held that he was a guest passenger. The Court said that it was simply the exchange of amenities between fellow employees. 

Anderson v. Conterio, 303 Mich. 75.

Plaintiff contended that the defendant was demonstrating the car for the purpose of making a sale and that he was not a guest. It was held that the testimony presented a question of fact. 

Brown v. Arnold, 303 Mich. 616.

Plaintiff was a guest in defendant's automobile and alighted from the car in front of her home. Plaintiff got out of the car, closed the door and took a step or two, and while in the gutter of the street was struck by the rear fender of the car, which skidded sideways as it was started. Plaintiff accompanied defendant on a motor trip from

Against Public Policy. 

Eskovitz v. Berger, 276 Mich. 536.

This accident occurred in Ohio in 1932 when there was no guest statute in effect in Ohio. The defendant contended that it was against the public policy of the state 100

[$40 of Michigan to permit actions by guests for ordinary negligence. It was held that it was not contrary to the public policy of the state. 

Sec. 39-b (New). Action for Loss of Services. 

Arritt v. Fisher, 286 Mich. 419.

The plaintiff in this case was the husband of a guest passenger of the defendant. It was admitted that there was no gross negligence. The Court held that the husband's right to recover depended upon his wife's right to recos.

Sec. 39-c (New). Abolition of Right of Action as Against Public Policy. 

Kaiser v. North, 292 Mich. 49.

Plaintiff was a guest of defendant and was injured in an accident in Ontario, Canada. An Ontario statute provided that in such situation plaintiff had no right of action against defendant. It was held that plaintiff could not recover; that the validity of the Ontario statute was not tested by the constitutional or statutory law of Michigan, and that the statute of the foreign jurisdiction did not contravene public policy here.

Sec. 40. Summary of Cases Under the Guest Statute. 

The decisions handed down in the last 10 years interpreting the so-called guest statute have placed the court in practical agreement that there is little difference in the meaning of "gross negligence" and "wilful and wanton misconduct" as the phrases are used in the statute. 

1. Meaning of gross negligence-It is impossible to find a satisfactory definition of the term gross negligence. By studying the facts of each case we can come to a definite conclusion as to what is not gross negli- 101

$40] 

gence. To merely drive a car too fast to hold the car on a curve is not sufficient, even though there were protests by the passengers. In driving onto the wrong side of the highway to pass another car the driver is not guilty of gross negligence int ordinary situation.

Failure to stop for a signal light or a stop sign may not be sufficient evidence. The plaintiff cannot recover by proving that the defendant could not stop within the assured clear distance. The Court has said that intoxication is not necessarily evidence sufficient to establish a case. To go to sleep at the wheel may not be gross negligence. 

What then is gross negligence? By studying the decisions under Sec. 37, one can discern a certain pattern of facts. In these cases the driver was very negligent over an extended period of driving. Accidents were. narrowly averted and yet the driver continued his reckless driving over the protests of the passengers. In most of the cases his frame of mind was ugly and he showed no desire to change his driving conduct. Finally, while still negligent, he has his accident. 

When is the plaintiff a guest-If the plaintiff is in the car for the purpose of business, or is rendering a service or benefit to the driver or owner, he is probably not a guest. If the driver and the plaintiff are sharing their cars in going to work, the plaintiff is a guest. If an adult is paying for the ride, and the payment is not toward expenses or merely incidental, he is not a guest. 

However, if the driver is a minor, the occupant will still be considered a guest though he pays for the ride, if the minor disaffirmed the contract. 293 Mich. 148.

Where there is a question concerning the payment being toward the expenses or merely incidental to a pleasure trip, see 294 Mich. 453; 295 Mich. 559; 297 Mich. 

616; 308 Mich. 234. 102

CHAPTER IV  Sec. 41. Ordinary Crossing Cases. 

McParlan v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 273 Mich. bobl 527. 

A minor occupant of an automobile which collided with defendant's train brought suit. The automobile was being driven on an icy street in Muskegon. The wind- 

Ishield was frosted. The driver testified that he was proceeding at a speed of 25 miles per hour; that he could see 50 to 70 feet ahead but did not see the train ahead of him until he was 25 feet from it. Over objection, testimony was introduced of two other similar accidents at the crossing in an attempt to prove that the street lighting blinded the drivers and created a special condition which placed a duty on the defendant to maintain special safeguards. Defendant introduced photographs and testimony to prove that one had a clear vision of objects 150 feet ahead. The Court held that plaintiff did not meet, by any evidence, defendant's testimony which indicated sufficient view to a careful driver to obviate the necessity for special protective devices. 

Proctor v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 273 Mich. 619.

In this case the plaintiff stopped his car at night 25 feet from the first track and looked to his right and saw nothing. He then started forward and was just crossing the second track when he saw a small white light and his car was struck an instant later. It was held that he was negligent in not stopping and making a proper observation before crossing the second track. 103

Rybarczyk v. New York Central Rd. Co., 276 Mich. 131.

In this case plaintiff testified that while driving west at 15 miles per hour he slowed to seven or eight miles per hour and looked to the south. He could see for 

275 feet but he testified that the train was not in sight. 

He looked to the north and again to the south, and saw the engine 125 feet south. He was then 25 feet from the track and when he applied his brakes his car skidded into the side of the engine. In holding the plaintiff guilty of negligence as a matter of law, the Court said that the physical facts did not square with the plaintiff's testimony. 

Simpson v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 276 Mich. 653.

The plaintiff was a minor occupant of an automobile, which collided with a railroad car, which had been standing on the crossing for more than five minutes in violation of a statute. It was held that the violation of the statute was not the proximate cause of the accident.

Mallory v. Pitcairn, 307 Mich. 40.

Defendant's engine and tender with three freight cars were being backed across a street at night. Plaintiff approached the crossing at a speed of 40 to 50 miles per hour. He had a clear view of the crossing and the train as it approached. Plaintiff, by reason of his injuries, had no recollection of the facts of the accident. The judgment for the defendant was affirmed on the ground of negligence of the plaintiff. 

Ortynski v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 307 Mich. 61.

Plaintiff's truck was being driven across a spur track at a speed of 10 miles per hour. The driver's view was obstructed by a trailer. When a few feet from the track he saw a Diesel locomotive coming out of the yard of the Chevrolet plant. Plaintiff testified that it had no headlight burning and no bell sounding. A collision resulted. 

It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. His contributory negligence was a jury question. There was no duty to stop at the crossing and look. 

Stuive v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 311 Mich. 143.

This accident occurred in the country on a clear day. 

Plaintiff was driving east and was crossing two tracks. 

When his car was 29 feet from the first track he had reduced his speed to 10 miles per hour. He looked to the right where he could see 250 feet. He then looked 106

SUPPLEMENT 

[$42 to the left, and when he next looked to the right he saw the train moving north on the west track. He heard no bell or whistle, although he listened for the noise of a train. He was too close to stop. It was held that plaintiff's negligence was a question of fact. 

Wiles v. New York Central Rd. Co., 311 Mich. 540.

At an unprotected railway crossing a number of freight cars were backed toward the crossing and then detached from the locomotive, coasting across the heavily traveled highway. It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the railroad, there being no flagman or warning signal.

Sec. 42. Summary of Ordinary Crossing Cases. 

Recent cases in this group have tended toward a more lenient attitude concerning plaintiff's duties. In 311 

Mich. 143, the Court seems to have decreased the duties. of an automobile driver in proceeding across a railway crossing in the country. It is difficult to reconcile this decision with many prior decisions. In 306 Mich. 95, the Court held that the 1921 statute, regulating the speed of a motor vehicle approaching a railroad crossing, had been repealed by the adoption of the Uniform Motor Vehicle Act. The Court will often permit the plaintiff's case to go to a jury where the train is being backed across the highway without lights. 301 Mich. 383; 306 

Mich. 246; 311 Mich. 540. Where the train is on a spur track across a city street at night, the case may go to a jury. 307 Mich. 61. For a case in which plaintiff attempted to prove a special condition, requiring the defendant to maintain special safeguards, see 273 Mich. 527. 107

§ 43] 

 Sec. 43. Protected Crossings. 

Lockett v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 272 Mich. 219.

Plaintiff testified that in the daytime she stopped her car a few feet from the first of five tracks and noticed that the signal lights were not flashing. Her view to the north was obstructed by a board fence. She started across, making no further observation and her car was struck on the fourth track. She had a clear view to the north after crossing the first track. In holding the plaintiff guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law the Court said: "She was then in a zone of safety for a distance of 37.5 feet, in which her view was totally unobstructed. She was no longer in a position to be warned by the signal lights. They were already in back of her and out of her sight. But she could have observed the approaching locomotive by the use of her own senses and we believe that her failure to look while traversing this zone of safety constituted contributory negligence as a matter of law.” 

Esterline v. Kennicott, 277 Mich. 130.

The plaintiff was a minor occupant of a car which struck a box car in a freight train. Plaintiff contended that because the wigwag signal was hidden by the box car from the sight of the driver a trap was created. It was held that after the train occupied the crossing, the purpose of the signal was ended, and that consequently plaintiff could not recover. 

Hart v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 278 Mich. 343.

In this case the defendant's witnesses testified that the locomotive bell was ringing and lanterns were swung at the crossing. The plaintiff gave negative testimony. 

He did not know that he was approaching a crossing. It 108

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 43 was held that there was no evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. 

Momany v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 282 Mich. 168.

The plaintiff contended that defendant was negligent in not operating the gates during the night. It was held that the crossing was not extra hazardous to the extent of making the railroad liable for not providing additional signals or operating the gates twenty-four hours. 

Spenclay v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 285 Mich. 421.

Plaintiff was driving across an 8-track crossing when struck by an unlighted freight car, which was being backed. There were warning signals at the crossing which were not functioning. Plaintiff had stopped before crossing the first track, and he testified that he continued to look for trains as he crossed. It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law. 

Cartwright v. Grand Trunk Western Railroad, 288 Mich. 316.

Plaintiff was driving his car across a railway crossing in Grand Rapids. It was claimed that a dense fog limited visibility to 100 feet. An order of the Public Utilities Commission required the crossing to be guarded. 

The defendant's testimony showed that a member of the train crew was at the crossing with a lantern. Plaintiff denied this. It was held that a question of fact was made out. The jury brought in a verdict for the defendant, and judgment was affirmed. 

Perch v. New York Central Rd. Co., 294 Mich. 227.

Plaintiff's decedent was in an automobile, which was standing at a crossing protected by gates which were 109

§ 43] 

down, when it was struck from the rear by another automobile and was hurled out onto the tracks. Defendant's locomotive struck the automobile 12 seconds later. The accident occurred at night and it was admitted that the headlight of the locomotive, because of a curve, would not focus on the crossing until it was too late. It was held that a question of fact was not presented as to whether defendant's negligence was a proximate cause of the collision. There was evidence that defendant's train was exceeding the speed limit set by the city ordinance. 

See Barnett v. New York Central Rd. Co., 295 Mich. 536. 

Benaway v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 296 Mich. 1.

Plaintiff contended that the flasher light signals were not working. The decedent was familiar with the crossing. The Court said that it was obvious that if the decedent had looked and listened, he would have seen the train in time to stop. Although he was entitled to place some reliance upon the automatic signal, he was bound to use some care. 

Jones v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 303 Mich. 114.

Plaintiff's decedent was driving his car in a westerly direction on McNichols Road in Wayne County. He approached the five-track crossing at a speed of 20 miles per hour and was struck by the train coming from the southwest. There was testimony that the train was traveling at a high rate of speed; that the whistle was not blown until close to the crossing, and that the warning signals at the crossing were not working. The decedent's view was blocked until he reached a point 39 feet from the track. A registered engineer testified that at 20 miles per hour decedent could not have stopped be- 110

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 44 fore reaching the track from the point where he could have seen the train. It was held that the decedent was not negligent as a matter of law in approaching the crossing at a speed of 20 miles per hour. 

Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co. v. Lovejoy, 304 Mich. 35. 

Defendant Lovejoy drove his car onto the track, and upon seeing the train approaching, attempted to back but was struck from the rear by the other defendant's automobile. Judgment against all of the defendants was affirmed. There were flasher lights and a one-lane gate arm at the crossing. There was testimony that three minutes elapsed between the collision of the cars and that of the train and Lovejoy's auto. The Court held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of each defendant, which was a proximate cause of the accident. 

Silanpa v. Thomson, 309 Mich. 326.

Plaintiff was driving west on a county road when his car came in contact with defendant's flat car which was being pushed in a northerly direction across the road. 

The rule and custom was for trains to stop at the road and a flagman was sent out to warn traffic. At the time of the accident there was no flagman present. The judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. The Court said that the crossing must be considered as a guarded crossing. 

Plaintiff's negligence was a question of fact.

Sec. 44. Summary of Protected Crossing Cases. 

Where the crossing is protected by warning signals which are not working, the driver is not negligent as a matter of law in approaching the crossing at a speed of 

20 miles per hour, although the view is obstructed. 303 

Mich. 114. Where there is a duty to have a flagman, the crossing must be considered as a guarded crossing. The 111

$45] 

rule of the railroad may require a flagman to warn traffic in certain instances. 309 Mich. 326. There may be no duty to operate gates at night. 282 Mich. 168. · Although the flasher lights are not operating, there is a duty to make observation. 296 Mich. 1. Where there are several tracks to cross, there is a duty to look while crossing, although the lights were not flashing. 272 

Mich. 219; 285 Mich. 421. Negative testimony is not sufficient to overcome the testimony of witnesses that lanterns were swung at the crossing, 278 Mich. 343.

Sec. 45. Automobiles Stalled on Track. 

Young v. Detroit Terminal Rd. Co., 287 Mich. 120.

Plaintiff was held negligent in not getting out of the car which was stalled on the tracks with a train approaching, even though the train was moving slowly and appeared to be slowing down when some distance away. 

Goldman v. Grand Trunk Western Ry. Co., 287 Mich. 289.

Plaintiff's car stalled on the railroad track at night. 

The testimony showed that the car was on the track for several minutes, and that the headlight of the locomotive could have been seen by the plaintiff more than onequarter mile from the crossing. In holding the plaintiff guilty of contributory negligence, the Court said that she failed to remove herself from a place of peril when she had an opportunity, in the exercise of reasonable care, to do so. 

It was held that the owner of the automobile could recover for its damage. 

Perch v. New York Central Rd. Co., 294 Mich. 227.

Plaintiff's decedent was in an automobile stopped at the railroad crossing. The car was struck from the rear and thrown onto the track when the train was 800 feet 112

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 46 away. Neither the engineer nor the fireman saw the car until the impact occurred. The train was traveling over 45 miles per hour, the speed limit being 30 miles per hour under the city ordinance. It was held that the negligence of the railroad was a proximate cause of the injuries. 

Carlson v. Grand Trunk Western Rd. Co., 308 Mich. 531.

Plaintiff was driving his car across five tracks in traffic. Traffic stopped and plaintiff was forced to bring his car to a stop on one of the tracks. A freight train was approaching on this track. Five occupants of the car observed the locomotive headlight and heard the whistle and alighted from the car, escaping injury. Plaintiff did not alight. He was held negligent as a matter of law. 

Sec. 46. Street Railway Crossing Cases. 

See Manoogian v. City of Detroit, 284 Mich. 432. 

Booth v. City of Detroit, 292 Mich. 102.

Plaintiff's automobile was being driven in a westerly direction on Grand River Avenue in Detroit. The east and west bound traffic lanes were divided by a center strip on which were located defendant's car tracks. Defendant's street car going west started to cross the west bound lanes at a point a short distance east of the Seven Mile Road. The street car was not stopped before turning. Plaintiff was driving at a speed of 40 miles per hour, the speed limit being 45 miles per hour. The physical facts indicated that the impact occurred almost instantly after the street car started its turn. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Secrist v. City of Detroit, 299 Mich. 393.

Plaintiff was making a left or U-turn in the middle of the block and was struck by the street car which was ap- 113

§ 48] 

proaching him. Plaintiff claimed that he was trapped and was forced to stop on the track. It was held that a question of fact was made out. 

Wilson v. City of Detroit, 299 Mich. 473.

Plaintiff, while driving east on Warren Avenue in Detroit, was struck by defendant's southbound street car. 

Plaintiff, on cross-examination, testified that after entering the intersection he looked once more to the north and saw the street car in motion. This was inconsistent with his testimony on direct examination and was contradicted on redirect examination. The Court held that it was for the jury to decide what testimony was the truth, and that a question of fact had been presented concerning plaintiff's negligence. 

Miller v. City of Detroit, 308 Mich. 611.

In this case plaintiff was held negligent in driving his car into the path of the street car which approached the intersection at a speed of 30 to 35 miles per hour.

CHAPTER V WRONG SIDE OF ROAD CASES Sec. 48. Wrong Side of Road Cases. 

Paton v. Stealy, 272 Mich. 57.

Defendant contended that he skidded to the wrong side of the road and that he was faced with an emergency in trying to avoid a pedestrian. It was held that the defendant turned to the left of his own volition and that he was not faced with an emergency inasmuch as he had time to stop. 114

SUPPLEMENT 

[$ 48 

Warwick v. Blackney, 272 Mich. 231. he Defendant was driving south in congested traffic on the east side of the road. Other cars ahead were also being driven on the wrong side. The Court said that the rules of the road are not abrogated by reason of congested traffic or unusual crowds in the absence of police officers ding traffic. In holding that there was no evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant, the Court said that defendant could not turn out of the lane of traffic because of the cars about him. 

Rosen v. Beh, 272 Mich. 487. 

Defendant, while driving his car west on a gravel road, turned to the south side of the highway to pass a parked car and trailer which occupied the north half. 

"It cannot be held, as appellant contends, that since the driver of the Ford automobile was proceeding on his left-hand side of the highway he was guilty of negligence as a matter of law. He had a right in passing the parked car and trailer to veer to his left and drive on the southerly or left-hand part of the traveled portion of the highway providing he exercised reasonable care in so doing." 

The plaintiff while riding a horse was injured when the automobile collided with the horse. The trial judge found no negligence on the part of the defendant and this was affirmed. 

Patterson v. Thatcher, 273 Mich. 597.

Plaintiff claimed that defendant drove his car onto the wrong side of the road and into the car which her husband was driving. Plaintiff's husband gave no testimony claiming loss of memory. Defendant and his two companions, the testimony of disinterested wit- 115

§ 48] 

nesses, the location of wheel and skid marks and the testimony of the plaintiff's statements at the scene of the accident refuted plaintiff's testimony. A judgment for the plaintiff was reversed and a new trial granted. 

Harding v. Blankenship, 274 Mich. 118.

A minor occupant of an automobile brought suit against the driver of the other automobile for injuries sustained in a head-on collision at or near the south end of a narrow bridge. Defendant's car was driven south. Plaintiff's car was on the left side of the road after the accident. There was testimony that tracks on the tarvia showed that plaintiff's car crossed from the right to the left side. Glass was found on each side of the road. There was testimony that defendant was driving at a speed of 70 miles per hour. In affirming the judgment for the plaintiff the Court said that there was evidence of negligence on the part of defendant in driving onto a narrow bridge at a high rate of speed, especially since the pavement was damp, and that there was evidence of proximate cause.  "The driver of plaintiff's car naturally was confronted with a sudden peril and the law makes allowances for fright and lack of coolness and judgment under such circumstances." 

Lindenfeld v. Michigan Interstate Truck Co., 274 Mich. 681. 

The driver of plaintiff's car testified that he was driving west on an icy pavement at a speed of 30 miles per hour. In reaching the crest of a hill he saw a truck and trailers 200 feet away approaching on the proper side of the road. When 100 feet from this truck defendant's eastbound truck turned onto the north half of the road to pass the truck and a collision resulted. The Court 116

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 48 held that plaintiff's testimony presented a question of fact and said that a driver, upon being confronted by an unexpected danger, is not required to be able to stop within 100 feet on a slippery downgrade pavement. 

Spillman v. Weimaster, 275 Mich. 93.

In this case plaintiff contended that defendant's truck was driven at an excessive rate of speed and onto the wrong side of the road. Judgment for the plaintiff was reversed and a new trial ordered because the trial Court instructed the jury that defendant's truck was restricted to 20 miles per hour by Comp. Laws 1929, Section 

4700 (b), Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1568 (b). This was in error as Act No. 253, Pub. Acts 1933, permitted a speed of 35 miles per hour for defendant's truck. The statutes being in conflict, the later one superseded the former. It was also held that defendant's truck was not a "slow moving vehicle" under Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4703, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1571.

Essmeister v. Roadway Transit Co., 275 Mich. 387. 

In this case it was held that the physical facts were sufficient to make out a question of fact concerning defendant's negligence. Both tractors were off the south portion of the highway facing in a southerly direction. 

The trailers were on the north half each headed the way they were traveling, the plaintiff's west and the defendant's east. Testimony was given that the marks on the pavement were on the north side until they came together. 

Brodie v. City of Detroit, 275 Mich. 626.

Defendant's bus was being driven south past another southbound bus when it struck the plaintiff. It was held that there was no duty on the part of the bus driver not to 117.

§ 48] 

drive on the left side of the street in passing the other bus. 

Bates v. Franson, 276 Mich. 79.

Plaintiff and defendant each contended that he was on the right side of the road. It was held that a question of fact was presented and that the physical facts did not show where the impact took place. 

Bowman v. Struble, 276 Mich. 311.

Defendant's truck and trailer were being driven up a grade in a northerly direction. The pavement was icy. 

As plaintiff's southbound car was passing the trucktrailer, it jackknifed across the highway into the path of plaintiff's car. It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant as the testimony showed that the truck-trailer had started backwards and the steering wheel must have been turned the wrong way. 

Hickey v. Smith, 277 Mich. 123.

Plaintiff testified that at night he turned his car to the left to avoid a horse and brought his car to a stop on the wrong side of the road. He claimed that it was stopped for ten to twenty seconds before struck by defendant's approaching car. It was held that plaintiff had as much opportunity to avoid the accident as defendant. 

It was the duty of plaintiff to remove his car from its dangerous location. 

DeForest v. Soules, 278 Mich. 557.

Defendant claimed that in driving his truck down a hill, the trailer jackknifed at a curve because of the unusually slippery condition of the road, and that this presented an emergency. In granting a new trial the Court said that defendant was entitled to an instruction that when an 118

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 48 automobile unexpectedly skids upon a slippery road through no fault of the driver, who does not know or has no reason to anticipate the danger, he may be excused from failure to comply with the statutes requiring a driver to keep to the right side of the road. 

Zullo v. Detroit Creamery Co., 281 Mich. 678.

Plaintiff and defendant each contended that he was on the right side of the road. The Court said that the testimony presented no issue of contributory negligence.

Plaintiff was granted a new trial because the trial Court did not give definite instructions upon the duty of the defendant and did charge upon defendant's claim of contributory negligence. 

Rollin v. Van Tine, 283 Mich. 208.

Each driver admitted that when the front end of the cars were opposite each other, each was on the proper side of the road. The defendant claimed that the rear end of plaintiff's car slued across the center line. The plaintiff claimed that the defendant turned to the left into his car as they were passing. One witness testified that the plaintiff's car left marks in the slush showing it went across the center line. The majority of the Court affirmed the judgment for plaintiff found by the trial judge without a jury. 

Odell v. Powers, 284 Mich. 201. 

Plaintiff testified that he was driving north on M-78. 

He saw a snow plow approaching throwing a cloud of snow across the east half of the road. He slowed to 15 miles per hour. After passing through the cloud of snow, plaintiff saw defendant's car coming toward him and but 10 or 15 feet away. It was held that a question of fact was presented. Judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 119

§ 48] 

Guye v. Domas, 284 Mich. 654.

Plaintiff testified that he was driving west at night at a speed of 40 miles per hour. The defendant's car was being driven in an easterly direction. Plaintiff did not see the approaching car and did not testify as to the position of his own car when the collision occurred. The 

Court said: "The failure of plaintiff to show that he was on the proper side of the highway when the accident occurred precludes recovery." 

Triestram v. Way, 286 Mich. 13. 

According to plaintiff's version of the accident, he first observed defendant's car approaching at least one-half mile away. As it approached it gradually crossed the center line and turned on to the plaintiff's side of the road until it reached the edge. The plaintiff continued to. watch defendant's car, and when the cars were 60 to 80 feet apart he turned his car sharply to the left. The defendant swerved his car back toward the center line and the cars collided. It was held that the plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law, there being evidence that the plaintiff was confronted with an emergency. 

Whether he should have slowed down or stopped was a question for the jury. 

Haney v. Beisel, 287 Mich. 239.

Plaintiff's car overtook a horse drawn wagon. The driver slowed down and applied his brakes. A patch of ice caused the car to skid to the left. On seeing defendant's car approaching, plaintiff's driver turned onto the shoulder and proceeded westerly on the south shoulder. 

The defendant instead of continuing on the pavement turned to the right onto the south shoulder, and the cars collided. It was held that plaintiff was negligent as a 120

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 48 matter of law. The Court said that plaintiff's driver was not faced with an emergency at the time of the collision as he increased his speed on the wrong side of the road, and deliberately assumed the burden of his decision. 

Patterson v. Jacobs, 289 Mich. 351.

Plaintiff's decedent was driving her car south on a street in Sault Ste. Marie. Defendant's car struck decedent's automobile headon, the impact occurring on the west half of the street. Defendant contended that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. It was held that she was not. The court said that the physical facts showed that decedent was operating her car on the proper side of the street. The skid marks left by decedent's car were within 2 feet of the parked car which she was passing. The traveled portion of the street was 

30 feet in width. It was claimed that decedent was negligent in driving at a speed of 25 miles per hour and that she should have stopped upon seeing defendant on the wrong side of the street. The Court said that she would have had the right to assume that defendant would guide his car to the proper side of the highway. 

Morton v. Peterman, 291 Mich. 442.

Plaintiff's car was being driven in an easterly direction, when defendant, driving south, made a right turn across the center of the street colliding with plaintiff's automobile. The defendant contended that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law in not applying the brakes as hard as he could upon seeing defendant's car. In affirming the judgment for plaintiff the Court said: "Some allowance must be made for time required for the requisite mental and physical operations in the application of automobile brakes." 121

§ 48] 

 Quick v. Western Michigan Transportation Co., 294 

Mich. 402. 1 In this case there was a dispute as to whether decedent's truck or defendant's truck was on the wrong side of the street at the time of the impact. There was conflicting evidence on the location of debris on the street. 

Defendant's driver was not permitted to testify to certain facts on the ground that they were equally within the knowledge of the decedent. It was held that plaintiff made out a case for the jury. The Court said that the photographs showing the damage to the trucks were not completely persuasive of the claim of either party. 

It should be noted that a police officer testified concerning the location of tracks left by decedent's truck. 

Williams v. MacSim Bar Paper Co., 296 Mich. 214.

Defendant contended that the verdict for the plaintiff was against the great weight of the evidence because of the testimony of witnesses concerning marks on the highway. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed by an equally divided court. 

Barkman v. Montague, 297 Mich. 538.

Plaintiff's car was being driven in an easterly direction. To avoid a car which had stopped at an intersection ahead of plaintiff the driver of plaintiff's automobile turned the car to the left side of the highway and came to a stop partly off the shoulder at the north side of the pavement. Defendant's westbound auto left the pavement and struck plaintiff's car. It was held that plaintiff's contributory negligence was a question of fact. 

Gibbons v. Delta Contracting Co., 301 Mich. 638.

Plaintiff contended that defendant's truck was driven across the center line of the highway into his car, which 122

Defendant produced proof of admissions made by the plaintiff that he had turned to the left to enter a driveway. There was conflicting evidence concerning the physical facts. It was held that there was a question of fact and that the verdict was not contrary to the great weight of the evidence. 

Smith v. Maticka, 305 Mich. 32.

Plaintiff testified that defendant drove his car to the wrong side of road and that plaintiff turned to the left to avoid collision. The trial judge refused to give plaintiff's requested instruction on emergency.

Pembor v. Marcus, 307 Mich. 279.

Plaintiff testified that the collision occurred on her side of the road and that defendant's car dragged her car across the road to the far shoulder. Defendant testified that he pulled to the right on the north shoulder where the cars collided and were located after the accident. The Court held that there was a question of fact in spite of the position of the cars. 

Gleason v. Hanafin, 308 Mich. 31.

Defendant was driving north in the easterly lane of a three-lane highway. A southbound car was driven into this lane. The defendant's car then went across the center of the highway, colliding with plaintiff's car which was proceeding south in the westerly lane. Plaintiff testified that defendant was driving 60 to 70 miles per hour.

There was a conflict of testimony as to whether there was a collision between the defendant's 123

auto and the third car. It was held that there was a question for the jury. The lower court had entered a judgment for the defendant because of the answer to one of several special questions. Under the ruling of the court the verdict of the jury was held consistent with the answer. 

Leete v. Gould, 308 Mich. 345.

Plaintiff's car was driven into the east and west street from the north. Plaintiff turned to go west and was struck by defendant's car which was eastbound and on the north half of the street. Plaintiff testified that before starting into Geddes Avenue she looked to the west and the only vehicle in sight was a cement mixer several hundred feet to the west. She did not again make an observation. Defendant testified that the front of plaintiff's car was over the center line. This was denied by plaintiff. It was held that plaintiff's contributory negligence was a question for the jury. 

In re Olney's Estate, 309 Mich. 65.

The impact occurred on plaintiff's side of the road. 

The defense contended that the skid marks and physical facts demonstrated that the defendant turned to the left to avoid plaintiff's car. The judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 

Anderson v. Kearly, 312 Mich. 566.

Plaintiff's car was being driven east on a 20-foot road. 

Defendant's car was westbound. At the close of plaintiff's proofs, defendant moved for a directed verdict. 

Plaintiff proved that plaintiff's car was on the south side of the highway facing west. Defendant's car was on the south side with the front end on the shoulder and pointing south and the rear wheels near the south edge of the pavement. All of the debris, including radiator 124

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 49 fluid and oil, was on the south side. The left front of plaintiff's car and the right front of defendant's car were damaged. It was held that the physical facts established a prima facie case. Defendant's witness testified that the collision took place on the south side of the highway. However, the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. The Court said that the testimony of this witness was impeached by showing that he stated on three different occasions that he was not present when the collision occurred.

Sec. 49. Summary. 

In recent wrong side of the road cases evidence of physical facts often plays an important part. The physical facts may overweigh the testimony of one of the parties. 273 Mich. 597. Evidence concerning the location of the vehicles may be sufficient to make out a case. 

275 Mich. 387; 289 Mich. 351; 294 Mich. 402. In 307

Mich. 279, the plaintiff was allowed to recover in spite of strong physical facts to the contrary. In 312 Mich. 566, it was held that the physical facts established a prima facie case.

A driver may not be negligent in being on the wrong side in greatly congested traffic. 272 Mich. 231. The same would be true in passing a parked vehicle. 272 

Mich. 487.

Where a car is stopped on the wrong side of the road, and.the driver has time to remove his car from the dangerous location, it is his duty to do so. 277 Mich. 123. 

In 297 Mich. 538, the question of plaintiff's negligence in stopping on the wrong side was for the jury. 

The party may be entitled to an instruction on emergency where his car skids onto the wrong side, 278 Mich. 

557, or is turned to the left to avoid the other car. 305 

Mich. 32. 125

§ 51] 

For cases in which one party contended that he turned to the left to avoid a car approaching on his side, see 

286 Mich. 13; 301 Mich. 638; 305 Mich. 32; 309 Mich. 65.

It is difficult to get a ruling that a driver is negligent as a matter of law in not avoiding a car on the wrong side. 274 Mich. 681; 284 Mich. 201; 291 Mich. 442.

CHAPTER VI  Sec. 52-a (New). Overtaking Vehicle.. 

Sec. 51. Left Turn Against Approaching Vehicle. 

Brown v. Tanner, 281 Mich. 150.

Plaintiff was riding a bicycle north on a street in Lapeer at night. He collided with defendant's truck which was driven south and which made a short left turn in violation of the statute. The lower Court entered a judgment for the defendant notwithstanding the verdict because plaintiff failed to see defendant's car and because he had no light on the bicycle. It was held that plaintiff was not negligent as a matter of law in failing to see defendant's car making a short left turn. Whether the absence of a light was a proximate cause of the injury was a question of fact for the jury. The intersection was well lighted. 

Butler v. Jones, 282 Mich. 346.

Plaintiff was driving west on Fenkell Avenue in Detroit. He saw defendant's car approaching about 400 feet west of the intersection. Plaintiff slowed his car to five to ten miles per hour and made a left turn to go south. 126

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 51 When his car was near the south curb of Fenkell Avenue the collision occurred. Plaintiff did not look west again until an instant before the impact, his car traveling sixty feet from the time of the first observation. It was held that plaintiff was guilty of negligence. The Court said that assuming defendant was exceeding the speed limit, plaintiff was not excused from making further observation and had he made proper observation he could have stopped or increased his speed. 

Hartley v. Rodd Lumber Co., 282 Mich. 652.

Plaintiff contended that while driving south on U. S. 

23, the defendant approaching her turned directly across her path. Defendant's version was that he stopped his truck with the front wheels at the center line and plaintiff swerved to the left driving the truck to the east edge of the pavement. It was held that the photographs of the vehicles and the physical facts disproved plaintiff's theory. Judgment for the plaintiff was reversed and judgment was ordered for the defendant. 

Duffy v. Enright Topham Co., 282 Mich. 662.

In this case plaintiff was riding a bicycle south on Bond 

Street in Saginaw. The bicycle was not lighted. Defendant's taxicab was driven north on Bond Street and went to the left side of the street before reaching the intersection in order to make a left turn. The plaintiff testified that he thought the cab would be turned back to the right side of the street so he kept pedaling. A verdict was rendered for the defendant. It was held that the verdict was not contrary to the law and evidence. The 

Court pointed out that when the plaintiff observed the taxicab was coming over to the left-hand side of the street he must have known that a collision was inevitable unless he stopped or the cab was turned back. 127

§ 51] 

Thomas v. Currier Lumber Co., 283 Mich. 134.

The defendant's car, being driven in excess of the speed limit, struck an automobile which was turned out from the back of a truck and made a left turn in front of the defendant. The defendant claimed that the car turned out when he was only 30 feet from it, and consequently excessive speed was not a proximate cause. 

There was some testimony that the defendant was partly over the center line. The Court held that a question of fact was raised concerning the issue of proximate cause. 

Fitzcharles v. Mayer, 284 Mich. 122.

The appellant made a U-turn, having noticed the other defendant approaching at a speed of 60 miles per hour. 

The other defendant turned to the wrong side of the road to miss appellant's car and struck plaintiff's automobile. 

It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of appellant. It was pointed out that the other defendant was driving at a speed in violation of the law and appellant was aware of the speed. 

Pugh v. Butler, 291 Mich. 446.

Plaintiff, driving north on M-78, drove his car partially off the pavement on the right to let a car pass to the north. While stopped plaintiff saw defendant approaching, some 80 rods away. When defendant was 

1,000 feet away, plaintiff attempted to drive his car across the pavement into his driveway, but his motor stopped and the car stalled when half of it was off the pavement. At this time defendant's car was 300 feet north. It skidded a distance of 88 feet into plaintiff's auto. It was held that plaintiff's negligence was a question of fact for the jury. The Court said that there was room for a fair inference that no accident would have occurred had not plaintiff experienced unanticipated trouble with his motor. 128

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 51 

Lemieux v. Ondersma, 291 Mich. 469.

Plaintiff's car was being driven toward Grand Rapids from Detroit on U. S. 16. His driver made a left turn to leave the highway at an intersection. He could see for a distance of 2,000 feet. After his car had gone 60 feet on an angle, and when the front wheels were off the pavement, he saw defendant's car 10 feet away. In holding plaintiff negligent as a matter of law, the Court said that during the entire period in which plaintiff's car was angling to the left at 2 miles per hour, the driver made no observation to the west. The only observation he made was when he was still on the right hand side of the highway. One second after he made this observation, defendant's car continued within his range of vision for 2,000 feet. 

Sheathelm v. Consumers Power Co., 293 Mich. 422.

At night, plaintiff was in a car driven south on U. S. 

127. Intending to turn left at an intersection plaintiff's driver slowed to ten miles per hour, and noticed a car approaching and at a bridge which was over 1600 feet south. Plaintiff's car was turned to the left and was struck by the approaching car at a point on the east shoulder. Plaintiff's car had traveled 24 feet after defendant's automobile was seen. The Court said that defendant's car must have been much closer, and consequently defendant was entitled to a directed verdict. 

Routt v. Berridge, 294 Mich. 666. 

Defendant was driving a truck north on U. S. 131.

Plaintiff driving south turned left to go into a gasoline station and a collision resulted. The trial judge instructed the jury that it was for them to find whether plaintiff's failure to look while making a left turn was negligence or not. The jury found for the defendant and 129

§ 52] 

plaintiff appealed. It was held that there was no error in the instruction. The Court also held that the subsequent negligence doctrine was not involved. 

Suarez v. Katon, 299 Mich. 38.

Plaintiff was driving his single seated motorcycle west on East Michigan Avenue in Ypsilanti at night. Defendant, driving east, turned his car to the left to go into a driveway and plaintiff's motorcycle struck the right side of the car at a point 3 feet from the north curb. 

Plaintiff was violating a statute by carrying a passenger on the motorcycle. It was held that there was a question of fact concerning defendant's negligence and plaintiff's contributory negligence. The court said that there was no persuasive testimony that plaintiff's carrying a passenger on his motorcycle actually contributed to the cause of the accident. 

Ruby v. Buxton, 305 Mich. 64.

Defendant was driving in a northerly direction on Dort Highway, a four-lane concrete road. Plaintiff's decedent had been driving south. He turned his car to the left, apparently intending to make a U-turn, and stopped with the front of the car one foot east of the center line. Defendant, who had just passed another northbound car occupying the most easterly lane, drove his car into decedent's automobile. The accident occurred at 11:30 p. m. Visibility was restricted, as there was a hard rain. It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 52. Left Turn Into Vehicle from the Rear. 

Filter v. Mohr, 275 Mich. 230. 

Defendant was attempting to pass decedent's motorcycle when the collision occurred. The testimony showed 130

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 52 that the impact took place 20 feet or less west of the intersection. The vehicles were proceeding in an easterly direction. The trial court instructed the jury on the statute prohibiting the passing of a vehicle at an intersection. It was held that this was error as the collision did not occur within an intersection. The Court said that there was sufficient evidence relative to the place and character of the collision, the skid marks and gouges on the pavement and the damage to the vehicles to present an issue of fact.  "There are some discrepancies between the testimony of the eyewitnesses and the physical facts shown by the officers. Whether the disclosed physical facts refute the claim of an interested witness is a matter for the trier of the facts, but it is also true that no testimony can refute the unquestioned physical facts, and no indulgence in arithmetical soliloquy can make it otherwise." 

Bugbee v. Fowle, 277 Mich. 485.

The driver of plaintiff's car testified that he gave a signal for a left turn and saw defendant's car five to six hundred feet back of him as he started his turn. Defendant claimed that he gave a horn signal and that plaintiff without any visible signal suddenly turned into his path. 

The case was tried without a jury. It was held that there was a question of fact as to contributory negligence and defendant's negligence. 

White v. Vandevelde, 284 Mich. 669. 

Plaintiff, riding a motorcycle in a southerly direction, collided with defendant's car which had stopped to make a left turn and then was driven across the east half of the road. Plaintiff testified that defendant's car was stopped, headed in a southeast direction, and that he 131

§ 52] 

gave a signal to pass, but that defendant started without signal to turn left, and a collision resulted. The accident occurred in a community of 200 inhabitants. It was held that the evidence regarding residence district was so vague that the trial judge did not err in submitting the question to the jury. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Buttermore v. Faleris, 304 Mich. 294.

Plaintiff was riding his motorcycle north on a cement highway. Defendant was driving his car in a northerly direction and made a left turn into a driveway leading to a public park. The plaintiff testified that he was 100 feet south of the driveway when defendant turned to the left; that he pulled to the left but could not avoid the collision. A witness, accompanying plaintiff on another motorcycle, testified that the plaintiff blew his horn and was going to pass at the driveway or near it and that plaintiff was quite close to defendant's car when the left turn was made. The trial court instructed the jury that plaintiff was not overtaking and passing at an intersection and therefore was not violating the statute. The judgment for plaintiff was reversed and a new trial ordered. The Court held that the driveway formed an intersection and there was a question of fact as to whether plaintiff was in the act of overtaking and passing a car at an intersection. The Court said that the jury had the right to disbelieve the plaintiff. 

McGrath v. Hargraves, 310 Mich. 510.

Plaintiff testified that he gave a signal and was passing defendant's truck when the truck was turned into the right side of plaintiff's car, no signal having been given by the defendant. The defendant contended that the collision was with the rear end of the truck. It was 132

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 53 held that there was a jury question and the judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 

Sec. 52-a (New). Overtaking Vehicle. 

Hetler v. Holtrop, 285 Mich. 570.

In this case verdict was rendered against the two defendants. One defendant's truck was passing the other defendant's truck. There was conflicting testimony as to whether the poles on second defendant's truck swayed from side to side; whether the truck was pulled over to the edge of the pavement, and whether the speed was increased. It was held that there was no error in the instructions, and the judgment was affirmed. 

Sec. 53. Summary of Left Turn Cases. 

Where a driver makes a left turn and his car is struck by an approaching car, he usually is held to be negligent as a matter of law. 282 Mich. 346; 291 Mich. 469; 293 

Mich. 422.

If the car is turned across the center line and stopped, the driver may be negligent as a matter of law. 305 

Mich. 64. Where the car stalls in making a turn, the driver's negligence may be a question for the jury. 291

Mich. 446. Where the approaching car is traveling at an excessive speed, the question of proximate cause may be for the jury. 283 Mich. 134.

It should be noted that the statute providing for limitation on passing at an intersection was changed in 1939. 

It is illegal to drive on the left side of the highway when approaching within 100 feet of any intersection. Comp. 

Laws 1929, Section 4707, as amended, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1575. A driveway into a public park would constitute an intersection. 304 Mich. 294. 133

§ 54] 

 CHAPTER VII REAR END COLLISIONS Sec. 54. Rear End Collisions. 

Patt v. Dilley, 273 Mich. 601.

In this case the plaintiff standing near the rear end of a parked car was struck and pinned against the car by defendant's automobile. It was held that defendant's testimony raised an issue of reasonable care and that the lower Court committed error in instructing the jury on the presumption under the rear end collision statute. 

Gates v. Pfeiffer Brewing Co., 275 Mich. 81.

The defendant claimed that the booster brakes failed on a downgrade and that the truck struck plaintiff's wagon from the rear through no negligence of the driver. 

It was held that a question of fact was made out as there was testimony that the proximate cause of the accident was the failure of the truck driver to turn to the left soon enough. 

Baumgartner v. St. Armour, 276 Mich. 650.

Plaintiff testified that she drove up to within ten or twelve feet of the rear end of defendant's trailer and turned to the left to pass when the trailer swerved three or four feet to the left into her path. A judgment for the plaintiff by the lower court was reversed. The Court said that the evidence of physical facts, and the improbability of a loaded trailer swerving at a speed of four miles per hour showed negligence on the part of the plaintiff. 134

SUPPLEMENT 

[$ 54 

Fugere v. Aronson, 285 Mich. 661.

Plaintiff, driving 60 miles per hour, was overtaking and about to pass the defendant who was driving at about 50 miles per hour. When plaintiff was 75 feet behind the defendant's car, and when he had turned to the left side of the road to pass, the defendant swerved to the left and stopped. Plaintiff testified that he was not positive that he could have stopped within 75 feet.

There was a 10-foot shoulder on the left. In holding plaintiff negligent, the Court said: "It then became his duty to do what he could to avoid the collision by either stopping or taking the shoulder of the road to the left of the pavement." 99 

Resnik v. Trumbull-Chevrolet Sales Co., 310 Mich. 214.

Plaintiff was driving in a northerly direction on 

Second Boulevard in Detroit. Plaintiff stopped suddenly because the car ahead was turned into the most easterly lane. Defendant's truck was driven into the rear of plaintiff's car. The jury returned a verdict for the defendant. In affirming the judgment, the Court said: "If plaintiff came to a sudden stop without giving ample warning to defendant's driver, then a jury could find that she was guilty of contributory negligence, or the jury could have found that under the circumstances of this case defendant's driver was faced with a sudden emergency and was not negligent."
