 CHAPTER VIII PARKING ON HIGHWAY 

Sec. 56. Parking on Highway. 

Lindenfeld v. Michigan Interstate Truck Co., 274 Mich. 681. case.

The co-owners of two trucks were defendants in this One truck, a 60-foot train, was having difficulty in climbing a hill because of a slippery pavement. The second truck following cut around first truck to pass and in doing so went to the wrong side of highway. 

Plaintiff's car collided with second truck which was in plaintiff's lane of travel.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment as to owner of first truck saying that the owner of the first truck was not guilty of negligence as a matter of law as there was no evidence that the first truck stopped in fact or within the meaning of the order of the public utilities commission (Rule No. 36), requiring the placement of flares before and behind the train. Furthermore, there was no evidence that the absence of flares had any causal connection with the accident. 

Park v. Gaudio, 286 Mich. 133.

Defendant's truck was parked in the south lane of a three-lane highway at night. The defendant contended that the truck was not illegally parked because the driver had stopped to give aid to others involved in an accident. 

There was conflicting evidence as to whether the truck was lighted. It was held that an issue of fact was presented as to the defendant's negligence. 

Marth v. Lambert, 290 Mich. 557.

Plaintiff, at night, stopped his car because of motor trouble. The car occupied 52 feet of the pavement which 136

SUPPLEMENT 

[$ 58 was 33 feet in width. He was standing at the left rear end of the car when defendant's automobile struck him. 

Plaintiff observed defendant's auto traveling in the center lane of the three-lane highway when it was 200 feet away. As it came within 60 feet of plaintiff it swerved toward plaintiff. It was held that plaintiff was not contributorily negligent as a matter of law. 

Bordner v. McKernan, 294 Mich. 411.

Plaintiff was a passenger in a taxicab which had been involved in an accident at night on Warren Avenue in Detroit. The driver left the cab in the middle of the street and went back to inspect the other car. Plaintiff remained in the cab and was injured when another automobile struck it. It was held that a question of fact was presented for the jury as to whether the driver of the cab exercised the high degree of care required in leaving his unlighted car standing in the middle of the street. 

Rossien v. Berry, 305 Mich. 693.

The defendant's car collided with the rear end of plaintiff's automobile. Defendant testified that plaintiff stopped on the pavement without a signal. It was held that defendant's testimony raised a question of fact and that defendant was entitled to an instruction on emergency.

CHAPTER IX  Sec. 58. Assured Clear Distance Cases. 

Patt v. Dilley, 273 Mich. 601. 

Plaintiff was injured while standing near a parked car which was struck by defendant, who saw the parked car when 150 to 175 feet away, and at that point was 137

§ 58] 

blinded by lights of approaching car. The approaching car passed when he was 75 feet from parked car. Defendant then swung back to center of street and when he could see again, plaintiff loomed up three or four feet ahead of him. The position of plaintiff in the road was disputed.

The question as to when defendant should have seen plaintiff was for the jury.  "When defendant's eyes were blinded by the oncoming car, he had seen the parked car and had a clear distance ahead to the parked car unless, and the fact was in dispute, plaintiff was in behind the parked car. If plaintiff was not there before defendant was blinded, then the question when defendant should have seen him was a matter of fact for the jury." 

Apparently, the Court does not intend, as a matter of law, to compel a driver to see an object when as a matter of fact he is unable to do so. The jury must decide. 

Plantz v. Imperial Oil Corp., 275 Mich. 570.

Plaintiff was a passenger in an automobile which collided with the rear of a parked truck shortly after vision of plaintiff's driver had been impaired by glare from headlights of other parked truck. The evidence was held ample to prove negligence of truck owner as well as contributory negligence of plaintiff's driver imputable to plaintiff. 

Lang v. County of Ingham, 277 Mich. 345.

Plaintiff drove over a depression in highway where county drain had been constructed and in doing so was injured so that he lost control of car. Evidence of plaintiff's speed and whether his rate of speed constituted con- 138

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 58 tributory negligence held sufficient to render such matters factual issues and to afford justification for finding for plaintiff thereon by trial judge sitting without jury.

Assured clear distance rule was not applied to a hole or depression in the highway. 

Braun v. County of Oakland, 279 Mich. 55.

There was an ice barrier across the highway caused by a leaky water main. This barrier was one to two feet in height. Lights were four or five feet off the highway but not over the highway at the point where ice barrier crossed the road. Plaintiff's automobile collided at night with this ice barrier. The Court held that the assured clear distance rule does not apply to a bump in the highway. The question of the contributory negligence of plaintiff was for the jury. 

Phillips v. Inter-City Trucking Service, Inc., 280 Mich. 30.

Plaintiff saw red lights and flares on four-lane highway some 700 or 800 feet ahead of him in the nighttime.

He knew the obstruction was standing still. He continued to drive toward the parked trailer and, when about 

25 feet south of the trailer, saw two automobiles from the opposite direction, side by side, and then another car swerved into lane of traffic being used by plaintiff at a rapid rate of speed. Plaintiff could not stop and struck parked trailer. The Court held that plaintiff's negligence could be conceded. "The rule makes no allowance for delay in action. 

Plaintiff must, on peril of legal negligence, so drive that he can and will discover an object, perform the manual acts necessary to stop, and bring the car to a halt within such range." 139

§ 58] 

 Stankrauff v. DeVoe, 281 Mich. 660. 

Plaintiff was injured when the car in which she was riding collided with a trailer parked on right side of pavement. The accident occurred on a dark and foggy morning late in January. The car had been driven at 

35 miles per hour or less and could have been stopped in 

30 to 32 feet. The brakes had been applied at several places to test the road. When 50 to 100 feet from the trailer plaintiff's driver applied the brakes and the car skidded and struck trailer injuring plaintiff.

This was a question for the jury as to whether plaintiff's driver was guilty of contributory negligence. The jury would be justified in finding that travelers found the road safe for a long enough distance that they would not be charged with anticipating an icy condition near place accident occurred. It should be noted that plaintiff's driver applied his brakes "in ample time to stop and avoid collision if the road had not been unexpectedly slippery; and consequently, that he was not guilty of contributory negligence. 

Zullo v. Detroit Creamery Co., 281 Mich. 678.

The Court refused to apply the assured clear distance rule in this case where there was a clear cut issue between parties as to which was on the right side of the street. 

Cook v. City of Otsego, 282 Mich. 248.

Plaintiff's decedent drove into a well lighted band stand on a dark misty night. It was negligence as a matter of law to drive at such a speed that the car could not have been stopped within the distance that objects can be seen ahead. Such a rule is not changed because of atmospheric conditions. 140

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 58 

Bard v. Baker, 283 Mich. 337.

Defendant's truck was loaded with road mats which projected over the sides thereof one and a half feet. The truck was parked and plaintiff's husband drove his car so as to clear the truck proper but the projecting mats, which were 42 inches above the ground, sheared off top of plaintiff's car. The Court held that plaintiff's driver was not contributorily negligent as a matter of law saying: "Our Court in placing a reasonable construction upon this statute [Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4697, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1565, as amended by Act 

No. 119, Pub. Acts 1933, Comp. Laws Supp. 1935, 

Section 4697], has held that a person should not be guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law in failing to see an object which was undiscernible to a person approaching the same in the exercise of ordinary care."

The mats were more than 42 inches above the pavement, which is the height the "main bright portion of the head lamp beams" of plaintiff's car were permitted to shine. Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4738 (b), Mich. Stat. 

Ann., Section 9.1606 (b), as amended by Act No. 59, Pub.

Acts 1931. 

Fors v. LaFreniere, 284 Mich. 5. 

While being driven througn a fog at night at a speed of 35 to 40 miles per hour defendant's car struck a pedestrian. The defendant did not see the pedestrian until he saw a couple of hands which seemed to come toward the side of the car. There was damage on the front of the car. Four justices held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant. 141

§ 58] 

 Odell v. Powers, 284 Mich. 201. 

The plaintiff was driving his car north on M-78 and slowed to a speed of 15 miles per hour as he approached a southbound snow plow which was throwing a cloud of snow across the road making visibility poor for 18 or 20 feet. After passing out of the cloud of snow plaintiff saw defendant's car coming toward him 10 or 15 feet away. The Court said that plaintiff was not obligated to bring his car to a complete stop when he saw the cloud of snow. Even if it was negligence to proceed the jury might have found that plaintiff would have been struck if he had stopped. 

Park v. Gaudio, 286 Mich. 133.

The plaintiff was driving his car in an easterly direction at night on a three-lane highway. He was driving 45 to 50 miles per hour in the south lane. A car was approaching in the center lane, and he dimmed his lights reducing visibility to 75 feet ahead. He slowed down to a speed of 30 to 35 miles per hour. Plaintiff saw defendant's truck when he was 70 feet from it, applied his brakes when 60 feet away, but could not stop because of mud on the pavement. The accident occurred in front of an Inn and there was testimony that cars had spread mud on the pavement. It was held that plaintiff's negligence was a question for the jury. 

Clark v. Jackson, 286 Mich. 355.

Plaintiff's driver while proceeding west on a street in 

Detroit, could see 60 to 65 feet ahead. The lights of an approaching car blinded him. He saw defendant's unlighted truck which was parked at the north curb, directly ahead, and could not avoid a collision. He was held negligent as a matter of law. 142

Vashaw v. Marquette Public Service Garage, 288 Mich. 363. 

Plaintiff, driving at night, struck a chain stretched across the highway between a wrecker and another car. 

The Court in holding that a question of fact was presented said that the "assured clear distance" statute did not apply to such an obscure menace to safety as a chain stretched across a public highway at night. 

Hautala v. Cochran, 289 Mich. 409.

At night plaintiff was driving down a long grade on a gravel road covered by packed snow. He saw the lights of a truck which was headed up the hill. This truck and trailer had stalled and jackknifed so that the trailer blocked plaintiff's path. Plaintiff testified that with the lights in his eyes he did not see the trailer until he was 60 to 75 feet from it. Plaintiff claimed that he could have stopped before reaching the trailer except for the icy condition of the highway near the trailer. This condition was unknown to plaintiff and disinterested witnesses corroborated plaintiff's testimony concerning the unusual condition at the point of the accident. It was held that plaintiff's negligence was a jury question. 

Maxson v. Bay County, 290 Mich. 86.

Plaintiff's car was driven into a ditch beyond the end of the road at night. Three posts 32 inches above the ground had been placed at the end of the road as a warning. The center post was broken off and the other posts were outside the traveled portion of the road. Beyond the drainage ditch was a flat open field. It was held that plaintiff's negligence was a question of fact for the jury. 143

$58] 

Schneck v. Genesee County Road Commission, 295 Mich. 482.

Plaintiff drove his car into the rear end of a trailer 10 feet wide on which there was a steam shovel. The trailer was painted gray, a color close to that of the pavement, and the platform was about 30 inches above the pavement. It was held that the testimony disclosed no fortuitous circumstances which excused plaintiff and consequently he was negligent as a matter of law. 

Cramer v. Detroit Edison Co., 296 Mich. 662.

Plaintiff drove his car into an electric light pole which was one foot back from the curb at the end of a parkway dividing the street. It was held that plaintiff was negligent and that defendant was not guilty of any actionable negligence. 

Meehl v. Barr Transfer Co., 296 Mich. 697. .

Defendant drove an unlighted truck out onto highway U. S. 12 into the path of plaintiff's car. It was shown that at a speed of 40 miles per hour plaintiff could not stop after the truck came to the edge of the pavement. 

The Court held that plaintiff's negligence was a jury question pointing out that this was not an intersection case. It was also explained that defendant was driving at such speed that he could stop within the assured clear distance. 

Burke v. County of Washtenaw, 301 Mich. 666.

In this case plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law in not seeing a tree in a parkway dividing the highway.

McNair v. State Highway Department, 305 Mich. 181.

In a 5-3 decision it was held that plaintiff was negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 59. Summary of Assured Clear Distance Cases. 

The Michigan Court in recent years has followed the assured clear distance rule but has established a number of exceptions. The driver is not required to stop within his range of vision to avoid a depression. 277 

Mich. 345; 309 Mich. 655. He may be excused from negligence in striking an ice barrier one to two feet in height. 279 Mich. 55.

For cases where a driver contends that an icy spot on the highway made it impossible to stop and was an unusual condition, see 281 Mich. 660; 289 Mich. 409. A driver is not required to see an object in the air more than 42 inches above the road. 283 Mich. 337. Mud on the pavement may be a recognized excuse. 286 Mich. 

133. The rule does not apply to a chain stretched across the highway. 288 Mich. 363.

A driver may not be negligent in driving into a cloud of snow, although he cannot see ahead. 284 Mich. 201.

There is no duty under the assured clear distance rule to see a rise in the road and a succeeding depression. 

305 Mich. 181. 146

CHAPTER X SKIDDING CASES 

Sec. 60. Skidding Cases. 

See Haney v. Beisel, 287 Mich. 239. 

Paton v. Stealy, 272 Mich. 57.

In this case the defendant claimed that he skidded to the wrong side of the road, and was not negligent. The lower Court decided that the defendant was on the wrong side of his own volition, and the judgment for plaintiff was affirmed because there was evidence of such fact. 

Grant v. Richardson, 276 Mich. 151.

Defendant's truck and trailer stopped on a hill and skidded backwards on the icy pavement. It was held that there was evidence of negligence of the driver in attempting to ascend the hill in its condition, and in jackknifing the trailer, voluntarily, while sliding downhill. 

Kolehmainen v. E. E. Mills Trucking Co., Inc., 301 Mich. 340.00 

Defendants' heavily loaded truck, occupying half of the highway, went into a skid after making a curve on an icy highway, and crossed the center of the road. It was held that there was evidence of negligence. A question was raised as to speed and whether defendant should have controlled the truck on the shoulder of the road. 

Brown v. Arnold, 303 Mich. 616.

Defendant stopped his car in front of plaintiff's home, parallel with the gutter and about 2 or 3 feet from the gutter. The center of the street was about 2 feet higher than the gutter and the street was slippery, being covered with ice and snow. Immediately after plaintiff 147

§ 60] 

alighted, defendant started the car turning toward the center of the street. The car skidded sideways and the rear fender struck the plaintiff. It was held that there was evidence from which the jury could conclude that defendant was negligent.  "Negligence may be inferred from the facts and circumstances. Physical facts may justify a jury finding that defendant is guilty of negligence. Negligence may be inferred from circumstances which place the case within the field of legitimate inferences from established facts.' 

Humphries v. Complete Auto Transit, Inc., 305 Mich. 188. 

Plaintiff was driving a car in a southerly direction in the extreme westerly lane of Telegraph Road. The pavement was icy and slippery. Defendant was driving a tractor and trailer north in the easterly lane of the fourlane highway. Defendant was driving at a speed of 25 to 40 miles per hour. He knew of the decline in the pavement but did nothing to retard his speed. When the truck was 150 to 200 feet from the point of impact, it went into a skid crossing the center of the pavement. 

It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the defendant.

Sec. 62. Closing Door on Occupant's Hand. 

Abent v. Michigan Cab Co., 279 Mich. 617.

Plaintiff in alighting from the rear door of a taxicab placed his hand on the standard to which the front door was hinged, with his finger tips in the door jamb. When the driver closed the door his finger tips were injured.

It was held that the plaintiff was negligent. 

Sec. 62-a (New). Pedestrian Walking in Center of 

Street. 

Reetz v. Schemansky, 278 Mich. 626. 

Plaintiff, at night, was walking east on a boulevard in 

Detroit, pulling a small express wagon. The defendant driving east in the center lane struck the wagon, and injured the plaintiff. Defendant claimed that plaintiff was negligent in not having a light on the wagon. The street was wide enough for four cars; the weather was 149

$63-al 

www clear and the street was well lighted. The majority of the court held that the statute did not require a light on the small wagon. Had a light been required, the question of the absence of a light as being a proximate cause was for the jury. The Court, by quotation, said that no statute required the plaintiff to walk on any particular part of the pavement.

Sec. 63-a (New). Cranking Car in Gear. 

See Sauer v. Rowland, 272 Mich. 520; Gordon v. Sears, Roebuck & Co., 278 Mich. 513. 

Marschall v. Glaeser, 284 Mich. 56.

The employee of the defendant garage asked the owner of the car to take it out of gear and to start the motor. 

The owner started the motor while the car was in gear and it pinned the plaintiff against a work bench. On rehearing it was held that the plaintiff was entitled to a new trial as to the theory that the owner of the car was made the agent of the garage.

Wallis v. Cox, 286 Mich. 76.

No signal was given. The plaintiff driving 15 to 20 miles per hour claimed that the defendant backed suddenly into the path of her car. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. It was held that the case was properly submitted to the jury. 150

Sec. 66-a (New). Duty to See if Children Are Near Car. 

Ravey v. Healy, 279 Mich. 323.

When defendant entered his car the plaintiff, 10 years old, got onto the right running board. Defendant told the plaintiff to get off. She disappeared from his sight and he started his car thinking she was off. Plaintiff was injured when he stopped the car after discovering her presence. It was claimed the defendant was negligent in starting his car without ascertaining that plaintiff was off the running board. It was held that there was no negligence on the part of the defendant. 

Also see Benedict v. Rinna, 257 Mich. 349. 

Bump v. Bellingar, 311 Mich. 254.

Defendant, a farmer, asked plaintiff, a 13-year-old boy, to go with him to pick up milk cans. On the route the defendant stopped his truck to pick up cans and he and the boy got out of the truck. When ready to go, the defendant saw the boy go around the rear of the truck to get into the cab on the right side. Defendant testified that he heard the door slam shut, and while glancing back at the load, he started the truck without looking to see whether the boy was in the cab. The plaintiff was on the running board and was thrown off and injured. The trial judge instructed the jury that defendant was negligent. This was held error on the ground that there was a question of fact. 

See In re Estate of Miller, 300 Mich. 703.

Sec. 66-b (New). Duty on Private Property. 

Reedy v. Goodin, 285 Mich. 614.

In this case plaintiff was working on a gas pump at a gas station. Defendant's truck which had stopped for 151

§ 66-c] 

gas struck plaintiff's leg when it was started. It was held that the question of negligence of the defendant and contributory negligence were questions of fact. 

Thurkow v. City of Detroit, 292 Mich. 617.

In this case the Court said that a lower degree of care and diligence is required of pedestrians upon private driveways than is required of pedestrians crossing a public street.

Sec. 66-c (New). Duty to Rescuer. 

Brugh v. Bigelow, 310 Mich. 74.

Defendant was involved in an intersection accident and was pinned under his car. Plaintiff heard the crash and defendant's cries, and in assisting in the rescue, was injured by the movement of defendant's car. It was held that defendant owed plaintiff a duty even though plaintiff was just a rescuer. The judgment dismissing plaintiff's action was reversed. 

Sec. 66-d (New). Car Door Opening. 

Hazen v. Rockefeller, 303 Mich. 536.

Plaintiff, a customs inspector, testified that he had inspected the contents of defendant's car and had walked to the customs office, when he was pinned against the building by the door of defendant's car as it was passing. The plaintiff testified that he neither opened nor closed the door. Defendant testified that he did not close the door, and that he thought the plaintiff did close it, as he heard a metallic noise. The case was tried without a jury and a judgment was entered for the plaintiff. 

This was affirmed., The Court said that from the evidence and circumstances a logical inference could be drawn that defendant did not properly close the door. 

Furthermore, a logical inference could be drawn that the 152

[§ 67 door swung open and struck the plaintiff because it was not properly closed.

Sec. 67. Bicycles. 

Stockfisch v. Fox, 275 Mich. 630. 

The defendant was

Plaintiff's decedent, 16 years old, was riding a bicycle in a westerly direction on an 18-foot paved highway. He had a 7-year-old boy on the bicycle. driving his truck and trailer west. signal on the truck. He turned to the left so that the right side of his truck was four to six feet south of the north edge of the pavement. The defendant testified that when the truck was six feet from the boys, the bicycle dropped off the pavement, and then jumped onto the pavement and into the path of the truck. A mark on the pavement, apparently made by dragging the bicycle, started 30 inches from the north edge of the pavement. 

The lower Court directed a verdict for the defendant. 

Judgment was reversed and a new trial ordered. The 

Court said: "It cannot be said as a matter of law that four or six feet from the right edge of an 18-foot pavement is a 'safe distance' to pass a bicycle when the truck steals up without warning at a speed of 25 or more miles per hour, although the bicycle occupies only 18 inches or two feet of the space and is traveling close to the edge."

The Court said that the jury could infer and find that the proximate cause of the accident was the defendant's approach without warning and so close to the boys that they were startled into running off the pavement, and being thrown in front of the truck.

Brown v. Tanner, 281 Mich. 150.

Defendant driving south on a street in Flint made a short left turn and struck plaintiff, who was riding a bicycle north. The Court held that plaintiff's failure to have a light on his bicycle might not have been a contributing cause of the accident, and it was a question of fact for the jury. 

Duffy v. Enright-Topham Co., 282 Mich. 662. 

Plaintiff, 12 years of age, was riding a bicycle south on a street in Saginaw. He saw defendant's taxicab northbound swing over to the west side of the street near the intersection. He kept pedaling ahead and the collision occurred near the southwest corner. The jury returned a verdict for the defendant. It was held that there was evidence of negligence on the part of the plaintiff in continuing ahead when it was apparent that the cab was turning in front of him. It was also admitted that plaintiff did not have his bicycle legally lighted. 

Ertzbischoff v. Smith, 286 Mich. 306. 

Plaintiff's decedent, 16 years of age, was riding a bicycle easterly on Gratiot Avenue in Detroit. The boy turned to the left and was struck by defendant's eastbound car, either while making the turn or after com- 154

SUPPLEMENT [§ 67-a pleting the U-turn. The defendant claimed that the decedent had completed the turn, and rode his bicycle on the wrong side of the street, without a light, head on into the car. There was conflicting testimony. One witness testified that the boy was turning and going in a northeast direction when struck. It was held that the boy's negligence was a question of fact for the jury.

The absence of proper lights might not have been a proximate cause. A new trial was ordered because of error in an instruction on lights. It was held that the subsequent negligence doctrine was not applicable. 

Swift v. Kenbeek, 289 Mich. 391. 

At night, the decedent, 19 years of age, was riding his bicycle westerly down a hill in the City of Kalamazoo.

Defendant's car proceeding easterly up the hill was turned left at an intersection striking decedent near the north curb line. It was claimed that the decedent was negligent in riding his bicycle at an excessive speed, and without a light or bell. The Court held that assuming decedent was negligent the question of proximate cause was for the jury.  "Suppose plaintiff's decedent had approached the point of collision at only 20 or 15 miles an hour, would every man acting as a juror in such case say that the accident would not have happened?"

Sec. 67-a (New). Stepping Off Elevated Car. 

Hartwick v. Lawson, 290 Mich. 91.

Plaintiff drove his car into defendant's garage to have it greased and the oil changed. It was driven onto a hydraulic hoist. Plaintiff later entered the car to clean a window. While in the car it was raised. He stepped backward out of the car and fell to the cement floor 5. feet below. Plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law for failing to observe for his own safety. 155

 Sec. 68-a (New). Running Off Road at Detour Sign. 

Cardinal v. Reinecke, 280 Mich. 15.

In this case defendant saw a detour sign and became uncertain as to whether to make the turn. She waited too long and went into a ditch. It was held that the issue of actionable negligence was for the jury.

Sec. 69-a (New). Striking Object Hung Over Road. 

Haszczyn v. Detroit Creamery Co., 281 Mich. 467.

The defendant's truck 9 feet 42 inches high struck a rope which was stretched across the street. The rope was less than 15 feet above the road in violation of Comp. 

Laws 1929, Section 4056, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.266.

It was held that the question of proximate cause was for the jury. The Court said that the rate of speed of defendant's truck and his failure to heed the warnings might have been the proximate cause of the injury. 

Van Wormer v. Kramer Brothers Freight Lines, Inc., 

284 Mich. 76.

Plaintiff helped to pile wire mesh on a trailer. The mesh was 92 feet in width making the vehicle more than 96 inches in width in violation of Comp. Laws 1929, Section 4728, par. (a), Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1596, par. (a). Defendant's truck struck the mesh injuring plaintiff who was riding on top of the load. It was held that the violation of the statute was not a proximate cause of the accident inasmuch as the defendant had a clear view of the plaintiff's vehicle for a long distance. 

Vashaw v. Marquette Public Service Garage, 288 Mich. 363. 

Defendant's wrecker was at one side of the highway with a chain attached to a car on the other side. The distance between the vehicles was 10 to 15 feet. The night 156

[§ 70 was dark and there were no lights turned toward the road or chain. Plaintiff approached at a speed of 15 miles an hour, but did not see the chain. It was held that the issues of defendant's negligence and plaintiff's contributory negligence were issues of fact. 

Sec. 69-b (New). Driving Through Narrow Space. 

School District of City of Ionia v. Dadd, 308 Mich. 220. 

This case was tried without a jury. The space between the scaffold structure and the building was 10 feet. 

The truck was 8 feet wide. While driving at a speed of 5 miles per hour the rear of the truck was passing the scaffold when it fell. The judgment for the defendant was affirmed.

Sec. 70. Avoiding Vehicle Coming Into Highway. 

Rasmussen v. McEachron, 274 Mich. 200.

Plaintiff's decedent, driving his car from a private driveway, attempted to cross U. S. 16, a trunk line highway, to the south side and collided with defendant's westbound car. The only eyewitnesses were the defendant and his sister. They testified that the decedent did not stop before entering the highway and entered when defendant's car was but 30 feet away. It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law in violating the statute, and that the defendant had a right to assume that the decedent would obey the statute and stop. 

Wilson v. Michigan Interstate Motor Freight, Inc., 286 

Mich. 99.

The plaintiff backed her car across a 26-foot street from the east side stopping near the west curb. She had seen defendant's truck coming from the north. When 157

§ 70] 

plaintiff's car stopped the truck was 200 feet away and was traveling 35 miles per hour. Plaintiff testified that she expected the truck driver to turn to the left and go in front of her. Plaintiff was held negligent as a matter of law.  

"The record is barren of any other warning to the truck driver of her intention, and she is not to be excused because of his failure to sense her expectation."

The subsequent negligence doctrine was not relied upon. 

Pierson v. Bailey Products Co., 298 Mich. 243.

Plaintiff's driver drove his car onto the highway from a private driveway. Entering from the north he could see to the east for 1,000 feet, yet he did not see defendant's truck until his car had reached the center of the highway. It was admitted that defendant's truck was turned to the south side of the highway where the impact occurred. The Court said that from the physical facts, such as the location of the automobiles and the damages to plaintiff's car as shown by photographic evidence, it conclusively appeared that plaintiff's car was still turning when struck. It was held that plaintiff's driver was negligent as a matter of law in not observing the approaching truck until too late to avoid the accident. 

Valenti v. Mayer, 301 Mich. 551.

Plaintiff was a minor occupant of a car being driven in a westerly direction on U. S. 12. There was testimony that defendant's decedent drove into the highway from a side road without stopping. Defendant contended that the sole cause of the collision was the speed of the plain- 158

[§ 70-a tiff's car and plaintiff's failure to see defendant's car in the intersection. It was held that the testimony raised an issue of fact as to this question. 

Moquin v. Nastwold, 313 Mich. 243.

Plaintiff's truck, 18 feet long, was parked at a loading dock near the east edge of the street. The plaintiff looked to the south and, seeing no vehicle within a distance of 200 feet, drove the truck out into the street, intending to turn south. He testified that when he reached the center of the street he saw defendant's car 250 feet south and moving about 40 miles per hour. The truck was struck at the left rear wheel and was pushed against a retaining wall. The defendant contended that the plaintiff drove the truck out in front of his car when he was but two car lengths away. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. Schmidt v. Willbrant, 313 Mich. 450.

Sec. 71. Speed on Rough Road. 

Salewsky v. Wright, 291 Mich. 587. nimpa Plaintiff was riding with the defendant, her daughter, but was not a guest. In driving through a mud puddle in a gravel road at a speed of 15 miles per hour, the jolt threw the plaintiff from the rear to the front seat and then back. Defendant had driven through the puddle twice before, and had experienced no trouble. It was held that there was no evidence of negligence. 

Sec. 71-a (New). No Contact Between Cars. 

Losey v. Wetters, 278 Mich. 422.

In passing the truck in which plaintiff's decedent was riding it was claimed that defendant cut in front of it too quickly forcing the truck off the highway. There was no contact between the vehicles, although there was testimony that defendant's car came within a foot of the truck. It was held that the testimony presented a question of fact. The Court said that even though the truck was exceeding the speed limit it was a question of fact as to whether such negligence was the proximate cause of the accident. 

Van den Heuval v. Plews, 291 Mich. 670.

Plaintiff's car was parked east of the highway and south of the intersection. Defendant was driving a truck south descending a hill. When 200 feet from the intersection he noticed cars approaching from the south. 160

McDuffie v. Root, 300 Mich. 286.

Plaintiff's car was forced off the highway by defendant driving on the wrong side. Plaintiff lost control of her car and it turned over in the ditch. It was held that a question of fact was presented.

CHAPTER XII DISTINCTION BETWEEN  Sec. 75. The Distinction Between Death and Survival 

Actions. 

Straub v. Andrews, 295 Mich. 129.

Suit was started in this case on September 28, 1939, one day prior to the effective date of Pub. Acts 1939, No. 297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 27.711 et seq. This statute changed the measure of damages in death actions.

It was held that the action was properly founded under the so-called Survival Act and that the new statute did not apply.

The legislature apparently abolished the distinction between death and survival actions arising out of injuries resulting in death by the enactment of this statute. 

Sec, 77. Interpretation of Word "Instantaneous." 

Anderson v. Jersey Creamery Co., 278 Mich. 396.

Suit was started under the survival act, and in answer to special questions the jury found that death by electrocution was not instantaneous. There was testimony that 162

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 78 the decedent showed signs of life for a few minutes. In holding that there was evidence of survival, the Court said that the question was an exceedingly close one. 

Gile v. Hudnutt, 279 Mich. 358.

In the face of testimony by a doctor that immediately after the accident the decedent showed no sign of life, a nurse testified that when the child was admitted to the hospital, she was bleeding from the mouth and her pulse was weak. The jury awarded $300 under the Death Act. 

Plaintiff appealed on the ground that the evidence showed a survival, and consequently, the verdict was against the great weight of the evidence. It was held that the verdict was supported by the evidence. 

Suit was brought under the death statute. The coroner testified that in his opinion the injuries would have caused instant death. Three other witnesses testified that the decedent was breathing several minutes after the accident. It was held that a question of fact was raised, and judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Sec. 78. Summary. 

Pub. Acts 1939, No. 297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 

27.711 et seq., abolished the distinction between death and survival actions where death resulted from injuries. 

Under the amended Death Act all actions for death and for injuries resulting in death are brought under the Act. bobour but, b0277 163

 CHAPTER XIII  Sec. 79. Death Actions for Minors. 

Rufner v. City of Traverse City, 296 Mich. 204.

The decedent was a 13-year-old boy who was earning about $3 per day. It cost about this sum to feed, clothe and care for him. He was to have continued through high school. A verdict of $2,500 plus expenses was held not excessive. It was also held that there could be a recovery for medical, hospital and funeral expenses although the estate might not be liable for them. 

Morris v. Radley, 306 Mich. 689.

This action was for the death of a child 4 years, 9 months old. There was no pain and suffering. A verdict of $2,539.50 was held not excessive. The court said that there was no precise yardstick with which damages could be measured in a case of this nature. The child's mother was permitted to testify that she was working in Detroit, that she made certain wages and that certain wages were made by women working in defense plants. 

The court found no reversible error in this. The verdict necessarily was based on uncertainty and was within reasonable probability. 

Covell v. Colburn, 308 Mich. 240. 

In this death case the decedent was a girl 15 years old.

There was no pain and suffering. The expenses were $596.47. A verdict of $650 was upheld. 

Anderson v. Kearly, 312 Mich. 566.

The decedent was 17 years old. He lived and worked on the farm operated by his father. His father worked 164

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 81 in a shipyard. Wages for farm help were $3.50 per day during the harvest season and $2 to $2.50 per day during the balance of the year. The funeral expense was $232.50. The court held that the $3,000 verdict, amounting to $2767.50 for loss of services for 3 years, 2 months, was not excessive.

Sec. 80. Summary. 

Under the Death Act, as amended in 1939, the damages include pain and suffering in addition to pecuniary injury. There may be a recovery for expenses, although the estate might not be liable for them. 296 Mich. 204.

The Michigan Court has definitely limited pecuniary injury to the minority period of the decedent. 308 Mich. 240. 

All of the old cases in this group are in point on the question of damages insofar as pecuniar injury is concerned. The measure of damages for the death of a minor is pain and suffering, expenses before and after death, and the pecuniary injury.

Sec. 81. Death Actions for Adults. 

Lindenfeld v. Michigan Interstate Truck Co., 274 Mich. 681. 

This was an action under the death act for the death of a housewife, 24 years of age. A verdict of $20,000 was held excessive and a new trial was ordered. The Court said that under the testimony the jury could not fairly find that the decedent's services were worth more than $25 per week, and her keep less than $5 per week. 

Nemet v. Friedland, 278 Mich. 541.

In a suit under the death act a verdict of $11,000 was rendered. The decedent was 40 years old and was earn- 165

§ 81] 

ing 35 cents per hour. He left a widow and four minor children. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

In an action for the death of a housewife, aged 30, a verdict of $6,558.95 was rendered. The husband testified at length regarding the surroundings of the parties and the nature of the services but did not place any money value on the services. It was held that the verdict was not excessive. 

Fors v. LaFreniere, 284 Mich. 5.

The decedent, 33 years of age, and an unmarried man, was living with his mother, a widow. He was working and contributing to his mother's support. He contributed $30 per month at times and worked about the home, receiving his board and lodging. A judgment of $3,600 was affirmed. 

See Pub. Acts 1939, No. 297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 

27.711 et seq., for change in measure of damages in death actions. 

Strong v. Kittenger, 300 Mich. 126.

Action was brought under the Death Act as amended in 1939. Plaintiff's decedent was a housewife 57 years of age. Verdict of $2,000 was rendered. Defendant claimed error in the instruction on damages because the Court did not charge the jury that cost of maintenance of the wife must be deducted from the value of her services to determine pecuniary injury. It was held that as defendants made no request for such instruction, they cannot successfully claim error. 

Kolehmainen v. E. E. Mills Trucking Co., Inc., 301 Mich. 340.

Decedent was 33 years old. He was survived by his widow and two children, 3 and 5 years of age. There 166

Defendant complained of the trial judge's action in instructing the jury that if a general verdict was rendered for the plaintiff the jury should inform the court how the amount was apportioned. The Court held that this procedure was proper in view of the statute requiring the Circuit Court to advise the Probate Court as to the amount of the judgment representing the pecuniary loss suffered by the surviving spouse and next of kin.

The wife of the driver of the car was killed in the accident. The wife and husband were each working and supporting ten minor children. The husband was severely injured in the accident. Sec. 82. Summary. 

The recent cases in this group are the same as the old cases insofar as pecuniary injury is concerned. Now, under the 1939 amendment of the Death Act, Pub. Acts 

1939, No. 297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 27.711 et seq., the measure of damages includes pain and suffering and expenses before death.

It should be noted that there may be no error in the failure to instruct concerning the cost of support of a wife or child in determining pecuniary injury, if there is no request for such instruction. 300 Mich. 126.

Where the husband of the decedent remarries, damages may be recovered for such pecuniary injury as continues. In other words, if the decedent performed services outside the family relationship, there could be a recovery for such services. 311 Mich. 143. The court 168

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 84 implies in this case that the remarriage cut short any recovery for the pecuniary injury arising out of the family relationship. 

CHAPTER XIV  Sec. 83. Survival Actions for Minors. 

Anderson v. Lavelle, 285 Mich. 194. 

The decedent, a girl 19 years of age, died a few minutes after the accident. She was moaning but made no voluntary movements. She had spent considerable time in a home for the feeble-minded and played with children 10 to 12 years of age. The defendant admitted liability but contended that there was no damage. 

A verdict of no cause for action was given by the jury. 

It was held that the trial court committed no error in charging the jury on conscious suffering and possible earnings and that they could bring in a verdict of no cause for action. 

See Pub. Acts 1939, No. 297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 

27.711 et seq., for effect on measure of damages where injuries result in death.

Sec. 84. 

Summary. 

The amendment of the Death Act, Pub. Acts 1939, 

Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 27.711 et seq., abolished the distinction between death and survival actions. All ac- tions for death and for injuries resulting in death must be brought under the Death Act. Hence the cases under 

Sec. 83 do not represent the measure of damages in actions for the death of minors. 169

§ 85] 

 Sec. 85. Survival Actions for Adults. 

Hanna v. McClave, 273 Mich. 571. 

A survival action resulted in a verdict of $5,266.25.

The decedent was 76 years old, and suffered for several hours before death. There was evidence that the decedent was in good health and that his work on the farm was worth $1.25 per day. It was held that the verdict was not excessive. 

Spillman v. Weimaster, 275 Mich. 93.

This was a survival action. It was held that burial expenses were not recoverable in such an action. 

Greene v. Richer, 278 Mich. 1.

In this survival case a verdict of $3,600 was held not excessive. The decedent lived for two days. He was not working at the time of the accident but when he could find work he earned $75 per month. 

Walker v. McGraw, 279 Mich. 97.

In this case it was held that the personal expenses of the decedent could not be subtracted from his earnings in finding damages. 

Zielinski v. Harris, 289 Mich. 381.

The deceased had an expectancy of more than 25 years. 

His earnings were more than $1,500 per year. His automobile damage was $625. He survived for 4 days suffering intense pain. It was held that the verdict of $1,000 was grossly inadequate and a new trial was ordered. 

Donahue v. Gordon, 292 Mich. 581.

The decedent survived the accident by more than 3 days. It was held that $1,200 was not excessive for pain and suffering. 170

Sec. 86. Summary. 

The amendment of the Death Act in 1939 abolished the distinction between death and survival cases. The cases in Sec. 85 do not represent the measure of damages under the Death Act. Some of the cases are valuable as demonstrating proper awards for pain and suffering.

Sec. 87. Actions for Loss of Services. 

Bugbee v. Fowle, 277 Mich. 485.

Plaintiff's wife survived the accident two days. The trial judge allowed plaintiff to recover for loss of services for her expectancy. The Court followed the decision of 

Hyatt v. Adams, 16 Mich. 180, and held that the recovery for loss of services was limited to the period from the time of the injury to the time of death.

Sec. 88. Pleading. 

Lucy v. Dowd, 285 Mich. 530.

Plaintiff tried to recover under both the Survival Statute and the death act in one count. There were no allegations of pecuniary loss. At the trial, the defendant did not object to the evidence of pecuniary loss, but moved to strike out such testimony at the end of the trial. 

It was held that the trial Court did not err in permitting the amendment of the declaration to show pecuniary loss. 

Plaintiff was permitted to correct the error, of alleging two separate causes of action in one count, in the Supreme Court. 171

§ 90] 

Susich v. Michigan Consolidated Gas Co., 292 Mich. 612.

It was held in this case that it was not necessary to refer to the survival statute in the declaration in a survival case.

Pub. Acts 1939, No. 297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 

27.711 et seq., now provides for action under the Death 

Statute, whether or not there is a survival. 

Sec. 90. Effect of Defendant's Death Upon Death Action. 

Godley v. Mueller, 280 Mich. 203.

In this case the question was raised as to whether the death action survived the death of the tortfeasor. 

Justice Butzel alone discussed this question in a dissenting opinion. The other members of the Court reversed the judgment on other grounds. Justice Butzel said that the action should survive, and for his reasoning, see opinion. 

Justin v. Ketcham, 297 Mich. 592.

Suit was started under the Survival Statute as the accident occurred before the effective date of the 1939 Death Act. The defendant's decedent, the wrongdoer, was instantly killed in the collision. It was held that plaintiff could recover. The Court said that common sense compelled the conclusion that the cause of death and the death itself did not occur in the same split second. 

In re Olney's Estate, 309 Mich. 65.

In this case it was held that an action under the Death Act survives the death of the wrongdoer. The wrongdoer died prior to the death of plaintiff's decedent. 172

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 91 

Sec. 90-a (New). Proof of Cause of Death. 

Frye v. City of Detroit, 256 Mich. 466.

In this case an automobile struck the decedent and threw him onto the street car track where he lay unconscious with blood flowing from cuts on his head. A street car fender then picked him up and carried him some distance. He died a few minutes later.  "But the evidence did not go beyond that, or furnish facts from which, by reasonable inference, it could be said, apart from mere guess or conjecture, that the street car, rather than the automobile, inflicted the injuries causing death.' 

Also see case of Dewitt v. Gerard, 274 Mich. 299. 

Kolehmainen v. E. E. Mills Trucking Co., Inc., 301 Mich. 340. 

Plaintiff's decedent's car was struck by an approaching vehicle and then by one following, causing death.

The jury answered a special question finding that the first collision caused the death. The Court held that there was sufficient testimony as to the cause of death. 

See Schmidt v. Willbrant, 313 Mich. 450.

Sec. 91. Other Miscellaneous Matters. 

Lindenfeld v. Michigan Interstate Truck Co., 274 Mich. 681. 

Plaintiff as special administrator of his wife's estate brought an action under the Death Act. Later he was appointed general administrator. Before trial the court allowed the general administrator to be substituted as plaintiff. It was held that the amendment was not error. 173

§ 92-a] 

In re Venneman's Estate, 286 Mich. 368.

In this case it was held that the amount recovered in a death action must be distributed according to the statute of distribution and not according to pecuniary loss sustained. See change as effected in Pub. Acts 1939, No. 

297, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 27.711 et seq.

CHAPTER XVI PRESUMPTION THAT DECEASED USED DUE 

CARE 

Sec. 92-a. Presumption Relied Upon as to All of the 

Actions of the Decedent. 

Rohrkemper v. Bodenmiller, 287 Mich. 311.

Deceased and her companion, at night, were walking in a northerly direction along the westerly side of the highway. Defendant, driving north and while passing a northbound car, struck deceased. The pavement was 16 feet wide with a shoulder of 4 to 6 feet. Defendant did not see the decedent until he was 5 feet from her. The case was tried without a jury. The trial judge found that the decedent was negligent. An evenly divided court affirmed judgment for the defendant. Four justices held that there was a question as to whether the decedent should have noticed the approach from the rear of defendant's car. Four justices held that the presumption of due care operated as there was no eyewitness who saw what the decedent did, and no testimony of negligence. 

See Jenks v. County of Ingham, 288 Mich. 600. 174

SUPPLEMENT [§ 94-a 

Delfosse v. Bresnahan, 305 Mich. 621.

The decedent, a pedestrian, was struck by the front of defendant's car. There was no eyewitness. The defendant did not testify, and several witnesses testified that after the accident defendant made the statement that he did not see the pedestrian. It was held that plaintiff was entitled to rely upon the presumption of due care.

Sec. 92-b. Presumption Relied Upon Only to Take Case to Jury. 

Arndt v. Grayewski, 279 Mich. 224.

Defendant testified that he did not see the decedent until his car struck him. The only testimony relative to the actions of the decedent was the statement of the driver of a car ahead of defendant's automobile. The 

Court said that this statement was contrary to physical facts and it was a jury question as to whether the decedent was negligent. 

Sec. 92-c. Where Circumstances Show Decedent Was 

Negligent. 

Essmeister v. Roadway Transit Co., 275 Mich. 387.

The defendant contended that because its driver was dead there was a presumption of due care on his part. 

It was held that the testimony of plaintiff's driver, coupled with the showing of the physical facts, overcame the presumption. 

See Waterstradt v. Lanyon Dock Co., 304 Mich. 437.

Material Actions Witnessed. 

Sec. 94-a. 

Foote v. Huelster, 272 Mich. 194.

In this intersection case it was held that the defendant and the occupant of his car were eyewitnesses and consequently the plaintiff could not rely upon the presumption. 175

§ 94-a] 

KLASSE "This is so even if the eyewitness is the adverse party."

It should be noted that the Court held that the evidence relative to the place and character of the collision and skid marks presented an issue of fact as to the care exercised by the decedent. 

Frye v. Brinker, 272 Mich. 339.

The defendants, the only eyewitnesses, testified that the decedent stumbled into the path of the car when it was two feet from him. It was held that the defendants being eyewitnesses, the presumption could not be relied upon. 

Buchel v. Williams, 273 Mich. 132.

It was held in this case that the defendants being eyewitnesses, the question of due care on the part of the decedent was one of fact and not of presumption. 

Rasmussen v. McEachron, 274 Mich. 200.

The only eyewitnesses in this case were defendant and his sister. They testified that the decedent drove out of a gas station onto the through highway without stopping and into the path of their car. It was held that the presumption of due care did not apply because there were eyewitnesses, and therefore the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. 

Collar v. Maycroft, 274 Mich. 376.

This case arose out of an intersection accident. The defendant was the only surviving eyewitness and he did not testify. It was held that the presumption could not be relied upon. The Court said that the defendant was at the trial and available to the plaintiff as a witness. 

Hence there was an eyewitness, and therefore there was no presumption of due care. 176

[§ 94-b 1 

Faustman v. Hewitt, 274 Mich. 458.

Plaintiff was adjudicated insane. It was held that inasmuch as the defendant was an eyewitness the presumption of due care could not be relied upon. 

Kalbfleisch v. Perkins, 282 Mich. 27. 

Plaintiff's decedent was killed in an intersection accident. It was held that the defendant being an eyewitness, the plaintiff could not rely upon the presumption. 

Peck v. Hampel, 293 Mich. 252.

In this case the Court held that the defendant was an eyewitness, and that although he did not testify, plaintiff could not rely upon the presumption of due care. 

Black v. Ambs, 307 Mich. 644.

Plaintiff introduced a statement signed by defendant that he did not see the decedent until he was 15 feet from him. Defendant and his wife testified that they saw the decedent walk from between parked cars. It was held that the defendant and his wife were witnesses and the trial court was correct in instructing the jury that plaintiff was not entitled to any presumption.

Sec. 94-b. Some of Material Actions Not Witnessed. 

See Fors v. LaFreniere, 284 Mich. 5; Rohrkemper v. 

Bodenmiller, 287 Mich. 311. 

Heckler v. Laing, 300 Mich. 139.

In this intersection case the decedent drove onto highway U. S. 2, striking defendant's car. There was no testimony as to observations made by the decedent. 

There was testimony that decedent stopped his car before entering the intersection. It was held that the decedent was negligent as a matter of law. 177

§ 95] 

Breker v. Rosema, 301 Mich. 685.

The driver of plaintiff's car in an intersection accident suffered a head injury, resulting in amnesia as to what happened immediately prior to the accident. This was proved by medical testimony. Plaintiff contended that there was a presumption of due care the same as if he had met his death. Defendant contended that the plaintiff was an eyewitness and therefore the presumption fell. The Court held that the presumption could be relied upon the same as if the driver were dead. The plaintiff was not able to testify as to what the driver did or what judgment he had. The Court said that whether contributory negligence existed frequently depends upon factors which are externally visible. Sometimes it depends on what passes through the mind. Obviously there could be no eyewitness to the latter type. of conduct. It was held that a jury question was presented.

Sec. 95. Summary of Cases Where There Are Witnesses. 

The opposite party, if an eyewitness, is sufficient to prevent the decedent's representative from relying upon the presumption as to those matters which were witnessed. It is not necessary that the opposite party testify. 293 Mich. 252. The plaintiff may be permitted to rely upon the presumption as to mental decisions although there is a witness. 301 Mich. 685. Loss of memory from a head injury is a reason for invoking the presumption. 301 Mich. 685. 178

Sec. 96. Liability of Owner. 

Miller v. Manistee County Board of Road Commission ers, 297 Mich. 487.

It was held that the County was liable by reason of the statute making the owner liable for the negligent operation of the motor vehicle. 

Mead v. Michigan Public Service Commission, 303 Mich. 168. 

In this case the decision in Miller v. Manistee County 

Board of Road Commissioners, 297 Mich. 487, was reversed. The Court held that it would not read into the statute, making the owner of a motor vehicle liable, a waiver of sovereign immunity. 

See Morris v. Radley, 306 Mich. 689. 

Wieczorek v. Merskin, 308 Mich. 145. There was a finding that the driver of the car was guilty of gross negligence. Plaintiff sought to have judgment entered against the driver and owner for gross negligence. It was held that the statute does not make the owner guilty of the gross negligence of the driver although the owner remains responsible for the injury resulting from the negligent act of the driver. 179

 Sec. 99. Joint Owner. 

Buchel v. Williams, 273 Mich. 132.

Chrystel and Jane MacFarlane were joint owners of an automobile. At the time of the accident Alice Williams, a schoolmate, was driving the car with knowledge and consent of both joint owners, although Jane Mac- Farlane was not in the car. The lower Court directed a verdict for Jane MacFarlane. The Supreme Court re versed the lower Court saying: "It was error to release Jane MacFarlane from liability, the car being operated at the time with her knowledge and consent and for the benefit of the joint owners." 

Moore v. Noorthoek, 280 Mich. 431.

The Supreme Court quotes ruling in Buchel v. Wil liams with approval.

Sec. 100. Presumption of Consent. 

Christiansen v. Hilber, 282 Mich. 403.

Plaintiff was injured by a truck belonging to defendant and driven by his son. Testimony showed that the truck was bought for business purposes and that the son only drove the truck when there was something to be done and that defendant never permitted son to use the truck for pleasure purposes. The son testified that the truck was used in camp for hauling supplies and that he used it on the occasion in question, for pleasure purposes. 

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the lower court against the father on the theory that the presumption of consent by virtue of Comp. Laws 1929, Section 

4648, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1446, was overcome by 180

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 100 1 direct and uncontradicted testimony. The Supreme 

Court said: "One who is driving a motor vehicle incident to the owner's business is presumed to be duly authorized so to drive the vehicle. But it is the established law in this state that such a presumption prevails in favor of the litigant relying thereon only so long as that phase of the case is not covered by testimony to the contrary." 

Morrow v. Trathen, 288 Mich. 172.

There was direct and positive testimony by the driver of defendant's truck that he had no permission to drive the truck, and that the defendant did not know that he was using the truck. It was held that the presumption did not prevail in the face of this testimony. Judgment for the defendant on a directed verdict was affirmed. 

Bushie v. Johnson, 296 Mich. 8.

Earl Johnson was using the car of his father with his consent. He permitted a friend to drive and he was in the car when the accident occurred. It was held that the car was driven with the consent of the owner. 

Sweeney v. Hartman, 296 Mich. 343.

The defendant owner permitted his son to use the car in going to and from work. He expressly directed the son not to carry passengers for hire. It was held that the owner was liable to an occupant passenger for hire in spite of this instruction. 

Brkal v. Pletcher, 311 Mich. 258.

This suit was against the owner of a car and his son who had used it. The plaintiff called the son for crossexamination under the statute. His testimony affirma- 181

§ 101] 

tively established the fact that the car was used contrary to the express prohibition of his father. It was held that the statutory presumption disappeared when plaintiff offered this testimony and rested his case. The son also testified on cross-examination that his grandfather was driving the car at the time of the accident against his protest and that the witness was asleep. 

It was held that the son, being plaintiff's witness, could not be held liable. His testimony could not be made a question of fact.

Sec. 101. Implied Consent-Question for Jury. 

Wingett v. Moore, 308 Mich. 158.

Defendant automobile dealer loaned a car to Anderson while the dealer repaired Anderson's car. The accident occurred more than 6 weeks later. Defendant testified that he loaned the car for Anderson to use in going to work. He admitted that he did not forbid him to use it for any other purpose. Held, that the question of implied consent was for the jury. 

Sec. 101-a (New). Consent of Owner for Limited Use. 

Merritt v. Huron Motor Sales, Inc., 282 Mich. 322.

Joseph Merritt, the plaintiff, started suit against the Huron Motor Sales, Inc., J. G. Clemmons, who was its sales manager, Thomas Schuon and Madeline Neumaier and others. J. G. Clemmons, the sales manager of the 

Huron Motor Sales, loaned an Oldsmobile automobile to defendant Schuon at Ann Arbor for the purpose of visiting a sick friend in the hospital at Brighton. The car was loaned on condition that the same would be returned to Mr. Clemmons at his home by 10:00 p. m. so that he could call for his daughter who was to attend a school party 182

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 101-a that night. It is claimed the failure of defendant Schuon to return the car after his trip to Brighton and within the time limit set and his violation of the agreement by driving the car to Detroit with three other companions brings appellant, Huron Motor Sales, within the protection of the statutory provision contained in Comp. Laws 

1929, Section 4648, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 9.1446; that is, that the owner of an automobile shall not be liable unless it is being driven with the express or implied knowledge or consent of the owner. 

A verdict was rendered against the Huron Motor Sales and others and the Huron Motor Sales appealed. Its contention before the Supreme Court was that the undisputed testimony showed that the automobile at the time of the accident was not being driven with the express or implied knowledge or consent of the Huron Motor Sales.

The entire case should be read because questions of evidence and impeachment of witnesses are also involved which it is not necessary to report here on this question. 

The Supreme Court's final conclusion was that if a record of testimony of both Mr. and Mrs. Clemmons who overheard the agreement with Schuon as to the limitations placed on the use of the car was undisputed, uncontradicted and credible, such testimony left no room for a contrary finding by the jury. There was no substantive testimony in the record supporting the essential elements of plaintiff's case; namely, that at the time and place of the accident the automobile was being driven with the implied consent or knowledge of the Huron Motor Sales. 

The Court stated further that the motion for judgment non obstante veredicto should have been granted on behalf of the Huron Motor Sales. 183

§ 102] 

Fischer v. McBride, 296 Mich. 671.

Defendant permitted his 17-year-old daughter to drive his car under the express restrictions that she should do the driving and not let anyone else use or drive the car. The daughter permitted another girl to take the car and drive it alone. It was held that the defendant owner was not liable. 

Roberts v. Lundy, 301 Mich. 726.

The owner permitted Rolling to use her car with instructions not to allow anyone else to drive the car. 

Rolling drove three adults and some children to Belle 

Isle. He parked the car, pulled the emergency brake, left the gears in neutral, and turned off the ignition, leaving the key in the switch. A 6-year-old boy was on the front seat with an adult. The motor of the car started and the car started back and injured the plaintiff. 

It was held that Rolling's conduct in leaving the key in the ignition switch was not negligence. It was also held that at the time of the accident the car was not being driven with the owner's consent.

Sec. 102. Owner-Certificate of Title. 

LaHay v. Nelson, 273 Mich. 435.

Plaintiff's decedent was fatally injured by a car which was claimed to be owned by Herbert Norton, an automobile dealer, and driven by one Nelson to whom it had been sold under an agreement containing a title retaining clause by Norton, salesman, and a Miss Roth, one of his clerks. This was a part of a series of transactions by which Miss Roth sold her own personal car to one Slade who was the former owner of the car which had been transferred to Nelson and who had injured the plaintiff's decedent. The certificate of title had been assigned direct from Slade to Nelson, and Norton, the 184

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 102 automobile dealer, was not mentioned in the assignment. 

The whole question was whether or not Norton had ever been the owner of the automobile causing the injury. 

Miss Roth, Norton's clerk, had used certain financial forms of Norton's in making out a new note and a title retaining contract. This, however, was without Norton's knowledge.

There are many outside facts introduced to show who was the real owner of the automobile such as insurance policies and other transactions. The Supreme Court stated that the evidence in the case did not show that Norton was the owner of the automobile stating that if the certificate of title was insufficiently assigned, title was still in Miss Roth and if the assignment was sufficient, it was either in Miss Roth's or Nelson's name. The testimony did not show that a certificate of title had ever been delivered to Norton. 

Gates v. Pfeiffer Brewing Co., 275 Mich. 81. 

Where the transfer of title was signed as follows: "Central Supply Co., transferor, K. T. Merritt, Prop. transferor," it was held that if Merritt was not at least a part owner it is difficult to understand why he was one of two parties who shortly after the accident signed an application for transfer and therein described himself as, "Prop., transferor." This was uncontradicted in the record and consequently it was a proper function for the jury to find at least part ownership in Merritt. 

Peters v. Youngblood, 287 Mich. 175. 

An Iowa dealer brought a purchaser to Detroit for delivery of a new car. The dealer's driveaway plates were put on the car and on the way back to Iowa it was involved in an accident. It was held that the dealer was not the owner. 185

§ 103] 

Wood v. Merchants Ins. Co., 291 Mich. 573.

The defendant insurance company claimed that the insured, a minor, was not the sole owner of the automobile as the car was registered in the name of the insured and his grandfather. It was held that the insured was the sole owner; that a mistake had been made in putting the grandfather's name on the certificate of title because he was the insured's guardian. The insured had paid for the car, and the grandfather had no interest in it.  "In the instance at bar the certificate of title was not conclusive evidence on the issue of ownership of the automobile, and the Court was not in error in so holding and deciding the issue of ownership upon the evidence." 

See Noorthoek v. Preferred Automobile Ins. Co., 292 

Mich. 561.

It should be noted that Act No. 127, Pub. Acts 1945, Mich. Stat. Ann., Sections 9.1708 (1) and 9.1708(2), abolished the defense of governmental function in actions for the negligent operation of a motor vehicle owned by a political subdivision of the state.

 Sec. 105. Liability of Employer.

Sec. 107. Deviation from Route by Servant. 

Phillips v. Fotheringham, 277 Mich. 566.

Fotheringham owned the automobile which was driven by Trombley at the time of the accident injuring Helen Phillips. Trombley testified that on the day of the accident he had driven his employer's car on business from 

Bay City into Saginaw County. On his return trip he passed through Solzburgh and there saw a friend who was intoxicated and not able to look after himself. 

Trombley was taking this friend home to the west side of Bay City when the accident happened. There was verdict and judgment for plaintiff and defendant contends the trial Court erred in refusing to hold as a matter of law that defendant Trombley was not at the time of the accident engaged in the course of his employment. 

The Supreme Court stated that the ruling in Foote v. 

Huelster, 272 Mich. 194, did not apply because Trombley on cross-examination made inconsistent and contradictory statements to those given by him on direct examination. Since such testimony gave rise to an inference that he had not departed from his route, an issue was raised for the jury. 

Kieszkowski v. Odlewany, 280 Mich. 388.

Defendant permitted John Wandor to use his truck to deliver wood. Bruno Jasinski, a minor, accompanied

Wandor. Wandor delivered wood and then instructed 

Jasinski to take truck back to defendant's store. Jasinski did not follow shortest route back to store because of heavy traffic on Joseph Campau but instead went three blocks east to Conant Avenue. From Conant he turned 188

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 107 west on Norfolk for purpose of seeing a friend, who was not at home. Jasinski then turned around but before reaching Conant the accident occurred. Was Jasinski deviating from his route to defendant's store when accident occurred? The trial judge thought, "the truck was being driven within the limits of permission." The Supreme Court clarified the situation and stated: "The deciding factor is not the degree of the deviation but rather, whether the owner impliedly consented to the route taken." It further stated: "but failure to specify a particular route does not, of itself, permit a personal use of the vehicle, and unless consent can be implied from some other source, such use is deviation. Such was the situation herein." The Court further stated: "Where a master and servant relation exists, the implied consent of the owner of the vehicle extends to the scope of employment. 

When the servant is outside the scope, he is outside the consent; the terms are co-extensive, and, as used in this sense have the same meaning." 

Rabaut v. Ford Motor Sales Co., 285 Mich. 111.

At the time the accident occurred the car, owned by a dealer and loaned to a doctor, was being driven by the doctor's chauffeur. The accident happened east of the doctor's home. His office was west of his home. The doctor testified that the chauffeur had been instructed to never use the car on personal matters, and had not been sent on any mission which would have taken him to was held that the evidence presented a question for the jury; that a presumption was raised that the car was being operated within the scope of the employment; that the doctor's testimony was negative and not sufficient to destroy the presumption; and that the only person who could have given dithe place of the accident. I h 189

rect and positive testimony was the chauffeur, and he was not produced. 

Kalinowski v. Odlewany, 289 Mich. 684.

The facts of this case, with another party plaintiff, were before the Court in 280 Mich. 388. It was held that the driver so deviated from his route for personal reasons that the lower Court was justified in directing a verdict for the defendant. 

Long v. Curtis Publishing Co., 295 Mich. 494.

McKay, an employee of the defendant company, made a business trip to Chicago from Detroit in his own car. 

He finished his business on Saturday at noon and was driving back to Detroit on Sunday when the accident oc-, curred. It was customary for the employees to use their cars on long trips, but they were reimbursed on the basis of railroad fare. No specific instruction was given as to the return trip. McKay visited his son near 

Chicago on Saturday and again Sunday morning. It was held that there was an issue of fact as to whether McKay was acting within the scope of his authority. 

Liability could not be avoided on the ground of deviation from route. 

Jeffries v. Jodawelky, 304 Mich. 421.

The trial court entered a judgment for the defendant, employer of the driver of a truck which struck the plaintiff, on the ground that there was a deviation from the business of the employer. The driver was not given any directions as to a particular route to follow. He testified that he was on a personal errand at the time of the accident. The Court said that statements taken from the driver before the trial, that he was not on a personal errand, did not rise to the dignity of substantive evidence and did not create a question for the jury. 190

Sec. 108. Implied Consent or Knowledge of Employer. 

Slinkard v. National Machine & Tool Co., 274 Mich. 662.

Defendant company owned a truck and had placed it in control of its employee, Donez, who used it in the company's business. Donez had been forbidden to use truck for personal use. The testimony showed that over a period of two years prior to the accident Donez had on several occasions used the truck to take his family for a ride. On the date of the accident Donez used the truck to drive from Jackson to Detroit with his family to attend the boat races. Otherwise the undisputed testimony was that Donez did not have the consent of his employer to use the car. The trial Court directed a verdict in favor of National Machine and Tool Company and the Supreme Court sustained this ruling on the ground that there was no testimony that the employer had any knowledge of the personal use Donez made of the truck, or that it either expressly or impliedly consented thereto. 

Weller v. Speet, 275 Mich. 655.

Benjamin Speet owned a dairy and had an employee named Den Uyl, who owned an automobile for his private use. Mrs. Speet, wife of Benjamin, owned no interest nor was she employed in dairy but sometimes received orders at her home for milk which she communicated to her husband. On the day of the accident in question, Mrs. Speet received a rush order for milk, and her husband and other delivery employees being out she asked defendant James Michielsen, a 16-year-old neighbor boy, to take Ford truck at dairy and make delivery. The boy ran truck out of dairy but Den Uyl, learning of the errand, told the boy to use his automobile, instead of the truck. The boy complied and on his way to deliver the milk the accident happened. The lower Court entered a 191

§ 108] 

judgment in favor of Speet notwithstanding the verdict. 

Was Michielsen a servant of Speet?

There was no implied agency here which would permit the wife, Mrs. Speet, to employ the boy and thereby create the relationship of master and servant between her husband and the boy. There were no acts and circumstances from which such implied authority could be deduced. 

Arnestad v. Point, 280 Mich. 339.

Arnestad was injured by Point's car, a dealer's automobile, which was driven by a prospective purchaser unaccompanied by the salesman of defendant who gave prospect the car for demonstration purposes. The defendant had issued instructions not to permit prospects to use his cars unless accompanied by the salesman. The testimony showed that Point himself had given out cars to prospective purchasers and also knew that his salesmen had done the same on prior occasions and that salesmen did not accompany prospects for demonstration. The 

Supreme Court refused to reverse judgment for plaintiff, on this point, saying that, "There was no such departure, by the sales employee from the instructions as to relieve defendant Point from liability." The testimony was such that consent was implied. 

Reitenga v. Kalamazoo Creamery Co., 288 Mich. 161.

Defendant company kept several special delivery trucks parked on a lot near the creamery in Kalamazoo.

Northrup, defendant's employee, testified that he had been given permission to use a company truck for transportation from his home to the creamery, and so used company trucks on an average of three to five times per week. This was contradicted by other witnesses. At the time of the accident Northrup had been visiting taverns, and was driving a company truck from the lot 192

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 115 to his home where he intended to spend the night. It was held that a question of fact concerning consent had been raised.

Sec. 110. Servant Acting Contrary to Instructions. 

Steudle v. Yellow & Checker Cab & Transfer Co., 287 

Mich. 1.

The defendant, a taxicab company, contended that it was not liable because its servant was acting contrary to orders.  "If he was engaged in the business of his master, the transportation of passengers for hire, appellant would be liable for his negligent acts even though at the time of the accident he was acting contrary to instructions."

See Holloway v. Nassar, 276 Mich. 212; Laughlin v.

Defendant Summers was a distributor of beer. Defendant Koss, the owner of the truck, was employed by Summers who paid an agreed price per case of beer delivered. The truck was involved in an accident with plaintiff's car. It was held that the question of whether or not Koss was an independent contractor was for the jury. 

Anderson v. Conterio, 303 Mich. 75. 

Defendant Conterio operated a garage. He owned his own demonstrator, and although he received a commission on all cars sold through his efforts, he was not under the control of the Gogebic Auto Company. It was 193

§ 117-b] 

held that the instructions were proper and that the verdict of no cause for action as to the Gogebic Company indicated that it was based upon a finding that Conterio was an independent contractor. 

Brinker v. Koenig Coal & Supply Co., 312 Mich. 534.

The defendant contended that the trial judge should have directed a verdict on the ground that it entered into an oral contract with the owner of the truck to deliver coal on a price per tonnage basis, and this made the owner an independent contractor. It was held that the driver of the truck was defendant's employee. 

Sec. 117-b. Wife Against Husband. 

Kircher v. Kircher, 288 Mich. 669. 

Plaintiff sued her husband to recover for injuries sustained in Colorado while an occupant of a car, driven by the defendant. The Colorado law permitted one spouse to recover from the other for a tort. The Court held that it would be contrary to public policy to allow a recovery.

Sec. 117-c. Wife's Cause of Action Against Owner Where Husband Is Driving. 

Watkinson v. Reichle, 292 Mich. 484.

The defendant, not being able to start her car, asked plaintiff's husband to ascertain the trouble. Defendant assured him that the car was not in gear. The car was in gear and plaintiff was injured. Plaintiff claimed that there was no negligence on the part of her husband, and that defendant was directly negligent. Judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 194
