[§ 119-a 

Sec. 118. Summary-Liability-Liability of Others. 

Where an employer attempts to escape liability on the ground that the employee deviated from his route, it may be necessary to introduce the testimony of the employee. 285 Mich. 111. On the other hand, inconsistent statements by the driver before the trial may not be sufficient to create a question for the jury. 304 Mich. 421.

Sec. 119. Imputed Negligence. 

On January 7, 1946, the Michigan Supreme Court decided the case of Bricker v. Green, 313 Mich. 218, overruling the rule of imputed negligence "so far as pending and future cases are concerned." In this unanimous decision the court, unmistakably, disapproved the doctrine of imputed negligence which had been followed in 

Michigan for more than 70 years.

In Bricker v. Green the suit was for the death of the wife of the driver and against the driver of the other car. 

The Court held that the negligence of the driver was not imputed to the decedent occupant. 

Mitchell v. DeVitt, 313 Mich. 428. 

This case was decided after Bricker v. Green, supra.

The defendant contended that the plaintiff, an occupant of a car, was guilty of contributory negligence in not warning the driver of the approach of defendant's car.

It was held that the plaintiff was not contributorily negligent as a matter of law.

Sec. 119-a. Fellow Servants. 

Hekman Biscuit Co. v. Commercial Credit Co., 291 Mich. 156. 

The plaintiff in this case attempted to recover on a compensation subrogation claim. The injured employee 195

§ 119-b] 

of plaintiff company was an occupant in a car driven by a fellow servant of plaintiff company. Plaintiff's driver was negligent. A judgment for defendant was affirmed. 

It was held that the plaintiff company was responsible for the negligence of its employee who was driving the car. His negligence was imputed to his employer. 

Utley v. Taylor & Gaskin, Inc., 305 Mich. 561.

In this case the court held that in a subrogation action to recover for compensation payments, the contributory negligence of plaintiff as employer would not defeat recovery against a third party. This seems to overrule 291 

Mich. 156.

Sec. 119-c. Minors. 

See Fabiano v. Carey, 279 Mich. 269.

Sec. 119-e. Private Conveyance for Hire. 

Wood v. Merchants Ins. Co., 291 Mich. 573.

The plaintiff used his car to go to and from school, a distance of about 7 miles. It was plaintiff's custom to carry other students each of whom voluntarily paid 75 cents per week. It was held that the automobile was not used as a livery conveyance for hire, and the occupants were not passengers carried for compensation. The 

Court said that the occupants voluntarily contributed toward the expense. The plaintiff carried them as a mere incidence and as an accommodation. 

See Brown v. Wood, 293 Mich. 148. 196

[§ 121 

Sec. 120. Summary-Imputed Negligence. 

The Michigan Supreme Court has unquestionably decided not to follow the doctrine of imputed negligence. 

313 Mich. 218. It should be noted that this change in the law will make more important the questions of contributory negligence of the occupant, assumed risk, and joint enterprise.

Sec. 121. Joint Enterprise. 

Schneider v. Draper, 276 Mich. 259.

In this case the driver of the car was going to the football grounds when two other players jumped on running board. Both were killed as a result of collision with a telephone pole. The Court cites the rule in Frisorger v. 

Shepse, 251 Mich. 121, with approval saying that in present case only the driver had control of the car and the other boys had no right to direct its movements. 

See also, Laughlin v. Motor Freight Lines, 276 Mich. 545. 

Also, Hopkins v. Golden, 281 Mich. 389, where the owner contributed the use of his car and bore depreciation thereon and the occupants, including plaintiff, contributed expense of operating machine and other expenses of the trip. Held: "All parties were engaged in a common enterprise for their mutual benefit and pleasure: the joint venture related to a single isolated transaction Under the facts stated, the common control and possession of the automobile is to be assumed." 

Johnson v. Fischer, 292 Mich. 78.

Plaintiff and her husband had a place near Pentwater where they went, over weekends, to fish. The plaintiff did not drive an automobile. Desiring to go fishing she asked the defendant, who was a sportswoman, to make 197

§ 123] 

the trip with her in defendant's car. Plaintiff directed defendant where to go, being familiar with the roads. 

It was held that this was a joint enterprise.  "This was a joint venture, not for profit, but for pleasure and recreation with a hope of prospective reward in acquiring fish, undertaken for the mutual benefit and satisfaction of each of the parties." 

It was held that plaintiff could not recover. 

See Bushie v. Johnson, 296 Mich. 8.

CHAPTER XVIII SUBSEQUENT OR DISCOVERED NEGLIGENCE Sec. 123. Subsequent or Discovered Negligence. 

Rosenfeld v. City of Detroit, 274 Mich. 650.

Plaintiff drove his car from a private driveway on the north side of the street to drive in eastbound lane, but was forced to stop on eastbound car track in front of approaching street car because of fast eastbound motor traffic. Held, justified in directing verdict for defendant since there was no showing the motorman could have brought street car to a stop in time to have avoided collision after he discovered or should have discovered plaintiff's peril. This was a case of concurrent negligence. Anderson v. Bliss, 281 Mich. 323, follows rule in 

Rosenfeld v. City of Detroit. 

Brodie v. City of Detroit, 275 Mich. 626.

A pedestrian walked in front of the bus, from which he had just alighted, four to six steps into the path of another bus proceeding in the same direction as first bus. 198

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 123 He did not look to his left at any time. The Supreme 

Court said although it was not necessary in deciding this case, that the testimony would not have justified the submission of the question of subsequent negligence to the jury. 

Hickey v. Smith, 277 Mich. 123.

Plaintiff's husband drove to wrong side of highway to avoid a horse which suddenly came onto highway. A head-on collision occurred when defendant's car, which was on the right of the highway, came along ten or twenty seconds later and after plaintiff's car had stopped. Held an unavoidable accident, or concurrent negligence. Defendant had no better opportunity to avoid accident than plaintiff's driver. The Court stated that the rule laid down in Krouse v. Southern Michigan R. Co., 215 Mich. 

139, is applicable because of failure of plaintiff's driver to make any effort to remove his car from its wrong and dangerous location. 

Brinker v. Tobin, 278 Mich. 42.

Doctrine of subsequent negligence held not involved where negligence of motorist and contributory negligence of infant in crossing the street concurred up to time of impact. 

Anderson v. Bliss, 281 Mich. 323.

Pedestrian, who had been standing talking with driver of truck headed south and parked three feet on westerly side of 20-foot pavement, then walked to easterly side of pavement without looking for northbound traffic and was run into by northbound truck. Driver had seen pedestrian 150 feet away and had not observed him again until instant of impact. It was held that plaintiff was not entitled to go to jury on ground of subsequent negligence 199

§ 123] 

because defendant was not bound to anticipate unexpected negligent conduct on part of the pedestrian which was also a proximate cause of the accident and the accident happened instantly after the driver discovered decedent in a place of danger. 

Duffy v. Enright Topham Co., 282 Mich. 662.

Plaintiff while riding a bicycle continued on his way after he had observed defendant's taxicab on the wrong side of the street near an intersection. Plaintiff knew a collision would be inevitable unless he stopped or taxicab returned to its side of the street. Held plaintiff's negligence concurred up to moment of impact and therefore was a proximate cause of collision. Doctrine of subsequent negligence not applicable. 

Ertzbischoff v. Smith, 286 Mich. 306.

A bicycle was ridden into the path of an automobile. 

It was held that the doctrine of subsequent negligence could not be applied. 

Beaulieu v. City of Detroit, 293 Mich. 364.

In this case it was held that subsequent negligence did not apply. The Court said that the motorman was not guilty of subsequent negligence in failing to anticipate that plaintiff's decedent would not remain in a place of safety. 

Davidson v. City of Detroit, 307 Mich. 420.

Plaintiff walked across the car track and was struck by the street car. The Court, in holding that plaintiff could not rely upon the doctrine of subsequent negligence because of concurrent negligence, said this: "In order to apply the doctrine of subsequent negligence, plaintiff's negligence must have put her in a 200

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 125 position of danger, must have ceased to operate as the proximate cause of the accident, the defendant must have discovered plaintiff's peril or should by exercise of ordinary care and diligence have discovered plaintiff's peril, the defendant must have had sufficient time and ability to avoid resulting harm by ordinary care and diligence in the use of the means at hand, and failed or omitted to use such care and diligence to avert the threatened injury." 

See Agranowitz v. Levine, 298 Mich. 18; Gallagher v. 

Walter, 299 Mich. 69; Secrist v. City of Detroit, 299 Mich. 

393; Ackerman v. Advance Petroleum Transport, Inc., 304 Mich. 96.

Sec. 125. Statutes of Limitation. 

Cugell v. San-Wash Laundry Co., 280 Mich. 286.

Suit was started in 1936, the action resulting from the death of a father in 1915. Plaintiff contended that the action was for the benefit of a daughter, who became 21 years of age in 1936, and therefore was not barred by the statute of limitations because of Comp. Laws 1929, Section 13978, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 27.607. The Court held that a minor has no severable and personal right of action for injuries to his parent. Under neither the death act nor the survival statute was the daughter a person entitled to bring the action. Hence it was barred by the statute of limitations. 201

127] 

 Sec. 127. Claims in Probate Court. 

See In re Chamberlain's Estate, 298 Mich. 278.

Sec. 129. Procedure Before Trial. 

Magel v. Kulczynski, 276 Mich. 424.

Plaintiff, under Rule No. 41 of the 1933 Rules, moved to take the defendant's deposition on a death case arising out of an automobile accident. The circuit judge limited the scope of the deposition to defendant's physical condition, and the mechanical condition of and the damage to the defendant's automobile. It was held that the circuit judge had not abused his discretion in limiting the scope of the deposition. The Court said that plaintiff had not shown that reasonable diligence failed to reveal the facts sought in the deposition.

Hallett v. Michigan Consolidated Gas Co., 298 Mich. 582. 

It was held that the Court did not abuse its discretion in entering an order for discovery by deposition under Court Rule No. 41 in conjunction with the production and discovery of books, papers, and documents under Court Rule No. 40, to enable plaintiff to declare. It was required that the order be clarified to exclude from its scope the production of confidential reports or any inquiry from any witness not based on actual knowledge. 

Sec. 130. Examination of Jury. 

See Rhoades v. Finn, 288 Mich. 262. 

Holloway v. Nassar, 276 Mich. 212.

At the request of plaintiff's counsel, the lower Court asked jurors whether they carried insurance in a certain mutual insurance company of Chicago. The Court substantially observed the precautions suggested in Harker v. Bushouse, 254 Mich. 187.  202

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 130 "We cannot say the record affirmatively shows error in this request because the Court evidently thought the questions proper under the circumstances, was convinced of the good faith of counsel, and the record affords no basis for a different conclusion. We suggest that where the court conducts the voir dire examination counsel have a right, upon request, to statement upon the record of the reason for such questions in order that the good or bad faith of counsel in requesting them may be reviewed. 

We also suggest that the court refuse to ask such questions except upon a showing, put upon the record and not in presence of the jury, which indicates their necessity to avoid injustice.' 

Campbell v. Osterland, 283 Mich. 175.

In this case the Court said that in Harker v. Bushouse, 254 Mich. 187, and Holloway v. Nassar, 276 Mich. 212, it had discussed the proper manner for examining prospective members of a jury. However, where defendant presented an affidavit showing five members of the jury panel were insured in a mutual company in which defendant held a policy, the plaintiff had the right to ask the jurors questions concerning their interest in the insurance companies which might be involved. 

Fedorinchik v. Stewart, 289 Mich. 436.

In this case it was held that where defendant was insured with a company paying dividends to policy holders and having a large number of insureds in the district, plaintiff was entitled on the voir dire examination to ascertain whether any of the jurors was insured in a mutual insurance company, and if so, what company. 

See Dewey v. Perkins, 295 Mich. 611; Grud v. Warren, 297 Mich. 546; Nicewander v. Diamond, 302 Mich. 239. 203

Sec. 133. Motion for Directed Verdict("Empson Act"). 

Hilliker v. Jewel Oil & Gas Co., 277 Mich. 615.

This case was tried without a jury. Motion was made by defendant for a directed verdict at close of plaintiff's proof. It was held that at the close of plaintiff's proof a case had not been made out and a judgment should have been entered for the defendant. The Court said that a motion for a directed verdict was proper even though there was no jury. The trial judge sat in a dual capacity. 

Sec. 134. Special Questions. 

Farr v. Haggerty, 273 Mich. 547. 

In this case plaintiff contended that the defendant in passing her car cut in too quickly and caught her left front fender with defendant's right rear fender. The defendant contended that the plaintiff ran into her car. 

A special question was put to the jury as to whether the defendant's car hooked the front end of plaintiff's automobile. The jury said "no," but returned a verdict for the plaintiff. The judgment for plaintiff was affirmed. 

The Court said that the special question was ambiguous, and the answer was not conclusive of the real issue.

Therefore it was not inconsistent with the general verdict. 

Ault v. Kuiper, 279 Mich. 1.

It was held in this case that submission of two special questions permitting the jury to separate the damages sustained in two separate injuries was not error, although plaintiff was permitted to recover only for the first injury. 204

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 134 

The following special questions were put to the jury and its answers are given. 

1. Was the deceased killed instantly as a result of injuries received in this accident? Yes. 

2. Did the deceased live for any period of time after the accident? No. 

3. Did the defendant, as a part of the consideration of hiring Viola Crook agree to furnish transportation to and from the summer camp? Yes.

The proper phrasing of the questions was not questioned. 

Dzikowski v. Michigan Central Railroad, 282 Mich. 337.

The special questions in this case were answered in favor of the plaintiff. The lower Court set the verdict. aside on the ground that the physical facts outweighed the verdict. Judgment for the defendant was affirmed. 

Hartley v. A. I. Rodd Lumber Co., 282 Mich. 652.

Judgment for the plaintiff was reversed. The Court said that the answers of the jury to the special questions found controlling facts contrary to the material allegations of the plaintiff's declaration and to plaintiff's testimony on her examination in chief. 

Case v. Klute, 283 Mich. 581.

In this guest case, the jury answered a special question in which they found that the cause of the collision was an error of judgment. A verdict was rendered for the plaintiff but the trial Court entered judgment for defendant in compliance with the jury's answer to the special question and this was affirmed. 205

§ 134] 

Herceg v. Wideman, 290 Mich. 52.

Schuckert v. Berdan Bread Co., 298 Mich. 379.

The jury answered this question in the affirmative: "Could the driver, where he stopped about 6 feet west of the paved portion of the highway, have an unobstructed view of vehicles approaching from the south on M-24 for approximately 1,100 feet?''

Smith v. Maticka, 305 Mich. 32.

Bathke v. City of Traverse City, 308 Mich. 1. 

In the course of its instructions, the trial Court used this sentence: "And it is the duty and obligation of every driver to avoid so far as possible, endangering the life or limb of other persons, as well as their property."

Sec. 138. Pleading Statutes and Ordinances. 

Grud v. Warren, 297 Mich. 546.

Plaintiff alleged duty of defendant to operate his motor vehicle as prescribed by statute but did not refer to any specific statute. It was held that the Court was in error in excluding the statutory provisions concerning speed, there being no surprise.

McDuffie v. Root, 300 Mich. 286.

Plaintiff's declaration alleged a fracture of the base of the skull and a resulting destructive lesion in the central nervous system. [§ 142-a This testimony was brought out in depositions taken some time before trial. It was held that the testimony was properly admitted, as the injury was the natural result of the injury alleged in the pleadings. It was not necessary to specifically plead it.

LONG

Sec. 142-a (New). Joint Negligence.

Sec. 142-b (New). 

Misjoinder of Parties. 

Kolehmainen v. E. E. Mills Trucking Co., Inc., 301 Mich. 340. 

Plaintiff's car was struck by an approaching vehicle and then was struck from behind by a following car. 

Suit was brought against the two owners of these vehicles. It was held that there was no misjoinder of parties. The Court referred to Court Rule No. 38, §3 (1933). Although joint negligence was mentioned in the declaration, the Court found that the allegations plainly charged concurrent negligence. 

Sec. 143. Variance. 

Ritter v. Terman, 285 Mich. 128.

It was held in this case that the allegation that the plaintiff was struck by defendant's car while walking in a southerly direction across the street was not in fatal variance with the evidence that she was standing when struck.

Sec. 145. Answers. 

Miller v. General Motors Corp., 279 Mich. 240.

Defendant in its answer did not set up any affirmative matter. It was held that the defendant was required to set up affirmatively those matters to be relied upon. 

In re Mueller's Estate, 280 Mich. 203.

In this case a claim was filed, in the nature of a declaration, against the estate of the driver of the car. It was a guest case. Plaintiff contended that it was the duty of the defendant to plead affirmatively in the Probate Court. It was held that inasmuch as the claim or declaration did not set out a cause of action, the defendant's procedure was proper. 

Hopkins v. Golden, 281 Mich. 389. 1 In this case the court in its opinion intimates that it is necessary for a defendant to plead the defense of joint enterprise in its answer, unless the plaintiff consents to such defense being offered.

Sec. 145-a (New). Reply to Answer. 

Dramis v. Dunbar, 280 Mich. 300.

Defendant contended that plaintiff in failing to reply to matters set forth in the answer, admitted same. The 

Court said that it was not necessary for plaintiff to reply unless defendant's answer alleged facts which would de. feat plaintiff's cause of action even though plaintiff proved all the allegations of his declaration. 211

§ 145-b] 

Park v. Gaudio, 286 Mich. 133.

Defendant's answer affirmatively charged that the proximate cause of the accident was the negligence of the plaintiff in driving at a speed greater than would permit him to bring the car to a stop within the assured clear distance ahead. Plaintiff in reply denied the affirmative allegations. At the trial plaintiff offered proof of mud on the highway as the cause of the failure to stop. Defendant objected to this testimony.  "Surely good pleading on the part of the plaintiff required them to state specifically this affirmative claim that the pavement was muddy." 

However, it was held that there was no error because there was no evidence that defendant was surprised. 

Sec. 145-b (New). Admitting Liability.

The Court said that any evidence not relating to damages was inadmissible. 

Sec. 147. Real Party in Interest. 

Wolverine Ins. Co. v. Klomparens, 273 Mich. 493.

Defendant's insurance company made a settlement with plaintiff's insured, the release including property damage as well as personal injuries. At the time this settlement was made plaintiff had paid the insured for his property damage under his collision coverage and 212

a SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 147 had taken an assignment. The defendant through his investigators and attorneys knew that plaintiff had made this payment when the settlement was made. It was held that the settlement did not bar plaintiff's action on its subrogation claim.

Associated Truck Lines v. Employers' Fire Ins. Co., 275 

Mich. 74.

The plaintiff corporation while carrying a cargo in a truck lost the equipment and cargo by fire. The equipment was insured with the Insurance Company of North America, which after paying the loss, sued the tortfeasor. 

The defendant company, which insured the cargo, demanded that the plaintiff, its insured, become a party plaintiff to protect its subrogation rights as the defendant company had not yet paid for the loss of the cargo. 

The insured refused to do this and the defendant used this as a defense in the suit against it on the loss of the cargo. The judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. The 

Court said that subrogation rights follow and do not precede payment. 

Woodley v. Lancaster, 307 Mich. 473.

Plaintiff, on cross-examination, was asked if she had an insurance policy with a hospital benefit association. 

On objection defendant's attorney stated that the question was material if plaintiff had assigned part of her claim. He was permitted to question plaintiff concerning any assignment to determine if she was the real party in interest. This was held to be proper. 

Bathke v. City of Traverse City, 308 Mich. 1.

Plaintiff, injured in an accident, had been given an assignment of her husband's claim. Plaintiff proved only expenses of husband arising out of her injuries and the 213

§ 149] 

instructions limited the damages under the assigned claim to expenses incurred by the husband. The jury was instructed that the loss of earnings of the plaintiff was within her original claim. It was held that there was no error in admitting the assignment in evidence. and allowing damages under such assignment.

Sec. 149. Matters Equally Within Knowledge of 

Deceased. 

Foote v. Huelster, 272 Mich. 194.

This was an intersection accident. Defendant King, the driver, was not permitted to testify to what occurred, on the ground that it was equally within the knowledge of the deceased. It was held that this was error, and was not cured by the failure to strike out the testimony given, as the ruling barred further legitimate inquiry and nullified the answers given. 

Collar v. Maycroft, 274 Mich. 376.

In this intersection case the defendant was not called as a witness by plaintiff, and did not testify in his behalf. 

No testimony was offered as to how the accident occurred. 

 "Hence there was an eyewitness of the accident who, in the absence of a showing that the subject matter of his testimony was equally within the knowl- 214

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 149 edge of the deceased, was competent to testify as to all facts and circumstances bearing upon the question of the negligence of the driver of the Dodge car.' 

Waldbauer v. Michigan Bean Co., 278 Mich. 249.

In this case it was held that the witness was an employee and not an officer or agent of the corporation. 

Consequently, he could testify. 

Pietrantonio v. Tonn's Estate, 278 Mich. 535.

In this case it was contended by defendant that the witness intended to file a claim against the estate and therefore was an interested party. It was held that the witness was not a party, and was not disqualified. 

Davis v. Belmont Creamery Co., 281 Mich. 165.

The defendant's driver was dead at the time of the trial and objection was made to certain portions of plaintiff's testimony. The Court cited Waldbauer v. Michigan 

Bean Co., 278 Mich. 249, evidently intimating that the driver was not an officer or agent within the meaning of the statute. 

In re Boyer's Estate, 281 Mich. 618.

Plaintiff was a passenger for hire in Boyer's car. 

Boyer died the next day. It was claimed that Boyer was on the wrong side of the road. Plaintiff was asked what side of the road his car was on when injured. On objection the answer was excluded. It was held that this was error. The Court said that drivers do not always know or realize their precise position on the highway especially at night. There was no evidence that Boyer had knowledge of his position with reference to the center of the road. 215

§ 149] 

Kalbfleisch v. Perkins, 282 Mich. 27. 

In an intersection case defendant was not allowed to testify as to the position of decedent's car when first seen by defendant and its speed. The Court said that it was at least a question of fact for the jury whether the proffered testimony related to matters that must have been equally within the knowledge of the deceased. 

Case v. Klute, 283 Mich. 581.

This was a guest case. Plaintiff's decedent was killed in the accident. Plaintiff objected to the admission of testimony by the defendant driver as to the occurrence of the collision and with regard to traffic just prior to the accident on the ground that such facts were equally within the knowledge of the deceased. It was held that there was no error in admitting the testimony as it did not affirmatively appear from the testimony or circumstances that such facts were equally within the knowledge of the deceased.

Plaintiff's counsel contended on appeal that the trial Court should have instructed the jury that they should disregard such testimony, if they found that the facts were equally within the knowledge of the deceased. The court held there was no error as no request for such an instruction was submitted. 

Quick v. Western Michigan Transportation Co., 294 

Mich. 402.

Defendant testified that he saw decedent slumped over the wheel. He saw him straighten up and stare at defendant. The trial Court refused to permit defendant to testify to anything that occurred after that until the time of the first impact. It was held that this was not error as the deceased was looking directly at defendant 216

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 151 from the time he was 60 feet away until the first impact. 

The Court said that according to every reasonable implication what happened in this interval was equally within the knowledge of the deceased. 

Benaway v. Pere Marquette Ry. Co., 296 Mich. 1.

Defendant's engineer observed decedent's automobile as it approached the crossing. It was held that his testimony as to the speed of the train, whether the bell was ringing, the headlight was on and the whistle blowing was proper as it was not affirmatively shown to be equally within the knowledge of the deceased. 

In re Orr's Estate, 297 Mich. 37.

The Court asked plaintiff if the Orr car stopped before it came onto M-46 and plaintiff answered, "It did not." It was held that it was error to admit this testimony as it was equally within the knowledge of the deceased. However, it was held that it was not reversible error as a distinterested witness had testified to such fact and defendant's counsel admitted in his brief that neither car stopped for the intersection.

Sec. 151. Physician-Patient Privilege. 

Mulvena v. Alexander, 278 Mich. 265.

Defendant called physicians as witnesses who had examined the plaintiff several years before upon order of the Probate Court on an application to have plaintiff admitted to an insane asylum. It was held that their testimony was not privileged as the probate records were public in nature and contained the findings of the physicians. 217

§ 152] 

 Sec. 152. Cross-Examination of Opposite Party or 

Agent. 

Frye v. Brinker, 272 Mich. 339.

Plaintiff called defendants under the statute. They were the only eyewitnesses. Their testimony was uncontradicted, and resulted in a judgment for the defendant. 

Spillman v. Weimaster, 279 Mich. 93.

Defendant's driver was called by plaintiff under the statute, and plaintiff attempted to impeach him by referring to his testimony at a previous trial and by statements made by him before the coroner. It was held that the plaintiff was within his rights. 

Anderson v. Bliss, 281 Mich. 323.

The driver of defendant's car was called for crossexamination under the statute. Plaintiff was not permitted to get an answer to the question as to what distance he would have had to swerve his car to miss the pedestrian. It was held that the exclusion of the answer was not prejudicial. 

Colvaruso's Guardian v. Stroh Brewery Co., 301 Mich. 245. 

Plaintiff called defendant's driver under the statute.

His testimony was not impeached nor contradicted and the Court held that plaintiff was bound by it. 

Sec. 153. Proof of Ownership. 

Davis v. Belmont Creamery Co., 281 Mich. 165.

The plaintiff, a pedestrian, testified that a man came over to him after the accident and gave him a paper with 218

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 154 a license number on it, and that he looked at the license and the numbers corresponded. He also testified that he noted the name of the defendant company on the side of the truck. It was apparently held that the identity of the truck was a question of fact for the jury. 

Sec. 154. Proof of Speed. 

Leitch v. Getz, 275 Mich. 645.

Plaintiff presented a witness to offer an estimate of the speed of defendant's car upon the basis of the weight of the cars, and the distance and direction they moved after the collision. It was held that the testimony was properly excluded. 

Tyler v. Weed, 285 Mich. 460.

The witness testified that he had observed the speedometers in automobiles in which he had ridden, and that he could give an opinion as to how fast defendant was going. It was held that the trial Court was in error in not permitting the witness to give his opinion regarding the speed of the car. 

Park v. Gaudio, 286 Mich. 133.

In this case an attempt was made to prove the speed of a car by a witness, who, at night, heard the hum or roar of the car but did not see it. It was held that the testimony was properly excluded. 

Jenks v. County of Ingham, 288 Mich. 600.

The trial Court refused to permit a 15-year-old boy to testify as to the speed of the Jenks car at a point 400 feet from the point of impact. It was held that this was error. 219

§ 155]  Zawicky v. Flint Trolley Coach Co., 288 Mich. 655. 

Plaintiff claimed that the defendant's bus was a vehicle and was being operated in Flint at an excessive speed in violation of the Motor Vehicle Law. The record did not show whether the district was either business or residential. The Court said that it would not take judicial notice of the character of the neighborhood. The question was not raised below. The Court said that on the record there could be no recovery for alleged violation of a statute. 

Hammock v. Sims, 313 Mich. 248.

The plaintiff, a pedestrian, testified that the defendant's car was coming fast. She was not permitted on re-direct examination to estimate the speed. It was held that this was error. Also it was error to instruct the jury that there was no evidence in the case of an unlawful or reckless rate of speed.

Sec. 155. Evidence as to Marks. 

See Quick v. Western Michigan Transportation Co., 

294 Mich. 402. 

Harding v. Blankenship, 274 Mich. 118.

It was claimed by plaintiff that defendant's car was on the wrong side of the road. Defendant relied upon testimony that plaintiff's car was on the wrong side of the road after the accident and that tracks in the wet tarvia showed that plaintiff's car crossed from the right to left side of the road. A witness for plaintiff testified that he looked for tracks and found none. Glass was found on both sides of the road. It was held that the positions of the cars and other physical facts were not absolutely determinative of just what happened. 220

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 155 

Faustman v. Hewitt, 274 Mich. 458.

The only evidence of this intersection case was based on physical facts. The front end of the defendant's car and the right side of plaintiff's car were damaged. There were marks on the gravel indicating the brakes of defendant's car had been applied. The Court said that from the position of the cars, the damage to each, and the marks on the road, the jury might be justified in finding negligence on the part of the defendant. However, it would be speculation for the jury to say that plaintiff was free from contributory negligence. 

Filter v. Mohr, 275 Mich. 230.

This case involved a collision between defendant's automobile and plaintiff's motorcycle. Evidence was offered concerning skid marks and gouges in the concrete; also there was evidence as to damage done to the motorcycle and marks made on the car. The Court said that there was sufficient evidence relative to the place and character of the collision, the skid marks and gouges on the pavement, the marks on the vehicles, to present an issue of fact. In quoting another decision the Court said: but it is also true that no testimony can refute the unquestioned physical facts, and no indulgence in arithmetical soliloquy can make it otherwise. The Court still heeds physical facts, even though disputed by testimony." 

Essmeister v. Roadway Transit Co., 275 Mich. 387. 

The Court held that the physical facts, such as the position of the tractors and trailers and the marks on the road, were sufficient, if believed by the jury, to stamp the defendant as negligent and to free plaintiff from negligence. The tracks left by defendant's tractor indicated it was on the wrong side of the road. 221

§ 155]  

Bates v. Franson, 276 Mich. 79.

Defendant contended that the physical facts showed that he was on the right side of the road. There was a conflict in the testimony on marks on the road. Oil and broken glass from plaintiff's car were found on plaintiff's side of the road. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed.  

"Unfortunately, physical science does not furnish us with any satisfactory rules by which we may deduce with any certainty from physical facts after the collision just what occurred immediately prior to and during the impact." 

Pearce v. Rodell, 283 Mich. 19.

In this case a pedestrian was struck by defendant's car on a country road at night. Testimony was received that the next morning a witness went to the scene and saw automobile tracks where they left the pavement, ran along in the ditch and then came back on the pavement. 

Because of the circumstances it was held that the evidence was properly received. 

Williams v. MacSim Bar Paper Co., 296 Mich. 214.

This was a wrong side of the road case. The Court was equally divided as to whether defendant's proof as to marks on the highway made the verdict against the great weight of the evidence. The opinion disagreeing with the defendant's contention pointed out the failure of the witnesses to connect the marks with the point of the collision.

Other Cases. 

Rollin v. Van Tine, 283 Mich. 208; Schuckert v. 

Berdan Bread Co., 298 Mich. 379. 222

See Lagassee v. Quick, 273 Mich. 295; Harding v.

Pembor v. Marcus, 307 Mich. 279.

Plaintif was driving east and the defendant west. 

Each testified that the collision occurred on his side of the road. After the collision the cars were on the north shoulder of the road. In holding that there was a question of fact, the Court said that the position of cars after a collision was not always indicative of the manner in which the collision occurred. 

Sec. 157. Photographs. 

See Quick v. Western Michigan Transportation Co., 294 Mich. 402. 

Hartley v. A. I. Rodd Lumber Co., 282 Mich. 652.

Photographs of defendant's truck showed damage. which was inconsistent with plaintiff's theory of case. 

Judgment for the plaintiff was reversed. 

Pearce v. Rodell, 283 Mich. 19.

Photographs taken some time after the accident, at the location thereof, were received over the objection that the pictures were taken with the plaintiff present and showing in the photographs. It was held that there was no error in admitting the photographs. 

Wallace v. Kramer, 296 Mich. 680.

Photographs of skid marks were taken 12 days after the accident under the direction of one of the witnesses. 223

§ 157-a] 

This was corroborated by another witness and in a general way by police officers. It was held that there was no error in admitting the photographs.

Sec. 157-a (New). Motion Pictures. 

Plaintiff's coun- 

Rogers v. City of Detroit, 289 Mich. 86. 

Plaintiff was unable to attend trial. sel offered moving pictures showing the rapid pulsation of plaintiff's throat. The trial judge viewed the pictures apart from the jury and felt that the jury would better understand the condition if the pictures were shown. It was held that there was no error. The Court said that the reception of such evidence should be left largely to the judgment and discretion of the trial judge.

Sec. 158. Res Gestae. 

Greene v. Richer, 278 Mich. 1.

There was testimony that immediately after the accident the driver of the car admitted in writing that he was working for the defendant. It was held that this created a question of fact. 

Sexton v. Balinski, 280 Mich. 28. 

Testimony that fifteen minutes after the accident the driver came to the police station and said that the defendant owned the car was held not part of the res gestae. 

Sheathelm v. Consumers Power Co., 280 Mich. 106.

After the accident plaintiff was unable to extricate his wife from the car. He ran over to where the other car had stopped and testified that the driver made certain statements. It was held that the statements could not be considered a part of the res gestae. 224

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 159-a 

Carter v. C. F. Smith Co., 285 Mich. 621.

In this case plaintiff tried to introduce testimony concerning a statement made by defendant's driver a few seconds after the accident. It was held that the testimony was admissible. 

Sec. 159. Admissions Against Interest. 

Sanderson v. Barkman, 272 Mich. 179.

In this case a question arose as to whether a statement made by plaintiff was admissible or should have been excluded as having been made in connection with a settlement conference. It was held that the testimony was admissible. 

Murner v. Thorpe, 284 Mich. 331.

In a guest case there was testimony that plaintiff's father told the defendant that suit was being brought ´against him and that the defendant said: "Go ahead; I hope she wins." Plaintiff contended that this showed an admission of liability. It was held that the testimony was admissible. 

Sexton v. Niewoonder, 296 Mich. 443.

Plaintiff's husband testified that defendant phoned him and said that he notified his representative to get in touch with him right away and make a settlement. It was held that the admission of this testimony was error and was prejudicial to the defendant. A new trial was ordered. 

See Secrist v. City of Detroit, 299 Mich. 393.

Sec. 159-a (New). Police Reports. 

Delfosse v. Bresnahan, 305 Mich. 621.

The records and briefs of this case show that the chief of police was questioned concerning an oral report made 225

§ 160] 

by the defendant concerning the manner in which the accident occurred. The lower court, on objection by defendant, excluded this report as privileged under Mich.

Stat. Ann., 1942 Cum. Supp., Section 9.1590. While this exclusion was not in issue on the appeal by the defendant, the Court seems to imply that the oral report was properly excluded. 

Baumgarten v. Tasco, 312 Mich. 161.

A police officer referred to his report concerning questions put to the defendant after the accident and the answers given. The Court held that the testimony of the witness as to what one of the defendants told him was clearly admissible. It was also held that the admission. of the accident prevention bureau's report, upon the condition that only that part of the report as came within the knowledge of the officer should be used, was not error. 

Sec. 160. Adjusters. 

Gegan v. Kemp, 302 Mich. 218.

Plaintiff's witness was confronted with a statement in writing contrary to his testimony. On re-direct examination plaintiff's attorney persisted in asking the witness leading questions concerning the claim agent for the insurance company which had taken the statement. 

It was held that the judgment for the plaintiff should be reversed, and a new trial was ordered because plaintiff's attorney reverted to the fact of insurance again and again after he had been warned by the trial judge. 

Boyce v. Shtukas, 306 Mich. 467.

This was an intersection case tried without a jury. 

An occupant of plaintiff's car, the sole survivor able to testify, testified that the car was stopped at the stop sign. Defendant introduced a statement by this occu- 226

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 164 pant in question and answer form and made in the hospital. The occupant was twice interviewed by an attorney and adjuster before a court reporter. The answers indicated that the car was not stopped, and that the occupants were busily engaged in conversation. The occupant at the trial denied giving the answers. Hospital records were introduced to show that she was suffering from shock and was being given narcotics and sedatives. It was held that it was a question of fact whether she made the impeaching statements or was in condition to give a true account of the accident. Judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed. 

Sec. 161. Credibility. 

Zimmerman v. Goldberg, 277 Mich. 134.

The defendant had pleaded guilty to a charge of reckless driving in the same accident out of which the civil case arose. The lower Court refused to permit him to answer as to this conviction. It was held that the answer should have been admitted. The Court said that it was cross-examination concerning defendant's plea of guilty to reckless driving arising out of the very accident involved in the principal case. 

Sec. 163.

Exclamations of Pain. 

Rogers v. City of Detroit, 289 Mich. 86.

Witnesses were allowed to testify as to exclamations of pain made by plaintiff. In holding that there was no error the Court said that the controlling test was spontaneity.

Sec. 164. Examination by Physician for Trial. 

See Krzywosz v. Crummett, 286 Mich. 649; DeVries v. Owens, 295 Mich. 522. 227

§ 165] 

Phillips v. Fotheringham, 277 Mich. 566.

In this case it was held that defendant's objection to the physicians testifying on the plaintiff's complaint of pain would not be considered because counsel did not state the reason for the objection at the trial. 

See McDuffie v. Root, 300 Mich. 286.

Sec. 165. Proof of Expectancy. 

Fortner v. Koch, 272 Mich. 273.

Mortality tables were not permitted to be proved in this case as the evidence showed that plaintiff was in poor health at the time of the accident.

Sec. 167. Miscellaneous Cases. 

Tanis v. Eding, 274 Mich. 288.

It was held in this case that the receipt of a map in evidence was not error, even though the map was not accurate in some unimportant details. Witnesses had referred to the map without objection. 

Madalinski v. Hill, 277 Mich. 219.

This was a pedestrian case. It was held that evidence as to the decedent's habits and drinking before the night of the accident was inadmissible. 

Gile v. Hudnut, 279 Mich. 358.

Hospital records were held admissible under Act 

No. 15, Pub. Acts 1935, amending Comp. Laws 1929, Sec tion 14207, Mich. Stat. Ann., Section 27.902.

For limitation on such admissibility, see Sadjak v. 

Parker-Wolverine Co., 281 Mich. 84. 

Patterson v. Jacobs, 289 Mich. 351.

Error was assigned because the court sustained plaintiff's objections to the following questions asked defendant. 228

SUPPLEMENT 

[§ 167 Q. Was there any possibility of avoiding the collision. at the time you first saw her car? 

Q. What in your judgment could you have done at that moment to avoid a collision?

Q. I am asking now for your judgment as an experienced driver, on all kinds of roads, with all kinds of cars, and I ask you what else or other you could have done to avoid a collision?

It was held that there was no error. 

Cook v. Vineyard, 291 Mich. 375.

A witness testified that she saw a car go by her house. 

She took a step away from the window and heard a crash. The court instructed the jury that this testimony was not entitled to a great deal of weight as the witness did not identify the car as the defendant's, and did not say how much time elapsed before the crash. It was held that this comment by the trial judge was not erroneous. It was pointed out that a step was not an interval of time but is frequently used to mean any short distance. 

Dewey v. Perkins, 295 Mich. 611.

Plaintiff called defendant as an adverse witness and asked him if he had not made a statement to a Mr. H. E. 

Griffin. Defendant moved for a mistrial on the ground that Mr. Griffin was known to be an insurance adjuster and that the sole purpose of asking the question was to inject insurance into the case.  "As the case must be retired, and the alleged error should not recur, we shall pass the question without further discussion, but with the comment that, in close cases, bringing in the question of insurance in an inadvertent manner by direct action of counsel may result in a reversal on this ground alone." 229

§ 169] 

Pacey v. Strange, 311 Mich. 40.

Plaintiff, in declaration, alleged that defendant violated the reckless driving ordinance of the City of Detroit. On direct examination the defendant was asked if he had been arrested or convicted of the charge of reckless driving. Plaintiff's attorney objected, saying that there was no claim to that. The defendant was permitted to answer in the negative. The Court held that in view of the statement of plaintiff's attorney, there was no reversible error.

Sec. 169. Excessive Verdicts. 

Arnestad v. Point, 280 Mich. 339.

In this case a verdict of $5,000 was reduced to $2,500. 

The plaintiff, an 18-year-old boy, had a fracture of the right fibula two inches below the knee from which he made a good recovery. 

Hartaugh v. Safeway Lines, Inc., 288 Mich. 471.

Plaintiff had a fracture of the left arm and a fracture of the right elbow. The doctor, who attended him, testified that the plaintiff had deformities of both arms and he believed they would be almost permanent. It was held that a verdict of $16,000 was excessive. www 230

SUPPLEMENT [§ 170 

Hartaugh v. Safeway Lines, Inc., 288 Mich. 703. 

Upon rehearing the Court held that the verdict was excessive but held that the judgment would be affirmed if the plaintiff filed a remittitur of damages in excess of $5,000. 

Bahlman v. Hudson Motor Car Co., 290 Mich. 683.

Plaintiff, a man 50 years of age, was given a verdict of $4,000. The sole injury was a cut on his head 5 or 6 inches long. This resulted in a scar visible at only a short distance. Nervousness developed since the accident. It was held that the verdict was excessive, and unless plaintiff consented to a remittitur so as. to reduce judgment to $2,000 a new trial was ordered. 

Pembor v. Marcus, 307 Mich. 279.

Plaintiff suffered two fractured ribs and her right leg was rather severely injured. It was painful at the time of the trial, 14 months after the accident. There was testimony that it was a permanent injury and the leg would always be larger than the other. The jury allowed more than $5,000 for pain and suffering. This verdict was held excessive and a new trial was ordered unless a remittitur of $2,500 was filed. 

Sec. 170. Sustained Verdicts. 

See Bates v. Franson, 276 Mich. 79; Lang v. County of 

Ingham, 277 Mich. 345; Murphy v. Sinen, 281 Mich. 274. 

Kemp v. Aldrich, 286 Mich. 591.

Plaintiff was a healthy woman, 32 years of age. She was permanently injured, one leg being a half inch shorter than the other. At the time of trial she was suffering pain and was using crutches. An $8,000 verdict was held not excessive. 231

§ 171] 

Cleven v. Griffin, 298 Mich. 139.

Plaintiff, 21 years old, sustained a slight concussion of the brain, a jagged cut above the eye resulting in scars, other cuts, and an injury to the ulnar nerve. For some time she suffered headaches, nervousness, shock and loss of sleep. It was held that the verdict of $2,000 was not excessive. 

Brown v. Arnold, 303 Mich. 616.

16 In this case plaintiffs produced testimony that the hospital and medical expense was $538.10. The verdict was $547.60. Plaintiff cross-appealed, claiming that the verdict was inadequate. The Court said that it was within the realm of possibility that the jury reached a compromise verdict, as the proofs showed that the defendant paid for plaintiff's care for two months after she left the hospital. The Court said that it would not substitute its opinion for that of the jury, and affirmed the judgment. 

See White v. Makela, 304 Mich. 425.

Mich. 19.

Plaintiff proved $700 in expenses and was given a verdict for $1,000. He testified, 18 months after the accident, that he was still suffering pain. The trial court instructed the jury that there was no proof as to permanent injury, but permitted an allowance for future pain. 

No instruction was given on present worth. The Court refused to grant a new trial, holding that there was 232

Sec. 173-a (New). Action for Prenatal Injury. 

Newman v. City of Detroit, 281 Mich. 60.

An action was started under the survival statute for prenatal injuries. The Court held that there was no right of action for a prenatal injury.

Sec. 175-a (New). Mitigation of Damages. 

Larabell v. Schuknecht, 308 Mich. 419.

Plaintiff had settled with one of defendants and had given a covenant not to sue. It was held that the remaining defendant had the right to show the amount paid as mitigation of damages.

Sec. 176. Miscellaneous Cases. 

Motts v. Michigan Cab Co., 274 Mich. 437.

Campbell v. Brown, 276 Mich. 449.
